J0.p: General heading for tales and sayings about how a person gains wisdom or knowledge and how they keep it.

J10.p: A person gains wisdom or knowledge by learning from their own experience, usually by suffering the consequences of mistakes.

J11.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 407), 110 (ST 219); Halm Aesop No. 370.
J11.p: A shepherd who was shipwrecked no longer trusts the sea, even though he once envied sailors and wanted their life.

J11.1.p: A man bitten by a snake becomes afraid of anything resembling a snake, even a rope.

J12.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 374), 110 (ST 221); Chauvin III 51 No. 7.
J12.p: A young donkey learns to avoid food that has been touched by animals bound for slaughter, and asks his mother to have the leftovers of the hog's food removed.

J13.r: BP III 239 (Gr. No. 157); Hervieux Fabulistes latins II 546 No. 70.
J13.p: Young sparrows have already learned from experience how to avoid men, and their father's quiz shows they know enough.

J14.r: Wienert FFC LVI *72 (ET 365), 140 (ST 466); Babrius No. 29; Halm Aesop No. 174.
J14.p: An old racehorse working in a mill laments the foolishness of his youth.

J15.r: Chauvin II 94 No. 43, 102 No. 62; Bødker Exempler 291 No. 47, 301 No. 67; Wienert FFC LVI *69 (ET 331), *127 (ST 352); Babrius No. 167; Jacobs Aesop 201 No. 6; Halm Aesop Nos. 96, 251, 350; cf. BP II 459; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J15.p: A serpent or snake-bird that was injured by a man refuses to be reconciled, because he knows neither can forget the injuries.

J16.r: Chauvin II 83 No. 6; Bødker Exempler 274 No. 7, 306 No. 82; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J16.p: A dove ignores past experience and rebuilds her nest in the same place where she lost her earlier brood, and loses another.

J17.r: *Type 157; BP II 96; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Hottentot): Bleek 47 No. 23; American Negro: Harris Nights 33 No. 7, 330 No. 57; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 262 No. 62.
J17.p: An animal learns from experience to fear men, but ignores another animal's warning, approaches a man, and is shot.

J17.1.p: A tiger, a jackal, and a bear each learn to fear man, after being told by others of his strength and tricks: he beat the tiger, swung the jackal by his tail, and made the bear fall from a tree.

J18.p: A disguised prince is beaten for his courtesy, realizes his folly, and goes home wiser.

J21.p: Advice that is later shown to have been wise, once its results are seen through experience.

J21.1.r: *Type 910C; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 20 No. 69; Alphabet No. 156; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 172, 283; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J21.1.p: A barber hired to cut a king's throat sees the words on the bottom of the basin, advising him to act wisely and consider the consequences; he drops the razor and confesses.

J21.2.r: *Type 910B; Chauvin II 157; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys. Cf. Wienert FFC LVI 37; Phaedrus III No. 10.
J21.2.p: A man returns home, sees someone sleeping with his wife, and restrains his anger; the sleeper turns out to be a newborn son.

J21.2.1.p: A piece of advice: before attacking anyone, draw and sheathe your sword three times first, so that anger cools and you do not act rashly. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.2.2.p: A piece of advice: sleep on it before killing yourself, because after a night's sleep your feelings about suicide will change. The note adds that this is the lesson learned from experience.

J21.2.3.p: A piece of advice: never draw your sword against an innocent person. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.2.4.p: A piece of advice: do not uncover or show your weapon in a public gathering. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.2.5.p: A piece of advice: never shed the blood of women. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.2.6.p: A piece of advice: keep your anger in check from the very start, before it grows. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.3.p: A piece of advice: do not go where an old man has a young wife. The note says that following this advice leads to discovering a murder at an inn.

J21.4.r: *Type 910A; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 115; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 52; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J21.4.p: A father's advice not to marry a foreign girl is shown to be wise after his son learns from experience. The counsel was proven right by what happened.

J21.5.r: Robbers encountered. *Type 910B; Scala Celi No. 788; Herbert III 99; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J21.5.p: A piece of advice: do not leave the main highway, because travelers who stray from it come to harm. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.5.1.p: A piece of advice: do not prefer a new road to an old, well-known one. The note says that travelers who take the new road are killed by robbers.

J21.5.2.p: A piece of advice: where three roads meet, take the side road rather than the main one. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.5.3.p: A piece of advice that a short way can turn out to be long, so the shortcut is not always quicker. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.6.r: Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 169ff. (Gonzenbach No. 81); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J21.6.p: A piece of advice: do not ask questions about extraordinary or strange things. The note says that those who ask such questions are killed.

J21.7.p: A piece of advice: do not cross a bridge while still riding your horse; get down first. The note says a man breaks his leg by ignoring this.

J21.8.p: A piece of advice: never bet more than a groat (a small coin). The note says a man loses his wife on a wager.

J21.8.1.p: A piece of advice: do not gamble or make wagers at all.

J21.9.p: A piece of advice: do not visit your friends too often. The note says that in the end the visiting man is treated shamefully.

J21.9.1.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 52; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J21.9.1.p: A piece of advice: do not stay too long on a friendly visit. The note says a guest stays so long that his host gives him black bread instead of white.

J21.10.p: A piece of advice: do not lend out your horse. It is considered wise because experience proved it.

J21.11.p: A piece of advice: do not walk half a mile with a stranger without asking his name. The note says a man unknowingly races his wife's lover and loses his wife on the wager.

J21.12.r: *BP IV 149 n. 2; Gaster Exempla 256 No. 390; *Paris Légendes du moyen âge 225ff.; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 24; Alphabet No. 191; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 167.
J21.12.p: A piece of advice: do not regret what is already past. The note says a man releases a bird, then believes its false claim that it holds a precious gem in its body, tries to climb a tree after it, and falls.

J21.13.r: (Cf. J21.12, K604.) *BP IV 149 n. 2; Alphabet No. 191; Gaster Exempla 256 No. 390; Paris Légendes du moyen âge 225ff.; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 167; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J21.13.p: Advice, proved wise by later experience, not to believe anything that is beyond belief. In one case a man believes a bird who claims she has a precious gem in her body.

J21.14.r: (Cf. K604.) *BP IV 149 n. 2; Alphabet No. 191; Gaster Exempla 256 No. 390; *G. Paris Légendes du moyen âge 225ff.
J21.14.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to try to reach what cannot be attained.

J21.15.r: Father has left money which will fall out when the spendthrift son goes to hang himself in despair. “The Heir of Linne.” *Type 910D; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 709; Chauvin V 133 No. 63, *VIII 94 No. 65; Child V 12f.; Clouston Tales II 53; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 2, Rotunda; Japanese: Ikeda.
J21.15.p: A piece of advice, later proved wise, that if you want to hang yourself you should use only the stone that is pointed out.

J21.16.r: Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 9 (*Lee 289); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J21.16.p: Advice to go to Goosebridge. A man with a disobedient wife goes there and finds mules being beaten and made to cross the bridge.

J21.17.r: *Cosquin Études 73ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 314, O’Suilleabhain 38; Icelandic: Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda.
J21.17.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to stay in church until mass is finished. Waiting saves a young person from death.

J21.18.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 22, 275, Neuman.
J21.18.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to trust those who seem overly holy. One example is a wife so modest she will not travel with her husband, who turns out to be an adulteress; another is a priest so pious he will not tread on a worm, who turns out to be a thief.

J21.19.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 100, 304, Neuman.
J21.19.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to start a journey early in the day.

J21.20.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 100, 304, Neuman.
J21.20.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to prepare the night camp while it is still daylight.

J21.21.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 100, 304, Neuman.
J21.21.p: Advice not to cross a swollen stream until the water has gone down is shown to be wise by experience.

J21.22.r: Nouvelles de Sens No. 7; Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *911; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 100, 304, *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J21.22.p: A counsel that a man at first doubts, such as not to tell a secret to a woman, is shown to be wise after he learns from experience that it is true.

J21.23.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to rise earlier. A man who wants to know why he is in debt gets up early and catches his servants stealing.

J21.24.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 52; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J21.24.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to make a horse run downhill. A horse that is made to run downhill breaks its neck.

J21.25.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to keep bad company. In one case, breaking the father's first counsel leads to the breaking of all his others.

J21.26.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to be too greedy in a trade. A man refuses fifty ducats for his horse, and the horse suddenly dies.

J21.27.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *911; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J21.27.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to adopt a child.

J21.28.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *911; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J21.28.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to trust a ruler who governs by reason alone.

J21.29.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to keep the head dry, the feet warm, and to eat meat. A king recovers from illness by following it.

J21.30.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, never to have to do with a woman unless you are wed to her.

J21.31.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, not to marry a woman before seeing her and finding her to be your equal.

J21.32.p: Advice not to marry more than one woman. A man who wanted three marries one and is greatly weakened.

J21.33.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to bathe by yourself and not in the common bathing place. A man forgets his purse in the bathhouse.

J21.34.p: Advice, proved wise by experience, to move a stool before sitting on it. A man saves himself from falling into a well by doing so.

J21.34.1.p: A traveler learns from experience to look around carefully when he finds himself in an unfamiliar place, and the advice proves wise.

J21.34.2.p: A person learns by experience to test a bed by touching it before sitting on it, and the advice proves sensible.

J21.35.p: Advice that a ruler should follow the majority opinion rather than his own whim proves wise through experience; in the tale a man finds money on the body of a dead traveler.

J21.35.1.p: Advice to pay heed to what four or five people say, and not ignore them, proves wise through experience.

J21.36.p: Advice not to travel alone proves wise through experience; in the tale a helpful crab saves a traveler from a crocodile.

J21.37.p: Advice not to follow a woman's counsel proves wise through experience.

J21.38.p: A greeting wishing to be spared from an evil man or woman proves wise: a man teaches a friend its meaning by borrowing money and then a coat from a creditor, who is discredited in court.

J21.39.p: Advice not to travel without money proves wise through experience.

J21.40.p: Advice not to expect honor or respect in a foreign country proves wise through experience.

J21.41.p: Advice to be cautious before falling asleep in an unfamiliar place proves wise through experience.

J21.41.1.p: Advice not to sleep in an inn proves wise through experience.

J21.41.2.p: A stranger should not close his eyes in sleep, lest he close them in death; this advice proves wise through experience.

J21.41.3.p: The saying that a person who lies awake gains while one who sleeps loses proves wise through experience.

J21.42.p: Advice to throw some food to an animal and watch its reaction before eating at an unfamiliar place proves wise through experience.

J21.43.p: Advice that a country not examined in disguise will always be ruined proves wise through experience.

J21.44.p: Advice not to rely on a relative in times of trouble proves wise through experience.

J21.45.p: Advice not to offer to settle a dispute as arbitrator unless asked proves wise through experience.

J21.46.p: Advice not to make friends with a policeman or soldier proves wise through experience.

J21.47.p: The saying that a man can only call his wife his own as long as she is with him proves wise through experience.

J21.47.1.p: Advice not to send one's wife away for a long visit to her parents turns out to be wise after experience shows it true. The saying is that a wife is yours only while she stays with you.

J21.48.p: Advice not to act without first investigating proves wise through experience; in the tale a gravedigger finds a purse of money in a dead man's pocket.

J21.49.p: A piece of advice, that one should never give a king a cup made of a single ruby as a gift, is shown to be wise only after experience proves it.

J21.50.p: A saying that idleness brings misery and work brings happiness is shown to be sound advice only after experience proves it.

J21.51.p: Advice not to stand by and watch two people fight; the person who does so is called on by both sides to testify for each, or is beheaded.

J21.52.p: A general heading for miscellaneous pieces of advice that are shown to be wise only after experience proves them.

J21.52.1.p: A disciple who stays in a city where everything has one fixed price finds that justice is not even to be found there.

J21.52.2.p: A saying that one should never be rude to a self-made man of low birth, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.3.p: A saying that hardened clay is hard to mold, meaning a person set in his ways is hard to change, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.4.p: Advice never to make a man's sin public if one can avoid it, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.5.p: Advice never to dismiss an old servant for his first fault, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.6.p: Advice that when a man attacks you, you should kill him whether he is king or prince, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.7.p: A boy who always claims "I know" gets into all sorts of trouble, and only learns to say "I don't know" after experience teaches him.

J21.52.8.p: The saying that nothing happens that does not work for one's good, shown wise by experience.

J21.52.9.p: The saying that a man who throws himself against a wave is overthrown by it, shown true by experience.

J22.p: A lion gives advice to his sons; only the younger one follows it and so succeeds.

J22.1.p: The lion's precept to his sons is to beware of man.

J22.2.p: The lion's precept to his sons is to honor the woods.

J22.3.p: The lion's precept to his sons is to keep peace with the neighbors.

J23.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 394; Irish: Beal XXI 307, O’Suilleabhain 25.
J23.p: Merchants try being honest for a year and find that honesty pays; a priest had advised this when they said they could not do business without cheating.

J24.p: Two fools who are always striking people end up striking each other until they come to appreciate the value of peace.

J25.r: Anecdote of Agesilaus. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 738.
J25.p: Why a great man plays with children; this can only be understood by someone who has children of his own.

J26.p: A person learns from experience that enemies are better won over by kindness than by cruelty.

J27.p: A man learns to fear death by meeting Life, an old woman who beheads him and puts his head back on backwards. He is left terrified for hours until his head is turned right again.

J30.p: A person gains wisdom by reasoning out conclusions from what they know, rather than by direct experience.

J31.r: *Wesselski Gonnella 118 No. 15, *Hodscha Nasreddin II 227 No. 481; Japanese: Ikeda.
J31.p: A man on his way to a city meets children who are so clever that he turns back home, reasoning that their parents must be even more clever and he would be outmatched.

J31.1.p: Two rival cities send wise men to dispute. One side disguises its wise men as peasants and debates the rivals, who withdraw fearing that the educated must be even more learned if their peasants are so clever.

J32.r: Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 316), 122 (ST 312); Babrius No. 1; Halm Aesop No. 403; BP II 99.
J32.p: A man sends an arrow to a lion as his message, and the lion concludes from the arrow how terrible man must be and so fears him.

J33.p: A blind man feels a young wolf and recognises from its nature that it will be savage.

J34.r: Wienert FFC LVI 76 (ET 416), 122 (ST 313); Phaedrus III No. 1; Jacobs Aesop 220 No. 81.
J34.p: A person judges from the smell of an empty wine cask how fine the wine must have been.

J50.p: A person gains wisdom by watching and noticing what happens around them.

J51.p: A man sees deformed witches and, on learning their deformity came from too much spinning, releases his wife from her spinning duty.

J52.p: A king watches animals take revenge on one another: a dog breaks a fox's foot, a man breaks the dog's, a horse breaks the man's leg, and the horse then breaks its own leg stepping in a hole. The king learns from this and becomes just.

J52.1.p: Someone comes to understand that death is universal by watching animals prey on one another.

J52.2.p: A king goes to the bottom of the sea in a glass barrel to learn wisdom by watching the fish.

J53.p: An army is saved from an ambush because its leaders notice birds flying up from the part of the woods where the enemy is hiding.

J55.p: A ruler learns a lesson from an exiled king and rewards the exile rather than a successful merchant.

J56.p: A person learns unscrupulous business methods by watching a usurer's own practices and then uses those same methods against him.

J56.1.p: A ruler learns a lesson after seeing a city governed by a king as uncharitable as himself.

J61.p: A hare tells his sons to use their eyes to their advantage, teaching them to learn by watching.

J62.p: A man spends a year observing dying people, and this turns his thoughts away from lust.

J64.p: Ducklings take to water by instinct, and this teaches a bridegroom about his bride's skill in lovemaking.

J65.p: Young birds learn which dangers to fear by watching, and their mother pushes them out of the nest once they have learned them.

J67.p: Small repeated actions, like drops of water wearing a hole in stone, gradually make an impression on the mind.

J67.1.p: A lazy student resolves to work harder after watching a man build a house one wattle at a time and seeing water fill a hole one drop at a time.

J80.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Bødker Exempler 272 No. 1; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J80.p: Wisdom or knowledge is conveyed through a parable, a short story that carries a moral lesson.

J80.1.p: Solomon is said to have told three thousand parables.

J80.1.1.p: Solomon uses a parable to show his mother that women's wisdom is inferior.

J80.2.p: A minister is taught through a parable that he should bow to the new king.

J81.r: *Basset 1001 Contes II 25; *Wesselski Märchen 209; Boccaccio Decameron I No. 5 (Lee 17), Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *981; Russian: Andrejev No. *981 (II); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J81.p: A man is shown through a comparison of dishes that one woman is just like another, and so gives up his desire to pursue her.

J81.0.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda, Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 10.
J81.0.1.p: A counselor refuses to arrange secret affairs for his lord, so the ruler serves him only his favorite food until he complains of the monotony and learns the point.

J81.1.p: Society is compared to a dish that is not fit to eat unless its ingredients, such as salt, pepper and fish, are properly mixed together.

J81.2.p: A hostess gives each guest a small portion of the food that suits them, with an explanation.

J81.3.p: Church canons are compared to a stew made from their separate meals.

J82.p: A priest walks through mud to show his congregation that they should not follow his evil ways.

J83.r: They are reconciled. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 401.
J83.p: A duke has two enemies pull out one of his hairs each, one gray and one black, and shows them that their quarrels hurt him equally, so they reconcile.

J84.p: Picking up water spilled on the ground is no harder than undoing the harm of slander.

J85.p: A chair set over a fiery pit is used as an image of how precarious life is.

J86.p: Falling rocks and a thread passing through a needle's eye are taken as hints of sexual intercourse, which explains how it began.

J87.r: (Usually connected with Jus Primae Noctis [T161]). Wesselski Archiv Orientální I 83f.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2429.
J87.p: Cowardly men are shamed when a woman stands naked before them.

J88.p: A cloud that either gives rain to thirsty crops or drops it into the ocean is used as a parable for wisdom.

J91.r: Wind, Water, and Modesty (Sense of Shame). The first two give their addresses but the third says she has no address as no one wants her. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J91.p: A monk shames his accuser by telling him a parable.

J92.p: A son saves his father's life by using a parable to show him how foolish it would be to plow up his own crop. The father had been persuaded to kill the child.

J94.r: Shown by test: holy man made to carry milk without spilling. So occupied he forgets to think of God. India: Thompson-Balys.
J94.p: It is hard to keep thoughts of God in mind when a person is busy with everyday worldly concerns.

J95.p: A fool digs holes along the edge of a road. Only those who stray from the straight path fall in, which shows a truth that is recognized only later.

J96.p: A man kills a nest of ants, and God punishes him for it. The moral is that cruelty to small creatures brings punishment.

J97.p: A lotus flower thrives only while it stays in water, so a king should not leave his castle. The plant is used as a parable for the ruler's need to stay in his own domain.

J98.p: Stones shaken in a jar stand for the difficulty of learning many dialects. The image makes the point that mastering many languages is hard.

J99.p: Wisdom or knowledge is passed on through a parable, a short story whose hidden meaning teaches a lesson.

J99.1.p: A parable teaches the relative pleasures of the sexes in love.

J99.2.p: A father leaves four pots to his sons. The eldest finds earth in his, the second finds bones, the third finds rice husks, and the youngest finds rupees. The pots stand for inheritance: the eldest gets land, the second cattle, the third grain, and the youngest keeps the money.

J100.p: Wisdom or knowledge is gained through necessity, meaning people learn out of real need.

J101.r: Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 272), 106 (ST 186, 246); Jacobs Aesop 213 No. 55.
J101.p: A crow, unable to reach water in a jug, drops pebbles into it so the water rises and it can drink.

J102.p: A bear learns to catch crabs by using his hairy claws.

J120.p: A person gains wisdom by learning from children, whose naive remarks reveal truths adults have missed.

J121.r: *Bédier Fabliaux 463f.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 436, 760; Crane Vitry 260 No. 288; Herbert III 25; *BP II 135, IV 172 n. 14; Scala Celi No. 530; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 41.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *996; Russian: Andrejev No. *982; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 256f. No. 201; Japanese: Ikeda.
J121.p: A son who has been ungrateful to his old father is shamed by his own young son, who copies the father's treatment. A man gives his old father half a carpet to keep warm, and his child keeps the other half, saying he is saving it for his father when he grows old.

J121.1.p: The ungrateful son is shamed by his own son's naive act of saving a wooden drinking cup or bowl for his father's old age.

J121.2.p: A father rebukes his undutiful son by telling him not to drag him past the threshold. He had once dragged his own father only as far as that point, when he had thought of putting him out of the house.

J122.r: You forgot to strike mother.” Wesselski Mönchslatein 170 No. 133.
J122.p: A father who habitually beats his wife says he has forgotten something, and his child naively replies that he knows, it is to beat his mother. The child's remark exposes the father's cruelty.

J122.1.p: A seducer is about to seduce a child's mother, but he stops when the child wisely says he is sad that his father has left his mother exposed to such dangers.

J123.r: *Wesselski “Der Knabenkönig und das kluge Mädchen” (Sudetendeutsche Zs. f. Vksk. [1930] Beiheft 1) passim; *Chauvin V 86 No. 26 n. 1; DeVries FFC LXXIII 323ff.; Scala Celi No. 895; Japanese: Ikeda.
J123.p: A child decides a lawsuit with wisdom. A king in disguise watches the child play a game that acts out the case, and the child's judgment settles it.

J123.1.p: A clever prince overrules the king's decisions, which seemed just but were wrong.

J124.p: A person learns patience by watching children who, when their food is stolen, calmly go looking for it instead of getting angry.

J125.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; West Indies: Flowers 474.
J125.p: Parents' wrongdoings are unintentionally revealed by their children's innocent remarks.

J125.1.r: She says, “You will not have to do that for mother poured a whole tubful into the cask today.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 374.
J125.1.p: A guest asks an innkeeper's little daughter for water to add to his wine, and the child's answer shows the wine is already watered, so no more water is needed.

J125.2.p: A woman's adultery is exposed by a small child's careless remark.

J125.2.1.p: A child unknowingly reveals that his mother has been committing adultery with the secretary: he warns his father not to step over a chalk line around the secretary, saying the secretary might do to him what he did to Mother.

J130.p: Wisdom or useful knowledge that people gain by observing animals.

J132.p: A mother mouse teaches her young to fear silent cats, since they are dangerous, but not noisy roosters, since their crowing is harmless.

J133.p: An animal sets a wise example that teaches a man a lesson.

J133.1.p: Two wild goats on a narrow cliff pass each other safely by one stepping over the other, showing that peaceful yielding is advantageous.

J133.2.p: A donkey stops drinking once it has had enough, teaching its owner a lesson about moderation.

J133.3.p: A trained deer drinks wine until it breaks its leg, then never drinks again, teaching its master a lesson about moderation.

J133.4.p: A woman refuses to follow a donkey that keeps to a safe path and is attacked by robbers as a result.

J133.5.p: A squirrel tries to empty a lake by dipping water out with its tail, illustrating how hard it is to reform the world.

J133.6.p: Big fish eat little fish, showing that a strong robber will plunder weaker neighbors.

J134.p: Behavior of animals teaches a person what to avoid doing.

J134.1.p: A cock's second mate lets her stepchildren starve, and a woman warns her husband to beware of such a stepmother.

J135.p: An animal that is leaving gives a man parting advice.

J136.p: A crow travels through the three worlds looking for happiness.

J137.p: A person gains wisdom by observing the behavior of insects.

J140.p: Wisdom or knowledge gained through formal education and study.

J141.p: A young person becomes wise by being taught by seven sages (wise teachers).

J142.p: Someone regrets having had a poor or missing education and wishes they had been taught properly.

J142.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 229), 145 (ST 502); Halm Aesop No. 217.
J142.1.p: A house dog blames its master for having taught it bad, lazy habits.

J142.2.p: A man blames his master or teacher for not correcting his faults when he was young.

J143.r: Wienert FFC LVI 71 (ET 361), 129 (ST 371); Halm Aesop No. 51.
J143.p: A colt (young horse) is badly behaved and untrained because its master neglected to train it.

J144.r: *Type 123; Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 262), 145 (ST 506, 535); *BP I 37; Dh IV 277f.
J144.p: A well-trained young goat (kid) refuses to open the door to a wolf, having been taught not to.

J145.p: Dogs that are hostile to each other become friendly when they are made to fight a common enemy, the wolf.

J146.p: Educated people are chosen as the best companions.

J146.1.p: A king prefers educated men as his companions.

J147.r: Useless. *Chauvin III 97 No. 1; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J147.p: A child is kept shut up so that he stays ignorant of the ways of the world.

J150.p: Wisdom or knowledge can be acquired in ways other than formal education.

J151.p: Wisdom is obtained from an old person.

J151.1.r: Type 981*; *Anderson FFC XLII 182 n. 1; *DeVries FFC LXXIII 220ff.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 446, cf. No. 538; Fb “gammel” IV 174a; Scala Celi No. 281; *Paudler FFC CXXI.—Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *995; Russian: Andrejev No. 981*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 995*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 910F*; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 115ff. No. 71.
J151.1.p: During a famine, all old men are ordered killed, but one man hides his father. When the young rulers fail, the hidden old man comes out, carries out the tasks set him, and saves the kingdom with his wisdom.

J151.2.p: Old men are preferred as advisers and councillors.

J151.3.p: Wisdom comes from God, who appears as an old, one-eyed man.

J151.4.p: An old man gives the advice to always say "if it pleases God" (insha'Allah) when speaking of future plans.

J152.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
J152.p: Wisdom or knowledge is gained from a sage or teacher.

J152.1.r: Chauvin IX 35 No. 27; Scala Celi No. 103; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J152.1.p: A cynical philosopher lives in a tub (barrel) and rejects ordinary comforts.

J152.2.p: Someone receives wise advice from a dervish (wandering holy man).

J152.3.p: A philosopher instructs a young person on how to behave.

J152.4.p: A wise philosopher comforts a woman who has lost her son, teaching her something that eases her grief.

J152.5.p: A philosopher teaches that infants, youths, and old people should each be greeted differently, showing the wisdom of respecting each age.

J152.6.p: A philosopher teaches that worldly honor is like a shadow: it runs away when chased, but follows and sometimes catches up with those who ignore it.

J153.p: A person gains wisdom or knowledge from a holy man, a religious figure who teaches or helps them understand.

J153.1.p: A holy man prays that all good things stay and all bad things vanish, and his prayer reforms a rich man because everything bad disappears from his life.

J153.2.p: A hermit explains to someone why anger is a sin.

J154.r: *Cosquin Études 85ff.; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 52; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Völsunga saga ch. 11, Boberg; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *911; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 230.
J154.p: A dying father gives his children wise advice, which later proves true through experience.

J154.0.1.p: A father gives his children wise words or advice.

J154.1.p: A dying holy person leaves his followers a puzzling message that only becomes clear later.

J155.p: A person gains wisdom or knowledge from women.

J155.1.p: A hero is given directions for his journey by a princess.

J155.1.1.p: A serpent is given directions for his journey by his beautiful wife.

J155.2.p: A king takes lovers among great men's wives in order to learn their husbands' secrets.

J155.3.p: Caesar ignores his wife's advice and suffers disaster as a result.

J155.4.p: A wife gives her husband wise advice.

J155.5.p: The wife of a usurer (moneylender) saves her husband through her prayers.

J155.6.r: (Cf. J154.) Icelandic: Völsunga saga ch. 33 (31); Þiðriks saga II 254—56, Boberg.
J155.6.p: A dying woman, a queen, leaves wise words for others.

J155.7.p: A person gains knowledge from mysterious women met in the forest.

J155.8.p: A harlot (prostitute) gives wisdom to a king.

J156.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 610; Irish myth: Cross.
J156.p: A person gains wisdom or knowledge from fools.

J156.1.p: A fool's remark teaches a wise person that it is better to make peace before a war than after it. The lesson is drawn from a foolish speaker.

J156.2.p: A wise person learns something from a fool who mocks or comments on the absurdity of a tightrope walker's performance.

J156.3.p: A nobleman gives a fool a gift and tells him to give it only to someone greater of a fool than himself. When the fool's master is dying and making no preparations for the journey the doctor warns of, the fool hands him the gift, and this shocks the master into repenting.

J156.4.p: A fool refuses to go to heaven because he wants to stay with his master, whom everyone says is bound for hell. The fool's loyalty is the foolish joke that teaches wisdom.

J157.p: A person gains knowledge or wisdom through a dream rather than through study or experience.

J157.0.1.p: In a dream a god appears to a person and gives them instructions or advice.

J157.1.p: In a dream a man is willing to receive the sacrament from an unworthy priest. The dream teaches him something about the priest and the sacrament.

J157.2.p: A person learns in a dream the fate of their dead parents: the mother is shown in Hell and the father in Heaven.

J157.3.p: A dream warns against spreading scientific knowledge among ordinary people.

J158.p: A person gains wisdom from an angel, who gives them knowledge or advice.

J158.1.p: Solomon heeds a warning given to him by an angel.

J161.r: Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 62 (Gonzenbach No. 8).
J161.p: A person rehearses a trial by setting up a stick in the ground as the judge and arguing the case before it, thereby gaining wisdom.

J162.p: A person gains wisdom by hanging in a tree for a long time.

J163.p: Wisdom or good sense is bought with money, as if it were a commodity for sale.

J163.1.r: Nouvelles de Sens No. 6; English: Wells 179 (A Peniworth of Witte); West Indies: Flowers 474.
J163.1.p: A man buys a small amount of wit, paying only a penny for it.

J163.2.p: A man is told to bring his wife a purseful of sense, so that she will be wise.

J163.2.1.p: A fool is told to fetch a pottle of brains. He tries to buy them, but finally learns that the real advice was to marry a clever girl.

J163.3.p: A person gives up one of their eyes in exchange for wisdom.

J163.4.r: *Types 910A, 910B; *Fb “råd”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 229.
J163.4.p: Good advice or counsel is bought, as if it were a purchasable item.

J164.p: Wisdom is given to a person directly by God.

J165.p: Wisdom is gained by eating or tasting from a magical tree of knowledge.

J166.p: A person acquires wisdom by reading books.

J166.1.r: (Sibylline). Nine books first offered at certain price. Finally after this is refused and the owner throws six of them into the fire, the king pays the same price for three of them. Finds them filled with wisdom. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 588.
J166.1.p: Wisdom is obtained from books, but the books cost a very large sum to buy.

J166.2.p: Wisdom is obtained from books that belonged to people who lived before the Flood.

J167.p: A person becomes wise by being constantly reminded of past foolishness, as when an unjust judge's skin is stretched over a footstool kept before judges so they stay just.

J168.p: Wisdom is taught in condensed form through inscriptions written on walls.

J171.r: (Cf. B82.6.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 213f., 216ff., 248f.; Jewish: *Neuman.
J171.p: Wisdom is given as short proverbial advice or counsels.

J171.1.p: A helpful horse gives the hero advice that leads to trouble whether he follows it or not.

J171.2.p: A king questions six doctors and receives wise answers to his questions.

J171.2.1.p: Asked what he likes best on earth, one doctor says that a man who does not have what he wants is not content.

J171.2.2.p: Asked what he likes best on earth, one doctor says that all joys are mixed with sorrow.

J171.2.3.p: Asked what he likes best on earth, one doctor says he likes that all evil and hypocrisy will one day end.

J171.2.4.p: Asked what most astonishes him on earth, one doctor says it is that the most respected people are the biggest fools.

J171.2.5.p: Asked what most astonishes him on earth, one doctor says it is that those who speak of spiritual matters are usually the most depraved.

J171.2.6.p: Asked what most astonishes him on earth, one doctor says it is that man lives in a state in which he cannot die.

J171.3.p: A group of other miscellaneous wise sayings is gathered here.

J171.3.1.p: A crow flying away says that a wise man does not stay in a place of calamity, but a fool stays there and suffers fear and sorrow.

J171.3.2.p: A proverb advises seeking to win over one's accuser so that he does not cause trouble.

J172.r: Type 756B; Andrejev FFC LXIX 120ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 324, 330, 332, O’Suilleabhain 63, 95, 100; India: Thompson-Balys.
J172.p: Hearing an account of the punishments prepared in hell leads a person to repent.

J173.p: A man, ordered by the Senate to make a tyrant stop killing, kills himself and his family so that the tyrant is shown the horror of his bloodlust.

J174.p: A wise person sees only the good in a worthless book, while a malicious person sees only the bad in a good book.

J175.p: A person gains wisdom from a young man, so that a wise lesson comes from someone younger or less expected.

J176.p: A person gains wisdom from evil spirits or demons.

J177.p: A person gains wisdom from his brother-in-law, that is, his sister's or wife's brother or a similar in-law.

J178.p: Robbers or thugs, disguised, show a cruel princess how she should treat her husband, and she gains wisdom from watching them.

J179.p: A miscellaneous category of other ways a person acquires wisdom or knowledge that do not fit the listed types.

J179.1.p: A humble Brahmin teaches a king the difference between what is his own and what belongs to others, that is, between "mine" and "thine."

J179.2.p: A person learns wisdom in an underground kingdom, where he finds that human passions cannot be satisfied on earth.

J179.3.p: A person gains wisdom from his neighbors.

J179.4.p: A person gains wisdom through fasting, going without food.

J180.p: General heading for tales and motifs about a person who has or possesses wisdom.

J181.p: A man says he is the youngest person present because he does not count the years before he became a monk or the like.

J182.p: Different kinds or types of wisdom that a person may possess.

J182.1.p: Forty-nine gates of wisdom are opened to Moses, and sometimes to Solomon as well, giving them complete wisdom.

J182.2.p: There are seventy-two kinds of wisdom.

J185.p: In a contest between wisdom and wealth, wisdom wins.

J185.1.p: A minister's clever daughter-in-law uses her wisdom to defeat a Brahmin's wealth in a contest.

J186.p: A person loses his wisdom by accepting bribes and gifts.

J190.p: Miscellaneous tales and motifs about acquiring and possessing wisdom that do not fit the other categories.

J191.p: Wise men, that is, people noted for their wisdom in general.

J191.1.p: King Solomon is portrayed as the archetypal wise man, famed for his judgment and knowledge.

J191.2.p: Other heroes from the Bible are portrayed as wise men.

J192.p: Certain nations are regarded as the source of wisdom, from whom others obtained their knowledge.

J192.1.p: Wisdom is said to have come from the peoples of the East.

J192.2.p: Wisdom is said to have come from Egypt.

J192.3.p: Wisdom is said to have come from the Greeks.

J192.4.p: Wisdom is said to have come from the Hebrews.

J200.p: A general heading for tales in which a character must make a choice, and the wisdom or folly of that choice is shown.

J201.p: A person is offered one option only, either to take what is put before them or to go without anything. Named after Hobson, a carrier who gave customers no real alternative.

J201.1.p: A person is given a choice between eggs, but only one egg or none at all is available.

J210.p: A character must choose between two or more evils, all of them bad, so that the wise choice is the least harmful one.

J210.1.p: Four choices are offered, all of them evil, and the person may make only one choice.

J211.p: A person must choose between being poor but free, or being rich but enslaved.

J211.1.p: A philosopher chooses poverty together with freedom over wealth that would bring bondage.

J211.1.1.p: A man gives away all his wealth, reasoning that it is better to die than to give up his virtue. He chooses poverty with freedom over riches that would enslave him.

J211.2.r: *Type 112; Crane Vitry 199 No. 157; Wienert FFC LVI *59 (ET 208), 124 (ST 325); Halm Aesop No. 297; Jacobs Aesop 202 No. 7; Albini Atene e Roma VI 175.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 15 No. 5; Japanese: Ikeda.
J211.2.p: The town mouse and the country mouse: the country mouse prefers simple poverty with safety to the rich but dangerous life in town.

J211.2.1.p: A fly mocks an elephant kept by a king, pointing out that the great beast lacks freedom.

J212.p: A person must choose between a plain life that is safe and a grand life that is dangerous.

J212.1.r: Jacobs Aesop 220 No. 78; Scala Celi 135a No. 744; India: Thompson-Balys.
J212.1.p: An ass envies a horse in fine trappings, but the horse is killed in battle while the ass lives content and safe.

J213.p: A person must choose between losing beauty or losing the power of speech.

J214.r: *Wesselski Märchen 236; Fb “rig” III 55a; Irish myth: Cross; English: Wells 114 (Sir Isumbras); Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *937; Russian: Andrejev No. *931 I; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 948*.
J214.p: A person must choose between suffering in youth or suffering in old age.

J215.p: A choice between two evils in which the person keeps the bad situation they already have rather than risk a worse one.

J215.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 186; Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 228), 115 (ST 255); Halm Aesop No. 36; Jacobs Aesop 215 No. 64; Scala Celi 21a No. 132; Alphabet No. 97; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 51; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 32; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J215.1.p: A wounded animal or man tells others not to chase away the flies, because the full flies will be replaced by hungrier, fiercer ones.

J215.1.1.p: A parrot left to guard figs eats his fill, and when he is replaced he argues that being full makes him safer than a new hungry guard would be.

J215.1.2.p: A king declines to banish his gossiping courtiers, reasoning that they would slander him among strangers, while at home they test his patience and help correct his conduct.

J215.1.3.p: A wolf is advised not to pull off the well-fed leeches, since hungrier leeches would take their place as he swims.

J215.1.4.p: An old man prefers the occasional loud chirp of swallows to the endless soft chirp of sandpipers, judging the constant noise worse.

J215.2.p: Oxen decide not to kill the butchers, because inexperienced killers might come in and make things worse.

J215.2.1.p: An old woman prays for the safety of a cruel tyrant, fearing that a worse ruler would succeed him if he fell.

J215.3.p: A heathcock prefers the hardships of home to the dangers of travelling in foreign lands.

J215.4.p: A monk flees to the wilderness to escape having to work with material goods, but finds he must work to survive and returns to the monastery.

J216.p: A person is forced to choose between two ways of dying and picks one.

J216.1.p: An army chooses to face the enemy rather than return in flight and be killed by its angry king.

J216.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 51 (ET 107), 115 (ST 253); Halm Aesop No. 273.
J216.2.p: A lamb prefers to be sacrificed in the temple rather than be eaten by a wolf.

J216.3.p: A crab would rather be killed outright than be imprisoned and starved.

J216.4.p: A defeated soldier lying helpless asks his enemy to stab him in the chest rather than the back, to preserve his honor; the captor spares him and they become friends.

J216.5.p: A person chooses to die young in exchange for lasting fame.

J216.6.p: A saint chooses to die in the pride of youth rather than live to suffer the misery of old age.

J217.p: A person would rather remain a captive than die.

J217.0.1.p: A person prefers a miserable life to death, and so does not want to die even though life is unsatisfying.

J217.0.1.1.r: (Compare C11 for a similar situation in which Death appears.) U.S.: *Baughman.
J217.0.1.1.p: A man prays for death to take him, and a trickster overhears; the trickster then comes to the man's house, often disguised, claims to be God or the devil, and the man tells him to take his wife, or the man runs away.

J217.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 71 (ET 354), 115 (ST 252); Halm Aesop No. 377.
J217.1.p: A lamb that escapes from the flock goes back to the shepherd rather than being killed by the wolf or butcher outside. He judges that captivity under a kind master is better than death.

J217.2.p: A discontented donkey wishes to die and be free of his hard life, but when he sees the skins of dead donkeys for sale at a fair, he changes his mind and decides to keep living.

J218.p: Two enemies choose to make peace instead of fighting to the death, usually because fighting would benefit someone else.

J218.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 72), 108 (ST 202); Halm Aesop No. 253.
J218.1.p: A lion and a wild boar, who are enemies, stop fighting and make peace, because killing each other would only give a meal to the vulture waiting above.

J221.p: A ruler or person accepts a small wrong or injustice on purpose, to avoid causing larger public trouble or disorder in the state.

J221.1.p: A king chooses to ignore his wife's unfaithfulness rather than cause upheaval in the kingdom by acting against it.

J221.1.1.p: A senator ignores his wife's adultery so that he will not damage his public reputation or position.

J221.1.2.p: A man scolds his servants when they tell him that his wife has been unfaithful, refusing to hear the news.

J221.2.p: A king accepts a small personal trouble or inconvenience for himself, so that his kingdom is spared great troubles. He suffers so that the realm is helped.

J221.3.p: A man would rather pay 500 florins that he does not really owe than let people say he failed to pay his debts.

J222.p: A person shipwrecked chooses to be rescued alone rather than be drowned together with his goods, so he gives up his possessions to save himself.

J223.p: A person must choose between two evils: paying a tribute or tax, or losing both money and life.

J225.p: A person accepts an event that looks unjust or wrong on the surface, because it prevents a greater wrong. Such choices are shown as wise despite appearances.

J225.0.1.r: *Type 759; *BP IV 326 No. 3; **DeCock Studien en Essays 178ff.; *Crane Vitry 179 No. 109; Herbert III 8; Fb “uskyldig”; Alphabet Nos. 68, 411; Scala Celi 15a No. 85; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 508b nn. 9—11; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 32; **O. Rohde Die Erzählung vom Einsiedler und dem Engel (Leipzig, 1894); *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 682. — Irish: Beal XXI 336; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 23, *296, Goebel Jüdische Motive in märchenhaften Erzählungsgut (Gleiwitz, 1932) 116ff., *Neuman.
J225.0.1.p: An angel takes a hermit along on a journey and does many things that seem unjust. Later the angel explains that each of these acts was in fact just.

J225.0.1.1.p: An angel explains to a hermit why God lets a sinner die peacefully with a grand funeral while a holy hermit is killed by a wild beast.

J225.0.2.p: God punishes many people because of the sin of one person, much as a man who destroys a whole beehive because a single bee stung him.

J225.0.3.p: An angel disguised as a young man shows a doubting hermit that the ways of divine providence cannot be understood by humans.

J225.1.p: A young man is made lame as punishment for having kicked his mother.

J225.2.p: A lion is sent to kill a man, but in killing him it frees him from the chance of sinning later and from a stay in purgatory.

J225.3.p: An angel takes a cup away from an old man. The angel does this so that the old man will not come to love the cup too much.

J225.4.r: *Type 759; Wesselski Mönchslatein No. 79; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J225.4.p: An angel, identified as Jesus, kills a man. The killing is done because the man is secretly planning a murder, so the act looks unjust but prevents a greater wrong.

J225.5.p: An angel kills a man because the man loves his child too much. The act seems unjust, but it is a choice made to avoid a greater evil.

J225.6.p: A saint gives generously to a gambler and only a little to a beggar. The gambler is generous with what he has, while the beggar hoards, so the saint's choice looks unfair but reflects their true characters.

J225.7.p: A forest-dweller who longs to do evil is sent to hell, while a writer who repents is sent to heaven. God explains to his wise man why this seemingly unfair outcome is just.

J225.8.p: An evil mother receives a fine funeral while a good father is buried poorly. The contrast looks unjust, and the tale presents it as an apparent injustice.

J226.p: Someone must make a hard choice between two relatives, where either choice means losing one family member's benefit or hurting another.

J226.1.p: A parent must choose which son to free: an adopted son or a long-missing natural son.

J226.2.p: A person must choose between a blind son who will live a long life and a healthy son who will die young.

J226.3.p: A man must choose between a foolish son who will always stay with him and four wise daughters who will leave him.

J227.p: Someone chooses death over other evils, judging that dying is less bad than the alternative.

J227.1.p: Someone chooses death rather than being taken captive.

J227.2.p: Someone chooses death rather than suffer dishonor or disgrace.

J229.p: A miscellaneous group of tales in which someone must choose between two evils, with no single theme.

J229.1.p: A man must choose between staying home with a loving wife or going to the tavern and having an unfaithful wife. He chooses the tavern.

J229.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 366), 115 (ST 251); Halm Aesop No. 382.
J229.2.p: A sheep must choose between an ignorant shearer and something worse. The sheep would rather die than suffer longer under the shearer.

J229.3.p: A person must choose between a big piece of cake with a curse attached and a small piece with a blessing.

J229.4.p: A man would rather send an ugly woman to the devil than a pretty one, and he chooses to keep the ugly mistress.

J229.5.p: A person must choose between a bad master, a bad official, or a bad neighbor. A bad master can do evil if he wishes, a bad official can harm a poor man and accuse him to his master, and a bad neighbor can betray his neighbors' secrets. The bad neighbor is judged the worst.

J229.6.p: A person must choose between a poor man and a miserly man as a leader, and the choice is a bad one because neither would make a good leader.

J229.7.p: A rower would rather be stoned by his master than stay out in the storm.

J229.8.r: Scala Celi 21a No. 128; Herbert III 35ff.; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 45; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J229.8.p: A person sticks with a bad master or situation because they fear that any replacement would be even worse.

J229.8.1.p: A weaver prefers his current master, who has only one hedgehog in the house, to later masters who have more and more hedgehogs. He insists his master remove the hedgehog, and when the master refuses he leaves, but after worse masters he returns to the first one.

J229.9.p: A man keeps a bride who has serious faults because he fears that another bride would be even worse.

J229.10.p: The idea that the smaller the evil, the better, so one should choose the smallest possible woman as a bride.

J229.11.p: A fool advises his uncle to accept money from his wife's lover rather than take revenge on him. In the note, the advice is in a letter that the fool never actually sends.

J229.12.p: Prisoners are offered a choice between being castrated or being blinded.

J229.13.p: As a punishment from God, a sinner may choose between twelve years of famine or twelve hours of heavy rain.

J229.14.p: A person would rather endure physical pain than live in poverty.

J230.p: A choice that tests whether someone can tell what is truly valuable from what only looks valuable.

J231.p: A person is offered anything and chooses wisdom over all other rewards.

J231.1.p: God allows Solomon to ask for anything, and he asks for wisdom. He is granted wisdom and also wealth.

J231.2.p: A choice is made between love and wisdom.

J232.p: Good health is chosen as the most precious thing a person could have.

J233.p: A person must choose between what they want and what they ought to do.

J240.p: A choice is made between something useful and something merely decorative.

J241.p: A fruit-bearing tree is chosen over a non-fruiting one because of its usefulness.

J241.1.p: Athena chooses the olive tree because it bears fruit.

J241.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 71 (ET 350), 143 (ST 494); Halm Aesop No. 102.
J241.2.p: A peasant is asked by sparrows and crickets to spare a honey tree. He refuses at first, but when he finds honey in the tree he agrees to leave it standing.

J242.p: In a contest, the useful thing beats the beautiful one.

J242.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 4), *142 (ST 484); Halm Aesop No. 384.
J242.1.p: A contest between a rose and an amaranth shows that worth does not lie in beauty.

J242.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 15), 74 (ET 398), *142 (ST 483); Halm Aesop No. 125.
J242.2.p: A pine tree and a thornbush argue over which of them is more useful. The point is that a plain, slow-growing but sturdy pine is worth more than a showy plant, since its beauty alone does not give it value.

J242.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI *43 (ET 1), 142 (ST 482); Halm Aesop No. 42.
J242.3.p: A fox and a panther compete in a contest of beauty. The fox's spirit is judged more valuable than the panther's handsome skin.

J242.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 63), 90 (ST 22), 142 (ST 480); Halm Aesop No. 398; Dh IV 185ff.
J242.4.p: A peacock is chosen as king because of his good looks, but he proves a bad ruler since he is too weak to defend his flock.

J242.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 3), 142 (ST 479); Halm Aesop No. 397.
J242.5.p: A peacock and a crane compete in beauty. The lesson is that it is better to be able to soar like a crane than to strut about like a peacock.

J242.6.r: Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 5, 9), 124 (ST 330), 142 (ST 482); Halm Aesop No. 415.
J242.6.p: In a beauty contest between swallows and crows, or between ants and flies, the winner is decided by usefulness, since real worth does not lie in beauty.

J242.7.p: A learned crow judges that a dead cat is worth more than a golden crown, because the cat is useful and the crown is merely ornamental.

J242.8.p: When dividing property, a clever younger brother claims the hind part of a buffalo, the upper part of a tree, and the use of a curtain at night, leaving his elder brother the less useful shares.

J243.p: Tales in which being useful is shown to be more valuable than being fast.

J243.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 19), 142 (ST 478); Halm Aesop No. 409.
J243.1.p: A dog and a hog dispute over their children, and the lesson is that worth does not lie in speed.

J244.p: Tales in which goodness is chosen over good looks.

J244.1.p: A father has a handsome son and an ugly daughter. He advises both to look in the mirror daily: the son so he does not trade his handsome face for bad character, and the daughter so she triumphs over her looks through good manners.

J245.p: Tales in which useful but plain things are preferred to costly, beautiful ones.

J245.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 164; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J245.1.p: A man is shown jewels that cost a great deal of money, but he replies that he has better stones, millstones, which earn that much money.

J245.2.p: A king dreams that he experiences the cultural civilization of a great empire, and on waking he would rather be poor and primitive.

J246.p: Tales in which physical strength is valued over cleverness.

J246.1.p: A man criticizes the devil because the devil's deeds are not fair. The devil replies that his deeds are strong nevertheless, so strong speakers are to be preferred to clever ones.

J246.2.p: A hero scorns weapons and fights with his fists alone.

J247.p: Tales in which goodness is chosen over wealth.

J247.1.p: A man is advised to choose a good but poor man as his daughter's husband rather than a rich man.

J251.p: Tales holding that practical know-how is more vital than book learning or theory.

J251.1.p: A bookish scholar and a boatman each look down on the other's skill, and the scholar's ignorance of swimming nearly costs them both their lives, so practical know-how proves more vital than book learning.

J252.p: A learned person is judged more valuable than two unlearned ones, because the learned person does not waste time on pointless things while the unlearned one does.

J260.p: A choice in which a person must pick between what something is truly worth and how it merely looks.

J261.r: Wienert FFC LVI 83 (ET 496), 142 (ST 485); Halm Aesop No. 369.
J261.p: The people who wail the loudest at a funeral are not necessarily the ones who grieve the most deeply.

J262.p: Things that make the most noise are often empty or hollow inside.

J262.1.r: Chauvin II 86 No. 21; Bødker Exempler 278 No. 20; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J262.1.p: A fox is fooled or amused by a drum that makes a lot of noise but turns out to be empty inside.

J262.2.p: A small coin rattling inside an empty bottle makes a lot of noise, showing that noise does not mean value.

J263.p: Even in a flood of empty talk, some wise words can be found.

J264.p: A ruler admires the beauty of jewels but never bothers to learn about their remarkable magical or healing powers, so the showy appearance proves to be of least importance.

J266.p: A traveler must choose between a short but dangerous route and a long but safe one.

J267.p: A person must choose between pleasant flattering lies and unpleasant but honest truths.

J267.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *244; Finnish: Aarne FFC V No. 33*.
J267.1.p: A raven drowns his young ones who promised to care for him when he is old. He spares one chick that admits it will not help him, because it would have to carry its own young.

J280.p: A choice in which quality is valued more highly than quantity.

J281.p: Parents or others prefer offspring of good quality over offspring of great number.

J281.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 20), 142 (ST 477); Halm Aesop No. 240.
J281.1.p: A lioness answers a fox, who mocks her for having only one cub, by saying that her single cub is a lion.

J310.p: A choice in which the present is preferred to the past.

J311.p: A person should not dwell on the past or worry about how things used to be.

J311.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 70 (ET 340), 144 (ST 496); Halm Aesop No. 60.
J311.1.p: A fox sees a man trying to count ocean waves and advises him to count only the waves coming toward him and ignore those that have already passed.

J311.2.p: A person should not ask why the former days were better than the present ones.

J312.p: What a person is now matters more than what they used to be.

J312.1.p: A wasp mocks a butterfly for coming from an ugly chrysalis, and the butterfly replies that where one comes from does not matter, only what one is now. Someone is judged by present worth, not by humble origins.

J320.p: People choose a pleasure or benefit now over a larger good later. The present is valued more than the future.

J321.p: A person keeps what they already have rather than risk it for something uncertain in the future.

J321.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 94), 105, 147 (ST 175, 525); Halm Aesop No. 9.
J321.1.p: Someone foolishly gives up a sure thing in hope of a bigger gain that never comes. The bird in hand is lost for the bird in the bush.

J321.1.1.p: A fisherman trades today's catch for the promise of a larger catch tomorrow, and loses out.

J321.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 308), 105 (ST 176); Halm Aesop No. 28; Jacobs Aesop 212 No. 53; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J321.2.p: A person keeps a small fish already in the net instead of waiting for the uncertain chance of a bigger catch.

J321.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 51 (ET 105), 106 (ST 180); Halm Aesop No. 254.
J321.3.p: A lion gives up a sleeping hare to chase a shepherd, and in the end catches neither animal.

J321.4.p: A person chooses what they have now over something in the future. This heading is a general statement of the same folly.

J322.p: A person should not harm themselves now in order to secure their family's future.

J322.1.p: A man bets he can run while his head is cut off. Asked what he will gain, he says his family will benefit.

J323.p: A man in heaven is offered to be reforged to improve him, but he chooses to stay as he is, preferring present unhappiness to change.

J325.p: A woman confesses that her child is not her husband's. The child chooses to keep the father it knows rather than the real father it has not yet met.

J326.p: A man prefers a servant girl who is present with him over her mistress who is absent.

J327.p: A soldier chooses to stay alive rather than die to take revenge on an enemy.

J340.p: A choice that brings a small gain at the cost of a big loss. This heading introduces such foolish bargains.

J341.p: A person keeps the weight or burden of a body part rather than lose it, even though losing it would be better.

J341.1.p: A fox would rather carry the weight of its tail than give part of it to an ape to be rid of the burden.

J342.p: Higher pay in a place brings higher living costs, so the extra money is eaten up.

J342.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 602; Scala Celi 60a No. 332; Alphabet No. 448.
J342.1.p: A barber leaves a cheap village for higher wages in a city, but finds the city's high living costs take all his extra earnings.

J342.1.1.p: A disciple stays in a place where everything is cheap, despite his master's advice to leave, and gets into trouble as a result.

J342.2.p: A wise man turns down an income worth half a kingdom, reasoning that the expenses of living at that level would eat up the gain.

J343.p: A man rejects a cure for his problem because the cure would bring him more trouble than the illness does.

J343.1.p: A drunkard refuses a cure for his fever because the cure would take away his thirst for drink.

J344.p: A person neglects what he already has while chasing after other things.

J344.1.r: *Chauvin II 104 No. 67; Bødker Exempler 302 No. 70; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J344.1.p: A monkey lets go of all the other lentils in his hand in order to search for one lentil he has lost.

J344.2.r: Chauvin II 106 No. 69; Bødker Exempler 303 No. 72.
J344.2.p: A host wants to learn Hebrew so badly that he risks forgetting his own language.

J345.p: A person neglects something valuable because he is distracted by something merely interesting.

J345.1.r: She-goats die; wild-goats run off. Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 368), 106 (ST 181); Halm Aesop No. 12.
J345.1.p: A herdsman neglects his own domestic she-goats in favor of wild goats.

J345.2.p: A man gives up farming to go fishing, and when the water dries up he has no food and goes hungry.

J346.p: It is wiser to be satisfied with what you have than to try for more and lose everything.

J347.p: A person gives up wealth and glory in exchange for freedom and virtue.

J347.1.p: A man turns down vast wealth because he knows that wealth would bring greed with it.

J347.2.p: A king sets down his crown because it brings too many worries.

J347.3.p: A prince chooses exile with honor over a shameful life at his father's court.

J347.4.p: A rich merchant turns out to be less happy than a poor man.

J347.5.p: A man turns down a rich marriage because the bride's house is full of dangerous wild animals.

J350.p: A choice where giving up a small amount brings a large gain.

J351.p: A person sacrifices a part of his body to save his life.

J351.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 264), 141 (ST 475); Halm Aesop No. 189.
J351.1.p: A beaver saves its life by biting off its own scrotum and leaving it for its pursuers.

J352.p: A person ignores discomfort or hardship once a prize or loot is within reach.

J352.1.p: A wolf is told that dust from a flock of sheep will bother him, but he decides it is useful and does not mind it, because the sheep mean booty he can take.

J352.2.p: A snake agrees to carry a frog king on his back, humiliating as that is, because the frog king feeds him frogs to eat.

J355.p: A person accepts a minor discomfort from the weather in exchange for a much bigger benefit.

J355.1.r: **Schiller Anthropos XII—XIII 513; DeVries FFC LXXIII 324ff.; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 67, *301, *Neuman.
J355.1.p: A king scolds the wind for blowing away a poor widow's last cup of meal, then learns the wind's act saved a shipload of people, and he is humbled.

J356.p: A person would rather fight on while tired than lose everything just to get a short rest, since the loss would cost far more than the discomfort.

J357.p: A priest sells his donkey because worrying about its safety keeps distracting him from his prayers.

J369.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a small inconvenience is accepted for a large gain and do not fit the more specific motifs in this group.

J369.1.p: Solomon turns down the water of immortality for himself when he learns he cannot also keep his possessions with it.

J369.2.r: *Crane Vitry 188 No. 127; Herbert III 11, 36ff.; Hervieux Fabulistes latins I 218 No. 47.
J369.2.p: An ape throws away a nut because its rind is bitter, missing the sweet kernel inside.

J370.p: Choosing between important work and unimportant work, and deciding which one deserves time and effort.

J371.p: A person should not waste time on minor quarrels when their life is in danger.

J371.1.p: A bull chased by a lion tries to hide in a cave, but a goat blocks the entrance; the bull does not stop to fight the goat and runs on, since the lion is behind him.

J372.p: A king is mocked for inventing a musical instrument, which is seen as a trifle, but is praised for building a great mosque.

J390.p: Choosing between kind strangers and cruel relatives, with the kind strangers chosen.

J391.p: A child or animal picks kind foster parents over cruel birth parents.

J391.1.p: A lamb chooses a she-goat as her foster mother, because the goat has cared for her more than her own mother, who has deserted her.

J400.p: Deciding carefully whom to keep company with and make friends with.

J401.p: Real friends are rare; most people who seem to be friends are not truly loyal.

J401.0.1.p: A saying that a true friend is recognized only when you are in need, because only then do friends show their loyalty.

J401.1.r: Criticized for its smallness he says, “I wish I had true friends enough to fill it.” Wienert FFC LVI 39; Phaedrus III 9.
J401.1.p: Socrates builds himself a small house, showing that he would rather have a modest home than a large one filled with many visitors.

J410.p: General heading for stories about whether it is wise to associate with people who are equal to you or with those who are not. It introduces the more specific motifs below.

J411.p: Someone of high rank refuses to associate with a person of humble status, and this refusal is treated as proper.

J411.1.p: A boar refuses to fight with a lowly ass, thinking it beneath him to match himself against such a creature.

J411.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 76 (ET 423), 120 (ST 297); Halm Aesop No. 153.
J411.2.p: Zeus refuses a wedding gift offered by a snake, because gifts should be accepted only from equals.

J411.3.p: A prince refuses to play with common children, regarding himself as too high-born for their company.

J411.3.1.p: Noble poets refuse to associate with a truly good poet because he was born of lowly birth.

J411.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 378), 120 (ST 299); Halm Aesop No. 3.
J411.4.p: A peasant is ashamed to have been thrown off by a donkey, since being unseated by such a lowly creature is disgraceful.

J411.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 82), 92 (ST 54); Halm Aesop No. 280.
J411.5.p: A wolf tries to make friends with a lion, and the lion kills him for presuming to be his equal.

J411.6.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 69), 92 (ST 45); Halm Aesop No. 116.
J411.6.p: A dolphin and a whale scorn a crab who offers to make peace between them, dismissing him as beneath their notice.

J411.7.p: A laurel and an olive tree, quarreling over which is more useful, scorn a thornbush when it is proposed as judge.

J411.8.r: Wienert FFC LVI *56 (ET 167), 113 (ST 238); Halm Aesop No. 257.
J411.8.p: A mouse climbs onto a lion's mane, and the lion is angered by the mouse's impudence.

J411.9.p: A knight ignores an insult from a servant, considering it beneath him to take offense.

J411.9.1.p: A king refuses to quarrel with a bird, thinking it beneath his dignity to contend with so lowly a creature.

J411.10.p: A leopard is ashamed to have been bitten by a lizard, since being hurt by such a small creature is humiliating.

J411.11.p: A rich man refuses to associate with his poor sister.

J412.p: General heading for stories in which an association between a great person and a lowly one turns out to be beneficial to both.

J412.1.r: First: an eagle, because it is ruler of birds; second: a falcon; because it is beloved by the nobles; third: a bird which flies with many others, so as to receive advice. King chooses third. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 677.
J412.1.p: A king asks his three sons what kind of bird they would prefer to be, and the one chosen is the prince who has democratic tastes and does not look down on ordinary people.

J413.p: General heading for stories in which an association between unequals brings no benefit and is harmful or unpleasant.

J413.1.p: A lion licks a sick man, who is disgusted by the attention from so unequal a creature.

J414.p: General heading for stories about whether it is wise to marry someone of equal standing or someone of unequal standing.

J414.1.p: A man is allowed to choose between a human wife and a fairy mistress, and he picks the human wife.

J414.2.p: A prince prefers his first love to the princess he later marries.

J414.3.p: A marriage between a jackal and a turtle fails because they have different habits.

J416.p: A person prefers to associate with their own kind rather than with strangers.

J416.1.p: A bird refuses to keep up a friendship with a bird of different habits.

J417.p: A man prefers to live with ordinary people rather than with a pious man, because he will look virtuous by comparison.

J420.p: Strong and weak creatures form a partnership or friendship with one another.

J421.p: The weak are made subordinate to the strong within an association.

J421.1.p: A lion, made king, appoints an ass as his lieutenant.

J421.2.p: A lion, made king, appoints a lame goat as his lieutenant.

J423.p: A stupid creature fears to keep company with a clever one.

J423.1.p: A jackal realizes the partridge was too clever for him and leaves.

J425.p: A weak creature fears to keep company with a strong one.

J425.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 76 (ET 414), *136 (ST 415); Halm Aesop No. 422; Jacobs Aesop 212 No. 51; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
J425.1.p: An earthen pot and a brazen pot are carried down a river together; the brazen pot wants to stay together for company, but the earthen pot fears its approach.

J425.2.p: A buffalo refuses a tiger's invitation to dinner because he sees a fire prepared to cook him.

J426.r: Chauvin II 101 No. 61; Bødker Exempler No. 66; India: Thompson-Balys.
J426.p: A rat allies with a cat in mutual danger, and once the danger has passed the friendship ends. The rat, threatened by a weasel and an owl, joins a cat caught in a net, is saved by her, then rescues her carefully and prudently ends the relationship.

J426.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J426.1.p: A mouse and a cat form an alliance that ends once the shared danger has passed.

J426.2.p: A snake and a frog are friends until the snake wants to eat the frog, and the friendship then ends.

J427.p: A cow and a tiger become companions, but the tiger eats the cow as soon as he is hungry.

J428.p: A tiger and a crane form a partnership, but they soon quarrel.

J429.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tales about the unwise choice of a companion who is stronger or weaker than oneself, with consequences for the one who chooses badly.

J429.1.p: A swan associates with a swallow and cannot fly away from danger, because the swallow's lighter, weaker nature holds it back.

J429.2.p: A swan keeps company with a crow and is wrongly blamed for the filth the crow drops, so that the bad friendship proves fatal.

J440.p: A general heading for tales about the choice of companions of different ages, where a young person and an old person keep company.

J441.p: A young and an old companion are joined together to their mutual benefit, with the association turning out well for both.

J441.1.p: An old ox is yoked together with a young ox, and the young one is kept in order and steadied by the older one.

J445.p: A general heading for tales where an association between a young person and an old person turns out badly because it is foolish.

J445.1.r: Herbert III 39ff.; Hervieux I 188 No. 14a; Heptameron No. 27; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J445.1.p: A foolish young man falls in love with an old woman who is ugly and who has been his mistress.

J445.2.r: Nouvelles Recreations No. 16; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 99; Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 341; Icelandic: *Boberg.
J445.2.p: A foolish marriage in which an old man takes a young girl as his wife.

J450.p: A general heading for tales about the choice of companions who are either good or evil, and what follows from keeping such company.

J451.p: Bad company spreads its faults to those who keep it, so that a person is corrupted by associating with wicked or lazy companions.

J451.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 376), 120 (ST 294); Halm Aesop No. 320; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J451.1.p: A man who buys an ass returns it because it has picked up lazy habits from lazy companions it kept.

J451.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 309), 120 (ST 296); Halm Aesop No. 100.
J451.2.p: A stork is killed together with cranes, because keeping such company brings it to a fatal end.

J451.3.r: Heracles on his arrival in heaven fails to greet Plutus, the god of wealth: he has seen him in too bad company. Wienert FFC LVI 76 (ET 418), 120 (ST 295); Halm Aesop No 160.
J451.3.p: The god of wealth falls into bad company and suffers for it.

J451.4.p: A mirror is dirtied by a snail that crawls across it, showing how a bad companion soils what he touches.

J452.p: A bishop's bad associates bring about his death: a doctor loses his life on his behalf and a lawyer loses his soul.

J455.p: A person comes to harm from keeping company with flatterers who tell him what he wants to hear.

J460.p: A general heading for tales about pointless choices, where someone makes a decision or debate that was never needed.

J461.p: People who are mutually useful to one another argue senselessly about which of them is most necessary or useful.

J461.1.r: *Prato Archivio per lo studio delle tradizioni popolari IV (1885) 25ff.; Penzer V 135 n.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 399; Wienert FFC LVI *43 (ET 6), 92 (ST 59); Halm Aesop No. 197; Jacobs Aesop 206 No. 29; *Crane Vitry 167 No. 73; *H. Gombel Die Fabel vom Magen und den Gliedern (Beihefte zur Zs. f. romanische Philologie LXXX [Halle, 1934]).—Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 71, *301f., *Neuman; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 139; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 393.
J461.1.p: The belly and the body's other members debate whether each is useful, though they all turn out to be mutually useful and need one another.

J461.1.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 58 (ET 187), 93 (ST 60); Halm Aesop No. 344; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
J461.1.1.p: A serpent's tail and head argue over which part is more useful. The point is that such a quarrel is pointless because each part needs the other.

J461.1.2.p: Fortune, Intellect, Knowledge, and Health argue over which of them is the greatest. The debate is foolish because each is useful in its own way.

J461.1.3.p: The tongue and the other parts of the body argue with one another about which is most important.

J461.2.p: A man's common wives, meaning everyday household items, each claim to have helped him most. The point is that every one of them was indispensable.

J461.3.p: Tobacco, a pipe, and a match argue about which of them is most useful to the smoker. Each is needed for the smoke, so the argument is pointless.

J461.4.p: A deer, an opossum, and a snake each give man indispensable help. They foolishly argue about which of them is most useful.

J461.5.p: Rice, wheat, and lentils argue over which is the best food.

J461.6.p: A hammer and an anvil argue over which is more important. Each needs the other to do any work.

J461.7.p: Wealth and wisdom argue over which of them is greater.

J461.8.p: An elephant and an ape argue about which of them is superior. An owl sets them a task that neither can do, which ends the pointless debate.

J462.p: Someone makes an unnecessary choice about what to believe, picking a faith or path when no choice was needed.

J462.1.r: King’s sons each choose a god: Jupiter for power, Saturn for wisdom, etc. Father says that a god of all combined would be better. Oesterley No. 243; Herbert III 204. Cf. Wienert FFC LVI 44 (ET 23), 135 (ST 410); Babrius No. 15.
J462.1.p: Someone makes an unnecessary choice among gods, worshipping or choosing a deity when no choice was needed.

J462.2.p: Aristotle drinks both red and white wine to show that every philosophy is good, so he has made an unnecessary choice between philosophies.

J462.3.p: Someone makes an unnecessary choice of religion, picking one faith when no choice was needed.

J462.3.1.r: All to be used. (Cf. J1262.9.) *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 70; Boccaccio Decameron I No. 3 (*Lee 6); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 150, 281.
J462.3.1.p: A father leaves his sons three jewels, standing for Christianity, Judaism, and Mohammedanism, and the sons must choose among them.
