J462.3.1.1.p: A father gives his son three rings that look the same, but only one of them is genuine. The religions are similar: only one is good, though all look alike.

J463.p: Someone makes an unnecessary choice between going uphill or downhill. A camel prefers the level ground.

J465.r: Both are good. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 105.
J465.p: Someone makes an unnecessary choice between praying and reading.

J466.p: People engage in pointless arguments about which thing is most useful, when each is useful in its own way.

J466.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 11), 74 (ET 390), 92 (ST 47); Halm Aesop No. 385.
J466.1.p: A pomegranate tree and an apple tree argue over which is worth more. A blackberry bush scolds them for their useless squabbling.

J466.2.p: A pointless argument over which of two saints with the same name is greater, showing a senseless debate about what is useful.

J480.p: A general heading for other foolish or wise choices people make when given a choice.

J481.p: A king prefers to have soldiers who inflicted wounds on others rather than soldiers who only received wounds, so he picks the fighters who gave the blows.

J482.p: Someone advises a king to marry a young unmarried maiden rather than a widow, because a widow would insist on having her own way.

J482.1.p: A woman turns down a second marriage: if her husband was good she fears losing him, and if he was bad she would regret the match.

J482.1.1.p: A widow refuses to remarry because her late husband still lives on in her heart.

J482.1.2.p: A widow refuses to remarry because her brother would kill any second husband she took.

J482.2.p: It is better to marry an ugly wife than a beautiful one, because an ugly wife is less hard to satisfy.

J482.2.1.p: It is better for a woman to marry a poor man than for a rich man to be without a husband, a joke turning on whether one lacks money or lacks a man.

J482.3.p: A young man is advised to choose as his wife a girl whose mother was chaste and faithful.

J483.p: Someone must choose between doing what they already know how to do and learning something new.

J484.p: A person chooses enjoyment and pleasure over becoming wealthy.

J485.r: Choice of three sins given him: adultery, murder (theft), drunkenness. He chooses drunkenness; the others follow. (Cf. J21.25.) *Type 839; **Taylor MPh XX 61ff.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 243; Chauvin VIII 129 No. 118; Herbert III *131; Köhler-Bolte I 583; Nouvelles de Sens No. 25; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 24; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 159, 282, Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. Wesselski Mönchslatein 22 No. 17.
J485.p: A hermit commits three sins, as listed in this tale.

J486.p: Someone chooses death over God and justice.

J487.r: Wienert FFC LVI *85 (ET 522), 145 (ST 503); Halm Aesop No. 390.
J487.p: A tame dog chooses its food bowl over chasing a fleeing hare.

J488.r: English: Wells 184 (The Fox and the Wolf).
J488.p: A fox would rather meet one hen than fifty women.

J491.p: A man picks his old sweetheart over a new one.

J493.p: A preacher prefers small men to big men, because the intellect has trouble reaching all the way down to a person's heels.

J494.p: Someone chooses death and revenge over living.

J495.p: A monk chooses solitude and loneliness over company and temptation, because living alone lets him avoid sin.

J496.p: Asked to choose between his friend and his mistress, a man picks his friend.

J497.p: An eagle prefers its own young to a changeling, a foreign young one substituted for its own.

J510.p: Wisdom in not reaching beyond one's station: being cautious about overambitious goals.

J511.p: Trying to change one's skin color is pointless, and a wise person does not attempt it.

J511.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *46 (ET 48), *87 (ST 5); Halm Aesop No. 13; India: Thompson-Balys.
J511.1.p: A Black man tries in vain to wash himself white.

J512.p: An animal that tries to become something other than its own kind comes to grief.

J512.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 91), 90 (ST 28); Halm Aesop No. 186.
J512.1.p: A crab comes ashore, and a fox kills it.

J512.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI *46 (ET 52), 90 (ST 27); Halm Aesop No. 170.
J512.2.p: A kite tries to neigh like a horse, loses its own voice, and gains nothing.

J512.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 46 (ET 46, 47), *88, 90 (ST 10, 20); Halm Aesop No. 182, 365.
J512.3.p: A camel tries in vain to dance.

J512.4.p: A donkey tries in vain to play the lyre.

J512.5.p: A wolf tries to be a doctor and only makes the patient suffer more.

J512.6.r: Chauvin II 106 No. 70; Bødker Exempler 303 No. 73; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J512.6.p: A crow tries to imitate the partridge's walk and only spoils its own.

J512.7.r: *Type 85; *BP I 206, III 558; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 135.
J512.7.p: A mouse, a bird, and a sausage keep house together; when they swap their duties, everything goes wrong.

J512.7.1.p: An elephant, a giraffe, a snake, and an ant try to keep house together, but their needs are different.

J512.8.r: Wienert FFC LVI 46 (ET 43), 90 (ST 24); Halm Aesop No. 337.
J512.8.p: A donkey wants a cricket's song, asks what crickets eat, eats dew as they do, and starves.

J512.9.r: Kills himself. Wienert FFC LVI 58 (ET 189), 93 (ST 62); Halm Aesop No. 388.
J512.9.p: A lizard tries to make itself as long as a snake.

J512.10.p: A fox disguises itself as a dove and, in doing so, forgets its plan to murder.

J512.11.p: A camel and a jackal exchange food. The camel is led by his friend to thorny fruit and gets a thorn stuck in his throat, showing that an animal should not try to change its nature.

J512.12.p: A frog wants to be shod like a horse.

J512.13.p: A jackal accidentally becomes king but still joins the other jackals in howling at night.

J512.14.p: A snake wants to be a household pet like a parrot and is killed.

J512.15.p: A frog tries to gather honey the way bees do and comes to grief, showing that an animal should not try to change its nature.

J513.p: Wise advice that it is best to leave things as they are rather than risk losing a good situation by seeking more.

J513.1.p: Birds who fly off in search of richer lands are almost all killed, and the survivors warn their friends to stay where they are.

J513.2.p: A barber tries and fails to become a merchant, and is worse off for having abandoned his trade.

J514.p: Advice that greed is dangerous, since grasping for too much can cost a person everything.

J514.1.r: Herbert III 40ff.; Hervieux IV 211 No. 38; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J514.1.p: A kite tries to carry off so many partridges at once that he drops them all and gets nothing.

J514.2.r: Chauvin II 95 No. 47; Bødker Exempler 292 No. 51; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
J514.2.p: A wolf, finding a hunter, gazelle, and wild boar all dead, tries to eat the bowstring first and is fatally wounded by the poisoned or tense bow.

J514.3.p: A greedy man keeps asking a complacent man for one more thing until, at last, he is struck blind by magic.

J514.4.p: A greedy pig looks up into a tree for figs and, distracted by the search, dies.

J514.5.p: A man not satisfied with his gold goes looking for jewels, finds only iron, and in the end gets nothing at all.

J514.6.p: A fowler offers two rubies as ransom for a goose he has caught, and ends up losing the goose and both rubies.

J515.p: A peacock spends so long preening for his coronation that the other birds grow impatient and crown the owl instead.

J530.p: Moderation in what one asks or takes from others, so as not to ruin the source of one's gain.

J531.p: A good shepherd shears his sheep rather than skinning them, and an emperor uses this image to answer a proposal for a new tax on the people by refusing to overburden them.

J550.p: Zeal can be wise and measured or foolish and excessive; this heading covers the difference.

J551.p: Excessive eagerness to tell the truth, regardless of consequences, which brings harm to the speaker.

J551.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 9; Oesterley No. 68; Herbert III 206.
J551.1.p: Cocks who loudly crow about their mistress's adultery are killed, while a discreet cock keeps quiet and saves his life.

J551.1.1.p: A bird warns its mistress against committing adultery and has its neck wrung for the warning.

J551.2.p: A fool is given the truth by being whipped on his bare back, with each blow named as the truth; when asked later to tell the truth, he says nothing is worse than the truth.

J551.3.p: A doctor loses a horse by telling the truth, while a doctor who flatters the lord is rewarded with a horse.

J551.4.p: A man is asked to tell the truth and blurts out that his host, his hostess and their cat have only three eyes between them, a rude remark that gets him driven away.

J551.5.r: When the magpie sees a bald man, she says, “You too must have tattled about the eel.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 6.
J551.5.p: A magpie blurts out to a man that his wife has eaten an eel, adding that she claimed an otter ate it, and the wife angrily plucks the magpie's feathers out.

J551.6.p: Only the youngest son tells the king the truth when asked where they got their food, and as a result he is banished.

J551.7.p: An honest servant tells people that the shop does not have many customers, and is dismissed for saying so.

J552.p: Fighting or quarreling to excess, showing a foolish and unrestrained eagerness to argue or battle.

J552.1.p: Two noblemen quarrel over a device or emblem, and the wiser of the two shows how foolish such a fight is.

J552.2.p: Noblemen ruined by a long lawsuit wisely decide to marry their children into each other's families, ending the dispute and saving their fortunes.

J552.2.1.p: A bishop who loves lawsuits is ordered by the king to settle them all, and he pleads that a few be left so he will have something to live for.

J552.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 401, 402), 98 (ST 119, 120); Halm Aesop Nos. 86, 126; Jacobs Aesop 206 No. 26.
J552.3.p: A serpent, called a weasel in some versions, tries to bite a file, wearing its teeth down on hard metal to no effect.

J552.4.p: A nobleman who is pestered by a quarrelsome woman leaves his helmet for her to quarrel with, saying she can talk to it instead of him.

J552.5.p: Two brothers settle their quarrel between themselves, so they do not have to pay a judge to decide it.

J552.6.r: “Each cock crows in his own barnyard.” Spanish: Childers (J500).
J552.6.p: A man boasts at home that his own king is the best, so that a Spaniard and a Portuguese each claim their own king is greatest, in a tale told of Castile and Portugal.

J553.p: Working to excess, pushing one's labor past sensible limits.

J553.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 40; Phaedrus III No. 14; Thiele Hermes XLI 585; Alphabet Nos. 6, 671.
J553.1.p: Aesop is caught playing with children and is scolded, so he unstrings a bow to show that relaxation is good and that it is needed to keep a bow working.

J553.2.r: When rebuked for making him a whistle he says: “I would have blown it for him had he asked me to do so.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J553.2.p: A ruler interrupts a meeting of the Senate to amuse his small son.

J554.p: Serving a master with too much zeal, so that the eager servant becomes a nuisance; here an emperor rebukes an overzealous servant for this.

J555.p: Obeying orders so rigidly and literally that the result is foolish or harmful.

J555.1.p: A mother gives her daughters instructions for married life, and the first daughter follows them literally and everything goes wrong, while the second, guided by her father's explanations, follows them sensibly and does well.

J556.p: Being honest to an excessive or foolish degree, carrying honesty past sense.

J556.1.p: St. George teaches a poor man that whoever steals a little and lies a little will get rich.

J556.2.p: A person who gives up God for five years is promised great wealth as the result, a tale of excessive honesty taken to a foolish extreme.

J557.p: Working too hard or taking on too much labor at once, showing a lack of moderation and sense.

J557.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 262; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J557.1.p: A monk is discouraged by the huge amount of work he faces, so he is advised to take on only a small amount each day, which he can actually finish.

J557.1.1.p: Even a single day of sincere penance has real value and is effective in atonement.

J558.r: Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 462), 138 (ST 431); Halm Aesop No. 161; Jewish: Neuman.
J558.p: Foolish excess in making sacrifices, giving up more than is wise or sensible.

J561.p: Pursuing something with reckless or excessive eagerness, so that the pursuit itself becomes foolish or harmful.

J561.1.p: A man tracking a gorilla gets so caught up in the chase that he notices the animal's great strength, which turns out to be a danger to him.

J561.2.r: Desists. Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 318), 109 (ST 213); Halm Aesop No. 83.
J561.2.p: A cowherd searching for a cattle thief finds him, but only recognizes him once he has become a lion, so the pursuit ends in a foolish mistake.

J562.p: Wasting effort on charity: helping those who do not deserve it or are ungrateful, or doing needless favors, is foolish. Example given: making a bed for a dog that lies down wherever it is tired.

J563.r: *Krappe Papers and Trans. of Jubilee Congress of Folk Lore Society (London, 1930) 277ff.; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 270, *357, *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
J563.p: A man brings a lion back to life, and the lion then devours him, a tale of misguided kindness.

J564.p: Excessive or foolish devotion in worship, going beyond what is sensible.

J565.p: Fasting to excess, denying oneself food beyond what is wise.

J565.1.p: A fool fasts while sitting on a roof until he grows so weak that he falls off.

J570.p: Wisdom in taking time to think before acting or deciding.

J571.p: Avoid making judgments in haste; take time before deciding.

J571.1.p: When angry, a man restrains himself by slowly saying the alphabet, which keeps him from judging in haste.

J571.2.p: A king is given three wheels to help him control his anger.

J571.3.p: A king, angry, punishes a misdeed on Easter day. Afterward he nearly kills himself in retaliation, and he submits, admitting he deserves that punishment for acting in haste.

J571.4.p: Avoid punishing others in haste, since acting while angry leads to unfair punishment.

J571.4.1.p: A man, to avoid being unfair while angry, has a disinterested third party punish his servant on his behalf.

J571.4.2.p: A master, while angry, refrains from punishing a servant who has ruined something important to him, so that he avoids a rash act he would later regret.

J571.5.p: A king is talked out of acting hastily in anger when someone tells him a story that makes him reconsider his judgment.

J571.6.p: A judge who has been harsh in condemning others is himself later brought to court and asks for mercy, and is rebuked with the saying 'Judge not, that ye be not judged.'

J571.7.p: A wise person postpones answering a fool's questions until the following day, so as not to respond in haste.

J571.8.p: An unpaid servant declines to speak ill of his master and is later rewarded for his loyalty.

J572.p: General heading for cleverness shown by waiting and thinking carefully before acting in a fight.

J572.1.r: Latter is bravest. *Chauvin II 152 No. 15; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J572.1.p: In battle, the truly brave man is the one who knows when to wait: one rushes at the enemy, a second waits a little, and a third holds back until the enemy attacks first.

J580.p: General heading for cleverness shown by being careful and avoiding danger.

J581.p: Foolish behavior of making noise while enemies are close enough to hear, thereby giving away one's position.

J581.1.p: A wolf, a guest at a dog's house, sings loudly after drinking too much, despite the dog's warning, and so gives himself away.

J581.2.r: Chauvin II 84 No. 12; Bødker Exempler 275 No. 11; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J581.2.p: A lover who insists on arguing with his mistress about how he should escape is caught by her husband, because the escape he is being given differs from what he had been told.

J581.3.r: Chauvin II 97 No. 53; Bødker Exempler 296 No. 58; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J581.3.p: A monk is saved when his enemies, a robber who wants his cow and a devil who wants his soul, quarrel over who should act first, which wakes him and his neighbors.

J581.4.p: Drones, ordered to make honey, dispute over who owns the honey, so their noise and quarrel reveal them.

J581.5.p: Kites and crows quarrel over how to divide a wounded fox, and their noise attracts attention.

J582.p: General heading for foolishness of showing oneself from hiding too early, before the danger has passed.

J582.1.r: Phaedrus II No. 8; West Indies: Flowers 476.
J582.1.p: A goat hides, but his horn sticks up above the ground and gives away his hiding place.

J582.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 286), *109 (ST 209, 521); Halm Aesop No. 127.
J582.2.p: A stag hides until the hunters have passed, but then begins eating a grapevine too soon and is discovered.

J585.p: General heading for cleverness in choosing what to eat, avoiding food that is dangerous.

J585.1.p: A clever girl refuses to eat figs, which would put her into a magic sleep.

J610.p: General heading for foresight in a conflict with others, anticipating what opponents will do and preparing for it.

J611.r: Wesselski Bebel II 110 No. 35; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 765.
J611.p: A wise man, before starting a quarrel, first thinks about how it is likely to turn out.

J612.p: A wise man checks who he is about to attack before he starts a fight.

J612.1.r: *Crane Vitry 159 No. 59; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XV 105; Wesselski Mönchslatein 87 No. 75; Alphabet No. 15; Scala Celi No. 430.
J612.1.p: A flea and a fever, each having troubled a person, swap lodgings: the flea goes to the washerwoman's cold river-washing and the fever goes to the abbess, and both succeed in escaping their pursuers.

J613.p: A wise person fears the weak more than the strong, because the weak can be dangerous when they unite or when their dangers are overlooked.

J613.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *76 (ET 421), 136 (ST 418); Halm Aesop No. 77; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3189; Legends Nos. 288f.
J613.1.p: Frogs fear that the sun will grow hotter and dry up all their puddles, so they worry about a danger that seems minor.

J613.2.p: Frogs watch two bulls fight and fear the defeated bull, knowing the loser will retreat to their marsh and trouble them there.

J620.p: Foresight used to stop others' plans before they can harm the wise person.

J621.p: A wise person destroys an enemy's weapons so that the enemy cannot fight.

J621.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 62 (ET 248), 118 (ST 277); Halm Aesop Nos. 105, 106; Dähnhardt IV 275; Herbert III 8; *Crane Vitry 176 No. 101; Jacobs Aesop 203 No. 12; Africa (Fang): Tessman 27ff., (Pangwe): ibid. 362ff.
J621.1.p: A swallow vainly urges other birds to eat hemp seed as fast as it is sown; when they ignore him he builds his nest among people, and later birds are trapped in nets made of that hemp.

J621.1.1.p: A snake gives away magic pills, and they are later used to kill him.

J622.p: A wise person prevents enemies from being born at all, stopping trouble before it starts.

J622.1.p: A wise man destroys a serpent's eggs so that no snakes hatch to become his enemies.

J622.1.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 255), 147 (ST 516); Halm Aesop No. 342.
J622.1.1.p: A swallow warns a hen not to hatch a serpent's eggs, since the hen would be hatching her own destruction.

J623.p: A wise person prevents hostility by making the enemy afraid, so the enemy does not dare to attack.

J623.1.r: Zeus: “If you had bitten the first foot that stepped on you it would not be done now.” Wienert FFC LVI 77 (ET 430), 128 (ST 364); Halm Aesop No. 347.
J623.1.p: A snake complains to Zeus that people step on him, hoping to be protected from them.

J624.p: Enemies or rivals set aside their quarrel and join forces to defeat a shared enemy.

J624.1.r: Chauvin II 87 No. 22; Bødker Exempler 279 No. 22; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
J624.1.p: Two sheep, who have been fighting and spilled blood, kill a fox that comes to lick up the blood.

J624.2.p: Sheep-dogs stop quarreling among themselves and join together to hunt a wolf that has raided the flock.

J624.3.p: Brothers who were enemies unite to fight a common enemy.

J625.p: To avoid violence while in danger, a person agrees to the other's heavy demands, and afterward goes back on the agreement. In the example, a barber demands much from a customer while holding a razor to his throat; the customer agrees, but after the shave throws the barber out.

J626.p: A person prevents trouble by taking away the weapons of a suspected wrongdoer before he can act. It later turns out the suspect was a fugitive murderer.

J628.p: Someone talks a foolish person out of killing himself, for example by describing hell as a place of pain and torment.

J631.p: A crab grabs a heron's neck, and fearing the heron will attack, cuts the neck and kills it.

J634.p: A king takes precautions to guard against being murdered by his enemies.

J634.1.p: To avoid being assassinated, a king singes his beard instead of letting a barber shave him, since a barber could be used to kill him.

J634.2.p: To avoid being assassinated, a king has the queen's quarters searched before he goes in.

J640.p: A character avoids coming under the power of others, escaping or staying out of their reach to stay safe.

J641.p: A character gets away before an enemy can attack.

J641.1.r: (Told also of fish.) *Type 246; Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 233), 108 (ST 205); Halm Aesop No. 85; Chauvin II 88.
J641.1.p: One bird flies away as a hunter bends his bow, while the other stays put and is shot.

J642.p: A character foolishly gives up his weapons and so becomes helpless against an enemy.

J642.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 32), 70 (ET 344), 107 (ST 198); Halm Aesop No. 249; *Basset RTP XXVI 126; Africa: Weeks Jungle 450.
J642.1.p: A lion who wants to marry a girl lets her family pull out his teeth and cut his claws, and he is then killed.

J642.2.p: Robbers are talked into handing a hero their swords, and he then kills them with those same swords.

J643.p: A people or animals take precautions so that they will not be ruled by a tyrant in future.

J643.1.r: King Log. Zeus has given them a log as king, but they find him too quiet. He then gives them a stork who eats them. Wienert FFC LVI *78 (ET 436), 110 (ST 217); Halm Aesop No. 76; *Crane Vitry 143 No. 24; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *277; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. *277; Russian: Andrejev No. 277; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J643.1.p: Frogs ask for a live king instead of a log, and so are ruled by a harmful king.

J643.2.p: A kite is made king of the chickens, showing a foolish choice of ruler.

J643.3.p: The lion is restored as king of the animals after the elephant grows tired of being ruler.

J644.p: A character avoids places where others have been killed or harmed, since those places are dangerous.

J644.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *53 (ET 131), 96 (ST 92); Halm Aesop No. 246, cf. No. 262; Jacobs Aesop 217 No. 73; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *50A; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A Indian (Tuxtapec): Mechling JAFL XXV 203; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 189, (Hottentot): Bleek 19 No. 10; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 243 No. 18.
J644.1.p: A fox sees many tracks going into a lion's den but none coming out, so he stays away and saves himself.

J645.p: A character avoids the power of a future enemy, dealing with a threat before it grows strong.

J645.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 55 (ET 149), 119 (ST 290); Halm Aesop No. 198.
J645.1.p: Birds flee from a cuckoo because they believe it will later grow into a hawk and prey on them.

J646.p: A person ignores the advice of someone who is their enemy, even though that advice might be sound.

J646.1.p: Palamides wounds Ulysses and then asks Ulysses for advice, and following that advice proves fatal to him.

J646.2.p: A bird overhears voices inside unhatched eggs plotting to eat their mother once they hatch, and flies away.

J647.p: A person takes steps to avoid being punished or harmed in revenge by an enemy.

J647.1.p: An old man advises a conqueror that to escape enemies' revenge he should either make peace and friendship with them or kill them all.

J647.2.p: Someone advises not to rob women when they are alone, because their husbands may return and take revenge.

J648.p: A person takes precautions to avoid being imprisoned in the future.

J648.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *61 (ET 240), 108 (ST 200); Halm Aesop No. 361.
J648.1.p: Monkeys planning to found a city give up the idea, reasoning that with walls it would be easier to catch them than before.

J651.p: A person pays no attention to danger that is near and is harmed by it.

J651.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 298), 107 (ST 195); Halm Aesop No. 194.
J651.1.p: A thrush focuses entirely on sweet fruit and so fails to notice a bird catcher, who catches it.

J651.2.p: A man, heedless of the danger of drowning, goes into the water to rescue a treasure and drowns.

J652.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; West Indies: Flowers 477.
J652.p: A person does not heed warnings given to them and suffers the consequences.

J652.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 59 (ET 203), 118 (ST 279); Halm Aesop No. 75; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 704.
J652.1.p: A frog keeps living in a puddle on the road, despite another frog's warning, and is run over.

J652.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 62 (ET 249), 118 (ST 277); Halm Aesop No. 417; Dh IV 274ff.
J652.2.p: Swallows warn other birds not to roost in a tree smeared with glue, but the birds ignore the warning and get caught.

J652.3.p: A man ignores a priest's warning that he will seduce the man's wife.

J652.4.p: Warnings given about certain peoples, who are to be avoided or feared.

J652.4.1.r: Warning disregarded. Disastrous defeat. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J652.4.1.p: Hector warns the Trojans not to attack the stronger Greeks, and they disregard him.

J652.4.2.p: A warning not to play tricks on the Gascons, who are known to be dangerous to trick.

J655.p: A person gets too close to danger or treats it too casually, and suffers for it.

J655.1.p: Birds stand around discussing a trap, and one of them gets caught in it.

J655.2.p: A fox mocks another fox for being caught in a trap, showing he is too casual about danger to be careful around it.

J656.p: A creature avoids things that are harmful by their very nature, so it does not get hurt by them.

J656.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 386), 122 (ST 310); Halm Aesop No. 32.
J656.1.p: A fox blames a thornbush for wounding him, though he should have known that thorns catch and tear whatever touches them.

J657.p: A creature takes care to choose a reliable animal or vehicle to carry it, so that it does not place itself under another's uncontrolled power.

J657.1.r: Thrown off. Wienert FFC LVI *71 (ET 358), 109 (ST 210; cf. 533); Halm Aesop No. 302.
J657.1.p: A young man trusts himself to a horse he cannot control, and so puts himself in danger.

J657.2.r: Dropped and eaten. *Wienert FFC LVI 46, 50 Nos. 51, 98; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J657.2.p: A tortoise lets an eagle carry it through the air, and the trusting ride ends badly for the tortoise.

J657.3.p: A crane offers to carry fish from one lake to another, then eats them instead.

J670.p: Defending oneself against others in advance, by planning ahead for attacks and conflicts.

J671.p: Defences that are either practical and workable or impractical and useless.

J671.1.r: *Type 110; Wienert FFC LVI 53 (ET 128), 96 (ST 97); Halm Aesop No. 15; Jacobs Aesop 216 No. 67; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 260 No. 213, *Arlotto II 226 No. 93; *Baum MLN XXXIV (1919) 462; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 634; Dh IV 145ff.; Herbert III 36ff.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; American Negro: Harris Nights 311 No. 53.
J671.1.p: Mice decide to hang a bell on the cat so they can hear her coming, but no one is willing to tie it on her.

J672.p: Defending oneself by strengthening one's own weakest points.

J672.1.r: Odysseus and the Sirens. Chauvin VII 98 No. 375 n. 4; Köhler-Bolte I 125; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 137, 263; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J672.1.p: Someone stops their ears with wax so that an enchanting song cannot lure them.

J672.2.p: Someone puts cotton in their ears so they cannot hear insults.

J673.p: Defence arranged for the moment when it will be most needed.

J673.1.p: Armor is ordered thin in front and thick in back, because the wearer would most need protection while fleeing.

J674.p: Defences that are either made in good time or made at the wrong time, out of season.

J674.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 237), 108 (ST 203); Halm Aesop No. 407.
J674.1.p: A wild boar sharpens its tusks even though no enemy is nearby, and tells a fox that there will be other things to do when an enemy comes.

J674.2.p: A man decides to make himself strong during peaceful times instead of waiting until he is attacked.

J675.p: A man kills another person so that he will not be killed himself.

J675.1.p: A son kills his father so that he will not be killed by him.

J676.p: A young fighter gives way to an angry opponent who has grabbed a pestle as a weapon, because he judges that two enemies are against him. The wise choice is to avoid a fight he cannot win.

J677.p: A king foolishly appoints a washerman as his chief minister, and the washerman makes no military preparations, so the kingdom is conquered. The point is the folly of choosing an unsuitable adviser and failing to prepare for war.

J680.p: Wise or foolish choice of allies, showing forethought in forming alliances.

J681.p: Alliances that leave both partners more open to harm than they were before.

J681.1.r: Carried off by falcon. *Chauvin II 123 No. 117; Scala Celi 73a No. 416; *Crane Vitry 135 No. 3; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 124 (cf. No. 125).
J681.1.p: A rat and a frog tie their paws together so they can cross a marsh, and the tie leaves them both in danger.

J681.1.1.p: A jackal and a leopard tie their tails together for mutual protection. Frightened, they run in different directions and injure each other.

J682.p: Choosing allies who are weak is a foolish mistake, since they cannot help when needed.

J682.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 64), 106 (ST 187); Halm Aesop No. 236.
J682.1.p: Foxes abandon their allies, the hares, when they see that the eagle will defeat them.

J683.p: Attacking those who are actually one's allies is a foolish act.

J683.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 375), 118 (ST 283); Halm Aesop No. 335.
J683.1.p: A donkey turns on his driver, who was trying to keep him from falling over a cliff.

J683.2.p: Tame doves help a trap catch wild doves, thereby aiding their common enemy.

J683.3.p: A tame fox helps dogs hunt wild foxes, and afterward the wild foxes no longer trust him.

J684.p: Choosing powerful partners as allies, and the risks or folly that can come of it.

J684.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *59 (ET 214), 92 (ST 58); Halm Aesop No. 41.
J684.1.p: A fox goes hunting alone under the protection of a lion, and is killed.

J684.2.p: A crow drives a sparrow out of its nest, showing the folly of allying with a partner too strong for you.

J684.3.p: A tortoise joins a peacock in a dance, and cannot escape when a hunter comes; the peacock flies away.

J684.4.p: A wise person who allies with the strong becomes so feared by others that they no longer dare to attack him.

J685.p: Choosing clever partners as allies, which is wise.

J685.1.p: A man, a lion and a bear are trapped in a pit. The bear advises against eating the man, since the lion would only grow hungry again, and suggests the man use his wits to get them all out.

J689.p: Miscellaneous tales and examples of forethought in alliances that do not fit the more specific headings.

J700.p: General forethought in providing for one's livelihood and needs in life, planning ahead for the future.

J701.p: General heading for acting now to secure one's future needs, such as planning ahead for later life.

J701.1.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 235 No. 516; Chauvin II 208 No. 75; Jewish: *Neuman.
J701.1.p: A man plants a tree knowing he will not live to see it mature, so he is planting for the generation that follows him.

J701.2.p: A king improves his kingdom before handing it on to his sons, even though he leaves it smaller in land but stronger and richer.

J702.p: General heading for the idea that people must work to support themselves, since living without labor is unwise.

J702.1.p: A dervish, seeing a bird feed its young, concludes that God provides for everyone so no one needs to work; he is then shown that he is mistaken.

J702.2.p: A king or queen teaches children to do all kinds of work so they will be prepared for whatever hazards life may bring.

J703.p: General heading for a person who behaves humbly or frugally now in order to secure a higher position later.

J703.1.r: Now he has them. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 500.
J703.1.p: A monk walks about with downcast eyes until he is made abbot, then lives in luxury; when asked, he explains that he had been looking for the abbey's keys.

J703.2.r: “Then I used small fish to catch big ones I have now!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J703.2.p: A bishop refuses to eat the small fish he was content with when he was an abbot, since he now expects larger ones.

J705.p: General heading for the idea that a secure livelihood should not be given up carelessly.

J705.1.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein No. 41; *Crane Vitry 234 No. 241; Herbert III 19.
J705.1.p: A priest gives up his parish and at once loses his fickle mistress, so he ends up with neither.

J706.p: General heading for the ways a person gets rich.

J706.1.r: Advice of a self-made man. Nouvelles Récréations No. 53.
J706.1.p: Advice that a person becomes wealthy by working diligently and spending little.

J707.p: A saying or teaching that money and wealth are the most important things in life.

J710.p: General heading for saving food ahead of time for future needs.

J711.p: General heading for the idea of saving during good times to prepare for hard times.

J711.1.r: *Type 249; *Chauvin III 58 No. 19; Wienert FFC LVI 55 (ET 156, 157), 126 (ST 347); Halm Aesop No. 295, 401; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 845; Jacobs Aesop 208 No. 36.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 451.
J711.1.p: A lazy insect (ant and grasshopper or cricket) is shamed by the thrift of an industrious one, and in winter it is left in distress.

J711.2.p: A careless mouse eats grain that was stored for a famine; when the loss is discovered and the grain moved, the mouse, having saved nothing, starves.

J711.3.r: *Crane Vitry 137 No. 9; Herbert III 63, 191; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 224; *Chauvin II 160 No. 49, 192 No. 9, III 101 No. 8; Scala Celi No. 134; Alphabet No. 655.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 36, 275f.
J711.3.p: A king who is to be deposed after a year secures provisions for his future by sending them to a safe place outside the kingdom.

J711.4.p: A wise man stores grain in advance against a famine he sees coming.

J711.5.p: A hardworking ant spends all its time on its harvest, drying the grain in the sun so it will keep. Stored food is brought out to dry to prevent spoilage.

J712.p: Having enough food is what really keeps a person from starving; money alone does not.

J712.1.p: A city that has plenty of money but no stored food will starve anyway.

J713.p: Crops must be planted and harvested at the right time of year, so people should act at the proper season.

J713.1.p: A lazy boy begs the God of the Seasons to hold back the plowing season so he can put off his work, but it does no good.

J715.p: Being kind is foolish when it puts your own food supply at risk.

J715.1.p: An eagle warns shepherds that a wolf is eating their sheep. A crow scolds the eagle for helping, since the sheep are the crow's own food supply.

J730.p: Planning ahead to have clothing ready for changing weather.

J731.p: Keep your warm clothes until cold weather is really over, rather than discarding them at the first warm day.

J731.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 70 (ET 348), 122 (ST 316); Halm Aesop No. 304.
J731.1.p: One swallow does not mean summer has arrived. A spendthrift young man sees a single swallow, decides summer has come, sells his clothes, and then freezes when frost returns the next day.

J740.p: Planning ahead to have adequate shelter.

J741.p: Build a shelter that will last through all the seasons of the year, not just the pleasant ones.

J741.1.p: A bear builds its house of wood, while a fox builds its house of ice. In summer the fox's house melts and fails him.

J751.p: Think carefully about the difficulties of a task before you start it.

J751.1.p: Telling the truth is better than lying. A servant about to be caught stealing rehearses a lie for his master, finds every version too transparent, and decides to tell the truth instead.

J751.1.1.p: A lady answers the queen so honestly and directly that she receives only a light punishment.

J752.p: Learn from past experience when planning what to do in the future.

J752.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 59 (ET 202), 108 (ST 201); Halm Aesop No. 74; Italian Novella: Rotunda (J742).
J752.1.p: Frogs whose spring has dried up consider jumping into a well, but decide not to because the well might dry up too.

J753.p: Clear obstacles out of your path so you do not stumble.

J753.1.p: A servant tells his master there is only one person in the public bath, but the master counts three hundred. Only one man had cleared a stone from his path and so avoided stubbing his toes; the rest had stubbed theirs, so only he deserved to be called a man.

J755.p: Every part of a plan has to be thought through in advance, because overlooking one detail can ruin the whole thing.

J755.1.p: A man is put in charge of the weather but forgets to ask the wind for help, so everything goes wrong and he has to give up control.

J756.p: Advice given after a misfortune has already happened is worthless, since it cannot undo the harm.

J756.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *84 (ET 509), 108 (ST 204); Halm Aesop No. 169.
J756.1.p: A doctor offers his advice only after the patient has died, and is mocked for having no foresight.

J758.p: Do not follow the advice of someone who stands to gain by it, since he is likely to be steering you for his own benefit.

J758.1.p: A fox that has lost its tail tries in vain to persuade other foxes to cut off theirs too, so that they will look like him.

J758.1.1.p: A man without a nose persuades foolish people to cut off their noses as well.

J758.1.2.p: A jackal that has lost its tail persuades other jackals to cut off their tails too.

J758.2.p: A crane advises a foolish man to drain his reservoir so he can harvest all the grain, but the crane is really after the fish left at the bottom and eats them.

J758.3.p: Fish turn down a fox's invitation to come live on dry land, where they would be safe from fishermen, because they see through his offer.

J761.p: A person must plan for old age in advance, because it comes whether or not they are prepared.

J761.1.p: A child finds a gray hair on his wicked father's head, a sign that the father is getting old and should change his ways.

J761.2.p: A miller has four horses to carry his grain but uses only one, so it dies early. The four horses stand for childhood, youth, manhood and old age, warning that one should not leave all the work of securing salvation to old age.

J761.3.p: An adulteress charges a pair of shoes for each man she sleeps with, and in old age she uses the shoes she has collected to pay men to sleep with her.

J762.p: Always leave yourself a way out of a difficult situation, so you are not trapped if things go wrong.

J762.1.p: A priest keeps a holy relic that cures plague when people kiss it, but he has them only kiss the container, so that if they die he cannot be blamed.

J765.p: When travelling in an unfamiliar country, mark the route you are taking so you can find your way back.

J766.p: Do not do your job so well that you make yourself unnecessary, because then you will lose your employment.

J766.1.p: A cat drives rats away but does not kill them, because if she killed them all she would have no more work.

J810.p: The wise way to deal with powerful people is to adjust your behaviour to suit them and their moods.

J811.p: Wisdom in giving way to the powerful: a clever person yields to the great rather than resisting them, because that is the safer course.

J811.1.r: Fox then divides: gives lion meat and he takes bones. *Type 51; Wienert FFC LVI 59 (ET 213), 110 (ST 220); Halm Aesop No. 260; Jacobs Aesop 200 No. 4; Herbert III *14, 39ff.; *Crane Vitry 199 No. 158.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; American Negro: Harris Nights 334 No. 58.
J811.1.p: A wicked or greedy ruler takes the whole share of spoils for himself, and the weaker partner who protested is eaten. The lion takes everything for himself, so the phrase means the biggest share taken by the strongest.

J811.1.1.r: “touch it if you dare.” Wienert FFC LVI *59 (ET 216), *148 (ST 530); Halm Aesop No 258; *K. Gorski Die Fabel vom Löwenanteil in ihrer geschichtlichen Entwicklung (Berlin, 1888).
J811.1.1.p: A lion divides the spoils and gives himself the best portion, justifying it by his rank as king of beasts, then by his strength and courage.

J811.2.r: Ass, hog, and fox as judges. Ass says she has bad odor: lioness slaps him. Hog says she has not: lion slaps him. Fox says that he has a bad cold and cannot smell. Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 29 No. 52*.
J811.2.p: A fox declines to act as go-between when a lion and his mate quarrel, and the lion decides to abandon the lioness because of her bad smell.

J811.3.p: A king gives equal honor to a poet and a critic: the poet is honored so he will praise the king, and the critic so he will not condemn him.

J811.4.p: A ruler angry at evil spoken about him is calmed by the gentle words of those who speak to him.

J811.5.p: A chief minister bribes a priest to tell the king that the ocean of milk the king wants to search for has curdled, so the quest is dropped.

J811.6.p: A fox who has three hundred fables ready to tell against a lion conveniently forgets them when he meets the lion.

J814.p: Flattering the powerful as a way of dealing with them: praising or agreeing with rulers to win their favor or stay safe.

J814.1.p: A musician is jailed because the king disliked the way he looked at him. When the king returns a year later as a conqueror, the musician says he had seen the king's victories in a vision and was blessing him, and he is honored instead.

J814.2.p: A flatterer agrees with the king even when the king holds opposite opinions, and when challenged he defends himself by saying he is the king's servant.

J814.3.p: A jackal meets a man with a musical instrument he does not recognize and greets him as Lord of Delhi. The man replies that the jackal is the Lord of the Jungle, and the jackal is flattered into agreeing.

J814.4.p: A wicked man is flattered to escape death at his hands: the approaching person sends a gift and calls himself his lord's humble servant, as Jacob did to Esau.

J814.5.p: A minister who disagrees with the king does not argue, but defers by telling him to do whatever seems good to him.

J815.p: Unpleasant truths should be kept from the powerful, since telling them can be dangerous.

J815.1.r: *Types 48*, 68**; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 381; *Gerber MLN IV (1889) 479; Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 53), 104 (ST 168); Alphabet No. 33; Scala Celi No. 36.
J815.1.p: A king of apes asks visitors what they think of his children, his courtiers. The honest visitor says they are very ugly and is punished, while the liar who praises their beauty is rewarded.

J815.2.p: Two brothers visit a land of naked people. The one who wears clothes is punished, and the one who adopts their nakedness is honored.

J815.3.p: A king with a blemish is given a muddy bath prepared for him, so that the flaw is hidden instead of pointed out.

J816.p: Tactful ways of correcting or rebuking powerful people so they will accept the criticism without anger.

J816.1.r: *Basset 1001 Contes II 452; Chauvin II 153 No. 21, *VIII 129f. No. 119; Wesselski Märchen 220 No. 34; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J816.1.p: A philosopher pretends to understand the speech of birds and reports what they say, so that the king hears his failing indirectly and is brought back to his duty.

J816.1.1.r: Asks if there is harmony among the cities and republics of Greece: philosopher tells him to ask it of his own house. Spanish: Childers.
J816.1.1.p: A king who has been living apart from his wife is reminded of his duty when a philosopher pretends to overhear birds talking about it. The wise man corrects the king indirectly rather than openly.

J816.2.p: A king mocks a poet by calling him a baker's son, and the poet answers by offering him only loaves of bread. The king recognizes the joke and rewards the poet instead of punishing him.

J816.3.p: A drunken king passes an unjust sentence, and a woman tactfully gets him to hear her case again. She asks to appear before him before he has eaten, and her case is retried once he has sobered and dined.

J816.4.p: A woman handles an amorous king with tact, turning him away from his advances without angering him.

J817.p: A gentle, respectful reply calms an angry person, so that a powerful man's anger is turned away. Used of dealing with the great and powerful.

J817.1.p: A nobleman calls a man a rogue, and the man makes a joke of the insult. The joke defuses the situation and he avoids trouble.

J817.2.r: “Don’t get angry,” he says; “rather than have you condemn me to hell, I would believe in four persons.” Wesselski Bebel I 163 No. 98.
J817.2.p: A physician who will believe in only four persons of the Trinity offends a theologian by questioning the doctrine. The physician's disputing of the doctrine angers the theologian.

J817.2.1.r: Flatterer agrees: it is the king he serves, not the wretched flowers. India: Thompson-Balys.
J817.2.1.p: A king makes an absurd statement about flowers, and the listener must respond to it with tact. The king's remark is a foolish claim meant to test or amuse.

J817.3.r: Relents when priest says, “Since there is no one here I may heed the call of Nature.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J817.3.p: A bishop angered by someone refuses to answer when addressed, and the one who speaks to him is left alone with his silence. Used as a joke on silent, angry dignitaries.

J818.p: Advice given to a king must be offered with great care, since a careless word can cost the adviser dearly.

J818.1.p: A yogi advises a king that the blood of a yogi will make the king's leaking tank hold water. The king takes the advice literally and cuts off the yogi's head.

J821.p: A person tries to stay on good terms with gods who are hostile to him, placating them with offerings and careful conduct.

J821.1.r: She will keep on good terms with me.” Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 231), 143 (ST 490); Halm Aesop No. 213.
J821.1.p: A dog asks a raven why he sacrifices to Athene, since she hates ravens for their gift of reading omens. The raven answers that the hatred is all the more reason to offer sacrifice.

J822.p: A man pretends to be a fool in order to protect himself when dealing with a king.

J822.1.p: A man pretends to be an idiot so he will not be drawn into trouble when two rival queens summon him to testify before the king. Feigning stupidity keeps him from taking either side.

J823.p: A man tells the king about an unpleasant event when the king is in a good mood, so the king laughs. The others who tell the king the same kind of story when he is in a bad mood are punished.

J829.p: Miscellaneous tales about dealing with powerful people, which do not fit the more specific categories of this section.

J829.1.p: A steward buys the king a pair of slippers, but the king thinks they cost too little and refuses them. The steward then buys an identical pair and charges a high price, and the king accepts them. The steward learns that this is how to deal with kings.

J829.2.p: A devil that is being driven out of a possessed man decides to leave of his own accord, so that the exorcists cannot claim they forced him out. He flees as the outcome becomes inevitable.

J829.3.p: A defeated ruler, disguised, gets an audience with the victor and asks what the victor would do if his enemy knelt and begged forgiveness. The victor says he would forgive, and the disguised ruler then reveals his identity and is pardoned.

J830.p: A general principle that the wise person adapts to a force too strong to resist rather than fighting it.

J831.p: A man wants a mountain or tree to come to him, and when it will not move he goes to it instead, so he adapts to the situation.

J832.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 174; Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 387), 107 (ST 190, 243); Halm Aesop No. 179; **E. Grawi Die Fabel vom Baum und dem Schilfrohr in der Weltliteratur (Rostock Diss., 1911).—India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.
J832.p: Reeds bend low in the wind or flood and survive, while a mighty oak is uprooted by it.

J833.p: A donkey is foolish to kick against the goads used to drive it, since kicking only hurts itself.

J834.p: A man who does not understand fire is burned by it, while someone who knows how to use it benefits from it.

J835.p: A clever person turns an unfavorable court decision into something flattering, interpreting the ruling as a great honor to himself.

J860.p: A general heading for comforting oneself in misfortune with some small, trivial thing.

J861.p: A person in misfortune finds comfort in food or something to eat.

J861.1.r: **Kuhn Der Mann in Brunnen (Stuttgart, 1888); *Chauvin II 85 No. 17, III 100 No. 6; Bødker Exempler 276 No. 16; Herbert Catalogue of Romances III 12; *Crane Vitry 191 No. 134; Alphabet No. 623.—Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J861.1.p: A man trapped in a pit surrounded by dangers comforts himself by tasting a drop of honey.

J861.2.p: A man on a sinking ship eats salt, so that he will feel thirsty and enjoy the large amount of water he must drink.

J861.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI *64 (ET 274), *143 (ST 495); Halm Aesop No. 292.
J861.3.p: A mouse or fly dying in a tub of meat is happy because it has eaten until satisfied.

J864.p: A person in misfortune comforts himself by imagining some impossible pleasure.

J864.1.r: When he stumbles he says, “What a fine opportunity to dance if I had time!” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 33 No. 135A, Espinosa Jr. No. 24.
J864.1.p: A fox chased from a chicken coop by dogs stumbles over a violin, and this is taken as a sign of music to comfort him.

J864.2.p: A fox about to be hanged asks to be allowed to see the geese first, comforting himself with a last pleasure he can never have.

J865.p: A person in trouble comforts himself by focusing on some good aspect of the situation.

J865.1.p: A dying toad comforts his lover, the frog, whom he is leaving neither married, widowed, nor a maiden, but pregnant, by saying it was with a fine fellow.

J866.p: A person in misfortune comforts himself by recalling happier times in the past.

J866.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 300), 133 (ST 324); Halm Aesop No. 23.
J866.1.p: Fishermen who catch nothing console themselves that their earlier high hopes make up for their disappointment.

J867.p: Two animals praise each other without deserving it: a donkey tells a camel what a beauty it is, and the camel replies with praise of the donkey's sweet voice.

J869.p: A miscellaneous category of comfort in misfortune through some small trifle that does not fit the other headings.

J869.1.p: Doves caught in a net comfort themselves, thinking the trapper's tears are pity for them. The trapper is in fact weeping for some other reason, so the doves' consolation is mistaken.

J870.p: A person consoles himself over losing or being unable to get something by pretending he never wanted it anyway.

J871.r: Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 267), 125 (ST 336); Halm Aesop No. 33; Scala Celi 52b No. 292; Jacobs Aesop 207 No. 31; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 30 No. 66a*; Jewish: Neuman.
J871.p: A fox who cannot reach grapes decides they must be sour, so he is not disappointed at missing them.

J871.1.p: A fox who asks a favor after being saved from dogs is set on by the dogs again. He is thankful merely to have escaped with his life.

J873.r: Wienert FFC LVI 62 (ET 244), 125 (ST 339); Halm Aesop No. 30; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 30 No. 66B*.
J873.p: A fox caught in a swollen river says he is only swimming to a town far off, pretending the crossing was his own plan.

J873.1.p: A jackal who cannot cross a stream says he is only looking for the shallowest part of it.

J873.2.p: A clever jackal who is clumsy at catching cows says he was running back and forth looking for the fattest calf.

J874.r: Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 322), 125 (ST 338); Halm Aesop No. 62.
J874.p: A dog thrown out of a dining room claims he was so drunk that he does not know how he got out of the house.

J875.p: A warrior who has lost his city says he never wanted to sell it for a higher price, so the loss does not bother him.

J876.p: A headless king and a tailless tiger, each afraid of the other's weakness, agree to be friends.

J877.p: A rejected suitor comforts himself by reasoning that a wife who did not love him would have been a constant source of trouble.

J880.p: A person consoles himself in misfortune by thinking of others who are worse off.

J881.p: A timid animal is comforted when he sees others that are even more timid than he is.

J881.1.r: Hares take heart when they see that frogs are more timid than they. *Type 70; *Dh IV 97ff.; Wienert FFC LVI *62 (ET 245), 116 (ST 266); Halm Aesop No. 237; Jacobs Aesop 204 No. 15.
J881.1.p: A creature is described as more timid than the hare, which was proverbially the most fearful animal.

J881.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 77 (ET 428), 116 (ST 267); Halm Aesop No. 261.
J881.2.p: A lion is comforted for his fear of the cock, because he discovers that the elephant is afraid of the gnat.

J882.p: A man whose wife is unfaithful is comforted by seeing others in the same situation.

J882.1.p: A man whose wife is unfaithful is comforted when he learns that the queen is unfaithful too.

J882.2.r: *Wesselski Märchen 185 No. 1; Köhler-Bolte II 625; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J882.2.p: A man whose wife is unfaithful is comforted when he sees a jealous husband who carefully guards his wife being cuckolded anyway.

J882.3.p: A man whose wife gives him a bath only once a week is comforted by a man whose wife does so only once a year.

J883.p: A poor man consoles himself by thinking about the misfortunes of the rich.

J883.1.r: Chauvin II 150 No. 10; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J883.1.p: A man forced to live on poor food like peas finds comfort in seeing a formerly rich man reduced to eating the husks. Seeing others worse off makes his own hardship easier to bear.

J883.2.p: A man suffering from cold comforts himself by imagining rich men suffering in hell or locked in prison.

J885.p: A lesser person is pleased when a clever person suffers a defeat. Someone else's downfall brings a petty satisfaction.

J885.1.p: A hare scolds a sparrow for letting itself be carried off by an eagle, but the hare is glad when a hawk then carries off the sparrow. Each mocks the other's misfortune.

J890.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tales in which people find consolation in their misfortunes.

J891.r: Chauvin II 150 No. 9; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J891.p: Enemy horses captured by a lion become friends with one another. Shared captivity or misfortune brings former enemies together.

J893.p: Comfort for worldly suffering comes in the form of a spiritual reward. Earthly losses are balanced by blessings of the soul.

J893.1.p: A priest comforts a blind man by pointing out that even flies have eyes, but only humans have the inner eyes of the soul. The blind man's loss of sight is made less important by this spiritual sight.

J900.p: A general heading for tales about humility, the virtue of modest, unpretentious behavior and not thinking oneself above others.

J901.p: A listing of seven figures who are said to be the daughters of Humility, representing the qualities that flow from humility.

J902.p: Angels are humble. Their humility is a characteristic of their nature.

J903.p: Humility is named as one of the qualities a prophet must have. A true prophet is expected to be modest.

J904.p: A judge ought to be humble and modest. Such qualities are expected of anyone who sits in judgment.

J905.p: The wise "Sons of the East" are humble. Their wisdom goes together with modesty.

J910.p: A general heading for tales in which great or powerful people show humility.

J911.p: A wise man admits that he does not know something. His willingness to confess ignorance shows his wisdom.

J911.1.p: A man is scolded for not knowing the answer to a question. He replies that he was chosen for his position because of what he knows, not for what he does not know, so he should not be blamed for his ignorance.

J912.p: A wise man stays humble even at death. He takes a modest view of his life and worldly status when dying.

J912.1.r: Herbert III 10; *Crane Vitry 185 No. 119; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 24; Wesselski Mönchslatein 67 No. 54; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J912.1.p: A king orders that a piece of cloth be shown after his death. It symbolizes that cloth is all he takes with him to the grave.

J912.2.p: A king refuses to have a grand tomb built for himself because he regards his time on earth as unimportant.

J912.3.p: A rich man comes to see that he cannot carry his wealth with him when he dies, and so becomes humble.

J913.p: A king has plain clay dishes set on his table among the gold ones, showing humility. He prefers the clay vessels because he once was a potter and made them himself.

J914.p: A king shows humility by mixing freely with ordinary people instead of keeping apart from them.

J914.1.p: King David dances with common young men before the Ark of the Covenant, humbling himself to please God.

J915.p: A king who comes from humble origins cannot be won over by flattery, because he knows his own lowly beginnings.

J916.p: To avoid vainglory, an abbot receives a judge while dressed in rags rather than in fine clothes.

J917.p: Two wise men who oppose each other each humble themselves, and they end up becoming friends.

J918.p: An empress sews with her own hands to show that her high rank does not make her too noble to do humble work.

J921.p: A noble holy man who is ugly embraces a man who calls him ugly, saying he loves those who see him as he truly is.

J950.p: Lowly people who pretend to be important or who presume to act above their station, and are exposed.

J951.p: A lowly creature disguises itself so that it passes as a great or noble one.

J951.1.r: **DeCock Volkssage 184ff.; Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 175, 176), *91 (ST 38), 93 (ST 69); Halm Aesop Nos. 333, 336; Jacobs Aesop 211 No. 49; *Chauvin II 224 No. 22. — Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer V 99 n. 3.
J951.1.p: An ass wearing a lion's skin is exposed as soon as he brays and raises his voice.

J951.2.r: Type 244; Wienert FFC LVI 47, 57 (ET 61, 173), *93 (ST 66, 67, 68); Halm Aesop Nos. 200, 201, 201b; Jacobs Aesop 205 No. 21; Scala Celi 80b No. 461; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J951.2.p: A jay dressed in a peacock's (or pigeon's) feathers is exposed and unmasked.

J951.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73, (ET 387), 92 (ST 42); Halm Aesop No. 212.
J951.3.p: A crow tries to prophesy like a raven, but he is found out by his voice.

J951.4.r: Detected. Wienert FFC LVI *53 (ET 133), 87 (ST 7); Halm Aesop No. 87.
J951.4.p: A weasel paints himself to look like something else in order to trick mice.

J951.4.1.p: A painted jackal is admitted neither to the peacocks nor to the jackals, so his disguise leaves him with no company at all.

J951.5.p: A king of jackals is captured because his large banner gives away his position.

J952.p: A lowly animal tries to move among its superiors and is punished or exposed for presuming to do so.

J952.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 58 (ET 188), 91 (ST 36); Halm Aesop No. 272.
J952.1.p: A wolf who presumes to mix with lions, and is called "Lion" by his companions, is only a wolf and is exposed.

J952.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 174), 92 (ST 53); Halm Aesop No. 323.
J952.2.p: An ass chases after a lion and is punished. A cock's crowing frightens the lion away, and the ass, thinking he himself scared the lion off, pursues it.

J952.3.r: Flees at lion’s roar. Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 184), 91 (ST 35); Halm Aesop No. 226.
J952.3.p: A lowly animal, a dog, tries to walk along with a lion as if it were his equal and is rebuffed or humbled for it.

J952.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 178), 91 (ST 39); Halm Aesop No. 104.
J952.4.p: A donkey that has worked alongside an ox begins to think he is the ox's equal.

J952.5.p: A frog hurls insults at a bullock, and the bullock ignores him with scorn.

J953.p: Lowly characters wrongly believe themselves to be more important, talented, or admired than they are.

J953.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 183), 91 (ST 34); Halm Aesop No. 224.
J953.1.p: A dog is proud of the clog tied around his neck, mistaking it for an ornament.

J953.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 481), 93 (ST 72); Halm Aesop No. 193.
J953.2.p: A poor singer believes he is talented and is driven out of the theatre for his bad performance.

J953.2.1.p: A bad writer praises his own work and is scolded for it.

J953.3.r: Punished for presumption. Wienert FFC LVI 81 (ET 478), 93 (ST 71).
J953.3.p: A flute-player thinks a song meant for the prince is being sung in his own honor.

J953.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 177), 94 (ST 74); Halm Aesop No. 324.
J953.4.p: A donkey carrying a divine image on his back thinks the people bowing are bowing to him.

J953.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI *55 (ET 150), 91 (ST 33); Halm Aesop No. 230.
J953.5.p: A wolf thinks he is scorning the dog, but he is actually fleeing from the dog's master, not from the dog.

J953.6.p: Gnats believe they have knocked a horse down, when the horse has only rolled over.

J953.7.p: A crow believes the harvesters are stealing his grain, when in fact the harvesters are just gathering their own crop.

J953.8.p: A vain woman in fine clothes in church thinks the congregation stands up to admire her, when they are really rising for the gospel reading.

J953.9.p: A spider believes it has stopped the wind from blowing.

J953.10.r: Wienert FFC LVI *57 (ET 186), 92 (ST 49); Halm Aesop No. 235; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 136.
J953.10.p: Gnats apologize to a bull for landing on his horn, since they did not realize they had any weight to press on him.

J953.10.1.p: A raven riding on a bull's horns believes he has brought the bull home by his own efforts.

J953.11.r: Penzer III 70 n. 1; Bloomfield Am Journ. Philol. XL 1.
J953.11.p: A crow lands on a falling tree and believes his own weight is what made it fall.

J953.12.p: A glowworm believes he shines as brightly as the stars.

J953.13.p: At sunrise a fox sees his long shadow and believes it makes him as large as an elephant.

J953.14.p: A jackal falls into a dye vat and tries to pass himself off as a peacock, but he is found out.

J953.15.p: Several animals each wrongly believe the moon shines only for their own benefit. The lowly creature's self-deception makes it foolish.

J953.16.p: An owl mistakes the echoes of its own hoots for other creatures praising it.

J953.17.p: A rat wrongly imagines that it owns a camel, though it is only tied to the camel by a string.

J953.18.p: A rag that has accidentally got into the king's wardrobe thinks it is a ribbon, believing itself to be a fine decoration.

J954.p: A lowly person foolishly boasts of having noble or famous ancestors.

J954.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 170; *Crane Vitry 147 No. 33; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 30; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J954.1.p: A mule boasts that it is descended from the king's war-horse, forgetting to mention that its mother was a donkey.

J954.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI *44 (ET 17), 100 (ST 140); Halm Aesop No. 43.
J954.2.p: A fox claims that certain statues are of his ancestors, but an ape exposes him as a liar.

J955.p: A lowly creature or person tries in vain to become greater or more important than it really is.

J955.1.r: Bursts. Jacobs Aesop 205 No. 22; Wienert FFC LVI 58 (ET 192), 93 (ST 61); Halm Aesop No. 84; *Crane Vitry 145 No. 29; India: Thompson-Balys.
J955.1.p: A frog tries in vain to swell itself up to become as big as an ox.

J955.1.1.p: A fish swells with pride until it bursts.

J955.1.2.p: A bird puffs out its feathers trying to look like a peacock.

J955.1.2.1.p: A titmouse ruffles its feathers to look as big as a bear, though its young ones know it for what it is.

J955.2.r: Master sees him and says, “Now that you are emperor remember your humble master.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J955.2.p: A servant pretends to be an emperor, playing at high rank.

J955.2.1.r: Master asks: “What would you do for me if you were king?” Answer: “Give you 100 ducats.” Master beats him for insufficient consideration. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J955.2.1.p: A page boy dreams of becoming a king.

J955.3.p: A servant asks his master for the arms of knighthood, and is given a stalk of garlic instead.

J955.3.1.p: A peasant asks to be knighted and is told he can be made rich but cannot be made noble.

J955.4.p: An old simpleton resolves to become a senator; he is tricked into believing he is wanted as an archer and is so frightened that he dies.

J956.p: An ambitious branch is chosen to be king of the trees, because the vine and the fig tree have refused the post.

J957.p: A presumptuous man standing before the works of Michelangelo declares that he too is a master.

J958.r: Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 260), 101 (ST 146); Halm Aesop No. 71.
J958.p: A mole pretends that it can see, smell, and hear, though it has fewer senses than that; its mother tells it to claim no more senses than it has.

J971.p: Flies try to drink water from an elephant's ears, and the elephant kills them. A small creature presumes too much and pays for it.

J972.r: Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 180), 92 (ST 56); Halm Aesop No. 21.
J972.p: A rooster who wins a cockfight crows over his victory and is carried off by an eagle. Another rooster, hidden until then, comes out and struts among the hens, taking the glory the first one claimed.

J973.r: (Bull in china shop.) Only breaks the pots *Wienert FFC LVI 40; Halm Aesop No. 190.
J973.p: A donkey wanders into a potter's workshop and presumes to act as an equal among the pottery, with foolish results. A lowly creature mistakenly thinks it belongs among fine craftsmanship.

J974.r: (Cf. J978.) Jacobs Aesop 204 No. 16; Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 162), 112 (ST 231); Halm Aesop No. 135.
J974.p: A young goat, perched safely on a house roof, mocks the wolf below. The taunting weak creature forgets its own vulnerability.

J975.r: Reprimanded for presumption. Wienert FFC LVI 57 (ET 181), 92 (ST 43); Halm Aesop No. 241.
J975.p: A hare insists that all animals should have equal rights, claiming the same privileges as the stronger beasts.

J976.r: Former reprimanded. Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 10), 92 (ST 52); Halm Aesop No. 133.
J976.p: The day after a feast day argues that it is as important as the feast day itself, claiming equal status to it.

J977.p: After only one day at school, children are told by their father to stop associating with uneducated people, looking down on those who have not been schooled.

J978.p: A person who boasts of defeating someone weaker is rebuked for the boast.

J981.r: Blacksmith: “You ruin my work!” Dante: “You ruin mine!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J981.p: An arrogant smith sings Dante's Divine Comedy. Dante throws his tools out into the street in response, as the smith's presumption is too much for him.

J981.1.p: Dante beats a mule driver who chants the Divine Comedy, punishing the man for presuming to recite verses he does not understand.

J982.p: Officials who presume above their station are ignored and disregarded by the council they serve.

J1010.p: Hard work and diligence are valuable and bring rewards, a general lesson about the worth of industry.

J1011.p: A lazy woman, seeing a little bird peck a hole in a stone through persistence, is inspired to return to her work.

J1020.p: People or creatures are stronger when they work together than when they act alone.

J1021.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 861; Wienert FFC LVI 83 (ET 491), 111 (ST 228); Halm Aesop No. 103; Jacobs Aesop 217 No. 72.—Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1021.p: A peasant ties twigs into a bundle that he cannot break, while single twigs snap easily. His quarreling sons learn from this that they are stronger together.

J1021.1.p: Sons who stay united make a living, while sons who separate fail to prosper.

J1021.2.r: when one is beaten the rest scatter. The enemy are like pigs—stick together in trouble. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1021.2.p: A preacher teaches the beaten Genoese the value of unity, comparing them to donkeys who are weak when divided.

J1022.r: Wienert FFC LVI *48 (ET 73), *112 (ST 229); Halm Aesop No. 394.
J1022.p: A lion can defeat bulls only when they separate from one another; while the bulls stand together, the lion cannot win.

J1023.r: Wolves are all of one kind. Wienert FFC LVI 47 (ET 57), *48 (ET 68), 112 (ST 230); Halm Aesop No. 267; BP III 545f.; Dh IV 104f., 290; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 107*.
J1023.p: A dog leader worries he will be defeated because his pack is made up of dogs of different breeds that do not work well together.

J1024.r: Cowell J[a]taka I 85 No. 33; Benfey Panchatantra II 156ff., 304f.; Bødker Exempler 290 Nos. 45—46; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1024.p: Quails caught in a net lift it together and fly off with it, escaping. They were caught only because they had quarreled.

J1024.1.p: Captured elephants escape a net by all pulling together at the same moment, so the net gives way.

J1025.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 70), 135 (ST 409); Halm Aesop No. 22.
J1025.p: Roosters that stay united beat a partridge, but they lose if they quarrel among themselves.

J1025.1.p: Cranes that fight alongside each other as allies defeat all their enemies, but if they quarrel they are doomed.

J1025.2.p: Cats join together in battle against a wolf and destroy it.

J1030.p: Relying on one's own efforts rather than depending on others for help.

J1031.r: Bolte) No. 867; Wienert FFC LVI *70 (ET 341), 126 (ST 351); Halm Aesop No. 210; Roumania: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 93*.
J1031.p: A farmer who stops waiting for neighbors and relatives and harvests his grain himself gets it cut. The larks nesting in the field, who heard him make that decision, then move their young away.

J1032.p: A stag hides in hay and escapes the servants who look for it, and is found only when the master comes to look himself.

J1033.r: Wienert FFC LVI 74 (ET 391), 145 (ST 508); Halm Aesop No. 191.
J1033.p: A gardener who plants a vegetable himself takes the best care of it.

J1034.r: Wienert FFC LVI *78 (ET 440), 138 (ST 436); Halm Aesop No. 81; Jacobs Aesop 214 No 61. Cf. also Halm Aesop No. 300.
J1034.p: Help from the gods comes only after a person makes his own effort. In the example, a driver whose ox cart is stuck must first put his own shoulder to the wheel before Hercules will help him.

J1040.p: Acting firmly and decisively without hesitating or waiting for everyone's approval.

J1041.p: It is impossible to please everyone, so one must act without waiting for everyone's approval.

J1041.1.r: Type 1830; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 218 No. 51; Wienert FFC LVI 83 (ET 495), 121 (ST 304); Halm Aesop No. 166.
J1041.1.p: People try to get the weather to suit everyone, but it fails, so weather is given without regard to what people want.

J1041.2.r: *Chauvin II 148 No 2, III 70, 145, VIII 140; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 244 No. 541; Herbert III 420; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 577; Scala Celi 135a No. 745; Alphabet No. 765.—England: Baughman; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1041.2.p: A miller and his son with a donkey are criticized whatever arrangement they choose: walking, riding, or any seating order. This shows that pleasing everyone is impossible.

J1050.p: Heeding warnings and taking them seriously.

J1051.p: Death sends three warnings to a man: loss of appetite, loss of desire for drink, and sickness. The man fails to recognize them as messages of death.

J1052.p: Cranes ignore warnings and are killed as a result.

J1053.r: Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 99), 60 (ET 219), 89 (ST 13, 281); Halm Aesop No. 346.
J1053.p: A snake ignores warnings to improve its manners and is eaten by a crab.

J1054.p: A man ignores his mother's warning and is punished for it.

J1055.p: A man ignores a priest's warning and is punished for it.

J1060.p: A collection of wise behaviors that do not fit under the other headings in this section.

J1061.p: A saying that something is worth only what it is actually used for; a possession that serves no real purpose has no real value.

J1061.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 28), 130 (ST 375); Jacobs Aesop 198 No. 1; Crane Vitry 157 No. 54; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1061.1.p: A cock scratching in a dunghill prefers one grain of corn to a peck of pearls, because the corn is useful to him. The lesson is that something's value depends on its real use.

J1061.2.p: A bald man finds a comb and realizes it is useless to him, since he has no hair to comb.

J1061.3.p: A foolish dog finds a treasure and stays with it until it dies rather than leave it, though the treasure does him no good.

J1061.4.r: Advised to imagine that his treasure is still there: he will be as well off as before. Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 503), 133 (ST 392); Halm Aesop No. 412; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 259 No. 201; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1061.4.p: A miser hoards his wealth and it is stolen, so the riches he never used are lost to him.

J1062.p: A saying that a person should first fix his own faults before trying to correct or heal others.

J1062.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 45 (ET 27), 57 (ET 179), 101 (ST 134); Halm Aesop No. 78.
J1062.1.p: A frog sets up as a beauty doctor but cannot cure his own ugliness.

J1062.2.r: Chauvin II 227 No. 8; Wienert FFC LVI 73, (ET 384), 136, 138 (ST 424, 432); Halm Aesop No. 312; Babrius No. 2.
J1062.2.p: A doctor who cannot cure himself is scorned by others.

J1062.2.1.p: A bald man tries to sell a hair restorer even though he cannot grow hair himself.

J1063.p: A saying that a person criticizes others for faults he himself has; the pot calls the kettle black.

J1063.1.r: Jacobs Aesop 211 No. 48; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1063.1.p: A mother crab scolds her children for not walking straight, though she walks sideways herself.

J1063.2.p: A drunk man mocks another man for being drunk.

J1064.p: A saying that it is pointless to try to teach someone who is foolish or stupid.

J1064.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 50 (ET 95), 118 (ST 284); Bødker Exempler 286 No. 34; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1064.1.p: A raven tries to teach apes that a shining stone is not fire, and the apes, refusing his teaching, kill him.

J1071.p: A saying that work done is lost in a moment of putting something off; delay can undo all the effort already spent.

J1071.1.p: An artist labors long to make a brazen head that can speak, but loses all his work by a moment of procrastination.

J1072.p: A tale in which a man is judged by his own qualities rather than by his clothing or appearance.

J1072.1.p: Guests strike a man who tries to stop their quarrel, not knowing he is their host in old clothes; they are humiliated but later forgiven.

J1072.2.p: A rich Brahmin dressed in poor clothing is treated as a beggar and turned away.

J1073.p: A saying that a person should never use all of his resources or abilities, but keep something in reserve.

J1073.1.p: A man never does any piece of work so well that he cannot improve it, so he never finishes anything.

J1074.p: The idea that keeping quiet can be more valuable than speaking. Wisdom often lies in saying nothing.

J1074.1.p: A clergyman, challenged to a debate or retort, declines to answer and explains that he has never regretted staying silent but has often regretted speaking.

J1074.1.1.p: A philosopher refuses to join in when others gossip, staying silent because he fears that one day he might talk too much and be unable to stop himself.

J1074.2.p: A man does not court an ugly woman, reasoning that she might say yes, so he keeps silent and never proposes.

J1075.p: The idea that over time anything, however remarkable, comes to seem ordinary and stops drawing notice.

J1075.1.p: A woman tests whether gossip will last by having a servant ride through the streets on a flayed donkey. By the third day no one pays attention, and she concludes that the same will happen with her planned marriage.

J1075.2.p: A fox is terrified the first time she sees a lion, but by the third meeting she is no longer afraid of him.

J1076.p: The idea that travelling far to get something is pointless, because the same result can be had nearby.

J1076.1.r: Told that he has now seen the world, for he will never see more than valleys, hills, fields, meadows, water, streets, cities, and villages. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 590.
J1076.1.p: A man who wants to travel is sent only six miles to deliver a letter, showing that the journey he desired was unnecessary.

J1081.p: The idea that a peaceful, untroubled night's sleep is worth more than wealth or comfort.

J1081.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 503; Herbert III 128 No. 79, 170 No. 35; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1081.1.p: A king buys a spendthrift's bed, reasoning that it must be an extraordinary bed since it let a man with so many debts sleep soundly.

J1082.p: The idea that trying to conceal an obvious deed is useless, because the evidence will reveal it anyway.

J1082.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 367), 102 (ST 154); Halm Aesop No. 17.
J1082.1.p: A goat's broken horn reveals what a herdsman did to her. When he begs her not to tell his master, she replies that the horn will tell the tale.

J1085.p: The idea that having a lot of money does not guarantee happiness.

J1085.1.r: *Type 754; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 420; *Crane Vitry 162 No. 66; Herbert III 281; Alphabet No. 276; Scala Celi 80b No. 459; Nouvelles Récréations No. 19; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 258 No. 204.
J1085.1.p: A happy friar grows unhappier as he receives more and more money. He gets rid of the money and becomes as happy as before.

J1085.2.p: A humble servant who acquires gold becomes arrogant.

J1085.3.p: A king sees a poor man who seems far happier than himself.

J1085.4.p: A poor man returns to the emperor all the gold he was given except enough for a comfortable living, because wealth would take away the happiness of his simple life.

J1086.r: “I don’t hear the unpleasant.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1086.p: A wise person refuses to react to unpleasant things, choosing to ignore them rather than be upset.

J1087.p: The idea that it is foolish to expect a stranger to care about your interests.

J1088.p: A man pleads with a thief stealing his figs, and when pleading fails he pelts the thief down from the tree with stones. The wise person switches to harsh measures when gentle ones do not work.

J1100.p: A general heading for stories of clever people and clever acts that outwit others.
