J1110.p: A general heading for stories about people who are clever and resourceful, outwitting others or solving problems through quick thinking.

J1111.r: **DeVries FFC LXXIII; *Chauvin VII 118 No. 387; Köhler-Bolte II 602 No. 1; *BP III 202; Bloomfield JAOS XXXVI 65.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
J1111.p: A general heading for stories about a clever girl who solves problems or outwits others through quick wit.

J1111.1.p: A princess who wins arguments and debates through skillful reasoning, often showing her cleverness in a contest of words.

J1111.1.1.p: A princess who is skilled at pleading a case, winning her point by clever persuasion.

J1111.2.r: Pierre Faifeu No. 43; Nouvelles de Sens No. 8.
J1111.2.p: The illegitimate daughter of a trickster inherits her father's talent for deceiving people and uses it herself.

J1111.3.p: A daughter-in-law who shows cleverness, often by solving a problem or outwitting others in her husband's family.

J1111.4.p: A clever daughter from a peasant family who solves problems or outwits others through quick thinking.

J1111.5.p: The clever daughter of a minister or high official who solves problems or outwits others through quick wit.

J1111.6.p: A clever female servant who solves problems or outwits others through quick thinking.

J1111.6.1.p: A clever slave girl who solves problems or outwits her masters through quick thinking.

J1112.p: A general heading for stories about a clever wife who solves problems or outwits others, often her husband, through wit.

J1112.1.p: A wife cures her wayward husband of his infidelity by a clever act: she gives a gift to his mistress so that the mistress can receive him properly, and the husband is shamed into mending his ways.

J1112.1.1.p: A wife disguised as a stranger has her husband dress in motley clothes when he goes to fetch a new bride; the prospective father-in-law mistakes him for a fool, and the wife then reveals herself to her husband.

J1112.2.p: A wife sends away the maid who is her husband's mistress and tells him the girl has run off. The husband understands the hint and mends his ways.

J1112.3.p: A clever wife advises her husband on how to succeed in his adventures.

J1112.4.p: Wives prevent a war by placing themselves and their children between the two armies, so that neither side wants to fight.

J1112.5.p: A clever wife gets her husband's secrets by questioning him cunningly until he tells her.

J1113.p: A general heading for stories about a clever boy who solves problems or outwits others through quick thinking.

J1114.p: A general heading for stories about a clever servant who solves problems or outwits his or her master through quick thinking.

J1114.0.1.p: A servant outwits his master through cleverness, showing a resourceful slave getting the better of those above him.

J1114.1.p: A man is tricked by the hired worker he employs, who cheats or fools him for his own gain.

J1115.p: A general heading for clever people who succeed by their wits in various trades and occupations.

J1115.1.r: Penzer IX 25 n. 1; Pierre Faifeu No. 10.
J1115.1.p: A gambler who wins or escapes losses through cunning rather than luck.

J1115.2.p: A doctor who solves a patient's problem through cleverness rather than medical skill.

J1115.2.1.p: A doctor refuses to give a purge to a man who drinks a great deal of liquid, reasoning that the drinking itself already flushes him out.

J1115.2.2.p: A doctor gets a pea out of a patient's ear by knocking the patient down so that the pea rolls out.

J1115.3.p: A barber who succeeds through cleverness in his trade.

J1115.4.p: A tailor who succeeds through cleverness in his trade.

J1115.5.p: A minstrel or entertainer who succeeds through cleverness in his trade.

J1115.5.1.p: A minstrel mends his tattered robe with scarlet cloth, and when mocked he remarks that he wishes the rest of the robe were that same material, so he is given a new robe.

J1115.6.p: A peasant who succeeds through cleverness, outwitting others by his wits.

J1115.7.p: A merchant who succeeds through cleverness in his business.

J1115.7.1.p: A merchant turns a loss to profit: monkeys steal his caps, and he catches them and sells them.

J1115.8.p: A prostitute who is clever and gives shrewd advice on many questions.

J1115.9.p: A shepherd who succeeds through cleverness in his work.

J1115.10.p: A government official who succeeds through cleverness in his office.

J1115.10.1.p: A governor who succeeds through cleverness in his office.

J1115.10.2.p: A minister who succeeds through cleverness in his office.

J1116.r: *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 184ff. nn. 18, 95, 173—176; Irish myth: *Cross.
J1116.p: A foolish person becomes clever, often through some change, gift or event that sharpens his wits.

J1116.1.p: A foolish person becomes clever by some means, and then shows his new cleverness, often as a madman who turns out to be shrewd.

J1117.p: An animal acts as a trickster, outwitting other creatures or people through cunning.

J1117.1.p: A jackal is the trickster animal who outwits others through cleverness.

J1117.2.p: A coyote is the trickster animal who outwits others through cleverness.

J1118.p: A bird shows cleverness, solving a problem or outwitting someone by its wits.

J1118.1.p: A parrot shows cleverness, such as repeating or using speech to outwit someone.

J1122.p: A younger person or generation shows more cleverness than the older ones.

J1122.1.r: Crow advises young ones to fly away if they see man stooping for a stone to throw. Young crows: “What if he already has stone in hand?” India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1122.1.p: A young crow shows alertness and sharp awareness of danger, outdoing older birds or others.

J1124.p: A court jester shows cleverness, typically through witty remarks or tricks that outwit others.

J1130.p: General cleverness shown in a law court, where someone wins a case or exposes a lie through shrewd argument.

J1131.p: General sayings or rules of thumb that are useful for winning or handling matters in a law court.

J1140.p: Cleverness in finding out the truth, such as exposing a guilty person or a false claim.

J1140.1.p: Solomon discovers the truth of a case without any witness evidence, relying on his wisdom.

J1141.p: A confession is obtained through a trick or deception rather than by direct proof.

J1141.1.p: A guilty person is tricked into making a gesture or act that reveals his guilt.

J1141.1.1.r: *Type 785; *BP II 149; *Chauvin VIII 101 No. 73; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 65 No. 9. Cf. American Negro: Harris Friends 160 No. 22.
J1141.1.1.p: A guilty man confesses his earlier crime in order to win the largest part of a prize.

J1141.1.2.p: A thief is caught when he touches his beard, which reveals the grease from the stolen fowl on it, after someone claims he has it.

J1141.1.3.r: Debtor: “That is a lie; it was only a span.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1141.1.3.p: A creditor, claiming a debt, says the destroyed bond was a cubit in size, and the trick exposes him.

J1141.1.3.1.r: Closing his bargain with the servant he had said: “May this stone be witness.” Judge orders stone brought to court. The farmer: “Oh, but the stone is too big (or very far away)”. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1549.
J1141.1.3.1.p: A stone serves as a witness, so that a farmer refuses to pay the wages due to his servant.

J1141.1.4.p: A guilty man is exposed when he is told his stick will grow during the night, and he cuts off the end of his stick to avoid being caught.

J1141.1.5.p: A guilty woman reacts to a trick by instantly touching her head, revealing she is the thief, because she thinks feathers stuck to her head give her away.

J1141.1.6.p: To tell which of two people is the master and which the servant, they are told to put their heads through a window, and the servant's head is to be cut off; the servant draws back and so reveals himself.

J1141.1.7.p: Someone must decide which of two figures is a real man and which is a demon in human shape; the decision is to go to whichever can pass through the end of a reed, and the demon is thereby revealed.

J1141.1.8.p: An accused woman is ordered to walk three times naked around a building; the guilty one begins to strip off her clothes in advance, thereby betraying herself.

J1141.1.9.p: A thief is convinced that the detective can read minds, and so he confesses.

J1141.1.10.p: A queen has suspects flogged, telling them to produce the stolen gem; the real thief, fearing more punishment, promises to produce it, thereby confessing.

J1141.1.11.p: A debt is confessed by having the defendant argue about whether a cat was present when the debt was made, thereby admitting that the debt was made.

J1141.1.12.p: B warns A not to tie his horse near B's horse; the horses fight and A's horse is killed. In court B pretends not to be able to speak, and A reveals that B could talk the day before and repeats their conversation, so the judge blames A for not heeding the advice.

J1141.2.r: Wesselski Märchen 186 No. 1; Chavannes 500 Contes I 378.
J1141.2.p: A magician is given three places at a table and is caught out; he confesses that he carries two persons inside his body.

J1141.3.p: Cheaters are questioned separately, and the first is made to repeat the paternoster; others believe he has confessed, and the truth comes out.

J1141.4.r: She does. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 723, *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 78; Köhler-Bolte I 535; *Wesselski Arlotto I 222f. No. 67; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1141.4.p: A thief is induced to confess by having an unjust lawsuit brought against him; a false message is sent to his wife to send the stolen jewel case to the judge as a bribe.

J1141.5.r: Confession follows. *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 70.
J1141.5.p: A bag of documents sealed to await the king is secretly opened, changed, and resewn by a repairer; the change is discovered and the repairer is in turn exposed when a fine carpet is repaired by him.

J1141.6.p: A man buries gold, and a thief steals it. The owner borrows scales, pretending to weigh money for burial, and the frightened thief, believing he is found out, hurries to return the stolen money.

J1141.7.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 99, 280.
J1141.7.p: A thief suspected of crawling through a hole is made to take off his clothes; he is covered in scratches, and he confesses.

J1141.8.r: Asks bystanders: “Who is right?” Silence. Newcomer states that the important man is wrong. “Had he been right the others would have said so.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1141.8.p: Silence is treated as a sign of guilt; an important man quarrels with a commoner, and the commoner's silence is taken as proof against him.

J1141.9.r: Owner greets everyone with: “I know about you!” No one pays any attention to him except the guilty one who says: “I did not do it.” Confesses. (Cf. N275.) Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1141.9.p: A person who is guilty protests innocence too strongly, which exposes him; animals are put to graze in a man's garden, and the protest reveals the culprit.

J1141.10.r: (Told that crossbow would shoot guilty person as he passed before it.) Pierre Faifeu No. 22.
J1141.10.p: A thief is made to fear for his life, and in his fear he confesses.

J1141.11.p: Husbands ask a suspected priest to talk to their wives about tithing, and the conversation gives enough evidence to convict him.

J1141.12.p: A guilty man who has been freed of a murder charge is tricked into making a false accusation, for which he is then sentenced.

J1141.13.p: A witness is always made to answer "No"; the trick works and he condemns himself.

J1141.14.p: A minister warns a congregation that a thief will be punished by God, and the thief confesses on the spot.

J1141.15.p: A thief is tricked into giving himself away while he is in church.

J1141.16.p: A thief is tricked into giving himself away during a supposed ordeal, such as a test of guilt.

J1142.p: Someone uses supposedly scientific tests, which in fact prove nothing, to find out who is guilty or who is lying.

J1142.1.r: *Chauvin VI 63 No. 231; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 155.
J1142.1.p: To decide which child belongs to which mother, a clever judge weighs each mother's milk, since the heavier milk is said to come from the mother of the boy.

J1142.2.p: A woman's secret love affair is revealed because her pulse quickens when her lover is mentioned.

J1142.2.1.p: A person's guilt is revealed because their heartbeat speeds up when the crime is mentioned.

J1142.3.p: A husband's wife is shown to have committed adultery because spit marks on the wall are too high to have been made by her husband.

J1142.4.p: A dead thief's body is carried through the street to see who weeps for him, since the weeper is presumed to be an accomplice or a relation who knows his guilt.

J1142.4.1.p: Someone arranges a reason for weeping so that the mother's tears over the thief seem natural and do not betray her as his accomplice.

J1142.4.1.1.p: A clever son falls from a tree so that his mother's tears over the carried body of his father will look natural and not reveal her guilt over the thief.

J1142.4.1.2.p: A woman breaks milk jars so that her weeping over the thief's body will look natural and not betray her.

J1143.r: *Type 950; BP III 395ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 200ff.; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1143.p: A thief is caught when a straw fire is built so that its smoke escapes through the secret hole the thief made to enter the building.

J1144.p: Those who ate stolen food are found out by clever means.

J1144.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda (J1142.4.); French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 24.
J1144.1.p: Those who ate stolen food are revealed by being given an emetic, which makes the stolen food come up.

J1144.2.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 27 n. 1.
J1144.2.p: An animal that has been stealing eggs is caught when it comes to a spring to drink, because all animals must explain why they are thirsty.

J1145.p: A criminal is found out with the help of an animal.

J1145.1.p: A murderer is revealed by the dead man's dog, which attacks the murderer whenever it can.

J1146.r: *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt I 117ff., 221ff.; *Gaster Germania XXV 290f.; Fb “mel” II 570; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 510 No. 109, 526 No. 111, 810 n. 410.
J1146.p: Ashes or sand are scattered on the floor so that an intruder, such as a lover, ghost or fairy, leaves footprints that give them away.

J1146.1.p: Pitch is spread on the floor so that the intruder's feet stick to it and leave tracks, or a shoe is left behind as a clue.

J1147.p: A wronged husband pretends to have had a dream and recounts it, so that his wife unwittingly reveals her adultery.

J1147.1.p: A husband pretends to tell a dream in which he describes his wife's adultery, and the shock of hearing it makes her die of fright.

J1149.p: A general heading for clever ways of finding out the truth or catching a guilty person that do not fit other categories.

J1149.1.p: A man feigns madness, but is exposed when someone threatens the child of the man pretending to be mad and he shows concern.

J1149.2.p: A cheat who swindled a man's wife is caught when the man arouses the cheat's curiosity by fishing in the street.

J1149.3.r: *Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7; Nouvelles de Sens No. 8; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1149.3.p: A man disguised as a maiden is exposed when a clever girl challenges him to undress during a dance.

J1149.4.p: A doctor learns from a patient's urine that the only cure for the illness is sexual intercourse.

J1149.5.p: A blind man's buried money is stolen, and he has a boy watch passersby and signal when one smiles at him, identifying the thief.

J1149.6.r: “How would you treat a woman who came into your possession?” Answer: “I would use her and then give her to the servants.” This reveals his true character. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1149.6.p: A thief is identified by the way he answers a question put to him.

J1149.7.p: A thief pretends to be a corpse, but is detected when the soles of his feet are pricked and he does not flinch.

J1149.8.p: A magistrate proves a thief's complicity by linking a cut-off hand found with the thief to his companion's severed head.

J1149.9.p: A magistrate convicts innkeepers of arson because silver buckles found in the ashes were not melted by the fire, showing the victims' goods were stolen before the blaze.

J1149.10.p: Spies listen at night to how the accused talk and react in private, and the truth is learned from what they reveal.

J1149.11.p: Accused people are each given a basin of water to wash their hands, and the guilty one wastes it uselessly, revealing guilt.

J1149.12.p: Ninety-nine wise men and one fool are ordered to pour milk into a tank all at once, and only the fool obeys, since the others see the impossibility.

J1150.p: A general heading for clever tricks connected with the giving of testimony by witnesses.

J1151.p: A witness's testimony is cleverly discredited so that no one believes it.

J1151.1.p: A witness is discredited by being tricked into talking foolishly, so that the rest of what they say is disbelieved.

J1151.1.1.p: A husband tells his talkative wife about a treasure he found, then adds impossible tales to her report, so that when she repeats everything, the whole story is disbelieved and he keeps the treasure.

J1151.1.2.r: “What fish?” — “Those I plowed up.” He is laughed to scorn. Bédier Fabliaux 196, 436; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1151.1.2.p: A wife hides fish in a furrow where her husband plows and he later finds them, so that when he asks at mealtime where the fish are, his absurd claim makes him seem untrustworthy.

J1151.1.3.r: Chauvin VI 126, VIII 35, 69; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 184, 195, 204 Nos. 347, 383, 407; *BP I 527; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No 4; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1151.1.3.p: A mother tricks her foolish son into claiming it rained sausages, so that when he testifies he killed a man on that night, his testimony is thrown out as absurd.

J1151.2.r: Trickster summoned to court on Jew’s complaint refuses to go unless he has a new coat: Jew lends him his. In court the trickster says that the Jew is a liar: “He will even claim that I am wearing his coat.” The Jew does so and no one believes him. *Type 1642; *BP I 65; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 220ff. No. 54; *Chauvin VI 126 No. 280; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1642A; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1151.2.p: A witness claims to have been wearing a borrowed coat, and the claim is shown to be false, so the testimony is discredited.

J1151.3.r: Witness agrees to the following facts in succession: that the person relating the facts may have been in anger, that he may have misunderstood, that he may not have heard it at all. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1151.3.p: A witness's testimony is discredited by gradually weakening it, step by step, until it no longer holds up.

J1151.4.p: A woman caught in adultery by a rejected suitor, who threatens to expose her, claims to her husband that the suitor has falsely accused her of sleeping with many men; when the suitor tells the husband the truth, the husband does not believe him.

J1152.r: (Cf. G1154.1.) Chauvin II 93 No. 41; Bødker Exempler 290 No. 44; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1152.p: Two parrots are taught to accuse their mistress in a dialect they cannot otherwise speak, so their testimony is discredited because they do not understand what they are saying.

J1153.p: Witnesses are questioned separately, and inconsistencies between their accounts discredit the testimony.

J1153.1.r: Witnesses discredited. **W. Baumgartner Susanna, die Geschichte einer Legende (Archiv f. Religionswiss. XXIV 259—80); *Chauvin VI 193 No. 362; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 361f., Neuman.
J1153.1.p: In the story of Susanna and the elders, the witnesses are examined separately, and their accounts of the exact circumstances of the deed do not agree, so their testimony is discredited.

J1153.2.p: A woman is claimed by two men, and the judge asks questions only the true owner could answer; only one man can answer exactly as she does, revealing who she belongs to.

J1154.p: A witness is discredited because they cannot give the details of what they claim to have seen.

J1154.1.r: (Cf. J1152.) *Chauvin VIII 35f. No. 3; Bødker Exempler 286 No. 35; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1154.1.p: A wife has her parrot describe a storm very realistically, and her husband notices that the parrot's account of the storm contradicts its tale of her infidelity, exposing the lie.

J1154.2.p: Witnesses claim to have seen a diamond, but cannot describe what it looks like well enough to be believed when asked to make a likeness of it.

J1154.3.p: False witnesses are unable to describe a stolen jewel accurately, which exposes them as liars.

J1155.r: *Type 1790; Wesselski Märchen 187 No. 2; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XV 69f.; *Hilka and Soederhjelm Neuphilologische Mitteilungen (Helsingfors, 1913) 15ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1155.p: A man who has confessed to a crime escapes blame by claiming the whole confession was only a dream, and that he woke up before it was real. The clever argument makes his evidence worthless.

J1155.1.p: A man confesses to a crime, then discredits his own confession by claiming to be a notorious liar, so the confession is not believed.

J1157.p: Bribed witnesses are thrown into confusion when the judge asks them an unexpected question, and so their false testimony falls apart.

J1158.p: A witness claims not to have seen the crime, and the claim is used to discredit or expose him.

J1158.1.p: A witness says a dust storm blew up and shut his eyes, so he did not see the crime.

J1160.p: A clever legal argument or pleading wins a case through skillful use of legal wording.

J1161.p: A pleading follows the literal wording of the law or contract, so that its letter is satisfied even though its intent is defeated.

J1161.1.r: *Type 1591; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 113; Scala Celi 7b No. 46; Alphabet No. 139; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 21 No. 77; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1161.1.p: Three joint depositors leave money that can only be withdrawn on their joint order; one steals it, and the banker, sued, agrees to return it when all three demand it, which the thief can never make happen.

J1161.2.r: *Type 890; Köhler-Bolte I 211f.; Wesselski Mönchslatein 172 No. 138; *Wesselski Märchen 252 No. 61; *Chauvin VIII 200ff. No. 245; *Taylor Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Fleischpfand”; Oesterley No. 195; Dunlop-Liebrecht 262; JEGPh. XXX (1931) 348—60; Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1161.2.p: A creditor is bound by a contract to take a pound of flesh as payment; the debtor wins by pointing out that the contract gives no right to shed blood, so the bond cannot be carried out.

J1161.3.r: *Type 1590; Herbert III 507 No. 62; *Anderson FFC XLII 362 n. 1; Fb “ed” I 234, “jord” II 45b; Künssberg Jahrbuch f. hist. Vksk. I 120f.; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn V (1897) 443ff., (1934) 324ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1161.3.p: A man accused of trespass defends himself by pointing out that he was standing on his own land, since the soil in his shoes came from there. He uses the letter of the law to escape blame.

J1161.4.r: *Köhler-Bolte I 137; *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 78; **Lewy ibid. XXXVII—XXXVIII 83; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman, *Gaster Exempla 210 No. 121a.
J1161.4.p: A cheat returns stolen money by hiding it in a hollow stick and handing that to the victim. He then swears on oath that he has repaid the debt, technically true but deceptive.

J1161.5.r: (God’s daughters). When the pope condemns him he says he will go to his brother-in-law (Christ: he has wedded God’s daughters). (Cf. J1764.5.) *Fb “nonne” II 693; Danish: Kristensen Jyske Folkeminder VII No. 36.
J1161.5.p: A clever boy is given a penance of abstaining from wine, bed, and prostitutes for three years. He follows the wording literally by sleeping on eiderdown in a convent among the nuns, outwitting the pope.

J1161.6.p: A barber is paid to change a woman's complexion and does so by burning her face with acid. He claims he has fulfilled the contract as agreed.

J1161.7.r: Smith reveals the solution on receipt of 100 crowns bearing the ruler’s likeness. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1161.7.p: A ruler forbids a blacksmith from revealing the solution to a riddle unless he has seen the ruler a hundred times. The blacksmith uses the literal wording to get around the ban.

J1161.8.p: A ruler orders a doctor to wear his hair and robe "not too long and not too short." The doctor obeys literally by having both cut half short and half long.

J1161.8.1.p: A bishop orders a priest to wear his beard and robe "not too long and not too short." The priest's literal compliance is a variant of the doctor story.

J1161.9.p: A drunk philosopher bets he can drink the ocean dry, on condition that the other man holds back the rivers flowing into it. The philosopher then wins by agreeing to drink only the ocean itself.

J1161.10.p: A master tells his servant he may have anything he can take with his teeth. The servant takes the master's cape in his teeth, following the words literally.

J1161.11.p: A thief arranges things so that the victim seems to have simply handed over the goods. The thief can then claim he only took what he was given, following the instructions literally.

J1162.p: A defendant admits the accusation but turns it around so that the accuser is embarrassed or defeated.

J1162.1.r: In court: “The child is indeed mine; give him to me.” The child belongs to a peasant. Nurse confesses and is punished. Wesselski Märchen 229 No. 40.
J1162.1.p: A nurse falsely demands payment for raising a child, claiming it is the hero's. The hero accepts her claim, and the child is then given to her as her own charge, exposing her falsehood.

J1162.2.r: In court: “The knife may indeed be theirs. I and my father were attacked yesterday by robbers. I fled. On returning I found my father killed and this knife in his body.” Robbers condemned. *Wesselski Märchen 229 No. 40. Irish myth: Cross (K448.1).
J1162.2.p: Robbers claim a man's knife as their own. The man admits this and counteraccuses them, turning their false claim against them.

J1162.3.p: A thief inscribes his own name on a stolen object so it appears to be his property. The mark is then used as proof of ownership.

J1162.4.p: A youth is brought to court for calling the king a fool. He proves his statement true by pointing out that the king let himself be tricked by an alchemist.

J1163.p: A lawyer defends an accused person by telling a parable or story whose lesson applies to the case.

J1164.p: A knight is brought before the king for fighting a blasphemer. He argues that if the king's honor is worth defending, so is the name of the King of Kings.

J1165.p: A defendant excuses a crime by arguing that the temptation to commit it was so great that it could not be resisted.

J1165.1.p: Thieves tell the judge that the walls of the houses were so weak that they could not resist the temptation to break in.

J1166.p: A defendant avoids blame by shifting responsibility for the offense onto someone else.

J1166.1.p: A barber performing an operation on a child's skin kills the child, and then blames the mother for the child's thin skin. The barber shifts the blame onto someone else to escape responsibility.

J1166.2.p: When an attacker assaults a royal mace-bearer, he throws away his mace. The attackers then accuse him of insulting the king, since the mace is the king's symbol and he has discarded it, and he uses this to shift blame.

J1169.p: A general heading for clever pleadings in court that do not fit a more specific category. Each is a trick of argument that wins a case or escapes blame.

J1169.1.r: She says that her sight is worse than ever for whereas she used to see many things in her house she now sees very little. Theft is thus revealed. Wesselski Mönchslatein 20 No. 15; Wienert FFC LVI 39; Halm Aesop No. 107.—India: Thompson-Balys.
J1169.1.p: A woman with bad eyes goes to a physician, who bandages her eyes and then steals from her house each day. When she refuses to pay his fee, he takes her to court.

J1169.2.r: Angry farmer: “Yes, behind the village he bought and paid for it” (meaning that he stole it from the pasture). Lawyer pleads successfully that it is as well to buy a horse outside as inside the village. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 838.
J1169.2.p: A lawyer unjustly claims that a stolen horse was bought and paid for, arguing for the thief in court.

J1169.3.p: A knight attacks an enemy against orders, and part of his army goes to help him and is killed. He then disclaims responsibility, saying he never asked for their aid.

J1169.4.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 507, 733; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1169.4.p: A king vows to sacrifice the first thing he meets, which turns out to be a miller driving an ass. The miller argues that the ass came before him, so the ass is beheaded instead of the miller.

J1169.5.r: Trickster: “If everyone laughs at the ass, how could the ass help laughing at her companion without a tail?” Freed. *Wesselski Gonnella 116 No. 12; U.S.: Baughman.
J1169.5.p: A king has a trickster's horse's tail cut off, and the trickster retaliates by cutting part of the upper lip off the king's ass. At the trial the animals are brought forth, and everyone laughs at the ass.

J1169.6.p: A tailor makes a coat for a Jew out of stolen goods. When accused of theft, the tailor says the Jew has the cloth, shifting the blame onto him.

J1169.7.r: Plea: he didn’t hire the ass’s shadow. *Wienert FFC LVI 37; Halm Aesop No. 339.
J1169.7.p: A man hires an ass and its driver for a trip across a plain. In the heat he sits down in the ass's shadow, and the driver pushes him away. A dispute over the ass's shadow follows.

J1169.8.p: A judge demands that a pseudo-prophet show a miracle. The pseudo-prophet offers to cut off the judge's head and bring him back to life. The judge agrees to be the prophet's first disciple instead of testing the offer.

J1169.9.p: A man is charged with three unlawful acts for killing one sheep, because two lambs were found inside it.

J1170.p: A general heading for wise or clever decisions made by judges in disputes.

J1170.1.p: A judge settles the quarrels of a village through a series of wise judgments.

J1170.2.p: Cormac mac Airt, a legendary Irish king, is famed as a wise judge and is known as the Irish Solomon for his clever decisions.

J1171.p: A judge settles a dispute by testing who truly loves the person or thing in question, revealing the rightful owner through their reaction.

J1171.1.r: *Frazer Old Testament II 570; *Goebel Jüdische Motive im Märchenhaften Erzählungsgut (Gleiwitz, 1932) 21ff.; *Gaidoz Mélusine IV 313, 337, 366, 385, 414, 446, 457; *Köhler-Bolte I 531; *Chauvin VI 63 No. 231.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “partage”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Menomini): Skinner and Satterlee PaAM XIII 397; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 348 n. 1; West Indies: Flowers 479. Cf. Cook Group: Dixon 37 (child actually cut in two to settle dispute).
J1171.1.p: Two women claim the same child. The judge offers to cut the child in two, and the real mother gives up her claim to save the child.

J1171.1.1.p: A ring is to be cut in two and divided between two quarreling persons. The real owner laments the waste of the gold, which shows that he is the true owner.

J1171.2.p: Three suitors dispute over a woman. When the judge proposes dividing her, the true lover is revealed by his response.

J1171.3.p: A woman has two husbands, and she is sentenced to be killed. One husband refuses to bury her, and so she is awarded to the other.

J1171.3.1.p: A judge rules that a man belongs to his third wife, because the first wife buried him when he died and the second did not protect him when he was alive. The judge uses this reasoning to decide who has the strongest claim on the man.

J1171.4.p: A colt is taken out in a boat to the middle of a river, and the mares are watched to see which one will swim out to it. The mare that swims to the colt is judged to be its real mother.

J1172.p: A judge punishes an unjust plaintiff with a clever ruling that teaches him a lesson for bringing a false or greedy claim.

J1172.1.r: Finder of a purse containing 800 gulden returns it to owner for reward. Latter says that purse had 900 gulden in it. In court. Decision: The rich man speaks truth. The purse found is not the one he lost. The finder may keep it. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 115; Chauvin IX 26 No. 15; Scala Celi 21b No. 135; Alphabet No. 650; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 44; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1172.1.p: A plaintiff claims a purse that was lost, but the judge shows that the purse produced is not the one that was lost, so the claim fails.

J1172.2.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No 48; Nouvelles de Sens No. 9; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 297.
J1172.2.p: A man is sued for payment because he enjoyed the smell of meat while roasting it. The judge makes him pay by letting the sound of coins clink in the plaintiff's hearing.

J1172.3.r: *Type 155; **Krohn Mann und Fuchs 38; **McKenzie MPh I 497ff.; Herbert III 14, 37, 54; *Köhler-Bolte I 50; *Chauvin II 121 No. 109; IX 18 No. 4; *Gaster Exempla 268 No. 441; *Crane Vitry 201 No. 160; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 745; Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 293), 147 (ST 515); Halm Aesop No. 97; *Fb “utak”; Scala Celi 86b No. 502; Alphabet No. 706; Oesterley No 174; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 39. -Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 27 No. 15; Indonesia: Dixon 197 n. 36; American Negro: Harris Nights 274 No. 46; Africa: Milligan Jungle 98f., (Cameroon): Lederbogen 63.
J1172.3.p: A man rescues an animal, often a snake or bear, which then tries to kill him in return. A judge, often a fox, advises the man to put the ungrateful animal back into captivity.

J1172.3.1.p: A man falsely claims a woman as his wife. The jackal judge tricks him by declaring that the real husband must enter the jar the woman carries on her head, so the impostor is shown to be a liar.

J1172.3.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Bushman): Honey South African Folk Tales (New York, 1910) 101f., (Tumbuka-Kamanga): Young Customs and Folklore of the Tumbuka Kamanga (Livingstonia, 1931) 233ff., (Shilluk): Oyler Sudan Notes and Records II 221f., (Tschi): Bellon Mitt. d. Sem. f. Orient. Spr. XVII (3) 20ff. No. 4, (Saho): Reinisch Die Saho-Sprache (Wien, 1889) I (5) 205ff. No. 17, (Senegal): Colin RTP I 140f., Zeltner Contes du Senegal et du Niger (Paris, 1913) 81ff.
J1172.3.2.p: Animals give a ruling against a man in a dispute because he has always treated animals unjustly, so the judgment goes against him.

J1172.4.r: Threatens him midway. Fox to be judge. Feigns deafness and makes turtle come so near shore man jumps and saves self. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1172.4.p: A man frees a turtle, and in return the turtle offers to carry him across a stream on its back.

J1173.r: (1) Man pulls off borrowed horse’s tail: he shall keep horse till tail grows on. (2) Man falls out of bed and kills a baby (or causes a miscarriage): he shall beget a new baby for the mother. (3) Man falls from a bridge and kills boatsman’s son: shall allow boatsman to fall from bridge and kill him *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 234 No. 515; *Köhler-Bolte II 578; Penzer VI 83f.; *Feilberg Danske Studier (1920) 2ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 131 No. 1535A*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1173.p: A series of clever but unjust judgments makes the plaintiff give up his case and withdraw it voluntarily.

J1173.1.p: A judge settles a dispute over a woman with an unusual ruling: her second husband must return her to her first husband in the same condition in which he received her, meaning pregnant.

J1173.1.1.p: A novel settlement decides that a snake's wife must wait to kill the prince until the princess has borne as many sons as the snake has sons.

J1174.p: Clever court decisions concern cases of kissing and rape, where the judge resolves the matter in an unexpected way.

J1174.1.r: Prince allows plea: “If we kill those who love us, what shall we do to those who hate us?” Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 120, 733; Alphabet No. 60; Mensa Philosophica No. 16; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 20; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1174.1.p: A young man is brought to court for kissing the prince's daughter, and he defends himself by saying he loves her.

J1174.2.p: A man steals a kiss from a woman and is complained against. The judge allows her to take one kiss in return.

J1174.2.1.r: Decision: deceived fiance is to sleep with seducer’s wife, if he ever marries. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1174.2.1.p: A man breaks his promise to sleep chastely with a woman, and the complaint is about that broken promise.

J1174.3.r: Decision: if she had shouted as loud before, the man could not have raped her. Youth acquitted. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 15; Herbert III 21; *Crane Vitry 242 No. 255.
J1174.3.p: A girl accuses a young man of raping her, but when he tries to rob her of money she screams for help, showing her accusation is a trap.

J1174.4.p: Girls who were rejected by a young man climb into his window at night, become pregnant, and demand marriage. They are branded as prostitutes and must pay him instead.

J1174.5.p: A man's torn garment is accepted as proof that he is innocent of rape, since if he had been the attacker the torn garment would have belonged to the woman.

J1175.p: Clever court judgments in cases of arson, where someone is accused of setting a fire and the judge decides the matter cleverly.

J1175.1.p: A cat with a broken leg is left in a warehouse under one companion's care; the cat scratches itself near a flame and starts a fire. Since the cat could not walk, the three traders' legs are blamed, so the three must pay the one who was left behind.

J1175.2.p: A rich man deliberately sets fire to his neighbor's tree to get rid of it, and the fire spreads to the neighbor's house. The judge orders him to pay four times the tree's value for the deliberate fire, but only the actual value of the house for the accidental spread.

J1176.p: A legal decision reached by carrying out a practical test or experiment to find the truth of a disputed matter.

J1176.1.p: A slave girl accused of being stolen is ordered to pour water into an inkwell, and she does it so skillfully that it is judged she must have learned the skill from the man who claims her.

J1176.2.r: Oesterley No. 246; Herbert III 237; Ward ibid. II 239; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 45; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1176.2.p: A man is accused of stealing wine after a neighbor left casks with him, some full and some half-full. The false accusation is exposed by measuring the leftover dregs in the casks.

J1176.3.r: (Cf. J1192.2.) Alphabet No. 261; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 58ff., 300f., *Neuman.
J1176.3.p: A woman leaves a honey-pot with gold hidden beneath the honey in the care of a neighbor. The neighbor steals the gold and replaces it with honey, but the thief is caught because gold pieces stick to the sides of the pot.

J1176.4.r: Jewish: Gaster Exempla 206 No. 113, bin Gorion Born Judas III 73, 302, *Neuman.
J1176.4.p: A two-headed man claims a double inheritance. Hot water is poured over one of his heads, the other head cries out in pain, and he is declared to be one man entitled to only one share.

J1176.5.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 247b; Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XVI 139.
J1176.5.p: To decide who a woman's true husband is, a man is given a task that only a superhuman could perform, and the impostor who manages it is revealed to be a god in disguise.

J1177.r: Judge tells story of the lady, her husband, her lover, and the robbers (H1552.1). Which was the most generous? Witness says that robber was. This shows that he has robber’s point of view. *Type 976; Jewish: Gaster Exempla 206 No. 111, bin Gorion Born Judas III 97, 303; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1177.p: A thief is found by telling a story to a group of suspects and watching how they react to it.

J1177.0.1.p: A story is told to the group on the condition that no one may interrupt or leave the room; the one who does so is revealed as the traitor or thief.

J1177.1.p: A miscellaneous group of different tales in which a story is told in order to discover the thief.

J1179.p: A miscellaneous group of clever court decisions that do not fit the other categories of judgments.

J1179.1.p: A flock of sheep ruins a field, and instead of paying money damages the owner is told to let the field's workers keep the flock until its milk and wool have covered the loss.

J1179.2.p: A hog belongs to whichever owner's place it walks to of its own accord.

J1179.3.p: A weaver makes a blanket shorter than ordered, and the judge orders him to add a piece to the blanket before he may receive full payment.

J1179.4.p: A robber is judged innocent because he is merely following the customs of his ancestors.

J1179.5.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 490; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1179.5.p: Merchants say a nobleman's servants robbed them, but the nobleman points out that the merchants were still wearing their good coats during the robbery, and he concludes his servants could not have been the robbers because they would never have left good coats behind.

J1179.6.p: Two people dispute ownership of a thread, and the thread is awarded to the one who can say what it was wound on.

J1179.7.p: A necklace is stolen, but the scent of the accused person does not match the scent that was found on the stolen necklace, so the accused is cleared.

J1179.8.p: A tenant who was advised by his landlord to steal in order to pay his taxes is acquitted of the theft.

J1179.9.p: A judge, tired of two men quarrelling over a tiny sum, settles the matter by paying the fine himself.

J1179.10.r: Pope’s decision: he may remain both a priest and husband but must not consort with any other woman. Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 42; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1179.10.p: A man who believes his wife is dead becomes a priest, and later finds she is alive, and the judgment on his situation is clever.

J1179.11.p: A judge rules that people who supply the same number of animals to pull a plow share the crop equally, regardless of how much work each one did.

J1179.12.p: A woman is awarded to the man who actually rescued her, since those who only watched could never have got her by merely watching.

J1179.13.p: A cardinal settles a long dispute by ruling that the monks who rise earliest may sound the matins bell, a privilege that had caused great argument.

J1179.14.p: A king's foster-son has his eye damaged by a bee's sting, and instead of the boy's friends getting the king's son's eye as payment, the king orders a swarm of bees destroyed so the guilty party perishes.

J1180.p: Cunning ways a person uses to avoid being punished by the law.

J1181.p: A condemned person escapes execution by using special privileges the law allows people in that position.

J1181.0.1.p: A king cannot execute a Brahmin, so he gets him drunk and so brings about his death indirectly, making the Brahmin kill himself.

J1181.1.r: One of the wishes: to have all blinded who saw him turn the plate. He is freed. *Wesselski Märchen des Mittelalters 230 No. 40; Herbert III 197; Oesterley No. 194.
J1181.1.p: A king decrees that a guest who turns his plate will be executed, but grants anyone condemned three wishes, and so the condemned escapes by using them.

J1181.2.r: Köhler-Bolte II 651—57; Zs. f. Vksk. XV 222; Icelandic: Boberg.
J1181.2.p: A condemned man uses his three wishes to become emperor, then judge, then the emperor's son-in-law for the last week of his life, and as judge he frees himself, so he is in effect set free.

J1181.3.p: A jester sentenced to leap from a height gets out of it through a clever remark: he asks for four more attempts, and the amused prince pardons him.

J1182.p: A person sentenced to punishment escapes it by outwitting the one who sentences them.

J1182.1.p: A trickster who has deceived a husband is to be beaten by the lady's women, but he is allowed one request, and he asks that whoever has most often deceived her husband strike first, so the beating never happens.

J1183.p: A condemned person escapes execution by appealing to the sacred rule that a host must protect a guest.

J1183.1.p: A prisoner who has drunk water provided by the king becomes the king's guest and so cannot be executed.

J1184.p: A person cannot be punished twice for the same offense, and this rule is used to escape a second punishment.

J1184.1.r: Herbert III 211; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 3.
J1184.1.p: An adulteress hurled from a high rock survives unhurt, and so she may not be punished again.

J1184.2.p: A prisoner condemned to have his ears cut off escapes a second mutilation because the executioner finds his ears are made of stucco, clipped for an earlier offense.

J1185.p: A condemned person escapes execution by telling stories that delay or charm the authorities.

J1185.1.p: A storyteller keeps telling a tale that never finishes, postponing execution night after night. The listener spares the teller so the story can continue.

J1189.p: Miscellaneous clever tricks by which a person escapes legal punishment.

J1189.1.p: A youth refuses to answer a king's question until he is seated on the throne. Once he is enthroned, he orders the executioners to punish the cruel king.

J1189.2.p: A condemned man escapes execution by threatening his executioners or judges with a curse.

J1189.3.p: A king takes the place of a condemned man after being told that whoever is executed that day will be reborn as king in his next life.

J1190.p: Miscellaneous clever acts and sayings in the courtroom that outwit judges, accusers or litigants.

J1191.r: *Chauvin VI 63, 231; *Zachariae Zs f. Vksk. XXX—XXXII 50 n. 2; *Wesselski Arlotto II 215 No. 73; India: Thompson-Balys; Oceanic: *Dixon 199 n. 37; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 197 No. 26.
J1191.p: A judge's ruling is shown to be absurd by carrying its logic to an even more ridiculous conclusion.

J1191.1.r: Real owner of the colt shows the absurdity (1) by fishing in the street or (2) by telling that his wife is shooting fish in the garden. Neither of these things are so absurd as the decision. *Type 875; **DeVries FFC LXXIII; India: *Thompson-Balys; Köhler-Bolte I 460; *BP II 349ff., 371; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 212 No. 434; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1191.1.p: A man ties his mare to another man's wagon, and the mare gives birth to a colt. The wagon's owner claims the colt, arguing that since the wagon carried the mare, the wagon bore the colt.

J1191.1.1.p: Someone answers an absurd court ruling about the colt by claiming that the sea is on fire, which is no more absurd than the judgment.

J1191.2.r: Countertask: harvesting crop produced from cooked seeds. *DeVries FFC LXXIII 244; Jewish: *Neuman.
J1191.2.p: A plaintiff sues for chickens that were supposedly hatched from boiled eggs, mocking an absurd legal claim.

J1191.3.p: A king gives a young woman to a gardener who already has a wife. She holds a funeral for the gardener's existing wife, and the king, amused by the joke, takes her into his harem.

J1191.4.p: A hired elephant dies, and its owner demands a live elephant in return. A god makes the owner break pots belonging to the other party, so that restitution cannot be made exactly.

J1191.5.r: No harder than for woman to bear objects.) India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1191.5.p: A slanderous accusation of giving birth to objects is refuted by showing it is as absurd as the claim itself. Later children tell toy animals to drink.

J1191.5.1.p: A rebuttal of an absurd accusation: it is as impossible for a woman to bear animals or objects as it is for someone to eat pearls.

J1191.6.p: A plaintiff beats a thief in court because the thief did not warn him in advance to bring witnesses to the robbery. The judge had refused to investigate for lack of witnesses.

J1191.7.p: A rice pot is hung on a pole while the fire is far away. The point is that cooking rice this way is as easy as warming a man from a distant lamp on a balcony.

J1192.r: *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 38; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1192.p: A judge whose decisions can be bought by bribes is shown to be corrupt.

J1192.1.r: *DeVries FFC LXXIII 263; Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 125, 128, 852, 853; Scala Celi 20a No. 122; England: Baughman; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1192.1.p: A judge gives his verdict to whichever side offers the larger bribe.

J1192.1.1.p: A judge who favors the bigger bribe is mocked with the absurd claim that a buffalo has eaten a turban.

J1192.1.2.p: A judge favors a poor defendant so that he can get money from the rich man without having to beg.

J1192.2.r: Reply: the decision was right; the error is in the honey. (Cf. J1176.3.) *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 252 No. 170.
J1192.2.p: A trickster bribes a judge with a jar that has honey on top of earth, and the judge issues a written ruling. When the cheat is discovered, the judge claims the ruling was a mistake.

J1192.3.p: A clever animal tells the court that she will drop dung on the ancestors of any judge who takes bribes, unless the judge confesses.

J1193.p: A person cleverly twists the meaning of a judge's words to get an advantage in court.

J1193.1.r: Type 1586; *BP I 519; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 271 No. 280; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 673; Fansler MAFLS XII 390, 435; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII 69 No. 4.
J1193.1.p: A boy takes the judge literally and kills a fly on the judge's nose, because the judge had said to kill a fly wherever he saw one.

J1193.2.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 254 No. 172; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 718; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1193.2.p: A judge awards a penny in damages for a blow. While the defendant goes to fetch the money, the plaintiff gives the judge a blow and says to use the penny as payment.

J1193.2.1.r: Judge has no change. Defendant strikes judge for the change. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1193.2.1.p: The court keeps the difference: a man is fined half a ducat in the tale.

J1195.p: A judge is frightened into giving a decision in favor of the clever party.

J1197.p: A judge decides that an offense is not so serious when his own son is the one who committed it.

J1198.p: Thieves or criminals are promised pardon if they confess, and they then confess.

J1198.1.p: A king promises thieves a pardon if they confess, and when they do he is pleased by their cleverness.

J1210.p: A clever person embarrasses another person and makes them lose their composure.

J1211.p: A person embarrasses another by telling scandalous or shameful stories about them.

J1211.1.p: A peasant, told by his bishop to speak the truth and spare no one, preaches about the bishop's love affair.

J1211.1.1.p: A bishop fines a priest for sexual misconduct. The priest hides and overhears the bishop's affair with an abbess, then works the overheard remarks into his Mass introduction. Asked to explain, he exposes the bishop, who returns the fine.

J1211.2.r: *Köhler-Bolte II 594; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 263 No. 236; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1211.2.p: A thief who has seen his victim in a shameful situation is allowed to keep the stolen goods as the price of his silence.

J1211.2.1.p: A thief caught by a drunken officer describes the officer's drunkenness in full, adding many shameful details. The officer denies that the mantle is his.

J1211.3.p: A courtier who has seen the king's love affair shields the king when asked what he saw, answering in clever proverbs, and wins a pardon.

J1212.p: A judge is made to lose his composure and is embarrassed by a clever party.

J1212.1.p: One litigant keeps the hens he was to give the judge hidden in his hand, and when the decision turns against him he makes the hens cry out, exposing the bribe.

J1213.p: A thief exposes the owner's unjust claim, embarrassing the owner.

J1213.1.r: The thief produces the calfhide: “You thief, to demand an ox for a calf!” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 209 No. 16, cf. 254 No. 177.
J1213.1.p: A thief steals a calf and keeps its hide, then the owner loudly complains about a stolen ox, and the thief uses this to show the owner's claim is unjust.

J1214.p: When an absurd claim is accepted without challenge, the person who made it ends up embarrassed and humiliated.

J1214.1.p: Two hunters dispute over game; one has a dog and the other only a dog's head, and the dog-head hunter claims it caught the game. When that claim is accepted, the other hunter raises a false alarm that the game's owner is coming to punish the theft.

J1216.p: A wine seller carries water into his cellar, and a man raises a false alarm that the house is on fire, pretending he thought so, which embarrasses the cheat.

J1217.p: A worldly man embarrasses a religious man by outdoing him in a clever way, leaving the religious man put out of countenance.

J1217.1.p: Two men agree to duel. The first says the odds are unfair because God helps his opponent, so the second agrees to fight without his brother's help if the first fights without God's help.

J1217.2.p: A simple holy man embarrasses a philosopher by telling him that wisdom came before learning, leaving the philosopher with no answer.

J1218.p: A man claims to be thirty years old, but he has been making that claim for the last twelve years, so his age is shown to be a lie.

J1221.p: An old man in love with a young woman silences his critics with a clever reply that leaves them embarrassed.

J1223.p: Someone is rebuked for telling a story that is both dull and long-winded.

J1224.p: A poet embarrasses others with a clever retort or performance, leaving them put out of countenance.

J1224.1.r: Vaults away from them saying: “You may tell me anything you wish—in your own homes! Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1224.1.p: A poet is pestered by admirers who keep asking him for things or favors.

J1224.2.p: A ruler tells his jesters to tease a poet, but the poet, Dante, answers their questions as if they were addressed to the ruler, putting him to shame.

J1241.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; West Indies: Flowers 481.
J1241.p: A clever dividing of goods or shares in which the person doing the dividing ends up with the best share.

J1241.1.p: A trickster is asked to divide two sheep and a ram among three friends, and he gives one sheep to two of them and keeps the ram and the other sheep for himself.

J1241.2.p: Four coins are divided among three persons: two are given to two persons, and the third person must wait until two more coins are found.

J1241.3.p: Two men who cannot divide three fish ask a trickster, who solves the problem by taking the third fish himself.

J1241.4.r: He is to divide. One lean fowl for the two fat people; two fat fowls for the one lean man. *Wesselski Märchen 229 No. 40.
J1241.4.p: At a meal with two fat fowls and one lean one, the hero takes the lean fowl while his two hosts share the fat ones.

J1241.5.p: Two men share a pot of eggs by taking turns putting a hand in; the trickster alternates so quickly that the other never gets a turn, until he finally puts his foot in the pan.

J1242.p: A dispute is settled by quoting scripture in a way that favors the one doing the dividing.

J1242.1.r: First: “And they cut one ear off” (takes ear). Second: “And they gave him a box on the ear” (takes other ear). Third: “And they took him away secretly” (takes whole hog away). BP II 361.
J1242.1.p: A pig's head is to be shared among three students, and the one who quotes the most scripture gets the largest portion. The division is decided by who can cite the Bible best.

J1242.2.p: Three men split a large fish by taking turns quoting scripture to decide each share. The trick is that the division is made by Bible verses rather than by fair measurement.

J1243.p: Three people share an inherited gold ring by selling it and splitting the money among them. A simple, practical solution to an unshareable object.

J1249.p: A general heading for clever tricks of dividing things fairly or cleverly among people, which do not fit a more specific category.

J1249.1.p: Five eggs are to be divided between two men and one woman. The woman gets three and each man gets one, with the joke that the men already have two of their own, meaning testicles.

J1250.r: Boccaccio Decameron Day 6 (Lee 176ff.); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1250.p: A general heading for quick, witty replies that outwit or silence a speaker.

J1251.p: A person who meets spite or ill will with ready, witty answers that leave the malicious speaker baffled.

J1251.1.p: A lover who is scorned by a disdainful mistress is humiliated when she answers him in a witty exchange of retorts.

J1252.r: E.g., Where are you going?—Forward. Where are you going to cut the tree?—At the foot. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1252.p: Answers that are technically true or deliberately twisted, so as to avoid giving the expected reply or to turn a question around.

J1254.p: A person avoids giving a straight answer to a question that is meant to trap them, so the questioner cannot catch them out.

J1255.p: A person refuses to say anything except "yes" or "no", which frustrates or outwits someone trying to make them talk.

J1260.p: A general heading for witty retorts that turn on the church or the clergy.

J1261.p: Witty replies that mock or treat sacred persons and things lightly, such as God, the sacraments or the clergy.

J1261.1.p: Jokes that treat the name of God lightly, often through irreverent or careless remarks about him.

J1261.1.1.r: Nuns tell a man that they are daughters of God. “Come and marry me; I should like such a rich father-in-law.” Wesselski Bebel II 120 No. 60.
J1261.1.1.p: A joke in which God is cast as a father-in-law, making a familiar family relationship out of a sacred figure.

J1261.1.2.p: A priest comforts a sick man by saying God chastens those he loves, and the man replies with a joke about why God has so few friends.

J1261.1.3.r: If I was the Almighty and had a moon, I’d hang it out on a night like this.” U.S.: Baughman.
J1261.1.3.p: A man stumbles in the dark and barks his shins, and he cries out an oath that mocks a sacred figure, using a joking substitute for God's name.

J1261.1.4.p: A farmer looks at his hay spoiled on the ground after rain and wishes he were God, saying he would then act more wisely than a fool.

J1261.1.5.r: He had but one ass to ride, while I have two.” U.S.: *Baughman.
J1261.1.5.p: A woman makes a disturbance in church and is carried out by force, and she excuses herself with a joke that she is more fortunate than her Lord.

J1261.2.p: A witty retort that mocks the sacrament or treats sacred persons and things with levity, showing disrespect for the church.

J1261.2.1.r: Sick woman calls the parson but recovers meanwhile He insists on her taking the sacrament and charges for it. “Set it here on the table; perhaps I can sell it again.” *Wesselski Bebel II 110 No. 36.
J1261.2.1.p: A joke about the sacrament being put up for sale, mocking religious rites by treating them as a commodity.

J1261.2.2.r: “If God can be brought by a man, he is too weak to help me.” Frey (ed. Bolte) *219 No. 10.
J1261.2.2.p: A priest offers to help a peasant carry the consecrated bread of the Lord, and the peasant answers that he does not trust God when God can be brought by a man. The joke mocks sacred things treated lightly.

J1261.2.3.r: Thief about to be hanged is told that if he truly repents he will eat Lord’s Supper in heaven. “If that is true, won’t you eat the supper for me; I’ll reward you well.” *Wesselski Bebel I 186 No. 42.
J1261.2.3.p: A clever retort in which a priest is said to be allowed to eat the communion supper himself. It is a joke that treats the sacrament with irreverence.

J1261.2.4.p: A witty answer that the sacrament is too precious to be bought, since if that were true no one would have given it freely to the speaker or the listener.

J1261.2.5.p: Dante is accused of failing to kneel before the sacrament, and he replies that his mind was on God and he did not notice what his body was doing, adding that his critics would not have noticed either if their minds had been on God.

J1261.2.6.p: A priest carrying the Host to a dying man sees a thief stealing figs from a fig tree and shouts insults at him, which is a joke about a holy man's irreverent outburst.

J1261.2.7.p: A priest throws the chalice at an owl, explaining that he thought the owl had stolen the Host. The joke mocks a clergyman's absurd and irreverent behavior.

J1261.2.8.r: Spectators tell him to thank God for not drowning. “I helped Him across!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1261.2.8.p: A priest carries the consecrated Host across a dangerous stream, a joke that treats the sacred object with levity.

J1261.3.r: Mule that carries him to scaffold goes very fast and criminal says, “At this rate I shall lunch with Christ.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 150 No. 1855*.
J1261.3.p: After confessing, a condemned man is told by the priest that he will dine with Christ that same evening. The joke treats the prospect of execution and heaven with flippant familiarity.

J1261.4.r: Old woman: “If your blessing had been worth a penny, you wouldn’t have given me that.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 344.
J1261.4.p: A beggar woman asks the pope for a shilling, then for a penny, and finally for his blessing, which he gives. She says the blessing is not worth a penny, mocking the pope's gift as worthless.

J1261.5.r: King asks how much his funeral will cost. “Give me the three hundred ducats now and when I am dead throw me into the Tiber.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 187.
J1261.5.p: A clergyman or heir jokes that he will spend the money meant for the funeral right away. It is a irreverent quip about the funeral fund.

J1261.6.p: At his mother's funeral a boy takes the money laid on the altar for masses. When the priest objects, the boy replies that the priest may take the money too when his own mother dies.

J1261.7.r: Bolte) No. 783; Irish: Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 76; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1261.7.p: A monk tells a thief he must return the stolen cloth on Judgment Day, and the thief replies that if he has so long a grace period he would like to take the whole monastery. The joke turns the threat of judgment into a boast.

J1261.8.p: A Franciscan claims his cord will save him from Hell, and a Benedictine answers with a dream in which St. Francis threw his cord to rescue members of his order from Purgatory, but so many clung to it that it snapped. The joke mocks the monk's cord as a weak guarantee.

J1261.9.p: Asked whether he would rather stay home to confess his flock or go to war against the infidels, a preacher answers that a living confessor is better than a dead martyr.

J1261.10.p: A joke asking how a goddess with a thousand faces blows her nose, which mocks the image of a many-faced deity with a silly question.

J1262.p: A category of witty exchanges in which clever retorts turn on points of church doctrine and theological debate.

J1262.1.r: Emperor: “God is a thief; he threw Adam into a sleep and then stole a rib from him.” Emperor’s daughter: “Would you call a man a thief who stole two earthen cups from you and replaced them by golden ones?” Jewish: Gaster Exempla 196 No. 55, *Neuman.
J1262.1.p: Earthen cups are replaced by golden ones, a witty doctrinal exchange in which a clever answer turns on the value or nature of the vessels used in religious practice.

J1262.2.r: The Jew agrees. The disputant condemns the Jew for believing that God could exist in a puddle and not in a pure virgin. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 154.
J1262.2.p: A Jew objects to the doctrine that God could dwell in the Virgin Mary, and a disputant asks whether he believes God is everywhere, then whether God is in a mud puddle. The joke traps the objector with his own logic.

J1262.3.r: “I am acting in accordance with the note.”—“The note is worse than the text.” *Wesselski Bebel II 118 No. 56.
J1262.3.p: A Jew slaps a Christian and tells him to turn the other cheek. The Christian beats the Jew, who replies that the Christian does not act according to his own Gospel.

J1262.4.p: A joke that treats passages of the Bible lightly, mocking or playing with scripture in a flippant way.

J1262.4.1.p: A joking reply that makes light of the Lord's Prayer (the paternoster) or a similar biblical passage, showing irreverent wit in a religious setting.

J1262.5.r: Is told that such return would take place in other world. “I won’t need money then, but I can use it now.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1262.5.p: A churchgoer hears the preacher promise that alms (charity) will be repaid a hundredfold and takes the words literally, acting on them in a way that surprises or embarrasses the preacher.

J1262.5.1.p: Someone who gives alms in God's name is promised tenfold return, and the preacher's wife gives sweets away to the poor, testing that promise in a joking way.

J1262.6.p: A witty defense of God against blame for evil creatures: just as a toolmaker is not blamed for tools that can be used for harm, God should not be blamed for making harmful beasts as well as good ones.

J1262.7.p: A wise man answers an atheist: if you cannot see the soul in a living person, you cannot expect to see it in a dead one, so the atheist's demand for visible proof fails.

J1262.8.p: A man examining a skeleton in a museum finds that no rib is missing, as the Adam story claims, and concludes that the ministers who told him the story were lying.

J1262.9.p: A ruler trying to seize a Jew's money asks him which religion is true, and the Jew answers that there are three: the one the Lord knows is right and two that his children believe are right.

J1263.p: Witty replies that mock abuses by churchmen, such as ignorance, greed, or luxurious living among clergy.

J1263.1.p: Witty replies that mock priests or clergy for being ignorant of their religious duties.

J1263.1.1.p: Explains why ignorant priests are favored: they can always find patrons who are as ignorant as they are.

J1263.1.2.r: “You did, the time I gave you ten florins.” Wesselski Bebel I 221 No 114.
J1263.1.2.p: A bishop, disgusted with a priest's ignorance, asks him who ever ordained him as a priest.

J1263.1.3.p: A priest who never reads the mass explains that his parishioners stand so close that they might memorize the words, so he does not read them aloud.

J1263.1.3.1.r: One clinches the argument saying: “You could not say it more quickly than I because I don’t read half of it!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1263.1.3.1.p: Two priests competing for a chaplain post argue about which of them can say the mass faster.

J1263.1.4.p: An ignorant student who fails his examination consoles himself by noting that Christ's own disciples did not pass theirs either.

J1263.2.p: Witty replies that mock clergy for selling church offices, sacraments, or favors for money.

J1263.2.1.r: Bishop is paid 100 ova (eggs) instead of 100 oves (sheep) for consecrating man as priest. To bishop’s protests the man answers, “You should have refused to consecrate me. If I had been worthy I should not have had to promise oves or ova.” *Wesselski Bebel I 221 No. 115.
J1263.2.1.p: Joke about how much a priest charges for consecration, the ceremony that makes someone a priest or bishop, showing that the church sells it.

J1263.2.2.p: A rich man pours ducats into the pope's lap, and the pope, saying no one could resist such an armored army, decides the case in the rich man's favor.

J1263.2.3.p: A priest refuses a small bribe, saying he will sell his soul to the devil only for a large sum.

J1263.3.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 777; Boccaccio Decameron I No. 2 (Lee 2); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1263.3.p: A Jew decides that Christians have a merciful God after considering the scandalous life of the papal court in Rome.

J1263.4.p: Witty replies that mock the luxurious living of churchmen.

J1263.4.1.p: A cardinal scolds an abbot for living in more luxury than the founder of his monastic order did, and the abbot replies by asking whether the cardinals of St. Peter lived in such luxury. The abbot's comeback turns the rebuke back on the cardinal.

J1263.4.2.p: A man mocks Saints Peter and Paul as fools for choosing poverty, since rich abbots get into heaven too. The joke is a sharp retort against the luxury of churchmen.

J1263.5.r: Many do not pray at all, many know their prayers by heart, and the great prelates look through their fingers *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 514.
J1263.5.p: A joke saying churchmen have no need of eyeglasses, implying they do not need to read or see well because they never work hard or study. It mocks clergy who are supposedly idle or self-indulgent.

J1263.6.r: Ruler explains: “I want a lying priest so that if he repeats my confession he will not be believed.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1263.6.p: A clever reply about choosing one's confessor, in which the speaker mocks a priest or the confession system. It is a joke aimed at clergy abuses.

J1263.7.p: A peasant sees a priest working in the fields and says he wants to confess. The priest tells him to put money in the box and do the same penance as last year, so confession is reduced to paying money.

J1264.p: A general heading for witty replies that mock priests, monks, or nuns for sexual misconduct or breaking their vows of chastity.

J1264.1.p: A priest accused of being too close to his parishioners' wives replies that the church is his wife, and that the men treat her far worse than he treats any woman.

J1264.2.r: Monk says, “I vowed three things: poverty in the bath, obedience at the table, and celibacy at the altar.” *Wesselski Bebel II 133 No. 100.
J1264.2.p: A joke about a priest who is celibate yet has a sexual or romantic matter arising at the altar. The humor exposes the gap between clerical vows and behavior.

J1264.3.p: The son of a priest is taunted that his father wears a crown but is not a king. The jab hints that the father, though a priest, has an illegitimate son.

J1264.4.r: She says, “It was during the silent period.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 716.
J1264.4.p: A nun is asked why she did not call for help when she was raped, and she answers with a witty remark that the silent period, or vow of silence, kept her from calling out.

J1264.5.r: He has nun as mistress. (Cf. J1161.5.) Wesselski *Bebel I 191 No. 58.
J1264.5.p: A youth explains that he has been keeping company with a pious person, a joke that hints at a sexual or unchaste connection with a religious person.

J1264.6.r: Defense accepted. Bolte Frey’s Gartengesellschaft *218 No. 6.
J1264.6.p: A nun, pregnant and asked about the father, claims the child is by the Holy Ghost. It is a mocking excuse for her pregnancy.

J1264.7.r: He answers: “God gave me five talents and I have added five more!” (Pun on word talent.) Nouvelles Récréations No. 4; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1264.7.p: A priest is assigned to reform five loose nuns but gets all five pregnant. He is rebuked for not using his talents, a pun on the parable, to resist temptation.

J1264.8.r: Man at his lady’s funeral says to priest: “You enjoy them when they are young and then give them to us to bury. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1264.8.p: A joke about returns or payments that are unequal, implying a clergyman's sexual or moral dealings have bad results. The title is a pun on an unequal exchange.

J1264.9.p: An abbess has twenty-four nuns but only twelve monks, so she assigns twelve nuns to the guests. The joke implies the nuns serve the monks and guests sexually.

J1265.p: A general heading for witty replies that rely on how the church is governed, such as the ranks and duties of bishops, parsons, and priests.

J1265.1.r: Parson: “Don’t let me be like Christ on Palm Sunday in Jerusalem” *Wesselski Arlotto I 173 No. 2.
J1265.1.p: A bishop seats a parson in the place of honor at dinner, and the parson fears this is a sign he will be punished, as though it were a last supper before execution. The joke compares the seat of honor to Christ's triumphal entry on Palm Sunday.

J1265.2.p: A priest is told he is unfit to care for his parish and offers to swap places with the bishop, turning the criticism into a clever challenge.

J1265.3.r: An abbot calls the monks together and asks, “Whom from all you fools can I appoint as steward?” A monk answers, “That should not be difficult since an abbot was found from the same company of fools.” Wesselski Bebel II 119 No. 58.
J1265.3.p: A clever remark that a group of clergy or officials are all the same company of fools, mocking church officials as a group.

J1269.p: A miscellaneous category of witty replies based on churchmen or the clergy that do not fit the more specific groups.

J1269.1.r: During the sermon the parson bids the sexton see if anyone is coming. The sexton: “A man is coming with a wheel on his shoulder”—Parson: “God gives it to you.” — Sexton: “Now a man is coming with half a hog on his shoulder.” — Parson: “God gives it to me.” Type 1829*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1829*.
J1269.1.p: A clergyman's clever retort about dividing up the offerings or fees between the parson and the sexton (church caretaker).

J1269.2.p: A man stays away from church because he does not want to hear people slandered there.

J1269.3.p: A chaplain accused of being the first to start every kind of trickery defends himself by claiming he is first in all things.

J1269.4.p: A priest who scolds others replies that he is only getting even, since he has to put up with a lot of scolding himself.

J1269.5.r: Blamed. If he can turn bread into the body of the Lord why can he not turn quail into fish? Frey (ed. Bolte) 247 No. 85; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 100; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1269.5.p: A bishop who receives quail on a Friday, when meat is forbidden, orders them cooked, and a clever answer turns the quail into something permitted for eating.

J1269.6.r: Abbess: “I can well believe that. The capon never loves the hen.” Wesselski Mönchslatein No. 59; Mensa Philosophica No. 115.
J1269.6.p: A bishop refuses a favor to an abbess on the grounds that he does not love her, answered with a witty comparison of a capon and a hen.

J1269.7.r: Gaster Exempla 194 No. 45; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 617.
J1269.7.p: A man who is praying refuses to salute a superior, explaining that while standing before the King of Kings he cannot show respect to lesser people.

J1269.8.p: A robber defends his theft from the rich by arguing that God will not let the rich into heaven unless their ill-gotten goods are taken from them.

J1269.9.r: Parishioner: “The ass, for he bore both the son and his mother.” Bolte Frey’s Gartengesellschaft 245 No. 81.
J1269.9.p: A riddle-like question asking who once carried the Savior on his back, answered with Saint Christopher.

J1269.10.p: A priest who is underpaid is criticized for not staying at home, and he replies that the mice are starving because he gets only forty florins a year.

J1269.11.p: Monks asking that quarters used by the king and his court be reconsecrated get the reply that their own quarters need it more.

J1269.12.p: A youth copies a priest's figurative language and announces a fire in the same manner, and the fire set by a cat's tail spreads.

J1269.13.p: A saint, invited to court by a king, replies that he cannot leave the court of God.

J1270.p: Clever verbal replies about who the parents of children really are.

J1271.r: When I look at you, I see that you are not even a man.” Wienert FFC LVI 40; Babrius No. 54.
J1271.p: A eunuch (castrated man) visits a diviner to find out whether he will become a father, and the diviner's reading of livers gives a sly answer.

J1272.r: children. Type 1548*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 654A.
J1272.p: Of three brothers, the shoemaker makes shoes for the queen and princess, the tailor makes clothes, and the fool gives a gift of his own, in a clever twist about who the children's father is.

J1273.p: A witty retort: an artist paints beautiful children but has ugly ones of his own, explaining that one kind is made by day and the other by night.

J1274.r: (Not son but brother.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 502; Mensa Philosophica No. 3; Nouvelles Récréations No. 15; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1274.p: A young man who looks like the emperor comes to Rome, and when asked whether his mother has ever been in Rome, he replies that his father has been there often.

J1276.p: A witty answer to a child that seems to have been born too early after a marriage, pointing to the question of its parentage.

J1276.1.r: Father-in-law to son-in-law: “Do like my grandson and you will always be ahead of others.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1276.1.p: A child is born just one month after the wedding, and a clever reply is given to explain it.

J1276.2.r: Husband returns wife to her father (uncle) saying: “I can’t afford a child every two months.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1276.2.p: A child is born two months after the marriage, and the witty reply is that the child is too much for the parents' income.

J1276.2.1.r: Groom leaves. Can’t afford a child every time he lies with his wife. Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 29; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1276.2.1.p: A child is born on the wedding night, so the parents' timing is questioned; a witty reply is given that the child's arrival was too much for the father's means.

J1279.p: A general category of witty replies to remarks about whether children are really their father's, where a clever answer turns the insinuation back on the speaker.

J1279.1.r: Youngest leaves his food to say: “Please, mother, give me a good father!” (Cf. J325.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1279.1.p: A dying mother tells her family that not all of her twelve children were fathered by their legal father, and names the true father of each child, so that they are left with a good father after all.

J1279.2.r: “Where does all this come from?” Wife: “God’s bounty.” Illegitimate child greets mother. Same question, same answer. Sailor: “I don’t want God to help me so much!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda
J1279.2.p: A sailor who has been away returns to find his poor hovel has been turned into a fine house, and he jokes that God has overdone it, hinting that the house is not his wife's doing or his own.

J1279.3.p: A suitor refuses to marry a girl because she seems too young or too delicate, and her father answers that she has already had three children.

J1279.4.p: A witty saying that strength comes from large numbers, illustrated by the claim that the Genoese children are strong because they have more help raising them.

J1280.p: A general category of clever replies made to a ruler, judge, or other person in authority.

J1281.p: When someone calls the emperor a tyrant, he replies that if he were one, the man would not dare say so.

J1282.p: A trickster is offered a reward by a ruler, choosing between a coin, an ass, a sheep, or a vineyard; he cleverly chooses so that he gets the coin and also effectively prays for the ruler.
