J1283.p: A king gives a man a coin, and the man makes sharp replies about brotherhood, saying that they share the Lord's Prayer and that if all the king's brothers gave as much, he would be rich.

J1284.p: A widow stops a ruler on his way to war and tells him he should not leave an act of justice undone for his successor, since he may be killed.

J1284.1.p: A wronged woman tells a ruler who ignores insults aimed at him to show her how it is done, implicitly rebuking him for his indifference.

J1284.2.p: A king says he is too busy to hear a widow's case, and she tells him to stop being a king; her boldness wins her an audience.

J1285.r: A thief condemned to the gallows tells the king, “I do what you do and it is against my will.” King: “You shall also be hanged against your will.” *Basset 1001 Contes I 507.
J1285.p: A clever reply or act is done against someone's will, typically when a person is forced to do or say something they did not want to.

J1286.r: “I was mistaken, you swine!” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 262 No. 223.
J1286.p: A peasant flatters a judge with grand titles hoping to win his favor, but the judge simply calls him a fool.

J1289.p: A general category of miscellaneous clever replies made to rulers or judges.

J1289.1.r: “I am a prophet, not a locksmith.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 258 No. 198.
J1289.1.p: A judge asks a pseudo-prophet to prove his powers by opening a difficult lock, and the man replies that he is no locksmith, exposing his fraud.

J1289.2.p: A peasant asks a bishop who rides with forty horses whether St. Kilian in Würzburg also rides that way; the bishop excuses the extravagance by saying he is also a prince and that the horses belong to the prince, and the peasant asks what the bishop would do if the prince became a fool.

J1289.3.p: A pope calls a persistent courtier a fool, and the courtier replies that others call the pope the same thing and that he will not try to correct them.

J1289.4.r: Philosopher: “If I am rewarded, I will say that you are right; I will no longer need money.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1289.4.p: A philosopher asks a ruler for money, and the ruler replies that philosophers do not need money.

J1289.5.r: Shivering king (rich man) to tattered peasant: “Aren’t you cold?” Peasant: “No, if you wore all your clothes as I do, you wouldn’t be cold either!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1289.5.p: A man who is being ordered to undress or is stripped answers cleverly by saying he is already wearing all his clothes, turning the demand into a joke at the ruler's expense.

J1289.6.r: King to son who has been accused of rape: “I never did anything like that.” Prince: “Your father was not king!” King: “Your son will never be one if you keep that up!” Spanish: Childers; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1289.6.p: A prince is given an excuse, a clever verbal reply that gets him out of trouble with a ruler.

J1289.7.r: Ruler: “I thought ruling was your business so I took your tools to learn shoemaking.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1289.7.p: A shoemaker criticizes the lord's rule, and the lord takes away his tools; the shoemaker begs for them back, saying he cannot earn a living without them.

J1289.8.p: A judge plugs one ear while the first side in a lawsuit speaks, explaining that he is saving the other ear for the second litigant.

J1289.9.p: A king is reproached by a philosopher who tells him to first bring harmony to his own household before asking about peace in his kingdom.

J1289.10.p: A king is persuaded by a philosopher to spare a city; when the king says he will not grant what is asked, the philosopher asks him to destroy the city, which saves it.

J1289.11.p: A man fined for breaking the sabbath asks for a receipt, arguing that if God asks for it he will not have to go to hell to get it from the judge.

J1289.12.p: A man arrested for drunkenness is so drunk that his trial has to be postponed; at the later trial he is told he kept calling the judge very wise, and he admits he must have been very drunk.

J1289.13.p: A weaver, hearing that a tax will be charged for every doorway of weavers, takes his door to the khan and refuses to come back for the side walls of his house.

J1289.14.p: A ruler offers a gem to whoever can first go all the way around the kingdom; a trickster goes around the king and declares that the king is the kingdom.

J1289.15.p: A thief brings the king buffaloes that he has killed in a hunt and then lost, and thereby reproaches the king for wasting his resources.

J1289.16.p: A jester flatters a prince for his generosity, claiming his palms have become hairless from so much giving and receiving gold.

J1289.17.p: The emperor asks which people have the biggest bellies, and the jester answers that it is the landlords.

J1289.18.p: A king asks a holy man for the heart of religion, and the holy man answers that since the king sits on a throne and he sits on the ground, he cannot tell him.

J1289.19.p: A tailor caught resting his head on the royal robe says there is no better resting place for the king's robe, since the head is the king of the body.

J1289.20.r: Smoker: “Donkeys don’t know how to enjoy themselves.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1289.20.p: A king tells a smoker that even donkeys will have nothing to do with tobacco, shaming him with a clever insult.

J1290.p: A question or proposal is answered by showing that following it leads to an absurd conclusion.

J1291.p: A question is answered not directly but with an absurd counterquestion.

J1291.1.r: Question: How can black beans make a white soup? Answer: How can a white whip on the naked flesh make black welts. *Wesselski Arlotto II 252 No. 168.
J1291.1.p: A riddle-like answer in which someone is asked to explain how one thing could produce something that seems impossible, such as black beans making white soup.

J1291.1.1.r: Answer: The same reason blackberries are red when they are green. U.S.: Baughman.
J1291.1.1.p: Someone asks why a black cow eats green grass yet gives white milk and yellow butter, an absurd question mocking a supposedly illogical puzzle.

J1291.2.p: Someone who asks about God's hidden workings is answered with a simple question about everyday nature, such as why a louse bite blisters but a gnat bite does not. The point is that if you cannot explain small things, you should not pry into divine secrets.

J1291.3.p: A question about how many priests a place should have is answered with an absurd counterquestion, such as asking how many fox tails it takes to reach heaven.

J1291.3.1.p: Asked how much cloth it would take to make God's coat, the clever answer is as much as for a person, since what is done for the poor is done for God.

J1291.4.r: “When your mother conceived where were you?” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1291.4.p: A trick question asks where the oil is in a sesame flower, meant to be an absurd question that a clever person turns aside.

J1292.p: A tide asks whether the moon is up yet, and a minnow mocks the absurdity, since the tide cannot rise without the moon, and tells it to wait until he has had a drink.

J1293.p: A general heading for tales where a proposal is shown to be absurd by carrying it to a ridiculous conclusion, so the proposer is made to see the folly.

J1293.1.p: A large bird wants to mate with a little bird, who replies that she is going to swallow a large eel. The large bird sees how absurd his proposal is.

J1293.1.1.p: A claim that the sea or a river is on fire, offered as a mockery, is no more absurd than a crow claiming a swan as a wife.

J1293.2.r: Judge shows criminal mercy: he will not punish him as he deserves, only take off his head. Nouvelles Récréations No. 82.
J1293.2.p: A proposal is shown to be absurd because, if the head is cut off, other punishments no longer matter.

J1293.3.p: Turning a king into a Brahmin is compared to turning a donkey into a horse, showing the proposal to be absurd.

J1293.4.p: A pot full of milk is taken as a sign that the city is full of fakirs, and a flower floating on the milk without disturbing it shows that one more will not matter.

J1293.5.r: Seller later buys all heads in butcher shop: demands heads of butcher’s family. India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1293.5.p: A butcher-buyer demands the saddle and ornaments along with the camel, as if all accessories were included in the sale.

J1300.p: A general heading for tales in which a meddling or foolish question is rebuked with a sharp answer.

J1301.r: “Mourn me as a man who was tormented by women talking foolishness.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 232 No. 86.
J1301.p: Women insist on knowing how a man wants to be mourned when he dies, and he answers in a way that rebukes their meddling.

J1302.r: “No, he isn’t; he can still carry all your and your brothers’ patience.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 473.
J1302.p: A priest complains that a miller's mule is overloaded, and the miller answers in a way that rebukes the priest's meddling.

J1303.p: Aesop borrows fire from a neighbor in daytime and carries a lantern to bring it back. When a fool asks what he seeks with a lantern in daylight, he replies that he seeks a man, not a busybody.

J1304.r: “I am wearing mourning for the father of my son.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 211 No. 27.
J1304.p: A man goes out in black clothes and people curiously ask him why.

J1305.r: “Yes, a crow.” And in what direction was his tail pointing?” Answer: “Toward the rear!”
J1305.p: A believer in omens asks a peasant woman whether she has seen a bird, in a tale about how a tail came to point in a particular direction.

J1306.p: A mother asks her newly married daughter whether she went to her husband on the first night, a nosy question about how the marriage was consummated.

J1309.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tales in which meddling or foolish questions are rebuked.

J1309.1.p: A man is asked by a naked Indian whether he is not cold; the man retorts that the Indian's face is not cold, so the question is foolish. In the note, the Indian asks if the man's face is cold, and the man replies that it is not.

J1309.2.p: A foolish questioner asks how often someone kills their ducks, and a witty person turns the absurd question back on them as a rebuke.

J1309.3.r: Disgusted father-in-law: “I have eaten half and your father half, to have such a fool son-in-law.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1309.3.p: Someone foolishly asks where the dirt went when a canal was dug, and is answered with a clever rebuke to the silly question.

J1310.p: A general heading for witty exchanges and clever replies about wine.

J1311.p: A servant is trained to bring cheap wine when good wine is asked for; when the guest objects, the host says the servant brought what was wanted, not what was asked for.

J1312.p: A general heading for tales in which wine is watered down and the server or host is mocked or outwitted for it.

J1312.1.p: The server of diluted wine is taunted by being told to serve the water and the wine separately.

J1312.2.p: The server of diluted Rhine wine is taunted with the claim that the wine was washed in the Rhine.

J1312.3.p: Since Christ turned water into wine, landlords have all tried to water their wine too, and a man prefers Jewish wine to the baptized kind.

J1313.r: Man given his choice of old or new wine says, “We must honor old age.” Wesselski Bebel I 163 No. 100.
J1313.p: A witty exchange about old wine.

J1314.r: To doctor: “If this is the way to get to Heaven (drinking) I don’t want to know any other!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1314.p: A witty exchange in which wine is connected with the road to heaven.

J1315.r: Man to friend who drinks very little: “If everyone drank as you do, wine would be cheap.” Answer: “On the contrary, it would be expensive because I drink all I want.” Spanish: Childers; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1315.p: A witty exchange in which the same thing is seen differently by two people, one of them through the lens of wine.

J1316.p: A guest complains that the host's serving of wine, said to be six years old, is very small for something so old.

J1317.p: A man asks for a large jug to be filled with wine and is told to go to the river; when he brings a small jug, he is served.

J1318.r: “Another drink and I could have slapped his face!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1318.p: An ambassador gains the courage to address the Pope only after drinking wine.

J1319.p: A miscellaneous heading for witty exchanges about wine that do not fit the other groups.

J1319.1.r: (Enemies are rum and hard cider.) U.S.: Baughman.
J1319.1.p: A man claims he loves his enemies and has great affection for those who hurt him, as a witty and ironic reply about wine.

J1320.p: A general heading for witty exchanges and clever replies about drunkenness.

J1321.p: A drunkard refuses to reform and keeps drinking despite warnings or examples, and is answered with a clever rebuke.

J1321.1.r: Instead of taking it as a warning the son says “Where does one get such good wine?” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 21, 814; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 115, 344, *Neuman.
J1321.1.p: A father shows his drunkard son a drunk man being mocked in the street, and the son asks where the drunk man got the wine.

J1321.2.p: An old woman is tricked into thinking she is already in hell, and she responds by asking for drinking companions, showing she is unrepentant about her drunkenness.

J1322.p: A clever reply or joke about someone who has an enormous, insatiable thirst for drink.

J1322.1.r: Doctors consult how to rid fever-stricken drunkard of his great thirst. “You take care of the fever; I shall take care of the thirst.” *Wesselski Arlotto II 267 No. 217; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1322.1.p: Someone promises to take care of a huge thirst, usually as a witty retort to a drinker being criticized.

J1322.2.p: A priest who drinks a lot is blamed, and he replies that people should consider his great thirst, since he has slept on a sack of salt and so has thirst enough for a week.

J1323.r: Drunkard’s wife takes him when he is drunk to a tomb and, masking as a ghost brings him food. “If you had known me better you would have brought me drink.” Wienert FFC LVI 38; Halm Aesop No. 108.
J1323.p: A witty retort in which someone says a person should have brought the drunk a drink, mocking the drinker's thirst or need for alcohol.

J1324.r: Doctor tells drunkard, “The goblet has stung you.” “If I had known that I would have drunk out of a glass.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 234.
J1324.p: A witty retort in which a drinker is said to have been stung by his goblet or drinking cup, a joke about excessive drinking.

J1330.p: A general heading for clever replies that people make when confronted by beggars.

J1331.r: Then he says he has nothing for him. “You made me come down for nothing; I make you come up for nothing.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 238 No. 113.
J1331.p: A beggar refuses to come inside and insists the householder come down to the door; when he asks for alms, the householder tells him to come upstairs instead.

J1332.r: Mother: “Tell him I am not at home.” Numskull: “He doesn’t want you, he wants bread.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 239 No. 528.
J1332.p: A foolish person reports to his mother that a beggar is downstairs asking for bread, and the joke lies in his simple-minded way of passing on the message.

J1333.r: Beggar: “Good day, you stingy fellows.” They: “We are not stingy fellows.” Beggar: “Then give and prove me a liar.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 202 No. 397.
J1333.p: A witty challenge in which someone, usually a beggar or poor person, dares another to prove that he is lying about his circumstances.

J1334.r: They say they have no meat, no bread, no wine, etc. “Then go beg; you have more need than I.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 236 No. 519.
J1334.p: A beggar tells a stingy person to go out and beg himself, turning the insult back on the miser.

J1337.r: Beggar protests. Emperor: “If all your brothers gave you that much you would be richer than I.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1337.p: A beggar claims to be the emperor's brother, and the emperor gives him a small coin; the joke rests on the idea that all men are descended from Adam.

J1338.p: A beggar asks a goldsmith to plate his club with gold, saying that asking costs nothing.

J1340.p: A general heading for clever replies made by people who are hungry or poorly fed.

J1341.p: A clever reply made by an underfed servant or child who is complaining about not getting enough food.

J1341.1.r: An avaricious master feeds bread-crusts to his servants. “The crusts are already getting soft.” Type 1567.
J1341.1.p: A hungry servant or child softens bread crusts, as a witty way of pointing out that he is given too little to eat.

J1341.2.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 247 No. 158; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 700; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1565; Italian Novella: Rotunda; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs. f. Vksk. 1954, 134.
J1341.2.p: Parents give a boy a small fish and keep a large one for themselves. The boy holds the small fish to his ear, says he has asked it a question, and reports that it told him to ask the large fish under the bed.

J1341.3.r: Given very thin rice soup, wit inquires about the master’s dogs. “He should have one to scent the rice in this soup.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 259 No 206, Arlotto II 75 No. 105.
J1341.3.p: A hungry servant or child is told to smell the rice, as a witty way of pointing out that he is given too little to eat.

J1341.4.p: A widow serves a tailor one egg, and he sings about it; she gives him two, and he sings that two eggs are two eggs, and each time he asks for more, with the joke continuing with a sausage added.

J1341.5.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 143 No. 1718, Keller.
J1341.5.p: A hungry apprentice gets his master's attention by telling lies about him, so that the master notices and feeds him.

J1341.6.r: They ask what the fifth calf does while the other four are nursing. “It looks on just as I am doing now.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 134 No. 1555.
J1341.6.p: A hungry shepherd answers a question with an absurd tall tale about a cow with four teats that bore five calves, a jab at being underfed.

J1341.7.r: One of them: “I wash out my insides so as to have more room for food.” She changes her practice. Type 1566*.
J1341.7.p: A servant or child, kept hungry by a stingy innkeeper who serves weak beer before meals, makes a clever retort that cures her of the habit. The note says she is given a pitcher of weak beer so she will fill up before eating.

J1341.8.p: A hostess praises the little lumps of sugar as sweeter, and a hungry servant takes the big lumps, saying he doesn't like sweets.

J1341.9.p: A hungry son slaps his brother for claiming he will get none of the father's cherries, and the father then shares the cherries with him.

J1341.10.p: A hungry student tells a mewing cat it cannot have the bones yet because no meat has been served, pointing out that the servant forgot to bring food.

J1341.11.p: Hired farm workers sing a song complaining about their food, then change the song once the food is improved.

J1341.12.p: A hired man says grace in a way that reveals better food has been served since unexpected guests arrived.

J1342.r: A guest is seen uttering a prayer before an underdone hen at the table. “She must be a goddess turned into a hen, for she has been over the fire and spared.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 193 No. 378.
J1342.p: A hungry guest says a prayer over a hen that is still underdone, mocking the poor cooking or stingy hostess.

J1343.p: A general category of jokes and retorts in which people show how much they love food and drink.

J1343.1.p: Asked what music he likes best, a hungry person answers that it is the sound of plates and spoons.

J1343.2.r: A priest, asked when he would have certain choice wine served, before or after the meal, replies, “The holy Mary was Virgin before, during, and after the birth.” *Wesselski Arlotto I 202 No. 33.
J1343.2.p: A greedy person answers a question about the timing of a meal by saying he is always thinking of food before, during, and after it.

J1344.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 10; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1344.p: An unwelcome guest, having seen his hostess hide food, reveals the hiding place by telling a story about it.

J1345.r: When host inquires, he replies, “If thou be the son of God, command that these stones be made bread.” Mensa Philosophica No. 171.
J1345.p: A person explains in a clever answer why he did not eat the bread that was offered.

J1346.r: “If both of us had been present at the miracle of the loaves and fishes you would have eaten me too!” Pilgrim: “I wouldn’t have eaten you but I would have chewed on you a bit!” Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 83; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1346.p: A maid scolds a pilgrim for eating too much, and the pilgrim answers back cleverly.

J1350.p: A general category of insulting, rude comebacks and verbal jabs.

J1351.p: Two women insult each other by calling one another prostitutes.

J1351.1.r: A woman having given her cook leave of absence for the next day asks her what day it is. “Saturday.” “No, it is the day on which the prostitutes wander.” The cook: “Yes, from one prostitute to another. Today I am with you, tomorrow with your sister.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 160.
J1351.1.p: Prostitutes are described as wandering from place to place.

J1351.2.r: The second: “You would like to be in my place but no one wants you.” *Wesselski Bebel II 127 No. 83.
J1351.2.p: An envious woman accuses another woman of being a harlot.

J1352.p: One person insults another by calling him an ass, a donkey.

J1352.1.r: King: “You have an ass’s load on you.” Fool: “Rather the burdens of two asses.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 239 No. 527; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1352.1.p: A king and his son, hunting on a hot day, load their fur coats onto a fool's back, so the fool ends up carrying the burden like an ass.

J1352.2.r: Oldster: “An ass of twenty is older than a man of seventy.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1352.2.p: A young rival mocks an old rival for being old, and the old man answers that age is a matter of perspective.

J1353.p: A witty comeback in which a man, asked why a stranger's errand concerns him, turns the question back by pointing out that the same logic applies to the questioner. The retort mocks someone who meddles in other people's business.

J1354.r: At market a man enquires of another: “How is the moon, three-quarters or full?” “I don’t know. I have neither bought nor sold one.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 209 No. 17.
J1354.p: A witty rebuff in which someone is told that a matter is outside his field or trade, so he has no business meddling in it. The joke is a polite-sounding insult.

J1355.r: You have everything for yourself alone; only your wife is public property.” Wesselski Bebel II 135 No. 104.
J1355.p: A flattering remark that is made to be an exception to a general rule, usually a sly compliment or ironic praise. The joke turns on the single person who is set apart as the exception.

J1356.r: One of them: “Who wouldn’t call that girl pretty?” The girl overhears and says, “No one would say it of you.” The man: “Anyone might say it who would lie as I have lied about you.” *Wesselski Bebel II 148 No. 155; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1356.p: A witty answer to flattery in which two men meet an unattractive young woman and one of them pays her an extravagant compliment that is turned back on him. The retort shows up the flatterer's insincerity.

J1357.r: To a prince who boasted that he was descended from the Trojans a doctor replies: “My people are of Nurenberg. Everyone knows who they are; but of the Trojans no one knows anything except that Aeneas was a traitor and Romulus a robber.” *Wesselski Bebel II 114 No. 46.
J1357.p: A witty retort about ancestry in which a person of humble origin is compared with an ancient, distinguished family, and the comparison is turned to the speaker's advantage. The joke pokes fun at boasting about birth.

J1358.r: A messenger tells a man that he has a newborn son. “Thanks are to God, but I am not beholden to you for it.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 223 No. 59.
J1358.p: A witty reply in which someone who brought a message is not thanked for it, because the message was not really his to bring or was no real help. The joke mocks thanks given to the wrong person.

J1361.p: A monk, taunted by women, answers by boasting of his sexual prowess, and a woman then calls on the devil to come and ride him. The joke is a bawdy rude retort.

J1363.r: Impoverished spendthrift sarcastically to thrifty person: “Stop spending so freely!” “It’s too late to give you the same advice.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1363.p: A witty retort in which someone is told that advice given to him comes too late to help, because the moment for it has passed. The joke mocks useless advice.

J1364.r: Asks worthy one: “Why is it that I am rewarded and you are not?” Answer: “Because you have found more of your kind that I have of mine.” (Also told of Dante and a minstrel.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1364.p: A tale in which an unworthy person is rewarded by people of his own kind, so that the reward goes to the undeserving. The point is ironic rather than moral.

J1369.p: A general heading for rude retorts that do not fit the more specific categories in this section. It collects miscellaneous insulting comebacks.

J1369.1.r: Friend: “You had better spend 200 so as to not be found out.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1369.1.p: A man decides to pay 100 florins to become famous, so that people will know who he is. The tale mocks the cost and vanity of seeking fame.

J1369.2.r: An old man says of a youthful prodigy: “He will be an idiot in old age because perfection before maturity brings on deterioration of the mind.” Youth: “You must have been very wise in your youth!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1369.2.p: A child prodigy gives a sharp, witty answer that shows unexpected cleverness. The retort surprises the listener with its wit.

J1369.3.r: One says: “I do not give every coxcomb the wall!” The other says: “I do, sir!” England: Baughman.
J1369.3.p: Two men meet in a narrow passage and neither will give way, so a rude or clever exchange follows. The situation sets up a witty quarrel.

J1369.4.p: Someone asks whose fool another is, and the reply is that he is the Bishop of Durham's fool, so the questioner must be someone else's fool. The joke turns the insult back on the asker. Found in England.

J1369.5.p: A soldier stays silent before the king, and the explanation is that he is always silent when questioned by a stupid person. The joke is a sly rebuke of foolish questioners.

J1370.p: A heading for witty retorts that cynically mock honesty, suggesting that people are not really honest or that honesty has little value. The jokes are sarcastic about truthfulness.

J1371.r: A king, hearing that a man keeps an account-book of people’s mistakes asks to see about his own record. He reads that the king has made a mistake in trusting a certain sum of money to a servant. King: “How if he comes back with it?” “I shall cross off your name and put him down for making a mistake.” *Wesselski Arlotto I 181 No. 5; Chauvin II 153 No. 20; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1371.p: A witty tale in which a person's record of wrongdoings is kept as an account book, with the mistakes listed as if they were business accounts. The joke is a cynical comment on dishonesty.

J1373.r: The Indian assures him that he can: “There is no white man within a hundred miles of here.” (Cf. X600.) U.S.: Baughman.
J1373.p: A white man asks an Indian whether he can safely leave some of his belongings in the Indian's lodge, and the Indian replies that they are safe because no white man is nearby to steal them. The retort is a sarcastic jab at white men's dishonesty.

J1380.p: A heading for witty retorts about debts, where someone answers a demand for repayment with a clever or sly reply. The jokes mock borrowing and the reluctance to pay back.

J1381.r: There is none there. “Then you didn’t return it as you said you would, and there is none to lend you this year.” *Wesselski Arlotto II 259 No. 186; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1381.p: A parson tells a borrower to get corn from the same place he got it the year before, which is a sly way of refusing to lend it. The joke mocks the borrower's request.

J1382.p: Someone who pays cash is treated better than someone who owes money. This is a witty reply in disputes about debts.

J1382.1.r: Finally one hands him a coin with the request. “You are the one who shall blow the whistle.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 246 No. 146.
J1382.1.p: Several people ask a man going to market to buy them a whistle, and he cleverly uses this to make them pay him or shows them who is truly reliable. Its point is that people who promise favors but pay nothing are not the ones to trust.

J1382.2.p: A man going on a sea voyage takes written orders from many people, some paying cash and some only promising payment later. On the ship he sorts the cards and pays only the cards that have gold on them, so the unpaid orders are blown into the sea by the wind.

J1383.p: A stag asks the sheep for a loan of grain and offers the wolf as security. The sheep replies that since both animals are so fast, nobody could know where they would be when payment is due.

J1384.r: Guests in inn discuss reincarnation. “Since we shall come back in three thousand years, the host might trust us till then.” Host: “You still owe me what you didn’t pay three thousand years ago.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 858.
J1384.p: A very old debt is claimed or disputed, and the reply is a witty comment about how ancient it is. The headline gives the exaggeration of its age.

J1390.p: A general heading for witty replies made when someone is accused of theft or caught stealing.

J1391.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian Coster-Wijsman Uilspiegel Verhalen 35ff. Nos. 17—22.
J1391.p: A thief caught in the act makes a weak, obviously false excuse, which is the joke.

J1391.1.r: Owner: How did you get into the garden? A wind blew me in. How were the vegetables uprooted? If the wind is strong enough to blow me in, it can uproot them. How did they get into your bag? That is what I was just wondering. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 207 No. 7, cf. II 214 No. 441.
J1391.1.p: A thief caught stealing vegetables in a garden blames the weather, claiming a big wind blew him in.

J1391.2.r: Owner: “Is this a ladder market?” “Can’t one sell ladders everywhere?” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 210 No. 18.
J1391.2.p: A thief climbs a wall using his ladder, and when caught in a garden he claims he is a ladder seller.

J1391.3.r: One says that he told the other than sheep have lower teeth but no upper, and that they caught the sheep to see. India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Vai): Ellis 221 No. 34.
J1391.3.p: Two thieves are caught with stolen sheep, and the joke concerns the sheep's teeth.

J1391.3.1.r: Man caught just as he knocks sheep in the head: The sheep bit me (or: I’m not going to let sheep butt me to death). U.S.: *Baughman.
J1391.3.1.p: One of the thieves caught with a sheep excuses himself by saying the sheep bit him.

J1391.4.p: A thief who steals meat escapes to a high place and claims he is only seeing how he would act if he were a hawk, as hawks steal liver too.

J1391.5.p: A fox caught near the farmyard claims he only went there to see whether any of his relatives were there.

J1391.6.p: A thief excuses himself from drinking the stolen liquid by saying he cannot drink because he has no teeth.

J1391.7.r: Accused, they say that they were merely measuring the cup to see how much it would take to fill it. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1391.7.p: A king orders each subject to bring milk for his new cup, and the subjects plan to cheat him by bringing water. The cup is then said to be only a measuring cup, which is the excuse for the trick.

J1391.8.r: Fox leaving merchant’s warehouse: “I had wanted a needle as big as an anchor and an anchor as small as a needle.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1391.8.p: A thief offers a ridiculous excuse involving needles and anchors, a silly explanation for what he is carrying or doing.

J1392.p: The owner of goods helps the thief carry them off or unknowingly assists the theft, which is the trick in the tale.

J1392.1.r: Comes to the thief’s door. Thief: “What do you want with me?” “What, isn’t this the house we set out for?” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 212 No. 32.
J1392.1.p: A thief ransacks a man's house and leaves, and the man gathers his remaining belongings and follows the thief home.

J1392.2.r: A buffoon says to robbers in his house, “You can’t find anything here in the dark, for I can find nothing in broad daylight.” *Wesselski Bebel I 132 No. 32; Scala Celi 104b No. 567; Mensa Philosophica No. 62.
J1392.2.p: Robbers are sympathized with after their theft goes badly, and the victim offers them help or comfort.

J1392.2.1.r: He is not yet in bed Spanish: Childers.
J1392.2.1.p: The owner tells the thieves to come back later, a cunning suggestion that lets the owner get the better of them.

J1392.3.p: A clever man helps a robber steal his money, so that he and the robber can both get some sleep. The owner's dry wit turns the theft into a joke.

J1392.4.p: The owner mocks a thief who breaks into his house and finds nothing worth taking.

J1392.5.p: A bridegroom bargains with a thief: he will give him spoils later if the thief agrees not to disrupt his wedding.

J1393.r: If I did that I should be a double fool.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 181 No. 342.
J1393.p: A simpleton is caught moving grain from other people's sacks into his own. When asked why, he admits he is a fool, and when told to put it back in their sacks, he says he is only a simple fool.

J1394.p: Thieves are said to work at night and keep odd hours, and this motif covers tales that play on that habit.

J1394.1.r: A thief having scorned Demosthenes for his constant study, the latter says, “I know that you have not failed to notice that I study much at night.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No 801.
J1394.1.p: A man who studies or works through the night is mistaken for a thief, or is joked about as one.

J1394.2.p: A king who rises too early is cured of the habit by having himself robbed. He replies that robbers get up even earlier than he does.

J1395.r: Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 504), 125 (ST 337); Halm Aesop No. 163.
J1395.p: A thief steals a hunter's hare, and the hunter replies that he was going to give it to him anyway, turning the theft into a joke.

J1396.r: I was trying to remove all chance of worry tomorrow.” Wesselski Mönchslatein 109 No. 92; Nouvelles Récréations No. 35.
J1396.p: A king catches a student who has stolen a capon and points out that the Bible says not to worry about tomorrow. The student answers that he took the capon so he would not have to worry about it.

J1397.p: A man takes a shirt to market for a friend who had stolen it, and it is stolen again there. He reports to his friend that he got back only the cost price, which is nothing.

J1398.r: The hangman takes off his hat: “One thief I hang, to the other I take off my hat.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 591.
J1398.p: A man praises a hangman for doing a good job hanging a thief, as a sarcastic jest.

J1399.p: A miscellaneous group of jokes and retorts in which someone answers a theft with a clever or mocking remark.

J1399.1.p: A parson hides his money in a holy place with a sign saying the Lord is there. A thief takes the money and leaves a sign saying the Lord has risen and is no longer there.

J1400.p: Witty replies in which someone exposes a reform that is not sincere, such as a person who gives up a vice only in appearance.

J1401.r: A tailor dreams that at Judgment Day he sees a flag made up of all the pieces of cloth he has stolen Upon waking he asks his servants to warn him if they ever see him tempted to steal again. This happens. He replies, “The piece I am about to steal does not fit into the flag.” *BP I 343; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 256 No. 190.
J1401.p: A tailor, whose dream or whose claim about it is turned against him, is shown up by a clever retort concerning a false reform.

J1410.p: Witty replies made about someone's fatness or corpulence.

J1411.r: The parson: “Why not; doesn’t the hay wagon get in?” *Wesselski Arlotto II 265 No. 209; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1411.p: A late-arriving parson asks to be let through a city gate, and the guard, seeing he is fat, jokingly says he does not know whether he can fit through.

J1420.p: Animals make witty replies about the dangers they face from predators or hunters.

J1421.r: Dogs appear; the fox flees. “The dogs have not heard of the new law.” *Type 62; *BP II 207; Wienert FFC LVI 52 (ET 120), 98 (ST 125); Halm Aesop No. 225; Jacobs Aesop 214 No. 59; *Chauvin II 202 No. 51, V 241 No. 141; *Lancaster PMLA XXII 33; *Graf FFC XXXVIII 26; Fb “ræv” III 114a.—Spanish: Espinosa III No. 225; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1421.p: In a peace fable, a fox tries to trick a rooster by reporting a new law that establishes peace among the animals, hoping to lure him down.

J1422.r: A cat seeing a mouse leave a bath says, “Good bath!” Mouse: “If I had not seen you!” Chauvin III 55 No. 11.
J1422.p: An animal jokes about its bath or washing, turning a dangerous situation into a witty reply.

J1423.r: The cock: “I have never seen a falcon roasted.” *Chauvin II 117 No. 96.
J1423.p: A falcon scolds a cock for running away from the master who fed him, an animal's sharp reply about ingratitude.

J1424.r: Two foxes in a trap converse: “Where shall we meet again?” “In three days at the furrier’s.” Chauvin III 77 No. 51.
J1424.p: A clever animal answer about where the foxes will gather, given as a retort about the dangers they face.

J1430.p: A group of witty exchanges between doctors and their patients, where one side gets the better of the other.

J1431.r: Sick man: “I came to a place I know not where; something happened I know not how; I am sick I know not where.” Doctor: “Go to the pharmacy and buy I know not what, and eat it I know not how, and you will become well I know not when.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 629; Scala Celi 47b No. 268.
J1431.p: A witty doctor-patient exchange whose punchline is the reply "I know not how."

J1432.r: A bad physician having predicted the immediate death of a patient meets him recovered. “How go things down below?” “They put you at the head of the list of bad physicians, but I maintained that you were no physician at all.” Wienert FFC LVI 39; Halm Aesop No. 168.
J1432.p: A witty doctor-patient exchange in which someone is said to have no physician at all, a sharp jab at a doctor's worth.

J1433.r: When patient reproves doctor for drinking wine the latter says: “Just now it is bad for you and good for me.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1433.p: A doctor forbids his patient to drink wine, telling him to follow his advice rather than his own example.

J1434.p: A doctor cures madness by throwing patients into a pit of water; a servant warns a strange-looking hunter to flee before the same thing happens to him.

J1438.p: A veterinarian becomes a doctor, because he had to pay for killing animals but not for killing people.

J1440.p: A miscellaneous group of witty retorts that do not fit the other repartee groups.

J1441.r: Question from the king: “Who are you?” “I am God.” “Make my eyes larger.” “I am only God of the earth and have power only below the girdle.” *Köhler-Bolte I 504; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 279 No. 326.
J1441.p: A witty retort in which someone is addressed as the god of the earth.

J1442.p: A collection of sharp, witty replies attributed to a cynic, a follower of the Cynic philosophers.

J1442.1.r: King (to cynic): “What can I do for you?” “Get out of my sunlight. Don’t take away from me what you can’t give me.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 802; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1442.1.p: A cynic's witty reply in which he wants sunlight rather than what is offered.

J1442.1.1.p: A cynic tells Alexander that the power of reason can make a poor man as great as a king.

J1442.2.r: Leaving an unclean bath house: “Where can I go now to wash?” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 802.
J1442.2.p: A cynic's witty reply told in the setting of a bath.

J1442.3.p: Asked why gold looks so pale, the cynic answers that it is in great danger.

J1442.4.r: Asked who will carry him to his grave if he has no friends: “He who needs my house.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 802.
J1442.4.p: A cynic's witty instructions about how his own body should be buried or left.

J1442.4.1.r: When told that the beasts and the birds will prey on him he says: “Put a stick at my side so that I may chase them away.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1442.4.1.p: A cynic asks that his body be left exposed to the elements instead of being buried.

J1442.5.p: Asked which wine tastes best, the cynic answers that it is the wine belonging to other people.

J1442.6.p: Arriving at a little town with very big gates, the cynic says to close the gate so the town will not run away.

J1442.7.r: Cynic: “Be careful; you might hit your father.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 802; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1442.7.p: A cynic's witty exchange involving a stone-thrower of illegitimate birth.

J1442.8.p: A cynic, hearing a man talk at great length about heaven, asks him when he came down from there, mocking his claim to know it.

J1442.9.p: A cynic answers a bald man's insults by sarcastically praising the hair that has left such an ugly head bare.

J1442.10.p: When a deceiver calls a cynic wicked, the cynic says he is glad to have him as an enemy, since such a man does good to his enemies and harm to his friends.

J1442.11.r: Friend: “Give me a shoot of that tree!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1442.11.p: A man tells a friend that his wife has hanged herself on a fig tree, and the cynic's response is the point of the joke.

J1442.11.1.r: When he learns that a woman has hanged herself from a tree he explains: “Would that all trees bore such fruit!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1442.11.1.p: In the fig tree story, the cynic voices a wish that is the punchline of the joke.

J1442.12.r: “One who has just escaped from drowning should not return to sea.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1442.12.p: Someone asks a cynic whether a widower should marry again, and the cynic gives a sharp, witty answer.

J1442.13.r: “Of an evil choose the smallest part.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1442.13.p: A cynical witty reply in which a man claims the smallest woman makes the best wife, using a joke to mock marriage choices.

J1443.r: Man ordered to number the fools in the city replies, “It is easier to number the wise men.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 241 No. 535; Chauvin VII 126 No. 393bis.
J1443.p: Foolish townspeople in a city are the subject of a joke in which their stupidity is shown through clever talk.

J1444.p: A wandering actor, rewarded by a city with a coat in their color, gambles it away; when scolded for giving away their gift, he replies that they did not want to keep it themselves.

J1445.p: A man is told by a seer that a believer can be recognized in two ways, but he has forgotten one and the seer has forgotten the other.

J1446.r: A man strikes a priest with a cane: “This is Moses’ staff.” The priest shoots with a pistol: “This is Aaron’s holy censer.” Type 1847*.
J1446.p: A witty answer or joke about Aaron's censer, a sacred incense burner from the Bible, in which a clever retort is made.

J1447.r: Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 161), 107 (ST 191); Halm Aesop No. 408.
J1447.p: A dog reproaches a sow that Venus will not let those who have eaten pork enter her temple; the sow replies that the goddess hates those who kill pigs.

J1448.r: A husband planning to punish his wife, who has yawned in church at the same time as a man, sees his error when his wife in the woods calls out, “The squirrels hop from bough to bough as the yawns from mouth to mouth.” Finnish: Aarne FFC VIII 6 No. 23; XXXIII 52 No. 23; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 141 No. 12; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 84 No. 35.
J1448.p: Yawns spread from one person to another, and a witty tale or retort turns on this contagious yawning.

J1451.r: Badger: “I was a hundred years old when grama grass first grew.” Crane: “My daughter was a hundred years old when grama grass first grew.” Wolf: “I am only eight years old, but we shall see who gets the beehive.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 31 No. *80, Espinosa III Nos. 268—270, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 26, 27.
J1451.p: Two people dispute who should get a beehive, and a clever answer settles the question in a humorous way.

J1452.p: A philosopher, asked why he is thin, explains that he feeds with his own blood a population as large as the Roman emperor's, the joke being that the feeders are lice.

J1453.r: Captain: “Good, it will be more comfortable fighting in the shade.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1453.p: A soldier tells his captain that the enemy is so numerous that their arrows darken the sun, so it is better to fight in the shade.

J1454.r: The lion: “If it had been a lion sculptor, the lion would have been standing over the man.” Wienert FFC LVI 70 (ET 343), 101 (ST 145); Halm Aesop No. 63; Jacobs Aesop 208 No. 35.
J1454.p: A man points to a statue of a lion being beaten by a man to show that man is superior.

J1455.r: Slave (workman) recommended to master whose recent slaves have died: “He has never died while I owned him.” *Clouston Book of Noodles 8; England, U.S.: Baughman.
J1455.p: A joke about a man or thing that claims it has never died yet, the humor coming from the absurd claim.

J1456.r: A man attempts to lie out of having called another a liar: “You lie if you say that I said you lied.” The other: “It’s a good thing for you that you didn’t call me a liar.” (Cf. J817.) *Wesselski Bebel I 204 No. 85.
J1456.p: A story or joke about a liar, in which his lying is shown up by a clever answer.

J1457.r: An old husband tells his young wife, who is concerned about his gray hair, “A gray fox is as good as a red one.” “But an old gray fox is not so good as a young red one.” Bolte Frey 242 No. 75.
J1457.p: A clever trickster called the gray fox outwits others through a witty reply or action.

J1458.r: We must now take an oath to break all the oaths we have taken.” Wesselski Bebel I 205 No. 88.
J1458.p: A village called on to join a war debates in a meeting, and a man reminds them that they have sworn oaths not to go to war, which is used to escape the duty.

J1461.r: Fool asked what made him gray-headed replies, “My hair.” *Wesselski Bebel I 228 No. 133.
J1461.p: A witty retort gives a humorous reason for why someone's hair has turned gray.

J1462.r: Man who wears a red cap after his father’s death says, “I can grieve just as much in red as in black.” *Wesselski Bebel I 125 No. 16.
J1462.p: A witty exchange turns on customary suits, using the word "suits" to make a clever reply.

J1463.r: Told that a forest dwarf with a long beard is a saint, a man replies: “If a long beard indicates sanctity, the goat is a saint.” *Wesselski Bebel I 129 No. 30.
J1463.p: A witty retort connects a long beard with holiness or sainthood.

J1465.r: Answered: “You may not fight, but you encourage your men to do so.” Jacobs Aesop 220 No. 79.
J1465.p: A captured trumpeter argues that he should not be punished because he never fought, he only blew his trumpet.

J1467.p: In a storm at sea a sailor jokes that everyone must now drink from the same cup, meaning the sea, since a man normally drinks from his own cup.

J1467.1.p: A sailor in a storm prays that the gods will sink the ship, reasoning that gods never do what people ask of them.

J1468.p: A famous glutton eats an enormous amount at a duke's invitation, then apologizes for eating so little, blaming illness and promising to do better next time.

J1471.p: A eunuch, reproached for his mutilation, replies that misfortune is no shame; the only shame is deserving the suffering you endure.

J1472.p: A princess asks three brothers what is the most beautiful thing in the garden, and the youngest answers "yourself," winning her hand.

J1473.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 206 (No. 5); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1473.p: A man dreams he is given nine coins and demands ten; on waking he realizes it was a dream and says he will accept the nine.

J1473.1.r: A joker sends him 999. He says that he will trust God for the other coin. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 220ff. No. 54.
J1473.1.p: A man prays for a thousand gold pieces and declares that he will not accept even one less.

J1474.r: Citizen: “Aren’t you afraid of drowning?” Sailor: “How did your ancestors die?” Citizen: “All of them in bed.” Sailor: “Aren’t you afraid to go to bed?” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 264.
J1474.p: A sailor remarks that all his ancestors drowned, a grim and ironic joke about his family's fate.

J1475.p: A peddler scolds his waiting dog and tells it to get ready to go, but the dog answers that it has nothing to carry and the peddler is the one who is late.

J1476.r: River: “What is your name?” Hide: “Hard hide.” River: “Hunt another name; I’ll soon soften you.” Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 403), 101 (ST 148); Halm Aesop No. 381.
J1476.p: A proud hide is humbled by being put into a river, in a witty saying about pride being brought low.

J1477.r: Reply: “No need to go to Rhodes. Show us your jump here.” Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 480), 100 (ST 135); Halm Aesop No. 203.
J1477.p: A boaster claims a great jump at Rhodes and says he could prove it if he were there; the witty reply is to demonstrate it right where he stands.

J1478.r: The husband is also burned and weeps: “I am weeping because your accursed mother didn’t take you with her when she died.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 238 No. 115; Köhler-Bolte I 498; Indonesian: Coster-Wijsman 71 No. 129.
J1478.p: A wife burns her mouth on overhot soup and weeps, then claims her late father loved soup so much that she cries whenever she eats it.

J1478.1.p: An abbot burns his mouth and, when asked, says he is crying because so many have left the monastery.

J1481.r: She goes to a dying neighbor and says, “If you die, as you surely will, and go to Heaven, as you surely will not, ask my husband where he left the hammer and anvil.” The dying man’s wife replies, “If you go to Heaven, as you surely will, if you die as you surely will not, do not run around and get into trouble, but sit down by the Eternal Father and observe and keep still.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 93 No. 805.
J1481.p: After her husband's death a woman claims she cannot find a hammer and anvil, a witty reply to a question about her loss.

J1482.r: The parson refuses; “If you can’t keep the secret, you must not expect me to.” *Wesselski Arlotto II 263 No. 199.
J1482.p: A man tells a parson a secret and asks him to keep it, setting up a witty exchange about keeping secrets.

J1483.p: A witty exchange concerns horses that have run away.

J1483.1.r: Jester: “You did have a swift horse. When I had to stop because my horse was tired out, you went two miles further.” Wesselski Bebel I 207 No. 94.
J1483.1.p: A king and his jester flee from danger, and the king boasts that his horse is the swiftest. The jester gives a witty reply that turns the boast against him.

J1483.2.r: A man on a runaway mule is asked, “Where are you going?” “Wherever my mule wants to.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 181 No. 343; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1483.2.p: A witty answer to a question about where a runaway mule goes, the point being that it goes wherever it wants.

J1483.3.r: He says, “There are no such storms on sea as on the land.” *Wesselski Bebel II 107 No. 21.
J1483.3.p: A clever saying that a person who rides a borrowed horse with no skill is carried wherever the horse runs. A lightly comic remark about a horse running off with an inexperienced rider.

J1483.4.r: The rider: “I couldn’t; you see, it ended there” (pointing to horse’s head). India: Thompson-Balys.
J1483.4.p: Someone is asked why they did not stay on the horse, and gives a witty reply to the question about their fall or loss of the horse.

J1484.r: The man: “What is that?” Barber: “A smith shoeing horses.” Man: “I thought it was someone being shaved.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 226f. No. 473.
J1484.p: A joke in which an incompetent barber keeps cutting a customer's face, and when a noise is heard the customer gives a witty explanation of what it is.

J1485.r: He is annoyed. She: “Pardon me, I did not know it was you” Clouston Noodles 94.
J1485.p: A bride creeps up behind her husband in the dark and kisses him, and he mistakes her for someone else, or the mix-up is played for a joke.

J1485.1.r: She runs her hand over his face, says: “Young man, if you’re goin’ to do anything, you’d better be agittin’ at it, ‘cause Old Whiskers’ll be here pretty soon.” U.S.: Baughman.
J1485.1.p: A farmer shaves off his whiskers and cuts his hair short, then comes home late and slips into bed beside his wife, who mistakes him for her lover.

J1486.p: A lazy young man explains that he stayed in bed late because he was listening to a debate between industry and laziness. A joke about an excuse for sleeping in.

J1487.r: One: “I am past Grace.” The other: “I am at the devil and all his works.” *Clouston Noodles 222; England: *Baughman.
J1487.p: A father sends his two sons to school and later asks how they are doing, and his answer shows a humorous twist on their progress.

J1488.r: The guide: “What did the bear say to you?” “He said, never trust a coward like you.” Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 319), 126 (ST 349); Halm Aesop No. 311; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 422; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1488.p: A paid guide climbs a tree and leaves the traveler alone with a bear. The traveler plays dead, the bear sniffs him and goes away, and the guide later asks what the bear whispered in his ear.

J1491.r: Owner: “You did not paint as many birds as I told you to.” Artist: “The windows were left open and most of them flew out.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1491.p: An artist is hired to decorate a room and paints too few birds, a joke about a trickster who cheats his employer.

J1492.r: King pretends to see the picture. Courtiers reveal that there is no picture. Spanish: Childers.
J1492.p: A trickster painter fools a king: a man whose wife has cheated on him cannot see the picture, so the painter's work is judged by the king's reaction.

J1493.p: A daydreaming servant breaks his master's pots while lost in thoughts of future profits. He argues that he has lost more than his master, so he should not be blamed.

J1494.r: The lame cannot flee from the enemy; the one-eyed soldiers will not see enough to make them afraid. Spanish: Childers.
J1494.p: A captain explains why he takes lame and one-eyed soldiers into his army, as a joke about their unfitness.

J1495.p: A person runs away from a real or imagined ghost, a comic situation in which fear makes the person flee.

J1495.1.r: The man stops to rest; the ghost stops, says, “That was a good run we had!” The man says, “Yes, and as soon as I get my breath, I’m going to run some more.” U.S.: *Baughman.
J1495.1.p: A man runs from a real or imagined ghost, and the ghost runs alongside him.

J1495.2.p: A man tries to spend the whole night in a haunted house. One cat after another comes in and asks whether everything will be all right when Caleb comes. Finally the man tells them to say he was there and left, and he leaves.

J1500.p: A quick, sensible reply in a practical situation, which turns the tables on the person who speaks.

J1510.p: A cheat is caught out by his own trick and is cheated in turn.

J1511.p: A rule that is used against someone must also apply to the person who made it, so the trickster is caught by his own rule.

J1511.1.r: At table the peasant says, “We will only act as if we were eating.” At work the servant replies, “We will only act as if we were working.” *Type 1560.
J1511.1.p: A trickster pretends to eat or to work, and the other party is cheated or shamed by that same make-believe. The point is that a made-up rule cuts both ways.

J1511.2.p: A master makes his servant call turnips bacon, and the servant later turns the rule back on him, making the master call a cat a rabbit.

J1511.2.1.r: When man asks for his fee, other takes a frog and gives it to him: “Know that the frog of the Ganges is a cow.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1511.2.1.p: A servant bathing a rich man uses sand in place of sandalwood and claims the sand is sandalwood, so the rich man must accept the same false naming.

J1511.3.p: A wife pretends to have a sickness that only a great number of delicacies can cure, and her husband pretends the same illness, so she is cheated by her own trick.

J1511.4.p: After dinner a servant fakes a fit and sleeps, so the master fakes a fit and beats the lazy boy, curing him of laziness.

J1511.5.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 372; *Wesselski Mönchslatein No. 106; *Crane Vitry 269 No. 310.
J1511.5.p: A host spills his guest's wine so the guest must buy more, then comforts him by saying it means a plentiful year. The guest returns the same remark while drawing wine from the host's cask.

J1511.6.r: The porter throws down the load: “When anyone tells you that any part of this load is not broken, don’t believe him.” *Basset 1001 Contes II 391; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 260 No. 211; Chauvin VIII 139 No. 136; *Fb “sandhed”.
J1511.6.p: A man pays a porter with three worthless pieces of advice, and the porter takes revenge by giving him three equally worthless pieces of advice in return.

J1511.7.p: Friends tell a man the next day is Judgment Day and urge him to hold a feast, then he burns their clothes, saying they will not need clothes on that day.

J1511.8.p: A husband forbids his wife to think. While he is away she eats the chicken and leaves only two drumsticks, and when he asks for the chicken she says she did not think of him because he forbade thinking.

J1511.9.p: A master claims to have eyes in the back of his head, so a servant holds food behind him and eats it, since the master has not objected.

J1511.10.p: A priest who lent money to a Jew but refused a farmer calls the money counterfeit. The Jew replies that he burned the money as soon as he heard it was false.

J1511.11.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2423; Russian: Andrejev No. *2082.
J1511.11.p: A father scolding his lazy son speaks in Latin, and the boy answers by pretending he understands only Latin.

J1511.12.r: When the thieves come, the serf barks: “Dress, dress .... They take, take .... They lead, lead .... “ The master does not understand the barking and pays no heed to it—is robbed of his property. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2421.
J1511.12.p: A master orders his serf to guard the manor at night in place of a watchdog, so the serf becomes the dog.

J1511.13.p: Oisin receives a tiny pancake and a speck of butter at Patrick's house, and later gives Patrick a quarter of a wild boar while his servant gets only an ivy leaf and a rowan berry, returning the poor treatment.

J1511.14.p: A man scolds another for picking cherries overhanging the road, and is told things on the public highway belong to no one. He then invites the man to climb the tree and drives off with his horse and buggy, using the same argument.

J1511.15.p: Priests at an inn insist on good wine only, claiming they may drink only one kind at a time. On their return the host serves them all bad wine, and they claim the rule has been changed.

J1511.16.p: A lazy monk criticizes other monks for working in the garden, and they reply that he should eat spiritual food rather than material food, meaning he should go without food.

J1511.17.p: A man is cheated into buying an ox with a load of wood attached, and later he sells a sharper another ox for a handful of coppers and claims the hand as well in court.

J1511.18.p: Priests tell a dying woman that her unfulfilled request for mangoes must be paid for in golden mangoes given to them, and they burn her with iron when she had asked to be cauterized.

J1511.19.p: A vizier advises a doctor to surrender his wife to a love-sick prince, since everything belongs to the sovereign. The doctor replies that the prince is in love with the vizier's wife, not his own.

J1511.20.p: A goldsmith sells cheap thinly gilded gold, and a peasant pays him back by fooling him with a pot of dirt topped with a little gold-looking bit. The cheat is turned back on the cheater, showing that a rule must work both ways.

J1512.p: Someone makes an impossible demand, and is shown up by a clever answer that makes the demand look foolish.

J1512.1.p: A king orders milk from a hornless cow from every house in the land, so that he can drink it. The people make wooden cows and substitute bog-stuff for milk, and the king is forced to drink it himself.

J1512.2.r: “Let me have your other so that I can see whether the one I bring you matches.” India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1512.2.p: A one-eyed man is asked to return an eye that he never had, or that someone took, and a clever answer turns the demand back on the asker.

J1513.p: A cheat or trickster is cured or punished using his own method, so he is healed with his own medicine.

J1513.1.p: A student who poses as a healer hangs a sign saying "If he does not live, let him die" around a sick calf's neck. Later, when he becomes a parson and falls ill himself, people propose to cure him with the same remedy.

J1515.p: A hard command is evaded by the person who is ordered to do it, who insists that the one giving the order go first and so avoids the task.

J1515.1.p: A condemned man insists that the priest, who is also guilty, must lead the way, so that the father of an illegitimate child walks in front of the cross.

J1516.p: Two rogues swap objects with each other and each ends up cheating the other.

J1517.p: Thieves are fooled by a prearranged conversation that they overhear, which is planned to mislead them into a trap or a wrong action.

J1517.1.p: Thieves overhear a conversation that says mustard has risen in price, and they steal mustard and leave everything else behind.

J1517.2.p: Thieves overhear someone say that money is hidden in the wall or field, so they take a box filled with stones or dig up the field in vain.

J1517.3.p: Thieves overhear someone say that their money is hanging in the tree, and they climb up and are stung by hornets.

J1521.p: A swindler's scheme is spoiled, and the plan he set up to trick someone is turned against him.

J1521.1.r: “Perhaps I shall find a nearer road home up there and shall need my shoes.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 233 No. 96.
J1521.1.p: Tricksters persuade a simple man to climb a tree, planning to steal his shoes while he is up there. He tucks the shoes into his belt and takes them up with him.

J1521.2.r: *Wesselski Bebel I 154 No. 81; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 497.
J1521.2.p: A monk at a dying old man's bedside asks whether he has not promised gifts to the church. The old man, too weak to understand, nods yes, and when his son asks whether to throw the monk down the stairs, he nods yes again.

J1521.2.1.p: The clever wife of a king's adopted son keeps the dying king distracted so that he cannot disinherit her husband.

J1521.3.p: A ruler who has received gifts from his subjects later demands them as a duty. A fool sets the nobleman's bed on fire, and when told to put it out he refuses, since then he would have to keep putting out fires forever.

J1521.4.p: A woman leaves three coins with a headsman, who denies her claim. She fails to prove it by ordeal, so she claims more, and this time she succeeds in the ordeal, so an unjust oath is answered by another oath.

J1521.5.p: A person is caught out through his own words, trapped by something he says.

J1521.5.1.p: A claimant is told he must be satisfied with 'something' as payment for his services, and the 'something' turns out to be a dead cricket. The trickster catches the cheat by taking his words literally.

J1522.p: A stingy person is taught a lesson or made to look foolish for his meanness.

J1522.1.p: A man asks for a half-price shave, and the barber shaves only one side of his face. The customer must then pay the full remaining half-price for the other side.

J1522.2.p: A stingy man's children are feasted in his absence, and people think he must have been generous. He is thus shamed when his stinginess is revealed by the reality of his household.

J1525.p: A prince tries to frighten a poor girl, but she turns the tables. Later she repeats the prince's mocking words back at him to frighten him in return.

J1526.p: A soldier gives a clever, sharp reply to a superior officer, turning the officer's insult or order against him.

J1526.1.p: An army major takes a sentry's rifle and scolds him for letting himself be disarmed. The sentry then pulls a concealed pistol and demands his unloaded rifle back.

J1527.p: Priests wrongly interpret a king's dream and take his horses as payment. A trickster advises the king to announce a second dream demanding that the priests be cauterized, and the priests return the horses to avoid this.

J1530.r: Brown JAOS XXIX 43 n. 40, Penzer III 241, 250f., V 64ff., IX 152, 155; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1530.p: A foolish claim or action is answered by another equally absurd one, shaming the first person.

J1531.r: England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, U.S.: Baughman.
J1531.p: A borrower of goods makes absurd excuses for failing to return them properly, and the lender answers with equally absurd counter-claims.

J1531.1.p: A man borrows a golden pumpkin and returns a brass one, claiming the gold turned to brass. The lender then keeps the borrower's son and returns with an ape, claiming the boy turned into one.

J1531.1.1.r: “Tank of water caught fire.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1531.1.1.p: A borrower says his borrowed mill has given birth to a horse. The judge, a jackal, arrives late to the hearing.

J1531.2.r: *BP II 372; Chauvin II 92 No. 37; B[ö]dker Exempler; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer III 250, V 62, *64; Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 299.
J1531.2.p: A borrower who is accused of losing or damaging something returns an absurd excuse, and the lender answers with an equally absurd counter-story; for example, a man claims mice ate the iron he was lent, and the lender claims a falcon carried off the borrower's son.

J1531.2.1.p: A man says insects ate a boy's dog that he was keeping. The boy in turn says a buzzard carried off a borrowed mule, and so he gets his dog back.

J1531.3.r: *BP II 372 n. 2; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 213 No. 35; DeVries FFC LXXIII 273 n. 1; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 1705*; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1531.3.p: A borrower returns a pot together with a small pot, claiming the pot had a baby. He later borrows it again, keeps it, and claims it died.

J1532.p: A woman's absurd explanation for an unexpected pregnancy or child is answered with an equally absurd reply, shaming her.

J1532.1.r: *Type 1362; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 208; BP IV 130; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1532.1.p: A sailor's wife has a son while he is away and claims the boy came from eating snow. Later the husband gets rid of the boy and says he melted in the sun.

J1533.p: Absurd explanations are offered for how animals or people are born.

J1534.p: One partner claims to have caught a deer in his bird-net, and the other answers by pretending to watch water flow uphill.

J1536.p: A ruler's foolish claim or order is rebuked by a courtier who makes an equally absurd request or point.

J1536.1.p: A courtier mocks a king's foolish decision to send a bishop on a military mission by asking the king to give him an church post as well.

J1536.2.p: A king is told that trying to convert him to Hinduism is as absurd as turning a donkey into a cow or a black dog white. The absurd demand is turned back on the ruler to rebuke him.

J1539.p: A clever person answers one absurd statement or demand with another absurdity, showing the foolishness of the original. This is a general category of such retorts.

J1539.1.p: A priest forbids his female servant to wash clothes, then ostentatiously washes his own clothes himself. A bishop reverses the order, so the priest's own foolish rule is shown up.

J1539.2.p: A scholar proves by logic that two eggs or chickens on a table are really three. His host or father then takes one for himself, gives one to the mother, and tells the son he may have the third.

J1540.p: A general category of witty exchanges in which a husband and wife trade clever retorts and try to get the better of each other.

J1541.p: A husband gets the better of his wife through a clever trick or retort, turning her own tactics against her.

J1541.1.p: A man promises to give his wife only good words, then hits her with a prayer book, which technically keeps his promise.

J1541.1.1.r: Beats her—a joy to him and a sorrow to her. BP III 277f.
J1541.1.1.p: A man promises to share his wife's joy and sorrow and then follows the instruction so literally that he shares it in an absurd way.

J1541.2.r: *Wesselski Bebel I 228 No. 139; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1541.2.p: A quarrelsome wife keeps scolding, and her husband silences her by playing the flute loudly until she gives up.

J1541.3.p: A woman rejects her ugly husband's advances, and he calms her by saying he wants a handsome child.

J1541.4.p: A husband and wife separate and divide their property, with the husband keeping the house and giving the wife the road.

J1545.p: A wife gets the better of her husband through a clever trick or retort, turning his own tactics against him.

J1545.1.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 117 No. 98; Mensa Philosophica No. 73.
J1545.1.p: A beaten wife tells the sick king that her husband is a skilled physician who will only practice when well beaten. The husband is seized and whipped.

J1545.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 793; Wesselski Mönchslatein 109 No. 93; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 5 (Lee 198); Scala Celi 49a No. 275; *Hibbard 41 n. 12; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No 78; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1545.2.p: A husband disguised as a priest hears his wife's confession. She lists her lovers as a servant, a knight, a fool, and a priest, which are all himself at different times: he was her servant, then her knight, then a fool for demanding confession, and a priest for hearing it.

J1545.3.r: *Wesselski Theorie 175; Plattdeutsch: Wisser Plattdeutsche Volksmärchen (Jena 1922, 1927) II 98; India (Kashmir): Knowles 245.
J1545.3.p: A husband keeps complaining about his wife's cooking, but she always has another dish ready. When he says he would rather eat dung, she produces some.

J1545.3.1.p: A complaining husband is shown up when his wife proves she does far more work than he does in one morning.

J1545.3.2.r: She: “You will have to have some shoes first.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1545.3.2.p: A fault-finding husband threatens to hit his wife with her shoes, and she turns the question back on him.

J1545.3.3.p: A man who keeps threatening to leave his wife is mortified when she tells him to go. After he leaves, he pretends his buffalo is dragging him home.

J1545.4.r: *Type 875; *DeVries FFC LXXIII 275—284 passim; *Fb “kjæreste” II 153a; *BP II 349; Fansler MAFLS XII 63; Jewish: *Neuman, *Gaster Exempla 224 No. 196; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1545.4.p: A wife driven from home is allowed to take her dearest possession. She takes her sleeping husband with her, and this brings about their reconciliation.

J1545.4.1.r: *DeVries FFC LXXIII 278ff.; *Gaster Germania XXV 285ff.; *Wehrhan Die Sage 31ff.; *Bolte Montanus Gartengesellschaft 615 No. 80.
J1545.4.1.p: When the women of a besieged city are allowed to carry out their dearest possession, they carry out their husbands. This is the Weinsberg tale.

J1545.5.p: A husband tells his wife to close up her private parts, and she replies that he is the one holding the key. Her quick comeback turns his crude remark against him.

J1545.6.p: A wife, using her wits, wins back the fortune her arrogant husband has foolishly gambled or lost, and so humbles him.

J1545.7.p: A wife laughs and answers so cleverly that her husband is put off and stops trying to fondle a maid.

J1545.8.r: He upbraids her; she replies: “If you had really died I should have given myself up to be burnt.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1545.8.p: A husband pretends to be dead, and his wife suggests cutting the corpse in two so it is easier to carry away.

J1545.9.p: A husband threatens to drown himself, and his wife calmly shows him a deep spot in the stream where he can do it.

J1546.r: *Crane Vitry No. 235; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 392; Herbert III 19; Alphabet No. 141; Gesta Romanorum No. 126; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 46; Scala Celi 46b No. 260; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1546.p: A nosy wife is told a false secret about the council's decision that each man may have many wives, and she gullibly believes it. Her husband's joke exposes her overcuriosity.

J1550.p: A general heading for witty replies to people who borrow money or ask for favors and to those who lend or give them.

J1551.r: *Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 209ff.; Hindu: Penzer V 132 n. 2, 133, IX 155f.; cf. Nouvelles de Sens No. 9.
J1551.p: A trickster pays or claims to pay a debt with something imaginary, so the creditor is satisfied with nothing real.

J1551.1.r: *Chauvin VIII 158 No. 163; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 810; *Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 209; Tupper and Ogle Walter Map 113; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1551.1.p: A woman demands payment for a visit she only dreamed she had with a merchant, and she is shown the money in a mirror as her payment.

J1551.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 298; *Wesselski Gonnella 110 No. 10; *Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 210.
J1551.2.p: A penitent confesses that he had merely thought of sinning, and the priest says the thought counts as the deed. The priest sets a penance of four florins, and the penitent replies that he only meant to give the money, so he should be credited with having given it.

J1551.3.r: *Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 211; Nouvelles Récréations No. 3; Hindu: Penzer V 132.
J1551.3.p: A singer is repaid for his song with a mere promise of reward, so that words are paid back with words.

J1551.4.p: A man who asks for directions for healing is paid with directions for getting pay, so that words are exchanged for words.

J1551.5.p: A monk gives a man a stick in place of a candle he wanted to burn before a holy picture, claiming it works just as well. The man repays him by letting the monk touch his purse, which is a substitute for money.

J1551.6.r: “It is the soup from the soup of the hare.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 234 No. 97.
J1551.6.p: A man is given a hare as a gift. Later crowds arrive claiming to be friends of the giver and expecting entertainment, and he serves them only clear water.

J1551.7.p: A man claims ownership of some bulls because he dreamed of them, and he is given only their shadows in payment or return.

J1551.8.p: A clerk tells a customer to imagine that blue cloth is green. The customer walks out without paying, and when the clerk asks for payment, he says the clerk should imagine he has been paid.

J1551.9.r: The monkey to the grocer: “You sold half water and half milk.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1551.9.p: A man pays only half his money, throwing the other half into a tank, as a way of settling a debt.

J1551.10.r: Shows him the Host through window, and says: “Have hope and imagine you receive it.” The man shows the priest a coin through the window, and repeats the same phrase. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1844.
J1551.10.p: A priest gives the sacrament or treatment to a man sick with an infectious disease, usually as a way of avoiding or turning aside a payment.

J1551.11.p: A jester is given half of a picture and told to imagine the other half. Later he redecorates a house using only fragments of pictures.

J1552.p: A general heading for tales in which requests for loans are turned down with clever replies or tricks.

J1552.1.r: The owner goes to see what the ass says. The ass is unwilling. Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 223 No. 60.
J1552.1.p: A man wants to borrow a donkey, and the lender answers by consulting the donkey itself as if it had a say in the matter.

J1552.1.1.r: “Will you believe an ass and not a graybeard like me?” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 224 No. 65; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs. f. Vksk. 1954, 128; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1552.1.1.p: A man tries to borrow a donkey, and the owner claims the donkey is not at home. The donkey then brays, exposing the lie, and the borrower protests.

J1552.1.1.1.r: Whereupon master sticks his head out of the window, saying “Thou who art moving about at this time art the big fool: I have been seated all day in my house.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J1552.1.1.1.p: When servants say their master is not at home, the visitor replies that only a fool would go out in the midday heat, so the master must be the fool hiding indoors.

J1552.2.r: He is refused on these grounds: either (1) he has never found anyone to trust him, (2) he has never bought anything, or (3) he is rich and does not need an extension of time. *Wesselski Bebel II 121 No. 65.
J1552.2.p: A man who has always paid cash asks for credit, and the lender refuses, giving three reasons for saying no.

J1552.3.r: Reasoning: “If he had lent his horse this would not have happened to mine.” Settled by compromise. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1552.3.p: A man refuses to lend his horse, so the neighbor borrows another horse, works it so hard it is ruined, and its owner sues the man who refused to lend his own.

J1552.4.p: Two farmers ask a priest to lend each of them two measures of grain. He refuses the loan but gives each one measure outright, so he keeps two measures in total.

J1556.p: A lender pays back a borrower who tricked him in a loan by playing a similar trick in return.

J1556.1.p: A borrower of butter is given a pot of cowdung with a little butter on top. The lender repays him with a wooden sword covered in thin iron, a trick of equal deception.

J1559.p: A collection of witty replies about borrowing and lending money or goods that do not fit a single category.

J1559.1.p: An abbot gives a lawyer a fine horse as a gift. When the abbot later comes to Rome seeking help, the lawyer returns the horse, saying he did not know the abbot had a lawsuit there, so the gift was really a retaining fee.

J1559.2.p: A young man is freed from captivity by offering God as surety for the ransom. When he fails to return, the creditor robs a rich abbot who claims to serve God, and the young man later says the debt was paid by God's servant.

J1559.3.p: A student leaving university sends back a small coin as payment for his learning, saying he is really paying far too much for what he gained.

J1560.p: A heading for witty replies and clever tricks concerning how hosts and guests treat each other.

J1561.p: A host who has been inhospitable is repaid in kind by a guest who gets revenge.

J1561.1.r: *Wesselski Arlotto II 247 No. 153; *Wesselski Gonnella 130 No. 23; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 240.
J1561.1.p: Told that the food cooking is clothes being boiled, a trickster retaliates by throwing his own dirty shirt into the pot.

J1561.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 60; Scala Celi 104a No. 565; Alphabet No. 357.
J1561.2.p: An abbot has his innkeeper neglect his guests shamefully. A guest retaliates by telling the abbot he was lavishly entertained, and the innkeeper is dismissed.
