J1561.3.r: “Feed my clothes,” he says, “for it is they that are welcomed.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 416; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 222 No. 55; *Prato RTP IV 167; Herbert III 70; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1561.3.p: A man in poor clothes is ignored at a banquet. He goes home, changes into fine clothes, returns, and is then honored, showing that the hosts respected the clothes rather than the man.

J1561.3.1.p: A poor suitor is served the good supper that was prepared for a rich one, and he recites a satirical rhymed grace over it.

J1561.4.p: A servant takes revenge on a stingy master or mistress by bringing about a humiliation or shortage that exposes their meanness.

J1561.4.1.p: A stingy hostess claims she has no spoons, so she cannot give the guest anything to eat. A joker then brings his own spoons to the feast, leaving her without excuse.

J1561.4.2.p: A servant pays back a stingy master or mistress by pretending to be blind. The joke is that the servant's apparent loss of sight is a punishment for the stingy hosts' poor hospitality; the note says the bread has no butter.

J1561.5.p: A father gives his inhospitable daughter deceptive advice about cooking, so that her feast for guests is spoiled.

J1561.6.p: A poor man who is refused hospitality claims a rich man is a relative, then explains a 'box connection': his cart is made of boxwood tied to the rich man's boxwood tree. Embarrassed, the rich man welcomes him properly.

J1561.7.p: A guest who was ignored at the meal gets his share of food anyway, because grace is said in the host's name so the food is blessed for him too.

J1562.p: A host who is stingy and greedy at mealtime, grabbing the best food for himself and shortchanging his guests.

J1562.1.r: B turns the plate around: “See how all things turn about in this world.” A turns it back: “However the world may turn, with good friends like us the plate will always remain the same.” *Wesselski Arlotto II 222 No. 89; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1568*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1568*.
J1562.1.p: A greedy host turns the serving plate or dish so that all the good portions end up on his own side.

J1562.2.r: He takes the whole chicken saying: “Since everyone has a bird, I must have one too.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 583.
J1562.2.p: A greedy host serves small birds to his guests and a roast chicken for himself. Each guest takes one small bird, so only the chicken is left when the plate reaches the host.

J1562.3.p: A greedy host hides meat in his clothing to eat later, but the smell attracts his dog and gives him away.

J1563.p: Tricks and methods a host uses to deal with guests who are unwelcome, troublesome, or who will not leave.

J1563.1.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 259 No. 200; Wesselski Arlotto I 130 No. 51.
J1563.1.p: A guest keeps asking for more blankets. The host finally piles a ladder, a trough and other heavy objects on top of him until he cries out for help.

J1563.2.p: Guests make impossible demands, and the host's servant gets rid of them by sending them off on a hard, nearly impossible errand so they leave.

J1563.3.p: A host bakes bread with onions in it for a guest he does not want, so the guest will find the food unpleasant and leave.

J1563.4.p: Guests insult each other by calling one another ox and ass. The host serves the one called ox green grass and the one called ass fodder.

J1563.5.p: A housewife drives unwanted guests away by a trick or by frightening them off.

J1563.5.1.r: They flee. Tells husband they left because she refused to give them pestle. Husband pursues to give them the pestle, but they run the faster. (Cf. K2137.) India: Thompson-Balys.
J1563.5.1.p: A wife gets the pestle ready and tells the guests that her husband uses it against guests, so they flee.

J1563.5.2.p: Servants touch the cooking pot, so the food is considered unclean and the guests leave hungry without learning the real reason.

J1563.6.p: When hints fail to make unwelcome guests leave, the host has to use force to remove them. This is how a man deals with his sons-in-law.

J1563.7.p: The host stages a mock fight to frighten the guests away.

J1563.8.p: A priest drives away parasitic guests by telling them he has just heard the confession of a man who died of plague.

J1564.p: A talker keeps a person from eating by constantly interrupting or distracting him with talk, so the meal goes unfinished.

J1564.1.p: A servant is asked a question each time he tries to eat a date, so he keeps spitting it out. That night he takes revenge by bringing up his answers at embarrassing moments, when his master is trying to carry on an affair with the maid.

J1564.2.p: A rabbi who was once treated rudely is later invited to dinner. He keeps the guests laughing with jokes so they forget to eat, and the feast is ruined.

J1565.p: A host is repaid for offering a guest something unsuitable or unpleasant, with a retort that returns the same kind of treatment.

J1565.1.r: *Type 60; Wienert FFC LVI 54 (ET 141), 98 (ST 123); Halm Aesop No. 34; *Crane Exempla 202 No. 165; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 64 No. 13.
J1565.1.p: A fox and a crane invite each other to dinner and each serves food in a dish the other cannot eat from: the fox uses a flat plate, the crane a narrow bottle.

J1565.2.p: At a feast given by bees, the bugs cannot eat the honey, and at the bugs' dinner the bees cannot eat the dung served to them, so each side is repaid in kind.

J1565.3.p: A parrot and a cat, who share a crop, take turns each day inviting the other to dinner, each trying to cheat the other out of the food.

J1566.p: A guest rebukes a host for extravagant luxury, usually with a pointed remark or action.

J1566.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 475; *Crane Vitry 195 No. 149; Scala Celi 140a No. 784; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 29, Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1566.1.p: A philosopher spits in the king's beard because the only clean spot he can find at the royal table, uncovered by gold and jewels, is the king's beard.

J1566.2.p: A ruler turns down hospitality from a subject who spends more than he earns, judging that such a host cannot afford to entertain him.

J1573.p: A host rebukes a servant who has been careless or lazy in carrying out his duties.

J1573.1.r: Servant who leaves off the salt is instructed to bring in the step-ladder so as to see what is missing. Wesselski Bebel II 71 No. 159.
J1573.1.p: A host rebukes a servant for doing his job badly by providing a step-ladder to reach the table, so the servant must climb to set it.

J1575.r: Spanish: Espinosa III No. 192; Italian Novella: *Rotunda, Boccaccio Decameron I No. 8 (Lee 23).
J1575.p: A guest brings his own food to a stingy host's table, rebuking the host's meanness.

J1575.1.p: A suitor who is refused use of the girl's lamp, since her mother will not let him burn her oil, brings his own lamp and oil the next night and tells her he will stay as long as he likes.

J1576.r: Boccaccio Decameron I No. 8 (Lee 23), Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1576.p: A hungry man, asked by his host to suggest a picture of something never seen, replies that it should depict generosity, which the host has not shown.

J1577.p: A host extends a feast invitation that is deceptive, meaning the guests are not really welcome or the feast is not really given.

J1577.1.p: A host invites to his feast only people whose households have never been touched by death, a condition that no one can truthfully meet.

J1580.p: A group of clever, practical retorts that are connected with giving alms to the poor.

J1581.p: A stingy giver of alms is repaid in kind by a clever response to his meanness.

J1581.1.p: A poet gives the emperor a poem hoping for a reward; the emperor answers with a poem of his own, and the poet sends back two pennies, saying that is all he has. The emperor laughs, sees he has been outdone, and becomes the poet's friend.

J1581.2.r: He then throws pellets made of herbs at the steward, saying that there is great power in words, herbs, and stones: he has tried two of them and plans to try the third. He is given alms. Wesselski Mönchslatein 20 No. 14.
J1581.2.p: A clown begs for alms and gets nothing, so he repeats or strengthens his request in a clever way.

J1582.p: Someone puts counterfeit or worthless coins into the church offering, and is then caught or repaid for it.

J1582.1.p: A peasant always puts a bad penny in the offering, so the priest bakes a penny into the communion wafer and gives it to him; unable to swallow it, the peasant believes he is possessed, and the priest gets him to confess and promise to reform.

J1582.2.p: A priest burns sulphur instead of incense after parishioners put base metal coins in the collection, telling them their money buys nothing better. A clever retort to people who give worthless offerings.

J1583.r: Preacher tells parishioners (regarding the day’s offering): “You will get back 100 for 1.” Donor of a penny: “I’ll be glad to get back my capital!” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1583.p: A clever person, when asked for something, replies that he is interested only in the capital and not the interest, so he refuses to give up a fixed sum or to pay out a bit extra. A witty dodge about money.

J1593.p: A stingy king tells a trickster to ask for any reward he likes. The trickster asks the king to do something disgusting, and the king, bound by his word, must give a costly gift instead.

J1600.p: A general heading for miscellaneous clever practical retorts, where people answer tricky or foolish situations with quick, witty actions or replies.

J1601.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 134 No. 1550C, Espinosa No. 54.
J1601.p: A fool who has bought a new ass is asked by everyone how much it cost. He gathers the whole crowd and then announces the price in a way that makes the question absurd.

J1602.p: A philosopher gives a penny to a man who has been throwing stones at him, but advises him to throw at a rich man instead, who could give more. The man follows the advice and is arrested and hanged.

J1603.p: A man suffering stomach ache from eating bad bread is treated for his eyes, so that he can afterward tell good bread from bad. A joke about absurd treatment.

J1604.p: A very annoying man holds up others while haggling with a butcher. Meanwhile a parson slips the three fish the man has set down into his large sleeves. When the man searches in vain, the parson shows them and advises him not to let people cheat him.

J1605.p: A man steals a large sum, keeps half, and gives the rest to five hundred people. He argues that he has done one wrong but five hundred good deeds.

J1606.r: (Cf. K1955.1.1.) *Köhler-Bolte I 137, II 5714; *Anderson FFC XLII 359; Boccaccio Decameron X No. 2 (Lee 311ff.); Scala Celi 126a Nos. 685, 686; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1606.p: Two monks, entertained by a lord, say they must go to certain waters to recover their appetites. Instead they are locked in a room for a day, and their appetites return without any journey.

J1606.1.p: A hungry man refuses to eat fish intestines one evening, but the next morning he eats them readily. He is caught out by his own hunger after his earlier refusal.

J1607.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 359 n 3; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 72; **Feilberg “Hundens Testament” Festskrift til E. T. Kristensen 11ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 96.
J1607.p: The owner of a dog has it given a Christian burial. The bishop then pretends that the dog has left the church a large legacy in its will.

J1608.r: (Cf. K551.18.) Herbert III 53; Crane Vitry 147 No. 33; Baum MLN XXXVII 350; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1608.p: An ass skips the parliament of beasts. When the lion sends the fox and the wolf to summon him, he pleads a charter of exemption and offers to let the fox read it written in his hoof.

J1611.r: *Type 1373; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 232 No. 87, *II 185 No. 348.
J1611.p: A man buys three pounds of meat, and his wife eats it, then says the cat ate it. The man weighs the cat and finds it does not weigh three pounds, which proves the wife's story false.

J1612.r: Type 211***; Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 372), 98 (ST 126); Halm Aesop No. 322.
J1612.p: A lazy ass, loaded with salt, falls down in the river so the salt dissolves and his load lightens. His master then loads him with sponges, which soak up water, so that the next time he tries the trick his load is heavier.

J1613.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 100 No 84; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 389.
J1613.p: A Jew who has fallen into a pit refuses rescue on Saturday, his Sabbath. The next day he calls for help, but the Christians refuse to rescue him on Sunday, their Sabbath.

J1614.p: A parson boasts that his maid always answers that work is already done. A guest bets she can be caught out, so he asks whether she has thrown the parson's suit into the tub of water. She overhears the bet and has the suit in the water before he asks.

J1615.p: A tenant promises his daughter to his master against her will. When the master sends for what was promised him, the daughter sends the horse, which is led into the master's chamber.

J1616.p: Soldiers are refused entry to both hell and heaven. They remind Saint Peter of his denial of Christ, and he admits them.

J1617.r: The man: “If God were so omniscient he might have found me for the priest.” Wesselski Bebel II 119 No. 57.
J1617.p: A woman tells her brother that God sees everything. When he is ill and the priest is called, he hides under straw to avoid being seen, and the priest leaves him alone.

J1618.p: A monk's guardian, allowed only one word to ask a busy prince for something, says "Soup" and gets all the food he wants.

J1621.p: Two friends agree to share everything they earn. One returns with many wounds instead of money, and the other gives up the claim to a share.

J1622.p: A blacksmith and a horse-trader forced to share a bed trade jokes: the blacksmith dreams he is working the bellows, and the horse-trader retaliates by dreaming he spurs a horse into him.

J1623.r: When he claims to see two roast chickens, his wife takes the one chicken away and he falls into the fire trying to find the other. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 140.
J1623.p: A drunkard who sees double is cured of the problem through a clever trick or retort.

J1624.p: A woman who crosses herself at the sight of a priest, believing priests bring bad luck, is knocked down and trampled by the priest, who says, as you believe, so shall it be.

J1625.r: The second replies with a small bag of peppercorns: “My army is small compared to yours but has all the power of the peppercorn compared to your lifeless seed.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 722.
J1625.p: One king sends his rival a large sack of seed to show how many soldiers he has.

J1626.r: He throws the harp at his master’s head and breaks it to pieces: “There you have your sound.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 722.
J1626.p: An apprentice harpmaker is blamed because the harp he made will not sound.

J1627.p: A nobleman who has embezzled public money, when asked for an accounting, replies he will give one once his counsellors have accounted for their own dealings, and they drop the matter.

J1628.p: A traitor hanged naked in effigy later meets the citizens wrapped in many blankets, claiming he caught cold from the night wind while hanging naked on the gallows.

J1631.p: A shoemaker's apprentice greases a pair of boots as if they were a fowl, and the angry owner returns and breaks a window.

J1632.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 139 No. 1695A*, Keller.
J1632.p: A cobbler learns a minstrel's songs and sings them to take away his trade, so the minstrel sews the cobbler's leather into odd shapes in return. When they sing together, people see the contrast and favor the minstrel.

J1633.p: A man who gets no alms in a village rings the church bell for mass and tells the sexton it is for the death of brotherly love; the sexton rings another bell for the death of the man's patience.

J1634.r: *Chauvin II 148 No. 1, III 98 No. 2; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1634.p: A king, to test a favorite, says he will retire from the world and offers him the regency. On his philosopher's advice, the favorite says he will go with the king into retirement.

J1635.r: Mensa Philosophica No. 53; Shakespeare Jest Books III (Certayne Conceyts and Jeasts) 11 No. 22.
J1635.p: A robber gives a priest double the penance the priest imposed on him, and then takes the priest's horse.

J1636.r: Ruler to servant stealing his game: “If you wish any I’ll send you some.” U.S.: Baughman; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1636.p: A man excuses himself from a demand or duty by saying he has a family to support.

J1638.r: “It’s against the rules of our order to have any money on us.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1638.p: An innkeeper's merchant guest loses his fowl to a monk who cites the rules of his order. Later the monk offers to carry the merchant across a stream, asks if he has money, and when told yes, drops him in the water.

J1647.p: A priest asked to preach a short sermon keeps it short by telling the congregation only that they are wicked.

J1648.r: —, I wouldn’t start from here.” U.S.: Baughman.
J1648.p: A traveler asks the way to a place, and the local man, exasperated, gives a joke answer that the traveler should not start from here.

J1651.p: An unfit abbot is dismissed when he cannot find the needle every monk is supposed to carry; his carelessness in small things shows he will be careless in great ones.

J1652.p: An oracle declares that the first of three sons to kiss his mother will become king; one son kisses the earth, the mother of all.

J1653.p: A poor peasant gets past a busy lawyer by bringing a lamb along, whose bleating makes the lawyer grant him an audience.

J1655.p: Clever ways of hiding jewels or treasure so that thieves or others will not find them.

J1655.1.p: Jewels are hidden inside cow dung cakes, where no one would think to look.

J1655.2.p: Valuable rubies are concealed by baking them inside bread.

J1655.3.p: Coins are hidden in a jar of oil or pickles so they go unnoticed.

J1661.p: Clever reasoning in which a wise person works out hidden facts from small clues.

J1661.1.p: A wise person works out facts about someone or something simply by carefully observing it.

J1661.1.1.r: Solution: She is recognized as a she-camel by the footprints; she is blind because she feeds on only one side of the road; the wine dropping down has soaked into the earth; the vinegar makes bubbles; the heathen is not so careful in his manners as is the Jew. **Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 198ff.; Gaster Exempla 195 No. 51; *Penzer VI 287; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 101 No. 55.
J1661.1.1.p: A wise man deduces from a passing camel's appearance and load that it is blind in one eye, carries wine and vinegar, and is led by a heathen and a Jew.

J1661.1.1.1.p: From the way a camel is ridden, a wise person deduces that a pregnant woman is riding it.

J1661.1.2.r: *Type 655; *Fischer-Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 198ff.; *Gaster Exempla 195 No. 51; Herrmann Saxo II 265ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1661.1.2.p: After seeing the king dance following a dinner, someone deduces he must be illegitimate, and the king's mother admits an affair with a dancer.

J1661.1.2.1.p: By observing the magistrate's behavior, a wise person concludes he is illegitimate.

J1661.1.3.p: Seeing that a loaf of bread falls apart, a wise person deduces it was kneaded by a weak, sick woman.

J1661.1.4.p: From the shape of a mare's hoofs, a wise person deduces that her mother was a she-buffalo.

J1661.1.5.p: Seeing that a horse has drooping ears, a wise person deduces it was raised on donkey's milk.

J1661.1.5.1.p: An animal that cannot get enough to eat is deduced to have been raised on dog's milk.

J1661.1.6.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1661.1.6.p: Noticing that a jewel is warm, a wise person deduces that an insect is living inside it.

J1661.1.7.p: A wise person deduces that a prince plays with children because he was denied a normal childhood.

J1661.1.8.p: A wise person deduces from appearance that a thief who is one-eyed and long-bearded is named Kale Khan.

J1661.1.9.p: A banker recognizes an honest merchant by examining a single hair from his mustache.

J1661.1.10.r: Thief has no taste of salt on his body: he must have been immersed in fresh water recently. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1661.1.10.p: A wise man works out that a cauldron was stolen and buried in a river, since it is the only explanation for its disappearance.

J1661.2.p: A clever person works out facts about a situation by using senses like taste, smell, or drinking, rather than by sight or direct information.

J1661.3.p: Someone describes a group of approaching warriors without realizing who they are, and another person then identifies them.

J1662.r: *Type 105; *BP II 119; *Fb “kat” II 108b, “ræv” III 114a; *Krohn Am Urquell III 177ff.; Magoun California Folklore Quarterly IV 390ff., Jacobs Aesop 209 No. 38; Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 303), 143 (ST 492); Halm Aesop 65; *Chauvin III 54 No. 10; *Herbert III 36ff.—Roumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No 33 I*; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; cf. Africa (Angola): Chatelain 215 No. 37 (turtle goes into hole).
J1662.p: A cat has only one trick for escaping danger, while a fox knows a hundred, yet the cat survives by using its one trick and the fox is caught.

J1662.1.p: A female jackal saves herself and her husband through quick thinking, showing that a little wit is worth more than a great deal of it.

J1664.p: A clever person settles a disputed question with a surprising, ingenious answer.

J1664.1.r: Solution by man as umpire: neither as cold as windy season. India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1664.1.p: Animals debate which is the coldest season, and the answer given is either the rainy season or winter.

J1671.p: A coachman comes up with a clever way to make his horses run faster: he ties a bundle of hay to the shaft so the horses chase it.

J1672.p: A clever person exploits human weakness: he charges every bad man one penny and every good man two pennies, so he collects two pennies from everyone.

J1675.p: A clever person manages to deal successfully with a king, outwitting or handling him skillfully.

J1675.1.p: Clever methods for getting a king's attention when ordinary means fail.

J1675.1.1.p: Someone starts a fight in order to get the king's attention, because nothing else would win it.

J1675.1.2.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 287, 378.
J1675.1.2.p: A wife accuses her husband of stealing from her, a false charge that brings the case before the king and exposes a corrupt judge who has imprisoned her husband and detained her.

J1675.2.p: Clever ways of delivering bad news to a king who would kill the messenger.

J1675.2.1.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 362; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 111 No. 925B.
J1675.2.1.p: A messenger reports bad news so that the king himself speaks the unwelcome words, phrased as a question, so the messenger is not blamed.

J1675.3.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 836; Boccaccio Decameron X No. 1; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1675.3.p: A nobleman mocks the king's unfairness by comparing him to an ass that pours water where it is already plentiful, and the king's wealth goes where it is not needed; the king replies that this is the nobleman's fate, and later events prove him right.

J1675.4.p: A one-eyed king orders rocks counted on pain of death, and a clever man avoids saying the word "one," which the king takes as a curse on his eye, by naming the first rock in another way.

J1675.5.p: An abbot gives the king a unique concert by sorting hogs into singing voices such as tenors and basses, then pricking them so they squeal a tune.

J1675.6.p: A poet goes to the king to complain that his dwelling was destroyed, but the king demands a story first, so the poet recites a list ending with the destruction of his home.

J1675.7.p: A clever hero pretends to be dull-witted in order to take revenge on the king.

J1675.8.r: When steadily unable to be admitted to presence of a king, a clever man demands an interview saying he is the son of God come down to earth and will condescend to see the king. When asked to show the king Heaven and the path to it, the pretender retorts that when he was sent down by the Father, he was told to look to matters relating to this earth. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1675.8.p: A character who is the son of God goes to see the king.

J1678.r: Marriage. “Now that you are relatives you can settle it between yourselves.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1678.p: Two men cannot agree on a bride's dowry, so a third party tells each one's parent that the other has already agreed, and the dispute is settled.

J1682.p: A charioteer taunts his losing master with insults to make him angry, so that he fights harder in battle.

J1684.p: A poet uses words so obscure that a student cannot understand them, and so the poet defeats the student in argument.

J1700.r: **Clouston Noodles; *Field Myth of the Pent Cuckoo; *Types 1200-1349, 1381-1387, 1430, 1450, 1642, 1643, 1653B, 1675, 1680-1696, 1725, 1750, 1775; *Bolte Frey’s Gartengesellschaft No. 1; Köhler-Bolte I 135. — Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 299 No. 18; Hindu: Penzer V 67ff., 80ff., 113ff., 117 n. 1; Oceanic (German New Guinea, Banks Is., New Hebrides): Dixon 124f.; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 295ff. nn. 81, 84-87, 92, 95, 103, 109f., 109h, 109k, 109y 109bb, 109dd, 270a-270c, 271b, 286.
J1700.p: A general heading for stories about foolish people, who are simple, ignorant, or unwise.

J1701.r: *Types 1380—1404; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 187b nn. 145 —149; Christensen DF L 35; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière.
J1701.p: A foolish wife, who acts stupidly or without sense.

J1701.1.p: A wasteful, extravagant wife whose husband constantly criticizes and finds fault with her spending.

J1702.p: A foolish husband, who acts stupidly or without sense.

J1703.p: A whole town or country whose people are all foolish, so that they act absurdly as a community.

J1705.p: A general heading for foolish people belonging to particular social classes or occupations.

J1705.1.p: A peasant or farmer who is portrayed as stupid.

J1705.2.p: A Brahmin, a member of the priestly class, who is portrayed as ignorant and stupid.

J1705.3.p: Learned scholars or experts (pundits) who prove to be foolish.

J1705.4.p: A king who is portrayed as foolish.

J1706.p: A general heading for stories in which animals are portrayed as stupid.

J1706.1.p: A tiger portrayed as a stupid beast that is easily fooled.

J1710.p: A general heading for stories about the trouble that comes from keeping company with fools.

J1711.r: (Cf. J1742.) *BP II 555; **Field Myth of the Pent Cuckoo.
J1711.p: Foolish people set off on a journey together and get into one absurd mishap after another.

J1711.1.p: Sheep, a duck, and a cock are stranded together at sea; the duck swims and the cock flies up to the mast to escape.

J1712.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 263 No. 237; Christensen DF L 91; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 484.
J1712.p: Three men are greeted by a stranger and quarrel over who was meant, each claiming the greeting was for the biggest fool. They settle it by a contest of telling tales.

J1713.p: A married couple who are both foolish, acting absurdly together.

J1713.1.r: Husband actually knows from observation but wife thinks he has supernatural knowledge and spreads his fame India: Thompson-Balys.
J1713.1.p: A man works out from clues that his wife is baking cakes, even though he was not told. The joke turns on a foolish married couple, where the husband's guess gives away what was meant to be secret.

J1714.p: Wise men are shown keeping company with fools, and the tale often shows the bad results of that association.

J1714.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 26; Herbert III 192; Alphabet No. 722; Oesterley No. 67; Scala Celi 75a No. 428; Africa (Vai): Ellis 242.
J1714.1.p: A wise man goes along with a fool against his own better judgment, and both are put to death for their foolishness.

J1714.2.p: A wise man is talked into tasting water that has turned many people into fools, and he becomes a fool too.

J1714.3.p: A wise man refuses to join a foolish crowd who stay out in an unexpected rain after a long drought, and they punish him for not acting as foolish as they do.

J1714.3.1.p: Forty wise men predict a violent rainstorm but cannot convince the people. They hide in a cave, come out after the shower, and the people call them fools.

J1714.4.p: An author concludes that his book must be stupid because stupid people and gossips are praising it.

J1714.5.p: A silent old man in the king's presence asks the king what the king himself does when he is in company with a fool.

J1715.p: A fool objects to having other fools as companions and leaves when he is seated between two fools at the table.

J1717.p: Three foolish scholars are sent to a raja as the two-footed cattle he had demanded, the joke being that they are taken for livestock.

J1730.p: A general heading for stories of absurd ignorance, where a character fails to know things that everyone else would know.

J1730.1.p: A hero does not learn his own name until after his first adventure, a joke on his ignorance of who he is.

J1731.p: A city dweller is shown to know nothing about farm life and country ways.

J1731.1.p: A city girl asks whether turnips grow in the ground or on trees, showing she does not know where food comes from.

J1731.2.p: A stupid man is too proud to admit he does not know what honeycomb is, so he asks the innkeeper's wife to roast a slice of it.

J1732.p: A general heading for stories where a character does not recognize certain foods and handles them absurdly.

J1732.1.r: Type 1316*; cf. Christensen DF XLVII 216 No. 76.
J1732.1.p: A fool who has never seen sausage squeezes out its inside and takes the casing for a sack.

J1732.2.r: (Similar for watermelon, plums.) England, Canada, U.S.: *Baughman.
J1732.2.p: A fool who does not know bananas throws away the fruit and finds the rest bitter.

J1732.3.p: A woman who does not know tea serves the boiled leaves with butter as if they were a vegetable.

J1733.r: Wienert FFC LVI 60 (ET 222), 91 (ST 32); Halm Aesop No. 115.
J1733.p: A sheep does not understand why a pig being led to slaughter shrieks, so the pig's cries puzzle it.

J1734.p: A layman, someone without medical training, shows absurd ignorance about medicine.

J1734.1.r: “You will soon see,” says the man, expecting the analysis to tell. (Cf. K2321.1.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 857; Christensen DF L 72; ibid. DF XLVII 202f. Nos. 42, 47.
J1734.1.p: A farmer takes his master's urine to a doctor for examination, and the doctor is asked to tell where the man comes from based on it.

J1735.p: A simpleton cannot tell which of his hands is his right one when it is dark.

J1735.1.p: A numskull keeps a candle at his right side when going to bed so that he can tell which hand is his right.

J1736.p: Foolish people meet an animal they have never seen before and react absurdly to it.

J1736.1.p: Fools who do not know what a crayfish is shoot it and build a rampart around it.

J1736.2.p: Fools who do not know what an owl is attack it.

J1736.3.p: Fools who have never seen a pig capture one by trapping it in a pit.

J1737.p: A besotted lover fails to see the faults of the woman he loves.

J1737.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 407; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1737.1.p: A foolish lover fails to notice that his sweetheart has only one eye, and realizes it only after returning from an absence.

J1738.p: Simple people show absurd ignorance of church teaching and religious matters.

J1738.1.p: An ignorant priest, giving the last rites to a dying man, forces rolls of cloth down his throat instead of bread.

J1738.2.r: Argument: living God takes less for upkeep and he can be killed later. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 409; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1738.2.p: Peasants take their old crucifix to an artist to have a new one made, and when asked whether they want a living or dead figure, they choose living.

J1738.3.r: Christensen DF XLVII 205 No. 53A; U.S.: Baughman.
J1738.3.p: Simpletons are astonished to hear that God has a son.

J1738.4.r: Christensen DF XLVII 205 No. 53B; U.S.: Baughman.
J1738.4.p: Simpletons are shocked to learn that God's son has died.

J1738.5.r: No one rises. “What, are there no friends of Jesus in this house?” A cowboy rises to his feet: “Stranger, I don’t know who this man Jesus is. I never heard of him before, but I’ll stand up for any man who hasn’t got any more friends than he has.” U.S.: Baughman.
J1738.5.p: A backwoods preacher asks friends of Jesus to rise, and the congregation responds in a foolish way, as if standing up for the friendless.

J1738.6.p: A backwoods preacher tells a couple that they are living in darkness, and the wife replies that she has long been trying to get her husband to cut a window in the house.

J1738.7.p: Ignorant people are told a religious holiday is coming the next day; when a camel appears, they feast it.

J1738.8.p: Foolish men hide themselves so that God will not see their sin, as if God could not see them.

J1741.p: Priests or schoolmasters, who are expected to know Latin, in fact do not know it.

J1741.1.p: A rival city insists that the Gospel of Luke be read as the Gospel 'according to Pergamum', a joke on a priest or schoolmaster who cannot read Latin and misreads the text.

J1741.2.p: An ignorant schoolmaster misreads Bible passages, taking the 'Agnus Dei' prayer as a request for money and reading other scripture as orders for priests to live in luxury.

J1741.3.r: (Essentially same as X111.9.) Nouvelles Récréations No. 7.
J1741.3.p: A tale type where memorized Latin answers prepared in advance do not always work, because the examiner asks questions in a different order or wording.

J1741.3.1.p: A foolish student memorizes set answers for an oral Latin examination, but the questions come in a different order, leading to comic mix-ups.

J1742.p: A simple country person who goes to the big city and is baffled by its ways, customs and comforts, making foolish mistakes out of ignorance.

J1742.1.p: A countryman traveling to another land expects to meet people from his own village there.

J1742.2.p: Asked where he lives, a countryman gives his village name and directs the questioner to a big high house, which is not a sensible address.

J1742.3.p: Country men in a city inn order a whole portion of mustard, not knowing it is a condiment meant to be taken in small amounts.

J1742.3.1.p: A countryman visiting a rich relative in town refuses dessert by saying he is not hungry, not understanding the custom of serving sweets after a meal.

J1742.4.p: A peasant is surprised to learn that the king is no bigger or different in appearance than other men.

J1742.5.p: A countryman misunderstands the comforts of city life, for example mistaking a latrine for a kitchen or fearing that tall houses will fall on him.

J1742.5.1.p: A boy who has never seen a real carpet hops around the edge of the room to avoid stepping on the cloth covering the floor.

J1743.p: Foolish ignorance of the calendar or of when events happen, such as mistaking the season or dating events wrongly.

J1743.1.r: A stupid man at confession says, “I confess myself guilty of all sins that I have committed since Christ’s birth.” “Are you so old?” “Yes, and I have a brother who is three years older than I.” Wesselski Bebel II 106 No. 17; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 295.
J1743.1.p: A simpleton blames or counts all sins as having happened since the birth of Christ, mixing up the time of events.

J1743.2.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 89; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1743.2.p: A family fails to notice that Lent has started until Palm Sunday arrives, then explains that Lent will be short because the winter was short.

J1743.3.r: Woman misinterprets calendar notation “February 22, Wash. B’day.” Washes their bee-hives. North Carolina: Brown Collection I 697.
J1743.3.p: A foolish custom or joke in which a day is named for washing bees, showing confusion about a holiday or calendar day.

J1744.p: Foolish ignorance of what married couples do together, leading to comic blunders around marriage.

J1744.1.p: A bridegroom does not know what to do on his wedding night and makes a series of blunders.

J1744.1.1.p: On his wedding night a clumsy groom, unable to find the way into bed past the drawn curtains, climbs a bedpost and onto the canopy, then falls onto his bride, who screams for help.

J1745.p: Extreme and comic ignorance of sex and how it works.

J1745.1.p: A fool cannot tell whether nude figures are male or female, reasoning that they have no clothes on to show their sex.

J1745.2.p: A foolish girl does not understand what is happening to her when she has her first menstrual period.

J1746.p: A fool is ignorant of reading and does not understand what written letters are for.

J1746.1.p: A fool who reads a book keeps weeping because he thinks the letters have shrunk, since they looked large and fat when he was at school.

J1747.r: Is told: “Their wives and family.” He asks the archbishop about his family. (Cf. J2461.2.) Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J1747.p: A fool, expecting guests, asks what he is supposed to talk about with them.

J1748.p: A fool is ignorant of how spectacles are used, not understanding that they help the eyes see.

J1749.p: A miscellaneous absurd ignorance: a fool shows foolish lack of knowledge in various ways not covered by other headings.

J1749.1.p: A fool wrongly thinks the word "aforesaid" is a title of honor, like a rank.

J1749.2.p: An ignorant notary is unable to draw up a legal document, because the names of the people involved differ from those in his sample form.

J1750.p: One animal is mistaken for a different animal.

J1751.r: “I know you well enough, you have put on a blue coat.” Type 1317*.
J1751.p: A dung beetle is mistaken for a bee.

J1752.p: A wolf is mistaken for a colt and, while the man is away, it eats the mare.

J1753.p: A bear is mistaken for a dog.

J1754.p: A donkey is mistaken for a hare.

J1755.p: A fool mistakes an earthworm for a snake or some other dangerous monster.

J1756.p: A hero searching for a monster brings home a dog, a zebra and other animals, thinking each is the creature he seeks, which he takes to be a giant cat.

J1757.p: A servant sent to bring in the cows is found chasing rabbits, having mistaken them for cows.

J1758.p: A tiger, lion or similar wild animal is mistaken for a domestic animal.

J1758.1.p: A fool trying to steal a goat in the dark catches a tiger instead, thinking it is the goat.

J1758.1.1.p: A fool rides a tiger, believing it to be a large male goat.

J1758.2.p: A tiger is mistaken for a dog.

J1758.3.p: A tiger is mistaken for a donkey, so the fool treats the dangerous beast as a harmless domestic animal.

J1758.4.p: A thief takes a leopard for a calf or donkey and tries to steal or handle it, with foolish results.

J1758.5.p: A drunkard rides a lion, thinking it is a donkey.

J1758.5.1.p: A thief mistakes a lion for a horse and tries to ride or take it.

J1758.6.p: A foolish husband mistakes tiger cubs for jungle cats, ignoring his wife's sensible judgment.

J1759.p: A general heading for other tales in which someone mistakes one animal for a different animal.

J1759.1.p: A Scotsman mistakes a moose for a mouse and asks what rats look like in this country.

J1759.2.p: A hunter mistakes a louse on his eyelash for a game animal and shoots at it several times before realizing his error.

J1759.3.p: A numskull believes fireflies are mosquitoes carrying lanterns to find their victims.

J1759.4.p: A bull is mistaken for a horse.

J1759.4.1.p: A calf is mistaken for a colt, a young horse, as part of the bull-for-horse mistake.

J1759.5.p: A cat's tail is mistaken for a worm.

J1760.p: A general heading for tales in which an animal or person is mistaken for something else.

J1761.p: An animal is mistaken for an inanimate object.

J1761.1.r: *Chauvin VII 9 n. 1 No. 373A; *Fb “fish” I 296b, “[ö]” III 1159b; Gunter 84; *Gaster Beiträge 53ff.; *Reinhard PMLA XXXVIII 448 n. 84.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; Hindu: Penzer II 193; B[ö]dker Exempler 286 No. 34; Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 210.
J1761.1.p: Sailors mistake a sleeping whale for an island and light a fire on its back.

J1761.1.1.p: A turtle is mistaken for an island.

J1761.1.2.p: A fool mistakes a serpent for an island, a foolish misunderstanding of what a creature is.

J1761.2.p: A white mare is mistaken for a church.

J1761.3.r: Chauvin II 90 No. 32; B[ö]dker Exempler 286 No. 34; Penzer V 58f.
J1761.3.p: A glowworm is mistaken for a fire, and a bird who tries to warn the monkeys is killed for her trouble.

J1761.4.p: A fish is mistaken for chewed sugar-cane, so foolish people throw their fish away.

J1761.5.p: A wolf is mistaken for a log of wood.

J1761.6.p: A person mistakes a snake for a flute and tries to play it, and the snake bites the would-be player. The tale is a joke about foolish misunderstanding.

J1761.6.1.p: A blind man takes a snake for a whip. He mistakes the living animal for an ordinary object.

J1761.7.p: A foolish person mistakes living toads or beetles for lost food and eats them.

J1761.8.p: A man mistakes a dragon for a log and sits down on it.

J1761.9.p: A bear is mistaken for a floating log or a blanket.

J1761.10.r: *Taylor English Riddles in Oral Tradition (Berkeley, 1951) 582 n. 11; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1761.10.p: Several blind men each feel a different part of an elephant and wrongly conclude that the whole animal is like the part they touched, such as a log, a rope, a fan, or something endless.

J1761.11.p: A fool mistakes dung beetles for fruit and eats them.

J1762.p: An animal is mistaken for a human being.

J1762.0.1.p: Animals are mistaken for messengers sent to deliver a message.

J1762.1.p: A goose is mistaken for a tailor. In a haunted house, the goose is thought to be a tailor who snips at the devil with scissors.

J1762.1.2.p: A crab is mistaken for a tailor, as the goose was in a similar tale.

J1762.2.p: A bear riding on a haywagon or horse is mistaken for a preacher.

J1762.2.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1705; Russian: Andrejev No. *2103.
J1762.2.1.p: A godless man is tricked into thinking a bear is a saint, attacks it, and barely escapes with his life.

J1762.3.p: A crab caught on a tiger's tail is mistaken for a man chasing the tiger.

J1762.4.p: A deer is mistaken for a man carrying a basket on his head.

J1762.5.p: Bees or wasps are mistaken for people such as Jutlanders.

J1762.6.p: A monkey dressed in clothes is mistaken for a nobleman.

J1762.8.p: A strong man meets a bear in the forest, takes it for a German, and wrestles with it. After strangling the bear, he fears he has killed a man.

J1762.9.p: A foolish wife believes goats' heads are human heads.

J1763.p: A person is mistaken for an inanimate object, such as a stone, a hat, or a statue. The fool takes a living human for a thing.

J1763.1.p: A small priest wearing a large hat is taken by someone to be just a hat lying about. The mistake comes from the hat hiding the person beneath it.

J1763.2.p: A girl sitting or standing still is taken for a stone. Her stillness leads someone to believe she is only a rock.

J1763.3.p: A soldier asleep on a tomb or in a chapel is taken for a stone statue lying there. His stillness makes him look like the carved figure.

J1765.p: A person is mistaken for an animal. The fool takes a human being to be a beast.

J1765.1.p: A shepherd is taken to be a she-ass, a female donkey. The mistake turns a man into a beast in someone's eyes.

J1765.2.p: A man is taken to be a sheep. Someone mistakes the human for a flock animal.

J1766.p: One person is taken to be a different person. Someone confuses one human with another.

J1766.1.p: Horsemen are thought to be men riding on cattle. Someone misreads the mounts, taking horses for oxen or cows.

J1769.p: Other creatures or beings are mistaken for something else, a catch-all for mistaken identity not covered by the more specific headings.

J1769.1.p: A giant is taken to be a hill. The fool mistakes the huge living being for a landform.

J1769.2.p: A dead man is thought to be alive. Someone mistakes a corpse for a living person.

J1769.2.1.p: A man who is horrified of corpses sleeps beside one, believing it to be alive. He does not realize the body is dead.

J1769.3.p: In the dark a fool lays his hand on a demon, believing it is a male goat he has come to steal. He discovers his mistake only after touching it.

J1770.p: An inanimate object is mistaken for something else. The fool confuses one thing with another.

J1771.p: An object is taken to be a living animal. Someone mistakes a thing for a creature.

J1771.1.p: A large tree is thought to be a snake, and people kill it with guns and spears. The fool attacks a tree believing it is a dangerous serpent.

J1771.2.p: An old sausage or sausage roll is taken for a frightening animal. Its shape or appearance makes someone think it is a creature.

J1771.3.p: An object is thought to be a turkey. Someone mistakes a thing for the bird.

J1771.4.p: A bush is thought to be an elephant. Someone mistakes the plant for a large animal.

J1771.5.p: A fool mistakes an island for a large dog. The idea is that something seen from a distance is taken for an animal.

J1772.p: A fool takes one object for a different one, with absurd results. This heading introduces the more specific mistakes listed beneath it.

J1772.1.r: *Type 1319; *BP I 317ff.; *Köhler-Bolte I 323; *Clouston Noodles 38; *Fb “æg” III 1142a; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 249 No. 163; Christensen DF XLVII 208 no. 63.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 157; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “oeuf”, “âne” “lièvre”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
J1772.1.p: A simpleton mistakes a pumpkin for an ass's egg and expects a colt to hatch from it. When a rabbit runs out, he thinks it is the colt.

J1772.1.1.r: “I don’t see how we raised this so quick.” U.S.: Baughman.
J1772.1.1.p: A small boy checks the bedbug eggs under his pillow each morning, and one day finds a terrapin there, so he thinks terrapins hatch from bedbug eggs.

J1772.1.2.p: Potatoes are mistaken for irregular eggs or eggs of the earth, a foolish misreading of what grows in the ground.

J1772.2.r: Cuts his mouth. Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 268), 107 (ST 199); Halm Aesop No. 223.
J1772.2.p: A dog mistakes a mussel shell for an egg and tries to eat or handle it as one.

J1772.3.p: Coins are mistaken for red beans, so a fool tries to cook or plant them as if they were beans.

J1772.3.1.p: Coins are mistaken for uncooked cakes, a foolish confusion of money with food.

J1772.4.r: N. A. Indian (Peoria, Kickapoo, Potawatomi): Michelson JAFL XXX 494.
J1772.4.p: A culture hero's pubic hair is mistaken for bear hair, a foolish confusion of body hair with an animal's fur.

J1772.4.1.p: A peasant up a tree sees the pubic hair of an ardent husband's wife and takes it for a calf's tail.

J1772.5.p: A man puts a food bowl on his head, thinking it is a helmet.

J1772.6.p: Fish bones in soup are taken for underdone peas, and the fool eats or serves them as peas.

J1772.7.p: Fools think the evening star is the morning star. The note adds the joke that they start a morning journey the evening before.

J1772.8.p: Cotton pods knocked off by a bullock are taken for lumps of the bullock's fat.

J1772.9.r: Christensen DF XLVII 192 No. 18; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1772.9.p: Excrement is mistaken for meat, and so a fool eats it.

J1772.9.1.p: A simpleton mistakes excrement for berries and tries to sell it.

J1772.10.p: A gun is mistaken for a clarinet, so one man blows into it while another presses its barrel as if it were the keys.

J1772.11.p: A boot is mistaken for an axe-sheath, a foolish misidentification of an everyday object.

J1772.12.p: A foolish tiger thinks a dog's tail is a gun.

J1772.13.p: A frog mistakes cattle for a distant country, not understanding what they are.

J1772.14.p: A fool sees a ferry boat with eight oars and mistakes it for an animal with long legs wading through the stream.

J1780.p: Foolish people mistake ordinary things for devils, ghosts, or other supernatural beings.

J1781.p: Someone takes an ordinary object for the devil.

J1781.1.p: A steamship is mistaken for the devil.

J1781.2.r: Knocked to pieces. Type 1321*; Christensen DF XLVII 187; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1679*.
J1781.2.p: A watch is mistaken for the devil's eye.

J1781.3.p: A glowing wheel is taken for the devil.

J1782.p: Someone mistakes an ordinary thing or creature for a ghost.

J1782.1.p: A robber or a dog in a church is taken for a ghost.

J1782.1.1.p: Cows in a church are mistaken for ghosts.

J1782.2.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 137 No. 101; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 47 No. 101.
J1782.2.p: Dough dropping onto the floor is mistaken for a ghost, and the man decides the place is haunted.

J1782.2.1.p: The sound of water dripping onto a dinner pail is mistaken for a ghost using a pick in a mine.

J1782.3.p: A noise in a house is mistaken for a ghost.

J1782.4.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3445, Legends Nos. 872ff.; U.S.: Baughman.
J1782.4.p: A man sleeping in a stable or abandoned cabin thinks the animals that come in are ghosts and kills them.

J1782.5.p: An animal carrying a lighted candle is mistaken for a ghost.

J1782.6.p: A person dressed in white is mistaken for a ghost.

J1782.7.p: A sleepwalker is taken for a ghost until people discover who it is.

J1782.8.p: A person in a haunted house shoots off all his own toes, thinking they are ghosts.

J1783.p: Something is mistaken for a corpse.

J1783.1.p: A butter cask is mistaken for a dead man, and fools knock it in two.

J1784.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3446, Legends Nos. 875-885.

J1784.1.p: A boy's laughter is taken to be the laughing of spirits, so the people who hear it wrongly assume ghosts are present.

J1785.p: A fool mistakes an ordinary animal for a devil or ghost and reacts with absurd fear or misplaced action.

J1785.1.p: A grasshopper is mistaken for the devil.

J1785.2.p: A crab is mistaken for the devil.

J1785.3.p: A donkey or ass is mistaken for the devil.

J1785.4.p: A man sees a Hereford cow at night, takes it for the devil, and defiantly declares his own piety, saying he is a psalm singer and a worshiper of God.

J1785.4.1.p: A man speaks to a colt, taking it for Satan, and declares that he is a righteous man and a psalm singer.

J1785.5.p: In the dark, a fool sees a cat's glowing eyes, mistakes them for embers, and when the cat attacks him he believes it is the devil.

J1785.6.p: A fox hidden in a coffer is mistaken for the devil.

J1785.7.p: A black sheep is mistaken for the devil.

J1786.p: A person is mistaken for a devil or ghost, and the mistake leads to a comic or frightening result.

J1786.1.p: A man dressed as a demon is taken for a real devil, and thieves flee in terror.

J1786.2.p: A woman is taken for a devil, and thieves run away in fright.

J1786.3.p: A man is mistaken for Famine or Cholera personified and is feared accordingly.

J1786.4.p: A priest who is exorcising a demon is himself mistaken for a demon and beaten to death.

J1786.5.p: A lion mistakes a man for a devil or ghost.

J1786.6.p: Men who see their wives with hair for the first time think they are witches and run away from them.

J1786.7.p: A lion thinks the man riding on its back is a monster and is frightened by him.

J1786.8.p: A man is falsely reported dead, so people flee from him as though he were a ghost.

J1789.p: At night, something harmless is mistaken for another frightening object, such as a ghost or devil.

J1789.1.r: Type 1322**; Christensen DF XLVII 212 No. 68; Russian: Andrejev 1322**; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1789.1.p: A windmill is mistaken at night for a holy cross, a church, or God.

J1789.2.p: A person mistakes the ticking of a clock for mice gnawing inside it.

J1790.p: A person takes a shadow for a real object or living being and reacts to it as if it were solid.

J1790.1.p: A foolish man sees his own shadow as another man chasing him and runs in fear.

J1790.2.p: A person mistakes his own shadow for a thief and beats it.

J1790.3.p: A monkey watching a tiger attack what it thinks is his shadow is so frightened that he falls out of a tree.

J1791.p: A person takes a reflection in water for the real object reflected and tries to get it.

J1791.1.r: Type 1335; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 241 No. 124; *Köhler-Bolte I 90, 498; Christensen DF XLVII 181.
J1791.1.p: A foolish man, seeing the moon reflected in a pool, thinks a cow has swallowed the moon when it hides behind a cloud, so he kills the cow to get it back.

J1791.2.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 241 No. 124; Christensen DF XLVII 217—18 no. 78; American Negro: Harris Nights 100 No. 19.
J1791.2.p: A foolish man sees the moon in the water and throws a rope in to rescue it, but falls in himself. Then he looks up and sees the moon in the sky, and is glad it was saved.

J1791.3.r: *Type 34; *Dh IV 230f.; *Fb “øst”; *Clouston Noodles 44; *Field Pent Cuckoo 18; Köhler-Bolte I 107; Christensen DF XLVII 217—18 no. 78; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 206f.; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 295 n. 81; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 357 (cf. J1791.4).
J1791.3.p: A man or animal sees the moon reflected in water, takes it for a cheese, and dives in after it.

J1791.3.1.p: A wolf, thinking the moon's reflection in a well is cheese, tries to drink the well dry to get it.

J1791.3.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 62 (ET 246), 119 (ST 287); Halm Aesop No. 218.
J1791.3.2.p: Dogs by a river, seeing food in the water, try to drink the whole river dry to reach it.

J1791.3.2.1.p: A demon tries to recover an object from a river by drinking the river dry.

J1791.3.3.p: Fools see the moon's reflection in water and take it for gold, diving in after it.

J1791.3.4.p: Jackals jump into a well after the sound of drums and are killed.

J1791.4.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 426; *Chauvin II 85; B[ö]dker Exempler 275 No. 13; Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 270), *105 (ST 178); Halm Aesop No. 233; *Crane Vitry 140 No. 18; Scala Celi 19a No. 111; Jacobs Aesop 199 No. 3.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 357 (cf. J1791.3).
J1791.4.p: A dog crossing a stream with meat in his mouth sees his reflection, thinks it is another dog with meat, dives for it, and loses his own meat.

J1791.5.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 270a.
J1791.5.p: A person tries to attack or catch an enemy he sees reflected in water, mistaking the reflection for the real enemy.

J1791.5.1.p: A person shoots at an enemy's reflection in the water, thinking it is the enemy himself.

J1791.5.2.p: A man throws a stone at his own reflection in the water, thinking it is someone else.

J1791.5.3.p: A frog leaps into the water to attack what it takes to be an elephant, but it is only the elephant's reflection.

J1791.6.r: Indonesian, Melanesian: Dixon 227 n. 34; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 270b.
J1791.6.p: A person dives into water after the reflection of a beautiful woman, thinking it is the real woman.

J1791.6.0.1.p: A woman dives into water three times, trying to catch the reflection of a man she has seen peering down at her from a tree. She mistakes the reflection for the real man.

J1791.6.1.r: *Type 408; BP II 121ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 9; Indonesian: Dixon 226.
J1791.6.1.p: An ugly woman sees a beautiful woman reflected in water and thinks it is herself, so she is proud of her beauty.

J1791.6.2.p: An ogre sees a beautiful woman's reflection in water and tries to drink the lake dry to get her.

J1791.7.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 276 No. 311; Penzer VI 86f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 17; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 441; American Negro: Harris Remus 68 No. 14.
J1791.7.p: A man fails to recognize his own reflection in the water and takes it for someone else.

J1791.7.1.p: A simpleton thinks his reflection in a jar of melted butter is a thief, so he strikes at the jar and breaks it.

J1791.8.r: Chauvin II 89 No. 28; B[ö]dker Exempler 284 No. 30; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1791.8.p: A goose dives for a star she sees reflected in the water, thinking it is a fish. The next day, when she sees a real fish, she lets it get away.

J1791.9.p: Foolish people see a bee's nest reflected in water and try to carry off the whole well to get it.

J1791.10.r: Thinks it is gold. Penzer V 115 n. 1.
J1791.10.p: A fool sees a golden-crested bird reflected in water and mistakes the reflection for the real bird.

J1791.11.r: Spanish: Espinosa III 206f.; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 37 No. 25.
J1791.11.p: Someone dives for fruit that is only reflected in water, while a rascal steals the real fruit.

J1791.12.p: An elephant is frightened by the moon's reflection in water, which appears to shake and move.

J1792.p: Someone mistakes a picture for the real thing it depicts.

J1792.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 276), 107 (ST 196); Halm Aesop No. 357.
J1792.1.p: A dove sees painted cups of water and dashes into them, thinking they are real water.

J1793.r: Jacobs Aesop 204 No. 20; Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 405), 124 (ST 333); Halm Aesop No. 47.
J1793.p: Someone mistakes a mask for a real face.

J1794.p: Someone mistakes a statue for a living person who is the original of it.

J1795.p: Someone mistakes an image seen in a mirror for a picture.

J1795.1.p: A foolish demon sees his reflection in a trickster's mirror and becomes convinced he has been captured.

J1796.p: Someone believes moonlight is a physical substance that can be gathered or handled.

J1796.1.p: Men build a hedge to keep the moonlight in, believing it is a substance that can be enclosed.

J1800.p: Miscellaneous foolish cases where one thing is mistaken for another.

J1801.p: Someone sees breath in the cold air and thinks it is tobacco smoke.

J1802.p: A foreigner hears words in a language he does not know and wrongly takes them to be insults.

J1802.1.r: (Cf. J1152, J1741, X111.7.) Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. III (N.F.) 173-8.
J1802.1.p: A foreigner asks several questions about ownership, a wife, or a funeral, and each answer is “I don’t understand,” which he takes to be someone’s name.

J1803.p: An uneducated person misunderstands learned or technical words and gives them a foolish meaning.

J1803.1.r: “No, I am not from that place; I am from Schmich.” *Wesselski Bebel II 126 No. 80.
J1803.1.p: A cleric is asked whether he is of legitimate birth, and the Latin phrase used is misread as a question about something else.

J1803.2.p: A simple person misunderstands the expressions a doctor uses and takes them literally or wrongly.

J1804.p: Two people try to talk using only signs and gestures, and each misreads the other's meaning.

J1805.p: Other cases where a word is misunderstood and the mix-up leads to a foolish result.

J1805.1.p: Two words that sound alike are confused with each other, causing a foolish mistake.

J1805.1.1.p: A man is told to cover the house with straw, but he hears a word that sounds like the word for wife and so covers his wife with straw.

J1805.2.p: A person does not know an unusual word and so misunderstands what is said, with foolish results.

J1805.2.1.r: Father finds Prince Sobur. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1805.2.1.p: A father asks his daughter what to bring back from his journey, and she answers “Sobur” (wait), which he misunderstands.

J1805.3.p: A dim-witted man who has forgotten a name keeps saying he has lost it, and people dive into a tank hunting for treasure he supposedly lost.

J1805.4.p: A fool is given money to buy food but goes around asking for something called “something” because he cannot name what he wants.

J1806.r: Christensen DF XLVII 176, 196; American Negro: Harris Nights 230 No. 39, Work JAFL XXXII 403, Parsons MAFLS XVI 32.
J1806.p: A person sees the setting sun and wrongly thinks it is a fire.

J1809.p: Other cases where one thing is taken for something else entirely.

J1809.1.p: An old woman sneezes, and the loud noise is mistaken for gunfire.

J1810.p: Natural events and physical happenings are misinterpreted by foolish or ignorant people.

J1811.p: The cry of an animal is misunderstood and taken to mean something it does not.

J1811.1.r: *Wesselski Bebel II 158 No. 183. Cf. BP II 535.
J1811.1.p: A lost simpleton hears an owl's hoot and takes it to be a message or an answer to him.

J1811.1.1.p: When an owl hoots, an old maid answers it as if it were a person, calling out “Anybody, Lord!” or naming the young man she hopes to marry.

J1811.2.p: A man mistakes the cries of a frog for something else and draws a foolish conclusion from it. The joke rests on the misreading of a natural sound.

J1811.3.p: A man who is lost in the woods hears a turkey's gobble and misreads it as a message or a sign. The humor comes from the mistaken meaning he gives the sound.

J1811.4.p: A fool hears a rooster crowing and takes it to mean something it does not. The crow is read as a message that makes no sense.

J1811.4.1.r: Hears a rooster crow, saying: “Cocky kuko! It’s the same everywhere!” He returns home. England, U.S.: *Baughman.
J1811.4.1.p: A henpecked husband hears a rooster's crow as a message about his situation and decides to leave home. He acts on the misreading of the crow.

J1812.p: A fool misreads some other ordinary sound as a meaningful message or a threat. The motif covers noises other than animal cries.

J1812.1.p: A fool thinks the rattling of seeds inside their pods is people insulting him. He reacts to the imagined insults, and in one version he burns a field.

J1812.2.p: Rabbits mistake the sound of waves for a great danger approaching them. They flee in panic from a harmless noise.

J1812.3.r: .” The rain drops: “Here he is..” The little bell: “He is hiding here..” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1264*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1264 I*.
J1812.3.p: A man hears fermenting dough make noises and takes them as a warning or a curse aimed at him. The bubbling dough is misunderstood.

J1812.4.p: A person hears the hissing of a fire and thinks it is the noise of muffins being cooked. The sound is misread as food cooking.

J1812.4.1.p: A person misreads the noises a fire makes and misunderstands what is happening. In one version a hunchback jumps into the fire and burns to death.

J1812.5.p: A person misreads the sound of someone snoring as a sign of something else, such as a request or a message. The snore is taken for speech.

J1812.5.1.p: A foolish thief hears a sleeping man snoring and thinks the snoring is the man asking for food. He takes the sound as an invitation.

J1813.p: A fool misunderstands what happens when food is cooked or prepared. He draws a mistaken conclusion from a normal cooking process.

J1813.1.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 412 No. 11.
J1813.1.p: A fool sees mushrooms shrink when put in water and thinks his wife has eaten part of them. He kills his wife over the mistaken belief.

J1813.2.p: A fool sees milk boiling and thinks it is overflowing, so he lets it run over. He fails to act because he misreads the boiling.

J1813.2.1.p: A numskull believes his prayers have stopped the milk from boiling over. In fact his wife has secretly added cold water to the pot.

J1813.3.p: A fool sees a boiling pumpkin and thinks it is talking. He mistakes the bubbling and noise of the pot for speech.

J1813.4.r: Christensen DF XLVII 177 No. 5, cf. 192 No. 18.
J1813.4.p: A fool sees a boiling pot sitting on the floor and thinks it is cooking itself. He takes the pot's activity for self-cooking.

J1813.5.p: Fish dance about in a cooking pot so that they seem to be many. A cook eats one of them, and then none are left to be seen.

J1813.6.p: A person takes a handful of black pepper and puts it into his mouth, instead of using it to season food while cooking. He misunderstands what pepper is for.

J1813.7.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2439*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1710*.
J1813.7.p: A peasant serving tea to a priest puts in far too many ingredients, including sugar and bacon, so the tea is salty and ruined.

J1813.8.p: A small boy left to watch the dinner runs to church and reports that the sheep's head has eaten the dumplings, when really he let it happen.

J1813.9.p: A fool cooks every bean he has for a single meal, and the resulting pile of food fills the whole room.

J1813.9.1.p: A foolish servant cooks all the rice for one meal, a stupid mistake in portion sizing.

J1813.10.p: A dim-witted person thinks a boiling pot is attacking him and smashes it to stop it.

J1814.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 210 No. 23; U.S.: Baughman.
J1814.p: A numskull, hearing a brook flowing while he urinates, mistakes the sound and waits a day and a half for his business to finish.

J1815.r: Type 1281; *Wesselski Bebel I 231 No. 144; Danish: Christensen DF L 65, Nyrop Dania I (1890) 283ff., cf. II 68ff.; U.S.: Baughman.
J1815.p: A fool takes the shoes from a hanged man's swollen feet, and a calf in his room is blamed for eating the body, so the people burn the house to destroy it.

J1816.p: A fool believes gold is being destroyed when snails crawl over it, mistaking the slime trail for damage.

J1817.p: A fool thinks his own belly is talking to him and stabs himself, because he misunderstands the noises of other animals shouting at him.

J1818.p: A fool misreads what an animal is doing and draws a wrong, absurd conclusion from it.

J1818.1.p: A fool sees a bull urinating and wrongly thinks it is bleeding.

J1819.p: Miscellaneous foolish misunderstandings of natural physical events, such as weather, objects, or processes.

J1819.1.p: Fools believe a thorn bush stops stinging at night, so they handle it without fear after dark.

J1819.2.p: A simpleton sleeping in a cold room breaks the window to let the cold out.

J1819.3.p: A fool wakes with a sleeping mat over his head and thinks it is still night, because he cannot see daylight.

J1820.p: A general category of foolish acts that come from a mistaken understanding of a situation.

J1821.r: They see a waving flax-field, and, thinking it is the sea, jump in to swim. *Type 1290; *BP III 205; Köhler-Bolte I 112; Christensen DF XLVII 195 no. 20; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “lin”, “pêche”; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1821.p: Foolish people take a literal, absurd action after misunderstanding a situation, such as swimming or fishing in a flax field. Their mistake leads them to act inappropriately.

J1821.1.p: A fool tries to swim in mist or fog, mistaking it for water.

J1822.r: Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 63 (to Gonzenbach No. 13).
J1822.p: A fool sweeps with a stick instead of a broom, having misunderstood what the tool is for.

J1823.p: A fool misunderstands church customs or ceremonies and acts inappropriately because of it.

J1823.1.p: A fool misunderstands the images of Christ and reacts absurdly to them.

J1823.1.1.p: A fool sees the image of Christ raised up to the church beams on Ascension Day and accuses Christ of tricking people into thinking he has gone to heaven.

J1823.1.2.p: A man refuses to go near a crucifix because a statue of Christ once fell on him in church and broke his arm; told it is a different image, he insists it is the son of the first and just as dangerous.

J1823.1.3.p: On Palm Sunday a maidservant meets priests leading the donkey that carried the Jesus figure, runs home and reports that the Lord has mounted and left.

J1823.1.4.p: A dim-witted man, seeing people wave palms on Palm Sunday, thinks they are trying to knock the figure of Jesus off the donkey.

J1823.2.r: The fools walks up and strikes the bishop: “You have made this shouting in the church.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 49.
J1823.2.p: At a wedding, after a period of silent prayer, the bishop starts a chanted responsive reading, and a fool takes this as a breach of the peace and a cause for a fight.

J1823.3.p: A dim-witted person thinks that putting out the lights in church means a fight is about to start.

J1823.4.p: A person decides to move away from Muslim land so that Allah need not be feared, misunderstanding the reason for the fear.

J1824.p: A numskull refuses communion because his sister died soon after eating the consecrated bread, thinking the bread caused her death.

J1824.1.p: Other foolish misunderstandings about the meaning or effects of communion.

J1825.p: A Turkish ambassador misunderstands Christian ceremonies and makes a ridiculous report about them to his king.

J1825.1.p: The Turkish ambassador reports that Christian laws are useless, since good people do not need them and bad people do not reform because of them.

J1826.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 52; *Wesselski Bebel I 194 No. 64; Alphabet No. 239.
J1826.p: A nobleman praises his falcon, and his fool, thinking the praise means the bird is good to eat, kills it and is disappointed by its taste.

J1827.r: I knew his father and mother and they were both honest people.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 51.
J1827.p: A pope writes to a king calling him 'our dear son Frederick,' and a fool protests that this is a lie because the king is no priest's son.

J1828.r: Left!” etc. He asks what kind of wood the boat is made of. Later he gets a log of that wood and tries to make it obey commands. Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 258.
J1828.p: A fool sees a boat with rowers obeying commands like 'Right!' and takes the boat itself to be obedient.

J1831.p: A landlord angrily throws a dish out the window, and a numskull throws out all the rest, thinking the landlord wants to eat outdoors.

J1832.p: One man accidentally jumps into a river, and when he calls out, his companions think he wants them to follow and all jump in and drown.

J1833.p: A numskull, seeing a fly on a bishop's nose while the bishop snores, thinks the fly is killing him, and strikes at it.

J1833.1.p: A numskull shoots at a grasshopper that has landed on his friend's shoulder and kills the friend.

J1833.1.1.p: A boy strikes at a fly on his sister's breast, which seems to turn into a nipple, and the girl thinks the brother caressed her.

J1833.1.2.p: One man strikes at a partridge that has landed on a second man's head.

J1834.p: Foolish men, mistaking the situation, bury a living person in place of the corpse they had lost.

J1835.p: A fool becomes angry at a goat chewing its cud, believing the goat is mocking him by imitating his chewing.

J1836.p: A fool sees coins lying by the road but leaves them there, not realizing they are money.

J1838.r: (Cf. J1782.8.) North Carolina: Brown Collection I 699.
J1838.p: A man mistakes his own toe for a snake's head and cuts it off.

J1842.p: A foolish person undergoes or performs a surgical operation that serves no purpose, done because of a misunderstanding.

J1842.1.p: A foolish female devil thinks her pubic hair has been lying to her, so she pulls it out along with the skin.

J1842.2.p: A fool cannot answer because his mouth is full, so people think he has abscesses in his cheeks and let them cut them open.

J1842.3.p: A bird is seen protruding from a king's stomach, and the king's men cut it out with swords, which kills the king.

J1842.4.p: A child's stomach is split open in an attempt to cure him of wandering.

J1845.r: The delegate slips and falls, cursing: “The devil may take you!” The serfs outside think this was the congratulation, and all cry in chorus: “You and your family!” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1708; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII 98 No. 14.
J1845.p: Serfs offer congratulations to their master on an occasion that is actually a misfortune for him, having misunderstood the situation.

J1846.r: (Cf. J1851, J1856, J1871.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1677*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1681 I*; Prussian: Plenzat 75.
J1846.p: A numskull prepares for his brother's wedding when the event is actually his father's funeral; on the way home from town he destroys what he bought.

J1849.p: A general heading for foolish actions taken because of a misunderstanding that do not fit other categories.

J1849.1.p: A fool takes a realistic story as true and acts on it.

J1849.1.1.p: Someone tells a fool a story about a deer, and the fool sets off to chase it.

J1849.2.p: A jackdaw tries to swallow sparks from a glowworm, mistaking them for food or fire it can eat.

J1849.3.p: A numskull strikes all the matches in a box one after another just to find out whether they work.

J1849.4.p: A soldier posted to guard a cannon decides to quit because nobody can move the cannon, so he judges his duty finished.

J1850.p: A general heading for stories where a fool gives gifts to, or sells things to, an animal or object as if it were a person.

J1851.p: A fool gives a gift to an animal or an object as if it could receive and value it.

J1851.1.p: A fool gives gifts to frogs, treating them as if they could receive and appreciate presents.

J1851.1.1.p: A simpleton throws money into a pond for the frogs, thinking they will count it.

J1851.1.2.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 139 No. *1693, Espinosa III 147.
J1851.1.2.p: A simpleton feeds his wheat to the frogs instead of taking it to the mill to be ground.

J1851.1.3.p: A simpleton throws money to frogs as payment, because they frightened his fleeing donkey out of the water.

J1851.1.4.p: A simpleton takes wool to a pond so that frogs and toads can weave it.

J1851.2.p: A simpleton hears birds calling and gives them gifts, as if they were people.

J1851.3.p: A simpleton gives a gift to an inanimate object, as if it could receive it.

J1851.3.1.p: A simpleton tries to stop up a hole by pushing money into it.

J1851.4.p: A grateful simpleton puts money into the anus of a sheep, believing the sheep has helped him.

J1852.r: *Type 1642; *BP I 59f.; *Chauvin VI 126 No. 280; Fansler MAFLS XII 352.
J1852.p: A simpleton sells goods to animals, expecting them to pay for what they take.

J1852.1.p: A simpleton sells a cow to a bird and expects payment; when he comes for his money, the bird flies to a rubbish heap where the fool finds a treasure.

J1852.1.1.p: A simpleton sells balls of thread to a great lizard, and the next day he finds a treasure at the same spot.

J1852.1.2.p: A simpleton sells oil to an iguana.

J1853.r: *Type 1642; *BP I 59; Köhler-Bolte I 135; Spanish: Espinosa III 147.
J1853.p: A simpleton sells goods to an inanimate object, as if it could pay.

J1853.1.r: *Chauvin VI 126 No. 280; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 211 No. 426; Fansler MAFLS XII 352; Clouston Noodles 144; Spanish: Espinosa III 147; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 4.
J1853.1.p: A simpleton sells goods to a statue, because he was told to avoid talkative buyers and the statue is the only one that never talks.

J1853.1.1.r: (Cf. J1852.1.) Type 1643; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 211 No. 426; Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 459), 138 (ST 430); Halm Aesop No. 66; Chauvin VIII 94 No. 65; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 4.
J1853.1.1.p: A simpleton sells goods to a statue, and when it will not pay he smashes it to pieces and finds a treasure inside.

J1856.p: Food is given to an inanimate object, as if it could eat.

J1856.1.p: A simpleton feeds meat to cabbages.

J1860.p: A simpleton or trickster punishes an animal or object absurdly, as if it were human and had done wrong.

J1861.r: The rascal: “Let me alone; he knows well enough what he has done.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 210 No. 20.
J1861.p: A rascal beats an ox for escaping from him, not realizing that the ox is the same animal that strayed onto his land and got away.

J1862.p: A man's coat is stolen while he leaves his donkey alone; he takes the donkey's saddle and says he will return it if the donkey returns the coat.

J1863.p: A cow is punished for the misdeeds of her calf. The fool thinks a parent should answer for the mistakes of its young.

J1863.1.p: A man beats the calves because the bull has butted him over the fence. He takes out his anger on the wrong animals.

J1863.2.p: A wolf is punished for the misdeeds of his father. The fool holds a son responsible for what his father did.

J1864.p: A man whips his gun when it fails to fire on a rainy day. When it finally goes off, he shoots a deer, so he thinks the beating worked.

J1865.p: In a land where sickles are unknown, a new sickle is punished by being drowned. The new tool cuts off a man's head, so the people punish it as a wrongdoer.

J1865.1.p: A sickle is punished by being tied in the top of a tree. The men who try this hang themselves in the attempt.

J1866.p: A man takes revenge on animals by killing them in great numbers. He avenges himself on a whole kind of creature instead of the one that wronged him.

J1866.1.p: A man avenges his brother's death by slaughtering wild pigs in large numbers. He takes revenge on the whole herd for one death.

J1867.p: A man punishes a part of his own body that has offended him. He blames his own body part for an error and punishes it.

J1867.1.p: A man beats his foot for slipping. He blames his own foot for the fall instead of the ground.

J1870.p: A fool shows misplaced pity for animals or objects, treating them as if they had human feelings and needs.

J1871.r: *Type 1291; BP I 521; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 250 No. 165; Missouri French: Carrière.
J1871.p: A numskull sees cracks in the ground and pities them so much that he greases them with the butter he is taking home.

J1872.p: A numskull hears limbs creaking in the wind and, feeling sorry for them, holds them apart. While he is stuck between them, his enemies take advantage of him.

J1872.0.1.p: A fool's creaking wagon stops making noise, so he decides it has died and cremates it.

J1872.1.p: A numskull climbs a tree to help a cuckoo so that it can call louder than the one in the neighboring forest. Meanwhile a wolf eats his horse.

J1873.p: A fool keeps animals or objects warm out of misplaced kindness, as if they felt cold like people.

J1873.1.p: A fool makes shoes for animals as well as for men, because he expects a cold winter.

J1873.2.r: Köhler-Bolte I 71; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 140 No. 1651; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1873.2.p: A fool gives a cloak to a stone to keep it warm.

J1873.3.p: A fool warms the stove by putting wool into it, wasting the wool while trying to keep the stove warm.

J1873.4.p: A king orders houses built to keep howling jackals warm in winter. A rascal takes the money meant for the building.

J1874.p: A fool shows absurd pity for a beast of burden by trying to lighten its load, even when that makes no sense.

J1874.1.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 229 No. 490; *Fb “sæk” III 720b; *Clouston Noodles 19; Field Pent Cuckoo 3; England, U.S.: Baughman; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1874.1.p: A rider lifts the sack of meal onto his own shoulders so that the donkey does not have to carry it.

J1874.2.p: A man hangs a bag of meal on one side of the saddle and balances it with a rock on the other side, to spare the animal.

J1875.p: A fool attributes human feelings such as fear, sorrow, or homesickness to inanimate objects.

J1875.1.r: The fool: “Everything tries to escape from death.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 183 No. 346.
J1875.1.p: A nut kernel that slips out of a fool's hand is imagined to be trying to escape its death.

J1875.2.p: A woman mistakes the bubbling of a boiling porridge pot for the pot complaining.

J1875.3.p: Foolish people try to carry a sea wave home in a bamboo rod, and when it stops moving they decide it is homesick for the sea.

J1875.4.p: A numskull believes a coin is weeping because it is damp with sweat from his hand after he has held it a while.
