J1879.p: A miscellaneous category of foolish sympathy shown to animals or objects that does not fit the more specific headings.

J1879.1.p: People drag their carts up onto the roof to shelter them from the sun.

J1880.p: A miscellaneous category of foolish behavior in which animals or objects are treated as if they were human.

J1881.p: A fool expects an animal or object to make a journey or do a task entirely by itself.

J1881.1.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 272 No. 281; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III 147; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 72 No. 130.
J1881.1.p: A fool sends an object off on its own to travel to a destination, expecting it to arrive without anyone carrying it.

J1881.1.1.p: A fool throws cheeses down a slope so they will roll home by themselves.

J1881.1.2.p: A fool lets one cheese roll downhill and then sends a second cheese after it to bring the first one back.

J1881.1.3.r: Clouston Noodles 36; Field Pent Cuckoo 5; *BP I 521 n. 1; England: Baughman; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa III 147; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 417f.
J1881.1.3.p: A fool sends a three-legged pot home to walk there by itself.

J1881.1.4.p: A fool throws a table off a sledge and expects it to go home by itself.

J1881.1.5.r: I came a shorter way.” Scotland: *Baughman.
J1881.1.5.p: A man sends his spinning wheel home by itself and then asks his wife whether it has arrived yet; when she says it has not, he replies that he thought as much.

J1881.1.6.p: A fool lays a sickle in the field and tells it to cut the grain.

J1881.1.7.p: A fool sends a letter home by floating it on a flooded river.

J1881.2.p: A fool sends an animal or object off alone, expecting it to find its own way to a destination without a person guiding it.

J1881.2.1.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 272 No. 281; Spanish: Espinosa III 147.
J1881.2.1.p: A fool loads a donkey with goods and orders it to go home by itself, as if it could find the way and deliver the load unaided.

J1881.2.2.r: Field Pent Cuckoo 6; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J1881.2.2.p: Foolish people send money by a rabbit, expecting the swift animal to carry it to the landlord in time.

J1881.2.3.p: A fool places fish in a stream and tells them to stop at his house, as if the fish could understand and obey.

J1882.p: A fool tries to teach animals skills or manners that they cannot learn, as if they were people.

J1882.1.p: A fool believes chickens can be taught to talk and tries to train them to do so.

J1882.2.r: *Type 1675; *BP I 59; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 224 No. 63; *Fb “tyr” III 908b; Christensen DF XLVII 229; England: Baughman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1882.2.p: A fool is told, falsely, that his donkey or ox has been educated and has become mayor, and he believes it.

J1882.3.p: A fool trains an elephant to beat a drum, as if the animal could be educated for that work.

J1883.p: A trickster joins a dance with bulrushes, mistaking their waving in the wind for dancing and taking part in it.

J1883.1.p: A simpleton speaks to a field of reeds as if they were people who could hear and answer him.

J1884.p: A woman tries to tire out her rival's boat to win a race, but ends up exhausting only herself, since the boat cannot get tired.

J1885.r: “Wretches, your house burns and yet you sing!” Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 291), 135 (ST 413); Halm Aesop No. 214.
J1885.p: A boy roasts snails and they make noise as they cook, and he is rebuked for it as though the snails were singing on purpose.

J1886.p: A fool dresses his hens in black clothes and tells people they are mourning their dead mother.

J1887.p: Fools chain a wheelbarrow that was bitten by a mad dog, to keep it from biting others.

J1888.p: An old woman, delighted by the sound of a cathedral organ, prays for the organ to come play at her house and tells it where she lives.

J1891.p: A fool blames an inanimate object for a misfortune that it could not have caused.

J1891.1.r: He says to the wines, “Have peace among yourselves and don’t quarrel or I’ll throw you out the window.” *Wesselski Bebel II 102 No. 14.
J1891.1.p: A man who has drunk many different wines becomes sick and blames the wines, which he imagines are quarreling inside him.

J1891.2.p: A carpenter on his deathbed refuses to forgive the nails that ruined his tools.

J1891.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 406), 123 (ST 317); Halm Aesop No. 94.
J1891.3.p: A fool accuses the sea of cruelty, though the sea says it was calm and the wind stirred it up and broke the ship.

J1892.p: A boy tells his mother not to catch the cock, saying it must keep its freedom or they will suffer for it.

J1894.p: A learned man speaks Latin while hunting, thinking that the birds will not understand him and so cannot escape. The joke is that he treats animals as if they could not understand ordinary speech.

J1895.p: A woman believes a calf's bleating is an accusation that she stole grain from the harvest, and she begs people not to believe what the calf said.

J1896.p: Foolish people believe that inanimate objects are born, grow, and die the way animals do.

J1896.1.p: Foolish people believe that stones reproduce and multiply like living creatures.

J1900.p: A general heading for foolish stories in which someone shows an absurd lack of knowledge about how animals behave or what they need.

J1901.p: Foolish people show absurd ignorance about how hens and other animals lay eggs.

J1901.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 362), 106 (ST 184); Halm Aesop No. 111.
J1901.1.p: A woman wants her hen to lay many eggs, so she overfeeds it, and the hen stops laying altogether.

J1901.2.p: A dim-witted person feeds hens hot water, expecting them to lay boiled eggs.

J1902.p: Foolish people show absurd ignorance about how eggs hatch.

J1902.1.r: (Sometimes puts on honey and feathers before sitting on the eggs.) Type 650; *BP I 316; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 212 No. 433; *Wesselski Bebel II 146 No. 148; Christensen DF XLVII 210 No. 63; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “oeuf”; Spanish: Espinosa III 147 Nos. 181—188; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 4.
J1902.1.p: A dim-witted person sits on eggs to finish hatching them, and warns others to be quiet so they do not frighten the eggs.

J1902.2.p: A dim-witted person tries to hatch a calf out of a cheese, as if a young animal could come from it.

J1903.p: Foolish people show absurd ignorance about how animals eat and drink.

J1903.1.p: When a calf will not drink, a peasant woman throws water on its back, as if it could drink that way.

J1903.2.p: A seller of milk is refused by the customer, so the dim-witted seller puts the milk back into the goat's mouth, thinking it will flow back into the udder.

J1903.3.r: When told to feed it three times a day he says, “A working man must have more to eat than a pig.” *Wesselski Bebel I 141 No. 56.
J1903.3.p: A farmer who wants to fatten a pig feeds it only twice a day, which defeats his purpose.

J1903.4.r: Decision: it lives on air. India: Thompson-Balys.
J1903.4.p: A puzzled person asks how an elephant can eat when it has a tail at each end, showing a silly misunderstanding of its body.

J1904.p: Foolish people show absurd ignorance about where an animal should be kept.

J1904.1.r: *Type 1210; *Köhler-Bolte I 66, 135; *Fb “ko” II 241a, “tyr” III 908b; Christensen DF XLVII 219 No. 81; English: Clouston Noodles 55; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 295 No. 15; Spanish: Espinosa III 147 Nos. 181—188.
J1904.1.p: A foolish owner takes a cow, or a hog, up to the roof to graze.

J1904.2.r: **Field Pent Cuckoo; Clouston Noodles 27; England: Baughman.
J1904.2.p: Fools build an enclosure to keep a cuckoo in. She flies over the hedge, and they claim the hedge was not built high enough.

J1904.2.1.p: Fools try to hedge in the cuckoo so they will have summer all year round, since the first cuckoo's call marks the coming of summer.

J1904.2.2.p: A foolish owner belles and fences in deer as if they were goats, and the deer simply jump the fence and run away.

J1904.3.p: A foolish owner makes hogs sleep in trees to break them of their dirty habits, ignoring what hogs are really like.

J1904.4.p: A foolish person builds a nest in a tree for a fish, not understanding that fish live in water.

J1904.4.1.p: A fool thinks fish will climb trees like buffaloes, so he expects them to be able to get up into the nest he built for them; a numskull also wonders what will happen if the river burns up.

J1905.p: A general category of foolish ignorance about how to milk animals, showing a lack of basic knowledge of livestock.

J1905.1.p: A fool stops milking his cow for a month, hoping she will then give a large supply of milk for a feast.

J1905.2.p: Foolish people try to milk a male donkey.

J1905.3.p: Two brothers share ownership of one cow, one owning the front end and the other the rear. The front owner tries to drive the cow while refusing to let the rear owner milk her.

J1905.4.p: A fool asks the owner of oxen why he does not milk them, since he is not working them.

J1905.5.p: Foolish people try to get cows to make curds before they are milked.

J1905.6.p: A fool kills a cow to get all her milk at once.

J1906.p: A general category of foolish ignorance about how to slaughter animals.

J1906.1.p: A fool tries to kill a bullock by striking its hindquarters instead of its head.

J1908.p: A foolish attempt to change an animal's basic nature, which cannot be altered.

J1908.1.r: *Type 217; **Cosquin Études 403ff.; *Fb “kat” IV 255a; *Wesselski Arlotto II 238 No. 131; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J1908.1.p: A man trains a cat to hold lighted candles on its head. When a king releases a mouse, the cat drops the candle and chases the mouse, showing its true nature cannot be trained away.

J1908.2.r: *Hertel Zs. f. Vksk. XXII 244; **Rohde Kleinere Schriften II 212ff.; Wienert FFC LVI *45, 71, 78 (ET 34, 351, 444), 86 (ST 1); Halm Aesop No. 88; Jacobs Aesop 218 No. 76; Spanish: Espinosa III 275-277; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1908.2.p: A cat is transformed into a maiden, yet when a mouse appears she runs after it, her animal nature showing through.

J1908.3.r: Africa (Nama): Des Schwartzen Menschen Märchenweisheit (Stuttgart, 1929) 140f. No. 27.
J1908.3.p: A frog-woman, disguised as a human, gives herself away by croaking like a frog.

J1909.p: A miscellaneous category of foolish disregard for how animals really behave.

J1909.1.p: A fisherman tries to make fish dance by playing his flute, but they do not respond. Later, when they are in his net, they jump about without any music.

J1909.2.p: A fool keeps trying to shoot an antelope dead so that it will come to him.

J1909.3.p: A dim-witted person tries to shake birds down from a tree as if they were fruit, not understanding that birds are not fruit that falls when shaken.

J1909.4.p: A fool claims that a mare bred to a donkey will produce a fine horse once the colt's body matches the size of its ears, showing he misunderstands animal breeding.

J1909.5.r: He says, “Such is bad conduct. If I were to do that they would say that I was eating it.” Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 587; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 33 No. 129*. Cf. Wienert FFC LVI *69 (ET 335), 94f. (ST 81); Halm Aesop Nos. 282, 330.
J1909.5.p: A sheep licks her lamb, and a wolf envies her for it, showing a foolish misunderstanding of how animals behave toward their young.

J1909.6.p: A dim-witted person tries to wash a black hen white, not realizing that scrubbing will not change her feather color.

J1909.7.p: A person fears that a frog may drown or get dirty in water, not understanding that frogs live in water.

J1910.p: A foolish person harms or kills someone through a mistaken ignorance of how the human body works.

J1911.p: A foolish person misunderstands what a baby is or how it is made, with harmful results.

J1911.1.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 215 No. 445; Spanish: Espinosa III 147; West Indies: Flowers 486.
J1911.1.p: A dim-witted person does not understand that a baby's skull is soft, and sticks a needle through it.

J1911.2.r: Wrings the child’s neck. Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 406 No. 3.
J1911.2.p: A foolish mother does not understand why babies cry and misreads their crying.

J1914.r: Dies. Type 1682; Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 364), 129 (ST 370); Halm Aesop No. 176.
J1914.p: A foolish owner trains a horse to go without food, and the horse starves or fails because the training ignores what horses need.

J1914.1.r: Fails in the war. Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 363), 129 (ST 369); Halm Aesop No. 178.
J1914.1.p: A warhorse is kept so underfed that it is too weak to be useful in battle, as a result of a foolish plan to feed it too little.

J1914.2.p: Three brothers share one mule and each assumes one of the others is feeding it, so none feeds it and the mule dies.

J1916.p: A foolish husband carries his wife across a stream with her head pointing down, and she drowns.

J1919.p: A miscellaneous group of foolish acts that harm or kill through a mistaken ignorance of the body.

J1919.1.p: A trickster cuts off a stork's bill and legs so that it will look more like a real bird.

J1919.2.r: The fool, “Those little ducks were able to cross here; why couldn’t a big fellow like you?” Wesselski Bebel II 146 No. 146.
J1919.2.p: A fool is asked where a river can be forded and says everywhere, so a man who tries to ride across nearly drowns.

J1919.3.r: A dog has eaten 14 pounds of butter; the fool squeezes 16 pounds from him. Fb “sm[ö]r” III 412b.
J1919.3.p: A foolish person's mistaken reckoning about weight adds two extra pounds to something, with harmful or absurd results.

J1919.4.p: A fool cuts off the tails of oxen so that they will look like fine horses.

J1919.5.p: Someone's genitals are cut off through ignorance, a foolish mistake with fatal or harmful results.

J1919.5.1.p: An ignorant bride castrates her groom after someone jokingly tells her to do so, taking the joke literally.

J1919.5.2.p: A nun tells a friar to get rid of a part of his body that offends her, and he takes her literally and cuts off his genitals out of ignorance.

J1919.5.3.p: A fool castrates himself, believing this will make him gain weight.

J1919.6.p: A simple man, not understanding how the body works, lets a priest share his wife.

J1919.7.p: A fool believes he has fathered a child with his sister by means of an earbox.

J1919.8.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2911; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 1543*.
J1919.8.p: A foolish wife gives her husband money to buy himself a penis, since he has none.

J1919.9.p: A cowboy shoots his wife when she breaks a leg or is injured in some other way.

J1920.p: Foolish people make absurd attempts to find things they have lost.

J1921.p: A needle or similar small object falls into the sea, and the fool plans to look for it the following summer.

J1922.p: Foolish people try to mark the spot where something was lost so they can find it again, but the marking does not work.

J1922.1.r: *Type 1278; *Fb “båd” IV 87a; *Clouston Noodles 99; Penzer V 92f.; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1922.1.p: Foolish searchers mark the spot on the boat's rail to show where a dropped object fell into the sea, rather than marking the place in the water.

J1922.2.r: Clouston Noodles 53; England: Baughman; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1922.2.p: Numskulls leave a knife in a field and mark its place by putting it under a cloud. The next day the cloud has moved and the knife is lost.

J1922.2.1.p: A fool searches for sown grain in the direction the cloud was in when he sowed it.

J1922.3.p: The owner of a vessel hides it under a mound of sand while swimming, and others make similar mounds so that the vessel is lost.

J1923.p: A numskull goes looking for bread he threw away a year earlier.

J1924.p: A numskull forgets the name of a certain food and thinks it has fallen into the sand.

J1930.p: Foolish people act as if natural laws do not apply to them.

J1931.r: *Type 1651; BP II 75; *Fb “penge” II 804a; Russian: Andrejev No. 842*.
J1931.p: To test whether money is genuine, people throw it into a stream to see if it floats, since good coins are supposed to swim and counterfeit ones sink.

J1932.p: Foolish farmers follow absurd practices connected with growing crops.

J1932.1.r: *DeVries FFC LXXIII 246; *Fb “så” Penzer V 67 n. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
J1932.1.p: Numskulls sow cooked grain, expecting it to grow.

J1932.2.p: A person sows cheese, hoping it will bring forth a cow.

J1932.3.r: *Type 1200; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 209 No. 423; Christensen DF XLVII 206, 231 no. 57; India: Thompson-Balys.
J1932.3.p: A person sows salt, hoping it will produce more salt.

J1932.4.p: A fool plants a hog in the ground, expecting it to sprout a crop of young pigs.

J1932.4.1.p: A fool plants an animal's tail in the ground, expecting new young animals to grow from it.

J1932.4.2.p: A fool plants bones in the ground, expecting an animal to grow from them.

J1932.5.p: A fool sows needles in a field as if they were seeds, expecting them to grow into a crop.

J1932.6.p: A fool harvests his crop early and gets only half of what he would have had by waiting.

J1932.7.p: A fool waters stones, hoping they will grow.

J1933.p: A numskull tries to dig up a spring of water so that he can carry it home with him.

J1934.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 227 No. 480; Christensen DF XL VII 201 no. 37; Jewish: Neuman.
J1934.p: A numskull digs a hole only so he has somewhere to put the earth he digs out of another hole.

J1935.p: A fool sends goods by telegraph, as if the telegraph could carry physical objects.

J1935.1.r: Type 1710; Christensen DF XLVII 204 no. 50; U.S. (Ozarks): *Randolph Devil’s Pretty Daughter (New York, 1955) 195.
J1935.1.p: A peasant hangs a pair of boots and a letter on a telegraph wire, expecting the boots to reach the city.

J1936.r: A man stands before mirror with his eyes shut to see how he looks in his sleep. Clouston Noodles 9.
J1936.p: A fool wants to know what he looks like while asleep, and tries absurd ways to find out.

J1936.1.p: A man takes a mirror to bed to see whether he sleeps with his mouth open.

J1937.p: A fool holds foolish beliefs about dead people and what can be learned from them.

J1937.1.p: A numskull asked to identify a corpse tries to recognize the dead man by his cough.

J1937.2.p: A numskull objects to a tomb being placed in an unhealthy spot, as if the dead would be harmed by it.

J1938.r: Type 1260; Clouston Noodles 44; Field Pent Cuckoo 17; Christensen DF XLVII 178; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 255.
J1938.p: Fools put meal into the boiling current of an ice hole to make porridge, then take turns jumping in to taste it.

J1941.r: A numskull cries from a tower and then runs away to see how far his voice will reach. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 191 No. 373.
J1941.p: A fool tests how far his voice will carry, in an absurd way.

J1942.p: A numskull ties yarn around a stove to keep the heat from escaping.

J1943.p: A numskull examines a sundial by candlelight in an attempt to find the time at night.

J1943.1.p: A fool covers a sundial to protect it, which makes it useless for telling time.

J1944.p: A foolish person tries to pick fruit from a tree that bears none. It is a standard example of absurd behavior ignoring how nature works.

J1944.1.p: Numskulls try to get pears from an oak tree, and afterward each accuses the other of eating all the pears.

J1945.p: A numskull tries to warm his hands at a fire by stretching them out across a river to reach it.

J1946.p: A numskull who has only ridden to town on a stick horse complains that he is as tired as if he had walked.

J1947.p: A fool tries to make salt by drying snow, ignoring that snow will not yield salt.

J1952.p: A fool mixes fire and water together to make a sacrifice, and is told that he needed only the two of them.

J1955.p: Someone demands that a murderer bring his victim back to life, as if the killer could simply restore the dead.

J1955.1.p: A widow chases after a guest to tell him he must restore her husband, whom he has accidentally killed.

J1959.p: A miscellaneous group of foolish acts that ignore natural laws and do not fit the more specific categories.

J1959.1.p: A simpleton drives goats into a well because he thinks it will be cooler for them.

J1959.1.1.p: A fool puts a hot sickle into water to cure its fever, as if it were a sick person.

J1959.2.p: A fool loses his mother's corpse on the way to her funeral, then mistakes an old woman for his mother and substitutes her.

J1960.p: A general heading for other foolish acts that ignore basic facts and do not fit the more specific categories.

J1961.p: A fool uses a white sheepskin as if it were a source of light, though it gives none.

J1961.1.p: A fool tries to catch light in a mousetrap, as if light could be trapped like a mouse.

J1962.p: An old woman forgets to knead yeast into her dough, so she throws the yeast into the stove afterward.

J1963.p: A fool puts only one stick of wood in the stove, expecting it to heat the room properly.

J1964.p: Foolish people lay tree trunks crosswise on a sledge, so that they stick out and cause trouble.

J1964.1.p: A fool tries to stretch a beam, as if a wooden beam could be lengthened by pulling.

J1965.p: Numskulls caught in a storm on the ice stick needles into the ice to keep from being blown away.

J1966.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 400), 123 (ST 319); Halm Aesop No. 402.
J1966.p: A man blames a wall for falling on him when it was really the man himself who used a crowbar to bring it down.

J1967.r: Italian: Gonzenbach No. 17, Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J1967.p: A dim-witted man, unwilling to wet his feet, sits by a stream waiting for it to drain away, then tries to empty it himself with a hazelnut shell for months.

J1968.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 254. Cf. Yeats’s “Cuchulain’s Fight with the Sea.”
J1968.p: A foolish person tries to punish or fight the sea, as if it could be defeated by force.

J1968.1.p: A foolish person attacks or fights the sun, as if it could be punished or driven off.

J1971.p: Foolish people try to cut with a buffalo's tongue as if it were a knife.

J1972.p: A stupid woman swims around on the roof of a house as if it were water.

J1973.p: A person pulls a tree down by the roots in order to give it water to drink.

J1974.p: A fool tries to purify cotton by burning it, copying how a goldsmith refines gold by fire.

J1976.p: Stupid people feel heat coming from a stove that has no fire in it.

J1977.p: A person stops up his mouth and ears so that wisdom will not escape from him.

J2010.p: A person is uncertain about who he himself is, a general category of foolish forgetfulness about one's own identity.

J2012.r: Fb “selv”; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs f. Vksk. 1954, 129ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2012.p: A person fails to recognize himself or herself, not knowing who he or she is.

J2012.1.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 274 No. 298; Christensen DF XLVII 27, 221 No. 83; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2012.1.p: A man whose beard has been cut off no longer recognizes himself and does not know who he is.

J2012.2.r: *Type 1383; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 274 No. 298; Christensen DF XLVII 35.
J2012.2.p: A woman whose clothes have been cut off no longer recognizes herself and does not know who she is.

J2012.3.r: *Type 1383; Fb “tjære” III 811a; Christensen DF XLVII 35; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2012.3.p: A woman covered in tar and feathers no longer recognizes herself and does not know who she is.

J2012.4.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 193 No. 152; Christensen DF XLVII 221 No. 83.
J2012.4.p: A fool dressed in new clothes no longer recognizes himself and does not know who he is.

J2012.5.p: A man cannot tell himself apart from another man who is dressed exactly the same way.

J2012.6.r: “You are me and I am you!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2012.6.p: A fool at the baths thinks he is someone else: he sees everyone naked, so he puts straw on his shoulder to mark himself, but the straw floats off to another bather.

J2013.p: A man is tricked into believing that he is someone else.

J2013.1.r: Clouston Noodles 7; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs. f. Vksk. 1954, 130; England, U.S.: Baughman.
J2013.1.p: A white man is made to believe he is a Black man: while he sleeps beside a Black man, his friends blacken his face, and when woken he insists they have woken the wrong man.

J2013.2.p: A man is tricked into believing he is a dog, and he behaves like one by barking at people.

J2013.3.p: A foolish man ties a pumpkin to his leg at night so he will know who he is in the morning. Someone secretly ties the pumpkin to another man's leg, and the fool is then unsure of his own identity the next day.

J2013.4.p: A numskull is tricked into believing he is an evil spirit.

J2014.p: A fool is so confused about who he is that he fails to recognize his own house and family.

J2015.p: Pupils mistake a dog's tail for their master's tail, grabbing it because they think it belongs to him.

J2016.p: A man fails to respond when his real name is called, because he is only used to hearing his nickname.

J2020.p: A foolish person cannot locate his own body parts or other things that belong to him.

J2021.r: (Usually get them mixed up when they sit down to bathe their feet.) Type 1288; BP III 150 n. 1; *Fb “ben” IV 32b; Clouston Noodles 32; Christensen DF XLVII 183.
J2021.p: Numskulls look for their own legs and cannot find them. A stranger helps them by striking them with a switch.

J2021.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Nouvelles Récréations No. 11.
J2021.1.p: A numskull asks a doctor which of his own legs is hurting him, showing he does not know which one is his.

J2022.p: A numskull searches for the donkey he is sitting on, unable to realize that it is beneath him.

J2023.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 234 No. 100; Italian Novella: Rotunda (J2043).
J2023.p: A numskull does not recognize his own horse and only finds it when the others ride away and he takes the one left behind.

J2024.r: “I didn’t get on backward but the horse seems to be left-handed.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 235 No. 100.
J2024.p: A numskull rides his horse or animal backward, facing the tail.

J2025.p: A person searches for something he is already carrying and cannot find it.

J2025.1.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 407 No. 4.
J2025.1.p: A man searches everywhere for his axe, not realizing he is carrying it on his shoulder.

J2025.2.p: A woman searches for a pastry that is stuck to her buttocks, unable to find it.

J2026.p: Fools fight a man they think is inside a drum and making the noise, but they are really pounding each other.

J2027.p: An opium smoker on a journey keeps asking the way and ends up back at his own house without realizing it.

J2030.p: Foolish people are absurdly unable to count correctly.

J2031.r: *Type 1287; *BP III 149 n. 1; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 267 No. 261; *Clouston Noodles 28ff., 192; *Field Pent Cuckoo 8; Köhler-Bolte I 112; Christensen DF XLVII 181ff.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 317 No. 153; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 66 No. 111.
J2031.p: Numskulls count their group but leave out themselves, so they wrongly conclude that one of them has drowned.

J2031.1.p: Numskulls count themselves by sticking their noses in the sand, and then they count the holes that result.

J2031.2.r: Why? *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 267 No. 261; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2031.2.p: A man counting ten horses gets only nine, because he leaves himself out of the count. When he mounts up, there are only nine horses under him, so he thinks one is missing.

J2031.3.p: A culture hero throws coconuts to different islands but forgets the one he is standing on, so that island has none. This explains why that island has no coconuts.

J2032.r: Numskull: “You should have taken one before they were all gone.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 246 No. 143.
J2032.p: Ten men are each supposed to take a goose, and when they all have one, there are ten geese. But one man is left without a goose, so the count seems to come out as nine or ten.

J2033.p: Three girls must go somewhere and come back together, but each has a different travel time: one takes half a month, one fifteen days, and one seven plus eight days. They find this seemingly impossible to arrange.

J2035.p: A merchant doing a calculation keeps stopping to ask the ages of his youngest daughter, elder daughter, and mother, and adds each answer to the total. So his sum never comes out right because the interruptions keep throwing it off.

J2036.r: Clouston Noodles 90; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 248 No. 161.
J2036.p: A numskull goes to buy goods for his wife and measures the length of the cloth or goods by stretching out his arms. He gets the measure by this foolish method.

J2037.p: Numskulls buy something together, but each one pays the full price instead of sharing the cost. The result is that they pay far more than necessary.

J2037.1.p: Numskulls buy a church together, and each one pays the full price rather than sharing the cost.

J2037.2.p: Three brothers buy a cow to share, but each one pays the farmer the full price for it.

J2040.p: A general heading for miscellaneous stories of foolish forgetfulness and absent-mindedness that do not fit the more specific types.

J2041.p: An actor forgets his role and starts speaking as himself instead of as the character he is playing.

J2041.1.p: In a Passion Play, the actor playing Christ says, "I am thirsty," and the thief on the left, forgetting his part, speaks up and says "I too."

J2044.p: A fool forgets his master's message. As a result, he is sent off carrying a heavy mortar to deliver, and the master makes him carry it back as punishment.

J2045.p: A fool believes a man's plea of not guilty even though he has seen that man injure him with his own eyes.

J2046.p: A law student forgets the speech he has prepared and cannot deliver it when the time comes.

J2047.p: A hero keeps leading his horse along, not realizing that the horse is dead.

J2048.p: A fool is given gifts for himself and his relatives but is so absent-minded that he forgets to take his own share.

J2050.p: A general heading for stories of foolish short-sightedness, where people fail to see the consequences of what they do or decide.

J2051.p: A wise man gives good advice, but people scorn him because they cannot see far enough ahead to recognize its value.

J2052.p: God's mercy is contrasted with man's short-sightedness, showing how people fail to see the wider good that God intends.

J2060.r: Air-castles. *Type 1430; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 249 No. 163; *Chauvin V 162 No. 85.
J2060.p: A general heading for stories of foolish plans, where people make schemes that are absurdly short-sighted or impractical.

J2060.1.r: *Type 1430; BP III 275; *Gerould MLN XIX 228; India: *Thompson-Balys; Arab: Azov JPASB (n.s.) II 402f.; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 269, Coster-Wijsman 65f. Nos. 107—110.
J2060.1.p: Two people quarrel and fight over the fine details of a daydreamed scheme that exists only in their imagination.

J2060.2.p: A man plants a hedge, expecting sheep to leave wool on the thorns so that he gets rich from it.

J2060.3.p: A fool plans to build a palace in the sky and lets a hawk fly off as its architect.

J2060.4.p: Foolish people draw lots to divide the purple cloth of a queen who is still alive.

J2061.p: A daydreamed plan collapses because the dreamer did not think ahead, and everything is ruined.

J2061.1.r: *BP III 261f.; *Chauvin II 101 No. 60; *Gerould MLN XIX 229; B[ö]dker Exempler 300 No. 65; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella; *Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 55, 277; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2061.1.p: A dreamer imagines selling a jar of honey, then in his excitement breaks the jar.

J2061.1.1.p: A dreamer imagines selling a basket of glassware, then in his excitement breaks all of it.

J2061.1.2.r: *BP III 265; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 520; *Fb “æg” III 1141b; *Gerould MLN XIX 226; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2061.1.2.p: A woman imagines selling a basket of eggs, then in her excitement breaks all the eggs.

J2061.1.3.p: A pot of flour is to be sold in a daydream, but the pot gets broken.

J2061.1.4.p: A dreamer imagines selling a jar of oil, and the jar is broken through his excitement.

J2061.2.r: *BP III 264; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 520; *Crane Vitry 154f. No. 51; **Gerould MLN XIX 225; Jacobs Aesop 219 No. 77; Nouvelles Récréations No. 12; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 55, 277.
J2061.2.p: A proud milkmaid imagining her future tosses her head or kicks in her sleep and spills the pail of milk she was to sell.

J2061.2.1.p: An old woman daydreams about the horse she will get from selling her milk, spurs it in her imagination, and spills the milk.

J2061.3.p: A man imagines selling the hide of a sleeping deer, and in his excitement he wakes the deer, which runs away.

J2061.4.p: A toad that has found money daydreams about what to do with it and gets run over while lost in thought.

J2062.p: A fool tries to make a point in an argument by acting it out in a foolish way.

J2062.1.r: “None.” “There is just that much wit in your heads.” *Clouston Noodles 26; Field Pent Cuckoo 2; England: Baughman.
J2062.1.p: Two men quarrel over which way sheep they have not yet bought should return, and a third fool shows them their foolishness by pouring out his meal into the water to reveal the empty sack.

J2062.2.r: “Does the ghee protect the saucer, or the saucer the ghee?” India: Thompson-Balys.
J2062.2.p: A foolish logician spills ghee while making an argument.

J2062.3.p: Foolish people argue over how a town was burned, and the question is absurd.

J2063.r: *Type 1450; *BP I 335; *Clouston Noodles 191; Christensen DF L 35; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 55, 277; India: Thompson-Balys; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 285 No. 125.
J2063.p: A girl sent to the cellar for wine weeps over troubles her unborn child might have if she marries the suitor, and her parents join her while the suitor leaves.

J2063.1.p: A queen grieves herself to death over what will happen to her children after she dies.

J2064.p: A servant plans to trick his master by refusing to eat, a foolish scheme that backfires.

J2066.p: A foolish character waits for something that can never happen.

J2066.1.p: A hungry fox waits in vain for a horse's lips (or scrotum) to fall off.

J2066.2.p: A daw waits in vain for figs to ripen in winter, which they never will.

J2066.3.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 410 No. 8; American Negro: Harris Nights 223 No. 38.
J2066.3.p: Men or animals wait in vain for nuts to fall from a tree.

J2066.3.1.p: Someone waits in vain for fruit to fall from a tree that bears no fruit.

J2066.4.r: Wesselski Märchen 250 No. 58; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 3.
J2066.4.p: A wolf turns down salted meat or similar food, hoping for other prey that never comes, and so goes without.

J2066.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 320), 102 (ST 156); Halm Aesop No. 275; Jacobs Aesop 211 No. 46; Japanese: Ikeda.
J2066.5.p: A wolf waits in vain for a nurse to throw away a child, though she has only threatened to give the child to him.

J2066.6.p: A dog waits to be hit with a piece of meat, as a butcher has threatened, hoping to get the meat.

J2066.6.1.p: A dog follows a washerwoman carrying a bundle, hoping it contains meat.

J2066.7.r: England, U.S.: Baughman; American Negro: Harris Friends 122 No. 16.
J2066.7.p: A gullible man waits for the rear wheels of a wagon to overtake the front wheels, believing this is how money is made, as he was told.

J2066.8.p: A hare waits in vain for the leaves to fall from a palm tree.

J2066.9.p: A hare waits in vain for a man's hand, which he sees dangling, to fall off.

J2067.p: A foolish bargain in which the sacrifice required is as costly as the reward to be gained.

J2067.1.p: A woman plans to sacrifice her only son so that the gods will allow her to bear another son.

J2070.p: Foolish or badly considered wishes, which bring trouble on the wisher.

J2071.r: Three wishes will be granted: used up foolishly. *Bédier Fabliaux 212ff., 471; Type 750; *Bolte Zs. f. vgl. Litgsch. VII 453; *BP II 212; *Fb “[ö]nske” III 1179a. — Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “souhaits”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 213, Coster-Wijsman 46 No. 56.
J2071.p: Someone granted three wishes wastes them on foolish things.

J2072.p: A wish that turns out badly because the wisher did not think ahead.

J2072.1.r: *BP II 213; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 180; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *775.
J2072.1.p: A wish that everything he touches turn to gold, which proves a disaster for the wisher.

J2072.2.p: A wish that grain grow without beards, a short-sighted request.

J2072.3.p: A short-sighted wish backfires: whatever the wisher pulls on comes out with it, such as a nose that pulls out long when he blows it.

J2072.4.p: A man wishes to be rid of his stomach, which he thinks enslaves him. Once it is removed, life seems dull to him, so he gets his stomach back.

J2072.5.p: A camel, granted a wish, asks for a longer neck, a short-sighted request that the tale treats as foolish.

J2072.6.p: An old woman, granted a wish, asks to have her nose cut off so she will remember the wish all her life, a foolish and self-harming choice.

J2073.p: The same wish produces opposite results depending on whether a wise or a foolish person makes it. The tale is told with two people receiving identical wishes.

J2073.1.p: A wish to keep doing whatever one begins all day: the wise person gets useful work done, while the foolish one, angry, must keep throwing water on a pig all day.

J2073.1.1.p: A wish for help in whatever one is doing: the wise person gets help with work, while the foolish one gets help in striking his wife.

J2074.r: *Type 1331; *BP II 219 n. 1; Crane Vitry 212 No. 126; Bédier Fabliaux 457; Wienert FFC LVI 79 (ET 446), 132 (ST 387); Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 647; *Reinhard JAFL XXXVI 383 n. 1; Scala Celi 106b No. 589; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 31.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2074.p: A wish that rebounds on the enemy: one person's wish is granted to the other with double effect, as when a covetous or envious man wishes his neighbor to be blinded and the wish is doubled.

J2075.r: *Type 750A; *BP II 220, 225; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 454.
J2075.p: A husband given three wishes passes one to his wife, who wastes it on something trivial. In anger he wishes the object inside her body and must use his third wish to remove it.

J2075.1.r: (J2075 contrasted with a married couple in which the wish is wisely used by the wife.) *BP II 223.
J2075.1.p: A transferred wish is used both wisely and unwisely, with good and bad results from the same transfer.

J2075.2.p: A wife uses two transferred wishes selfishly; the husband kills her and uses the last wish to his own advantage.

J2075.3.p: A woman scornfully throws away pills and is punished with sores over her body. She must then use the pills to heal herself.

J2075.4.p: A wife granted a wish for beauty elopes with a prince. Her husband wishes her into a pig, and their son must use a third wish to restore her.

J2076.p: A fool, granted any wish he likes, chooses something trivial instead of something valuable.

J2076.1.p: A modest wish that no lights may burn on a certain night except in the wisher's own house, a petty request that gives her an odd privilege.

J2079.p: A miscellany of foolish wishes that do not fit a more specific category.

J2079.1.p: A wife wishes to be turned into gold, a foolish wish that has her transformed into a precious metal.

J2079.2.p: A foolish wish to destroy every fly and spider, a wish to wipe out all such creatures.

J2080.p: Bargains that the person making them is foolish to accept, usually because they turn out badly for him.

J2081.p: A foolish bargain in which the terms grow steadily worse for the one who made it, each step leading to a bigger loss.

J2081.1.r: *Type 1415; *BP II 199; English: Wells 118 (Octovian); India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 57 No. 84; N. A. Indian (Zuni): Boas JAFL XXXV 74 No. 3. Cf. Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 128.
J2081.1.p: A fool keeps trading each animal for a lesser one (a horse for a cow, the cow for a hog, and so on) until he has nothing left.

J2081.2.r: Chauvin II 83 No. 10, cf. II 89 No. 28.
J2081.2.p: A fool trades a good fish for a worthless shell, and then a shell containing a pearl for a small fish.

J2081.3.p: A fool trades his wife for an ox, then wrongly thinks something is wrong with her head because her hair parting is marked with red.

J2081.4.p: Fools sent to buy a cow come back with a monkey instead.

J2082.p: A fool who has paid twice the usual price for a shave settles the account by having the barber shave his wife.

J2083.p: A fool tries to cheat the buyer in a sale, but his own trick ends up costing him.

J2083.1.p: A fool sells a third of a cask of grain for the price of a fourth, thinking he is cheating the buyer.

J2083.2.p: A fool sells two fox skins stuck together as if they were one, for the price of one.

J2083.3.p: A seller of fox skins mixes otter skins in among them, hoping to cheat the buyer.

J2083.4.p: A fool buys nine eggs and sells ten for the same price, then says that business is improving.

J2083.5.p: A fool hands over a heaped measure while being paid only for a level one.

J2083.6.p: A seller measures out more yards of cloth than the money paid for.

J2085.p: A fool offers a reward for a lost item that is worth more than the item itself.

J2085.1.p: The owner of a lost ass offers the ass along with its saddle and bridle as the reward to whoever finds it.

J2085.1.1.p: A man trades his only horse for a set of harness.

J2086.p: A woman sells cows on credit and takes one of them back as a pledge for the unpaid price.

J2087.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 276 No. 309; Clouston Noodles 72; U.S.: Baughman.
J2087.p: An auctioneer praises a man's worthless cow so highly in his sales speech that the man decides to take her back himself. The persuasive talk backfires on the seller.

J2088.p: A fool selling an over-short turban at auction honestly warns the prospective buyer that it is too short.

J2088.1.p: The fool honestly tells the buyer that the horse is worth little, since otherwise his father would not be selling it.

J2088.2.r: Breton: Luzel Legendes chrétiennes de Basse Bretagne (Paris, 1881) I 16.
J2088.2.p: A seller warns the buyer that the cow is a thief.

J2091.p: A foolish man helps a thief by telling him where valuables are hidden while warning him not to steal them.

J2091.1.p: A fool hides treasure and marks the spot with a sign reading 'Here it is,' and a thief answers with a sign reading 'Here it is not.'

J2092.r: Chauvin II 82 No. 2; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 179; B[ö]dker Exempler 272 No. 2; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2092.p: A man who finds a treasure hires porters to carry it away for him, and they rob him instead. The fool's own trusting choice of helpers leads to his loss.

J2093.p: A fool gives away or sells valuable things for almost nothing, out of ignorance or carelessness.

J2093.1.p: A simpleton gives away an old water bag without realizing that money is hidden inside it.

J2093.2.p: A woman trades a valuable jewel for a salad, and the person she gives it to does not know its worth either.

J2093.3.p: A fool who does not know a jewel's value throws it away as worthless.

J2093.3.1.p: A boy turns down pearls in exchange for worthless stones, and a jeweler recognizes the pearls for what they really are.

J2093.4.p: A man gives away good timber for useless wood because his wife tells him the good wood will bring only sickness and trouble.

J2093.5.p: Someone trades sacks of gold and silver for sacks of rice, a foolish exchange of great riches for ordinary grain.

J2093.6.p: Gold and jewels are sold for a trifling price, through foolishness or ignorance of their worth.

J2094.p: Someone burns costly wood to make charcoal, wasting something far more valuable than what is produced.

J2095.r: Choice of eating 100 onions, receiving 100 blows, or paying 100 coins. Fool tries onions in vain, then the blows, and finally must give the coins. *Zachariae Kleine Schriften 170; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 349; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2095.p: A foolish person is said to eat a hundred onions, a boastful or absurd feat of eating.

J2096.p: A stupid boy believes that trading all his silver for a worthless cup will win people's respect.

J2099.p: A miscellaneous foolish bargain, where someone makes a bad trade that does not fit the more specific categories.

J2099.1.p: A woman swaps her horse for a sack of bones, because she has been falsely told the sack is full of gold.

J2100.p: A cure or remedy turns out to be worse than the problem it was meant to solve.

J2101.r: *Type 1281; BP II 72 n. 1; Christensen DF XLVII 219ff. no. 82.
J2101.p: People who have never known cats buy one at great price, and it kills many mice. Mistaking it for a monster, they burn down the house to get rid of it.

J2101.1.r: Clouston Noodles 65; Wesselski Märchen 251 No. 59; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2101.1.p: A woman tries to punish a cat by tying cotton to its tail and setting it alight, and the fire spreads until the whole village burns.

J2102.p: A costly or extreme method is used to get rid of insects, and it does more harm than the insects.

J2102.1.p: A person sleeps in shoes to avoid being bitten by insects, a ridiculous and impractical precaution.

J2102.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 49), 128 (ST 363); Halm Aesop No. 393.
J2102.2.p: A snake wants to be rid of wasps, so it lets a cart wheel run over it along with them, a futile and self-destructive remedy.

J2102.3.r: Jacobs Aesop 204 No. 18; Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 313), 128 (ST 361).
J2102.3.p: A bald man tries to swat a fly on his head and hurts himself instead of getting rid of the insect.

J2102.4.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 37; *BP III 288; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 244 No. 137; Christensen DF XLVII 219ff. No. 82; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 267.
J2102.4.p: A fool burns down his own house in an attempt to get rid of insects living in it.

J2102.4.1.p: A fool burns down his house to get rid of a lizard, a far worse loss than the pest itself.

J2102.5.p: A nest of wasps is burned out, and the house catches fire and burns down along with it.

J2102.6.r: Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 288), 128 (ST 362); Halm Aesop No. 411.
J2102.6.p: A fool burns his clothes to rid them of insects such as lice or fleas.

J2102.7.p: A fool burns his crop to rid it of insects, destroying the harvest he meant to save.

J2102.8.r: Snakes eat numskull’s family. India: Thompson-Balys.
J2102.8.p: A fool introduces frogs to eat the insects, then snakes to eat the frogs, creating a new pest problem.

J2103.p: A fool goes to great and foolish expense to kill off rodents, costing more than the damage they cause.

J2103.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 35; *Crane Vitry 138 No. 11; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2103.1.p: A farmer troubled by mice eating his cheese puts a cat in the cheese tub, and the cat eats both the mice and the cheese.

J2103.1.1.p: A woman puts a cat in a flour bin to catch a mouse, but the cat eats the pie kept there and loses interest in the mouse.

J2103.2.p: A peasant asks a nobleman to help against a rabbit that is raiding his garden, and the nobleman chases it on horseback so long that he ruins the peasant's crop.

J2103.2.1.p: A king ruins his own garden in an effort to get rid of a viper hidden there.

J2103.3.p: A fool burns down his house to get rid of rats.

J2104.p: When a fireplace gives off too much heat, foolish people decide to move it rather than simply put out the fire.

J2104.1.p: A cow fouls a church, and foolish people try to clean it by moving the whole church with ropes.

J2105.p: To keep croaking frogs from disturbing his sleep, foolish men shoot at the frogs all night long.

J2106.p: A man kills himself so that his quarrelsome wife will become a widow and be free of her.

J2107.p: To tame a bull, a man cuts off its horns, which only makes the animal more violent.

J2108.r: Wienert FFC LVI 85 (ET 520), 116 (ST 265); Halm Aesop No. 221.
J2108.p: After a dog bites a man, he rubs bread on the wound and feeds it to the dog, so every dog later bites him to get the double reward.

J2112.p: A man tries to cure his gray hair by pulling it all out, leaving himself bald.

J2112.1.r: Soon all are gone. *Chauvin II 128 No. 134; Fb “hår” IV 241b; Crane Vitry 215 No. 201; *Herbert III 16; Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 489), 129 (ST 372); Halm Aesop No. 56; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2112.1.p: A young wife pulls out her husband's gray hairs and an old wife pulls out his black ones, so that he ends up bald. A fool's remedy for gray hair that leaves him worse off.

J2113.p: A calf gets its head stuck in a pot, and a fool cuts off the calf's head and then breaks the pot to free it. A foolish fix that destroys more than the problem.

J2113.1.p: A man cuts off his donkey's head as a punishment for it. A foolish act of punishment that kills the animal.

J2114.p: Snakes in a pond are to be killed, but the eels are killed too. A foolish attempt to get rid of a pest that also destroys harmless creatures.

J2115.p: Fools take an overdose of medicine and die from it. A foolish remedy that proves fatal.

J2119.p: A general category of foolish remedies that are worse than the illness, not covered by the more specific motifs listed under it.

J2119.1.p: A man cuts off his nose to get it out of the light. A foolish attempt to solve a simple problem by destroying the body part.

J2119.1.1.r: Penzer V 68f.; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 21 No. 76.
J2119.1.1.p: A man tries to improve his wife's looks by cutting off her nose. A foolish cure for a supposed flaw that disfigures her.

J2119.2.p: The straightest path is not always the shortest way to get somewhere. A tale theme in which a fool assumes the direct route is quickest.

J2119.2.1.r: Farmer takes a few feet off his journey and lifts a wheelbarrow over 22 stiles in so doing. Clouston Noodles 54; England: Baughman.
J2119.2.1.p: A fool takes a shortcut that turns out to be longer or worse. A foolish decision to cut across instead of taking the usual route.

J2119.2.2.p: Two contestants race: one goes straight through the stones, while the other goes around in circles and wins. A race where the roundabout runner outpaces the direct one.

J2119.3.p: Noodles push their parents over a rock as a favor to them. A foolish kindness that harms the people it is meant to help.

J2119.4.p: Numskulls drill a hole in their boat to get the water out. A foolish scheme that makes the problem worse by letting water in.

J2119.5.p: A stupid giant, seeing how fat he has become, wants to eat himself up. A foolish response to his own size that would be self-destructive.

J2119.6.p: A boy holds rice in his joined hands with his arms around a pillar, afraid to move lest he spill it. The roof is removed and he is lifted over the pillar to save the rice.

J2119.7.p: Stupid cowherds apply a hot iron to the temples of an unconscious man to revive him. A foolish attempt at first aid that harms the injured person.

J2119.8.p: A cow is tied down tightly with stones so it will not blow away, but then it cannot do all the other things a cow should do. A foolish precaution that defeats its own purpose.

J2119.9.p: A hero beheads an old woman who asks him to cure her of old age. A grim tale in which a request for a cure is answered with a fatal misunderstanding.

J2120.p: Foolish heedlessness about danger to objects or animals, where a person ignores a risk that could damage or destroy them.

J2121.p: A fool tries to dry snow by placing it on the stove. A foolish act that shows a complete misunderstanding of what snow is.

J2122.p: A foolish person puts a candle into the oven to dry it out, and of course the candle melts.

J2123.r: Type 1245; *Fb “lys” II 483b; Clouston Noodles 58, 64; Christensen DF XLVII 215 No. 74, ibid. DF L 49.
J2123.p: Foolish people try to bring sunlight into a house with no windows by carrying it in baskets. When that fails, they start tearing down the house to let in light.

J2124.p: A fool sets fish aside to save them for Easter, putting them in one big pool, where an eel eats them all.

J2124.1.p: A numskull sends meat home by tying it to a kite bird, and the kite eats it on the way.

J2125.r: BP III 337ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 139 No. 1692.
J2125.p: Foolish people try to guard their chickens from a fox by tying up the chickens' beaks and weighing them down in a river with stones.

J2126.r: Von der Leyen Das Märchen 78 and Herrigs Archiv CXIV 20 n. 2.
J2126.p: A numskull tries to water the roots of a tree by pouring water on the top, and so digs up the tree to reach the roots.

J2126.1.p: Foolish people cut down trees in order to gather their fruit.

J2127.r: Penzer V 84; Von der Leyen Das Märchen 78 and Herrigs Archiv CXIV 20 n. 2; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2127.p: A numskull is told to carry a can of oil carefully because it has a small hole. To find the hole, he turns the can around and lets all the oil run out.

J2129.p: A general category of foolish disregard for the safety of objects or animals that does not fit the more specific motifs.

J2129.1.p: Foolish people steer a boat so that it goes over a cliff.

J2129.2.p: Heirs quarrel over an inheritance until they destroy the whole property.

J2129.3.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 53; Scala Celi 4b No. 21.
J2129.3.p: A peasant kills his hen so that he can get all the eggs she would lay over the next year at once.

J2129.4.r: It is lost. Type 1696; *BP I 314; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 141 No. 1703.
J2129.4.p: A fool sticks a needle into a haywagon, having been told to stick it in his sleeve.

J2129.5.p: Foolish people patch old shoes with new leather instead of mending them properly, so the result makes no sense.

J2129.6.p: Numskulls take the clothes out of their trunks and cover the empty trunks to keep rain off them.

J2129.7.p: Foolish people drag a horse back and forth across ice until its skin is rubbed off.

J2129.8.p: A fool plants his mother's seed rice in other people's fields.

J2130.p: A general category of foolish disregard for one's own safety.

J2131.p: A numskull gets hurt through his own foolish act.

J2131.0.1.p: Numskulls try to kill mosquitoes with bows and arrows, and only wound themselves.

J2131.1.p: A foolish character is beaten as a result of his own absurd lack of foresight or judgment about personal danger.

J2131.1.1.r: U.S.: Baughman; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 138 No. 1690.
J2131.1.1.p: A fool tries to preach while the priest is already preaching, and is beaten for interrupting him.

J2131.2.p: A foolish character is stung, usually by bees or insects, because of his own careless behavior.

J2131.2.1.p: A fool catches bees in a sack and then opens the sack at home, so the bees sting him.

J2131.3.p: A foolish character injures his own arms or legs through absurd behavior.

J2131.3.1.r: Fb “hæl” I 727; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 111—112, Espinosa Jr. No. 119.
J2131.3.1.p: A girl cuts off part of her own heel so that she can fit her foot into a shoe.

J2131.3.1.1.p: A fool cuts off his own arms so that he can wear a sleeveless sweater.

J2131.3.2.p: A gullible person is talked into cutting off part of his own body.

J2131.3.3.p: A man lays a piece of wood on his leg in order to saw it, and so saws his own leg off.

J2131.4.p: A foolish character blinds himself through his own absurd action.

J2131.4.1.p: A numskull, who is a stupid ogre, looks through a gun barrel and is shot in the eye.

J2131.5.p: A foolish character gets his head stuck in some object or opening.

J2131.5.1.p: A trickster puts on a buffalo skull as a disguise and gets his head caught in it.

J2131.5.2.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 263, Coster-Wijsman 62 No. 98.
J2131.5.2.p: A numskull licks out a pot and gets the pot stuck on his head.

J2131.5.3.p: A numskull sticks his head into the branches of a tree and gets caught there.

J2131.5.4.p: A numskull sticks his head into the hole of a millstone, and the stone rolls into the lake with him.

J2131.5.5.p: A wolf trying to catch a camel's tongue puts his head into the camel's mouth and is killed.

J2131.5.6.p: A jackal gets his head caught in a pot of blue dye. The animals make him king, but recognize him by his cry and drive him out.

J2131.5.7.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *66; Russian: Andrejev No. *64.
J2131.5.7.p: A fox tries to drown a jug by sticking his head into it, and he drowns himself.

J2132.p: A foolish character is dragged along, usually by an animal or vehicle, as a result of his own absurd behavior.

J2132.1.p: A foolish man ties a rope to a buffalo he wants to catch, and the animal drags him to his death.

J2132.2.p: A numskull ties a rope to his own leg while a cow is grazing on the roof, and when the cow falls off he is hauled up the chimney.

J2132.2.1.p: A fool ties a rope to his leg and also to a dog, so the two animals or he are dragged along by the rope.

J2132.2.2.p: A person binds his hand to a dog's leash and is dragged along when the dog runs off.

J2132.3.p: A milker foolishly ties a cow's tail to his own body, and the cow's reactions drag or injure him.

J2132.3.1.p: A jackal ties a captive crow to his tail, and the crow pecks itself free and injures the jackal's tail.

J2132.4.r: (Cf. J1758.1.1.) Dragged to his death (or injured). India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2132.4.p: A numskull foolishly rides on the back of a tiger.

J2132.5.p: An animal lets itself be tied to another animal's tail and is dragged to death.

J2132.5.1.p: An animal's tail is tied to a tiger's or leopard's tail, and the animal is killed when the tiger flees.

J2133.p: A numskull falls, typically because of his own careless or foolish action.

J2133.1.r: Falls and is killed. *Chauvin III 49 No. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2133.1.p: A camel with a donkey on its back dances, and the donkey is thrown or falls off.

J2133.2.r: Falls to his death. Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 79.
J2133.2.p: A monkey jumps over a ravine while wearing his sword, and falls in.

J2133.3.p: A cat climbs to a steeple and tries to fly, and falls.

J2133.3.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 85.
J2133.3.1.p: A coyote tries to fly from a treetop and falls to the ground.

J2133.4.r: *Type 1240; Köhler-Bolte I 51, 135, 486ff.; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 216f. No. 49; Chauvin II 201 No. 47; Clouston Noodles 158; Fb “træ” III 967; Christensen DF XLVII 229; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 293 No. 2; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2133.4.p: A numskull cuts off the tree limb he is sitting on, and falls.

J2133.5.r: They all fall. *Type 1250; Köhler-Bolte I 113; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 242 No. 124; *Bolte Schweiz. Arch. f. Vksk. XXIII (1920-21) 36ff.; Clouston Noodles 46; Christensen DF XLVII 179ff., 193 No. 7; Virginian: Parsons JAFL XXXV 302; Chinese: Chavannes II 324.
J2133.5.p: Men hang down in a chain from a tree or height, and the top man must spit on his hands before he can climb or hold on; the chain depends on his action.

J2133.5.1.p: A wife is carried up a tree toward the sky in a bag held in her husband's teeth; she asks him a question, and when he answers she drops.

J2133.5.1.1.p: A servant carries his master across a stream and answers a question with a gesture that throws the master off.

J2133.5.2.p: A numskull, going to heaven while holding the tail of a divine elephant, lets go to make a gesture and falls, and everyone holding onto him falls too.

J2133.5.3.p: Three men in a tree sing a song and clap their hands, and they fall down and die.

J2133.6.r: Type 121; *BP II 530 n. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
J2133.6.p: A group of wolves climbs on top of one another to reach a tree, but when the bottom wolf runs off, the whole pile collapses. The fool is the one who makes this mistake or is caught in its outcome.

J2133.6.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 141 No. 1703, Espinosa III 147; Africa (Ashanti): Werner African 125.
J2133.6.1.p: A fool tries to measure a tower by stacking hampers on top of one another. To get the height right, he has the two bottom hampers taken out, which defeats the purpose.

J2133.7.p: A wolf that breaks into a house through the chimney falls down it and dies. It is a foolish, self-inflicted death from entering where it should not.

J2133.8.r: Wienert FFC LVI 85 (ET 514), 107 (ST 194); Halm Aesop No. 72; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2133.8.p: A stargazer, so busy looking up at the sky, does not watch where he is walking and falls into a well.

J2133.9.r: Chauvin II 157 No. 34; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2133.9.p: A blind man leads another blind man, and both fall into a pit. The foolish guide's lack of sight leads to disaster.

J2133.10.p: A monkey jumps into the water after a butterfly, mistaking it for something worth catching, and drowns or is lost in the water.

J2133.11.p: A hedgehog and a crab jump from a boat after a turtle. They fall into the water, but they land on floating leather, which is the joke of the note.

J2133.12.p: A woman tries to climb a rope made of excrement and urine. The foolish attempt is absurd and disgusting, and she cannot succeed.

J2133.13.p: A fool hanging from a tree by his hands tries to clap them together and lets go, so he falls.

J2133.14.p: A fool re-enacts an accident he has seen, and in doing so he falls again and injures himself and others.

J2133.14.1.p: When asked how a pigeon was killed, a fool aims a stone at the questioner while saying he struck it like this, so he re-enacts the killing on a person.

J2134.p: A numskull makes himself sick or uncomfortable through a foolish act, such as eating or taking something harmful.

J2134.1.p: A trickster eats scratch-berries, which cause intense itching, and so makes himself miserable.

J2134.2.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 303 n. 109h, (California): Gayton and Newman 83.
J2134.2.p: A trickster eats medicine that makes him physically ill, purging him, because he takes it without sense.

J2134.2.1.p: Numskulls eat medicine that makes them ill. In one version, people pour medicine into rice to make broth for cooking rice.

J2135.p: A numskull starves himself through foolish reasoning, even though food is available.

J2135.1.p: A numskull who has food for eleven of twelve months fasts for the entire first month to get the hardship over with, and so starves while still having eleven months of food.

J2136.p: A numskull brings about his own capture through a foolish action that leaves him trapped.

J2136.1.p: A coyote wears a fox's rattle, gets caught in brush because of it, and is injured.

J2136.2.p: A trickster is caught on a fishhook, usually after going after bait or food without care.

J2136.3.r: Fox says, “If your sense were as long as your beard, you would look for exits as well as entrances.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 33 No. 128.
J2136.3.p: A goat sneaks into a garden to eat and gets caught because of its own carelessness.

J2136.4.r: B[ö]dker Exempler 281 No. 26; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 60, 62, 63; West Indies: Flowers 488.
J2136.4.p: A trickster is caught and pinched by a crab or other shellfish, through his own foolishness.

J2136.5.p: A thief is caught because he is careless and makes mistakes that give him away.

J2136.5.1.r: Caught. Scala Celi 58a No. 324; **Zachariae Studien zur vgl. Litg. IX 284ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2136.5.1.p: A thief pauses to admire beautiful objects instead of quickly grabbing them, and so gets caught.

J2136.5.1.1.p: A thief keeps debating which of two or more things to steal, wasting time until he is caught.

J2136.5.2.r: Zachariae Kleine Schriften 179; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 22 No. 101; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 66; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 66 No. 112.
J2136.5.2.p: A thief who talks too much gives himself away and is caught.

J2136.5.3.p: A thief who has stolen a deer cuts it into pieces and keeps counting the pieces, so he is caught while doing so.

J2136.5.4.p: A foolish helper of a thief wakes the owner of the house, and when caught he argues that he was trying to wake the household to stop the theft, and he is believed.

J2136.5.5.p: A foolish thief cooks food in the house during a robbery, and the smell or noise wakes the household.

J2136.5.6.p: A foolish thief asks the owner of the house to help him with the theft, and so is caught.

J2136.5.6.1.p: A fool sent by thieves to rob a house is told to bring out the heaviest thing, and he cannot carry the grain-grinder alone, so he wakes the master to help him.

J2136.5.7.p: A thieving numskull finds a drum, trumpet or similar instrument in an outhouse and beats or blows it, raising the alarm and getting caught.

J2136.5.8.p: Thieves are caught and killed one at a time because none of them will help the others, since fewer thieves means more loot for each survivor.

J2136.5.9.p: A thieving wolf is tricked into singing, which gives away its position so it is caught.

J2136.6.p: An animal is trapped while feeding inside the carcass of another animal.

J2136.6.1.p: A greedy jackal gets trapped in the carcass of a dead bullock while eating it.

J2137.p: A character dies because he failed to think ahead and protect himself.

J2137.1.r: Chauvin II 89 No. 27; Spanish Exempla: Keller; B[ö]dker Exempler 283 No. 29; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2137.1.p: A louse invites a flea to share its home, and the flea bites the man and jumps away while the bed is searched and the louse is killed.

J2137.2.p: Wolf-colored dogs join a pack of wolves to help kill other dogs, and then the wolves turn on them.

J2137.3.p: A bee lands on a water lily, which closes over it at night and drowns or kills it.

J2137.4.p: A crocodile swallows a water-snake, and the snake kills the crocodile from inside. The crocodile dies because it did not foresee the danger of eating the snake.

J2137.5.p: Sheep are slaughtered by a butcher after being persuaded that he will spare them. Their trust leads them to their deaths.

J2137.6.r: *Chauvin III 49 No. 1; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos. 199-201, 204-5; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2137.6.p: A camel and a donkey are caught together because the donkey sings and gives away their hiding place.

J2137.7.p: A king tries to visit the spirit world beneath the ground and dies in a tunnel he dug for the journey.

J2143.p: A foolish person meddles in a quarrel between powerful beings, and the weak one caught in the middle is killed by the fight.

J2143.1.p: A sparrow tries to stop a fight between elephants and is crushed to death when they trample it.

J2146.p: A person makes a reckless jump to recover something they have lost and is seriously harmed or killed by it.

J2146.1.p: A miser leaps into a ravine to recover a single grain he dropped and breaks both legs.

J2146.2.p: A man jumps into a river to save his treasure and drowns in the attempt.

J2160.p: A general category of other foolish acts done without thinking ahead.

J2161.p: Foolish mistakes made while getting dressed, showing a lack of foresight.

J2161.1.p: A fool tries to pull on both trouser legs at the same time by jumping into the breeches.

J2161.2.r: *Type 1285; *Fb “skjorte” III 269a; Clouston Noodles 209; Christensen DF L 49.
J2161.2.p: A foolish man, dressing, pulls on a shirt that has been sewn shut at the neck, so he cuts off his own head to get it on.

J2161.3.p: A fool laces a bedcover onto his shoe as though it were a shoelace.

J2162.p: Foolish misuse of fire that causes harm instead of helping.

J2162.1.p: A person burns down a temple in order to become famous.

J2162.2.p: A fool whose house is on fire adds wood to the flames.

J2162.3.p: People trying to put out a burning boat row to shore to fetch water from a spring, instead of using the water around them.

J2163.p: A foolish person carries the plow horse instead of leading it, so as not to trample the field, and so is absurdly short-sighted.

J2163.1.p: Foolish men carry each other through mud, taking turns being carried so that none of them gets dirty.

J2163.2.p: Sedan-bearers must carry their master around searching for his dog, because they refused to help search for it themselves.

J2164.p: Foolish acts done while rowing a boat, showing a lack of foresight.

J2164.1.p: Two people rowing a boat pull in opposite directions, so the boat goes nowhere. It is a foolish act of short-sightedness.

J2164.2.p: A fool rows a boat that is still tied to the dock, so he makes no progress. He does not think to untie it first.

J2165.p: A fool carries a log or millstone up a hill, then realizes he could simply have rolled it down. So he carries it back up again just to roll it down.

J2166.p: A lover who is too short-sighted is slow to act when his chance comes, and so loses the advantage he had gained.

J2167.p: A foolish person eats porridge in one room and drinks the milk in another, so the two never meet. The porridge and milk are kept apart by mistake.

J2168.p: In preparing to slaughter an ox, its feet are cut off the evening before, so the animal cannot be walked to the place of slaughter. It is a foolish blunder of timing.

J2171.p: A foolish or clumsy carpenter does his work in a way that defeats its own purpose. This is the general heading for the carpentry blunders that follow.

J2171.1.p: A fool tries to build a boat in a way that cannot work, such as from unsuitable materials. This heading covers the boat-building blunders that follow.

J2171.1.1.p: A fool builds a ship with a wooden saw. The ship has no bottom and is so narrow that nothing can get inside it.

J2171.1.2.p: An ogre covers the hero's boat with tar, meaning to harm him, but the tar actually helps or fails to hurt him as intended. The ogre's short-sighted scheme backfires.

J2171.1.3.r: It melts. (Cf. J2186.) Japanese: Ikeda; American Negro: Harris Friends 69ff. No. 9.
J2171.1.3.p: A gullible person is tricked into building a boat out of mud, which obviously cannot float.

J2171.1.3.1.p: A fool tries to make a canoe out of sand, which cannot hold its shape or float.

J2171.1.3.2.p: A fool tries to build a boat out of clay, which cannot float.

J2171.2.p: A fool makes mistakes in putting roofs on houses. This heading covers the roofing blunders that follow.

J2171.2.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 599; Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 269), 134 (ST 402); Halm Aesop No. 222; Japanese: Ikeda. Cf. Russian: Andrejev No. 72.
J2171.2.1.p: A fool does not bother with a roof while the weather is fine, then cannot put one on when it rains.

J2171.2.2.p: A fool builds the roof on the inside of the house instead of the outside, so it does not keep out the weather.

J2171.3.p: Builders keep throwing away the beams of their scaffolding until nothing is left to support the structure, and it all collapses.

J2171.4.r: Type 1246; Fb “hammer” IV 199a; Christensen DF XLVII 194.
J2171.4.p: Several workers each throw their axe down in the same place where the first man's axe fell, so the axes are lost in one spot.

J2171.5.p: A bird builds its nest out of salt, which melts away in the rain and so the nest disappears.

J2171.6.p: A man riding a camel, too high to fit through a doorway, has the doorway broken down so he can ride in. It does not occur to him to simply climb down.

J2172.p: Foolish carelessness in looking after herd animals, where a person's shortsighted handling of sheep, cattle or other livestock brings loss on themselves.

J2172.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 508), 104 (ST 172); Halm Aesop No. 353; Jacobs Aesop 210 No. 43; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 489.
J2172.1.p: A shepherd raises false alarms about a wolf so often that, when a real wolf attacks, nobody comes to help him.

J2172.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 317), 136 (ST 414); Halm Aesop No. 250.
J2172.2.p: A shepherd shuts a lion into the yard with his livestock, hoping to trap it, and ends up losing all his animals.

J2172.2.1.r: The dog: “What good to lock us up from the wolf when he is with us?” Wienert FFC LVI 68 (ET 327), 135 (ST 411); Halm Aesop No. 371.
J2172.2.1.p: A shepherd tries to lock a wolf into the stable, but the wolf almost gets locked in with his animals instead of outside.

J2172.2.2.p: A shepherd ends up with a wolf locked in among his sheep, so the wolf can attack them freely.

J2173.p: A shortsighted fool loses food he had meant to eat or keep, through his own foolish action or delay.

J2173.1.p: A trickster steals a feast, but then falls asleep before eating it, and someone else takes the food.

J2173.2.p: A numskull sees a cheese by the road and tries to lift it with his sword, which is too short; he leaves to fetch a longer sword and someone else takes the cheese.

J2173.3.p: A bird boasts about catching a rabbit, but while he is busy boasting, other birds eat the rabbit.

J2173.4.p: A fool celebrates catching a deer too early, and while he celebrates, the deer escapes wearing his clothes.

J2173.5.p: A fool kills chickens by throwing them off a balcony onto a stone, and kites carry the dead birds away.

J2173.6.p: A crocodile seizes one of two children bathing in a river, leaves him waiting in his hole, and goes back for the other, but both children escape.

J2173.7.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 83.
J2173.7.p: A traveller goes off while fish are cooking, and the fish burn up because he left them unattended.

J2173.8.p: A man avoids the trouble of carrying milk by milking a cow straight into his mouth.

J2173.9.p: A foolish method for removing hairs from salt: wash the salt in water so that it melts away.

J2174.p: A condemned person makes foolish or irrelevant demands just before execution, showing he has no sense of his real danger.

J2174.1.p: A man about to be hanged keeps asking for his red cap, which he left in prison, and never considers his real peril.

J2174.2.p: A man about to be hanged is very fussy about his bread, worried it will harm his health.

J2174.3.p: A man who hurt his head trying to hang himself has a doctor dress the wound, and then goes off and hangs himself.

J2174.4.p: A condemned man asks to be hanged at once so he can get back to his work.

J2175.p: A general heading for foolish shortsightedness in how people treat their children, where a parent or caretaker acts in a way that ignores the obvious danger or need.

J2175.1.p: A schoolmaster whips his pupils in advance to stop them from misbehaving, rather than waiting until they have actually done wrong.

J2175.1.1.p: A priest beats his wife before going to buy food, because he wants her to cook it in a particular way.

J2175.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 486), 102 (ST 155); Halm Aesop No. 352.
J2175.2.p: A foolish person scolds a child who is drowning instead of rescuing him.

J2175.3.p: An absent-minded nurse lowers the child into the well on the rope instead of the bucket.

J2175.4.p: A man lets his infant son play unattended in a river, putting him in danger of drowning.

J2175.5.r: (Cf. J2465.4.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1677; Russian: Andrejev No. *1681 II.
J2175.5.p: A dim-witted person sent to fetch children either smothers them on the way home or scalds them while bathing them.

J2175.6.p: A numskull kills his own children while trying to cure their illness.

J2176.r: *Type 1387; BP I 316, 521ff.; *Fb “tosse” III 832a, “t[ö]nde” III 935a, “[ö]l” III 1175; Christensen DF L 49; Italian Basile Pentamerone I No. 4.
J2176.p: A fool leaves a tap open on a wine barrel in the cellar, so the wine runs out while he is distracted, for example by falling into a study or chasing a dog.

J2176.1.p: A fool tries to soak up spilled wine by sprinkling meal (flour or ground grain) on it.

J2176.2.p: A fool tries to drink gruel by making a hole in the pot, so the gruel simply runs out.

J2178.r: Herbert III 54, 82; Scala Celi 76a No. 433; Alphabet No. 245.
J2178.p: A peasant on his way to a feast drinks so much ditch-water that he is too full to eat the feast.

J2178.1.p: A master sets his servant an example by eating the rind of a fruit first, fills up on it, and never reaches the fruit inside.

J2181.p: Foolish men who have bought a charter from their lord get drunk to celebrate, use the charter's seal as a candle, and so burn it and lose their charter.

J2182.p: A fox fleeing loses an eye in briars, then returns the next day and eats it, thinking it tastes like chicken.

J2183.p: A general heading for foolish hesitation, where someone who cannot decide what to do loses the chance and suffers harm.

J2183.1.p: A dog runs back and forth between two castles on opposite hills, chasing the music played during each meal, and gets nothing because the music switches before he arrives.

J2183.2.p: Overpolite travelers each insist that the others board first, so the train leaves and they are left behind.

J2183.3.p: A bird that is overly careful to choose food matching its color is caught and killed by an eagle while it hesitates.

J2183.4.p: Two prisoners who have one hour of freedom waste it arguing over which road to take home, and so lose their chance.

J2183.5.p: A princess is so picky about suitors that she ends up marrying a foolish man, after hesitating too long over better choices.

J2183.6.p: A foolish person fails to act quickly when a fire breaks out, so the blaze gets out of hand.

J2183.6.1.p: People argue over whose job it is to put out a fire, and they keep investigating instead of acting, so the fire burns the whole town.

J2184.p: A Brahmin washes his clothes to purify them, then fears a passing dog has polluted them. After testing it by crawling on all fours with a leaf for a tail, he decides the clothes are tainted and destroys them rather than washing them again.

J2185.r: “I wish I had drowned; then you would all have been disgraced.” *Wesselski Bebel I 181 No. 27; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2185.p: A foolish priest is pushed into the water and suffers an embarrassing setback that brings him shame he could have avoided.

J2185.1.p: A man who is about to be hanged tells his captors that hanging him would have caused them real trouble, a remark showing that he is the one who has the upper hand.

J2186.p: A trickster makes men out of his own excrement, or something similar, and his false creations melt away in the sun, exposing his deceit.

J2187.p: A bear riding a horse lets his paws slide down the horse's flanks, and when the horse runs under a tree the bear is snagged and tears his claws into the horse's flesh.

J2188.p: A husband with food for every day of the year except one decides to fake his death for that day, hoping his servants will be too grief-stricken to eat. They eat as usual, so he rises to scare them, and a servant who thinks he is possessed by devils kills him.

J2191.p: A foolish servant lets a bear loose while his master is away, and the bear wrecks the place. When the master threatens to cut off the meddler's ears, the fool begs his dog not to tell on him.

J2192.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 731; Christensen DF XLVII 201 no. 38, 204, 221; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2192.p: A fool is told to take letters to a neighboring castle, but he sets out without getting his instructions, and he returns carrying a bag of stones as his reply.

J2192.1.p: A fool is sent to tell his master's wife that his master will not be home for dinner, but he waits a whole week before delivering the message.

J2193.r: Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 271, Coster-Wijsman 53 No. 78.
J2193.p: A fool has himself buried alive because he thinks he stinks.
