J2194.r: N. A. Indian (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXII 223 No. 1 (32); Boas RBAE XXXI 722.
J2194.p: Raven steals the robes of the Red Willow Men and finds that they are of no use to him.

J2195.p: People foolishly throw food at one another instead of eating it.

J2196.p: People try to cut grain by shooting it down with guns, because they do not know how to use a sickle.

J2197.r: The fool: “Why go to all that trouble? Just enjoy yourself with wine, women, and song.” Wesselski Bebel I 179 No. 22.
J2197.p: An abbot plans to build a grand palace while life is short, and the joke is that he is wasting his time on something he may never enjoy.

J2198.p: A person mourns or laments a misfortune that has not happened and may never happen.

J2199.p: A miscellaneous category of foolish acts done through poor foresight that do not fit other headings.

J2199.1.p: Someone sounds an alarm for no good reason, causing needless panic.

J2199.1.1.p: A fool rings a bell to announce a chess victory, so when his house catches fire and he rings the bell for help, no one comes because they have learned to ignore his foolish alarms.

J2199.1.2.p: A woman who is to ring a bell when she goes into childbirth is talked into ringing it falsely, so that when she really needs help, no one answers.

J2199.2.p: People build a wheelbarrow that is too big to get out of the shed they built it in.

J2199.3.p: Nine men try to lift a bull over a fence, when it would be far easier to lead it out through the gate.

J2199.4.p: A miscellaneous act of foolish short-sightedness in which someone saves money or effort in a way that costs them more later.

J2199.4.1.p: A dim-witted person is pleased that he hurts his feet rather than his shoes, as if that saved money.

J2200.p: A general category of foolish behavior in which people reason absurdly or illogically.

J2210.p: Foolish reasoning that follows logically from a wrong starting assumption, producing an absurd conclusion.

J2211.p: A fool ignores the basic differences between kinds of animals and so draws absurd conclusions about them.

J2211.1.r: “What would you do if you had to live here always?” Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 163), 90 (ST 30); Halm Aesop No. 327.
J2211.1.p: A donkey laments after falling into a bog, and frogs who live there scold him for complaining, since falling into mud is normal for them.

J2211.2.p: A magpie, thrown into a mud puddle by his master, sees a muddy sow and assumes she too has quarreled with her master.

J2211.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 377), 106 (ST 189); Halm Aesop No. 95.
J2211.3.p: Dogs run away from their master because in a famine he has killed his cattle, reasoning that he will surely kill the dogs next.

J2211.4.p: A donkey brays when it hears a conch shell, and its owner foolishly thinks the donkey must have been a saint in a former life.

J2212.p: Foolish reasoning in which the effects of age or size are applied in absurd ways.

J2212.1.p: Asked to bring two fifteen-year-old slaves, a fool brings one who is thirty years old.

J2212.1.1.p: A priest asks for a maid at least fifty years old, and the fool brings one aged twenty and one aged thirty, which misses the instruction.

J2212.2.p: A fool buries himself in an old grave, thinking that the angel who comes to question the dead will pass him by because he seems to have been dead a long time.

J2212.3.p: A fool thinks a wooden anchor would hold if only it were bigger.

J2212.4.p: Sailors judge that the old reef will be worse than their new ship in a collision, reasoning that the ship will endure the shocks better.

J2212.5.r: You should have seen him run when he was only a calf.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 228 No. 73.
J2212.5.p: A fool rides an ox to a tournament, and when ridiculed he claims the ox is swifter than a horse because it is still young.

J2212.6.r: “Hasn’t it had time in these fifty years to become a goat?” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 235 No. 105.
J2212.6.p: A fool born under the sign of the Kid claims he was born under the Goat, reasoning that the sign has grown up in the meantime.

J2212.7.p: A fool expects a small boat to grow into a ship as it gets older or bigger. He reasons from age and size in a ridiculously literal way.

J2212.8.p: A peasant decides he no longer needs a horse because the newborn foal is too heavy to carry. He applies the idea of size and age to the animal in a foolish way.

J2212.9.p: Fools think it strange that a grown stranger does not know a local road that their young children know. They assume that age should bring knowledge of the place.

J2213.p: Fools reason badly with numbers, drawing ridiculous conclusions from counting or quantities.

J2213.1.r: (Sometimes solved by placing an object on one side of the bed.) Type 1289; Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 416 No. 15.
J2213.1.p: Two people each insist on sleeping in the middle of the bed, so that neither can have the edge. The fools fail to see that the arrangement cannot work.

J2213.2.p: A priest boasts that his fight with peasants was profitable because he received three blows for every one he gave. He treats getting beaten more often as a gain.

J2213.3.r: *Von der Leyen Das Märchen 78 and Herrigs Archiv CXIV 20 n. 2; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2213.3.p: A fool eats a number of cakes and only feels satisfied after the seventh. He regrets not having eaten the seventh first, since that was the one that satisfied him.

J2213.4.p: A fool reasons that because a horse can pull one load, it can surely pull two. He ignores the limits of the animal's strength.

J2213.5.r: “Twenty.”—“There are only four.”—“I said that there are twenty; that is even better.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 261 No. 222.
J2213.5.p: Asked how many daily prayers there are, a numskull answers twenty, reasoning that twenty is more than ten and so must be the right answer. The motif turns on this faulty comparison of numbers.

J2213.5.1.p: Asked how many commandments there are, a numskull says twenty. Told that the minister would not accept that answer, he concludes there must be more than twenty.

J2213.6.p: A man who owns half a house wants to sell his half so he can use the money to buy the other half and so own a whole house. The plan goes in a foolish circle.

J2213.7.p: A dentist is tricked into pulling two teeth for the price of one because the patient complains that the work is expensive. The fool is duped by a misjudgment of cost and number.

J2213.8.p: A man prefers small oysters because he will get more of them per hundred. He ignores the fact that the total amount is the same.

J2213.9.p: A numskull discovers that one feather makes a hard pillow, and so he concludes that a sackful of feathers would be unbearable. He reasons that a small amount makes a difference, so a large amount must be far worse.

J2214.p: Fools draw a sweeping general rule from a single unusual event, and then act on that rule as though it always holds.

J2214.1.r: I burned my mouth with hot peas the other day.” Clouston Noodles 77; French: Irwin Verville No. 83.
J2214.1.p: A fool warns travelers riding through a field of peas that they will burn their horses' feet. He wrongly assumes that peas burn in the way that one incident suggested.

J2214.2.r: Reason: he tried in vain as a youth to lift a certain stone; he has also tried in vain as an old man. Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 265 No. 240.
J2214.2.p: Fools conclude that youth and age are alike, drawing a foolish general conclusion from a limited observation.

J2214.3.p: After a thief steals a salted cheese, the fools wait at the well, reasoning that since people always go to the well after eating salted cheese, the thief will come there too.

J2214.3.1.p: Having waited at the well for the thief in vain, the fools decide to wait in the graveyard instead, reasoning that the thief must eventually come there.

J2214.3.2.p: After the cover is stolen, the fools wait for the thief to come back for the bolster, concluding that he will certainly return for it.

J2214.3.3.p: A man waits by the well for the thief to come back and return the goods he stole, as if thieves returned what they took. The fool's expectation is absurd.

J2214.4.p: A fool decides that human milk is the best food for a baby, so he feeds the child only milk from his wife and the baby starves.

J2214.5.p: A fool concludes from the fact that people supply feed to animals that humans must be the animals' servants.

J2214.6.r: Fish so reason. (Cf. B233.1.) India: Thompson-Balys.
J2214.6.p: A fool reasons that because people enjoy milk they must once have been calves.

J2214.7.p: A fool decides that oil must be cheap, or that spilling it brings good luck, and so he breaks oil vessels on purpose after hearing this.

J2214.8.p: A fool carries his sick wife to the remedy instead of carrying the remedy to his wife, reversing the sensible course.

J2214.9.p: A fool dips himself into cold water to cure a fever, reasoning that since hot iron is cooled by water, the same will cool his body.

J2214.10.p: A fool refuses to feed a starving colt, reasoning that a fed colt would become fiercer, so the hungry colt stays fierce.

J2214.11.p: The daughter of a widow, who earns her living by spinning, sees much warm cloth coming from England and concludes that England must be full of widows, since widows wear such goods and spin.

J2214.12.p: A traveler misjudges distance in the clear air of mountain country, thinking a far-off mountain is near.

J2214.12.1.p: A newcomer strips to swim across what he thinks is a narrow five-foot stream, not realizing the mountain he has walked toward all morning is actually sixty miles away.

J2215.p: Foolish reasoning about God, where a person draws absurd conclusions from events or circumstances concerning God.

J2215.1.r: He complains to God, “What was the use of taking from me what you were going to give back to me after stealing from another?” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 212 No. 34.
J2215.1.p: A man is robbed and later the same day is given a large sum of money, and he complains that God is wasteful in this way.

J2215.2.p: A man who says he serves God is put to work and beaten, while his companion who serves someone else is treated well, and he cannot understand why God's servant is treated worse.

J2215.3.r: When reproached he says “How should it be unclean when God has killed it instead of men?” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 270 No. 273.
J2215.3.p: A fool finds a dead hen, cooks it, and serves it for dinner, honoring it above God who did not provide live food.

J2215.4.p: A fool sits idle and waits for God to provide food for him instead of working for it.

J2215.4.1.p: A fool who has waited for God to provide blames God when food is scarce.

J2215.5.p: An old man blames God for heavy rain, though as an elder he should have known that more rain was unwelcome.

J2215.6.p: Someone blames God for letting pumpkin vines bear fruit larger than the fruit of nut trees, thinking the arrangement is backwards.

J2216.p: A poor man decides that an idol in a temple must be poorer than he is, since the idol is naked and has no clothes.

J2217.p: A general type of tall tale in which a speaker exaggerates by claiming something is many times greater or better than the superlative allows, usually through false reasoning.

J2217.1.p: A man boasts that his horse is the best in England, then claims he has another at home worth ten times as much, so the superlative is outdone.

J2217.2.r: “One is bottomless; the other is deeper than that.” England: Baughman.
J2217.2.p: A man describing lakes gives an exaggerated, absurd account of their size or number, going far beyond what is believable.

J2220.p: A miscellaneous group of foolish stories in which people reason in absurdly illogical ways.

J2221.p: A country person refuses to believe a priest's reports about hell because the priest has never been there himself.

J2222.p: A numskull tells his father that it would have been better if he had never been born, so that the son could inherit his grandfather's estate.

J2223.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 231 No. 83, Mönchslatein 170 No. 134.
J2223.p: A fool lies still while a thief enters his house, hoping the thief will find something he can then take back from the thief.

J2223.1.p: A robbed man blames the thief for not warning him in advance, so that he could have had witnesses present to the theft.

J2224.p: A numskull plants seed in the daytime and then digs it up at night to keep it safe, reasoning that treasures must be guarded.

J2225.r: (1) Student has only one eye: Aristotle says to beware of those whom nature has marked. (2) Student comes from Bremen: no one of consequence comes from there. (3) His name is Nicholas: no one with that name can succeed. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 611; cf. Type 1661.
J2225.p: A person gives three absurd reasons for refusing to give alms to the poor.

J2226.p: A person is foolish enough to try to learn swimming only after getting into the water, as if it were a matter of ordering the steps backward.

J2227.p: A queen, told that peasants have no bread, responds that they should eat cake, showing her ignorance of their hardship.

J2227.1.p: A king who is unaware of famine says that the people can live on pulse (sugar) and rice instead.

J2228.p: A sheep believes it lost an eating contest because of its weak legs, misidentifying the real cause.

J2231.p: A person asks why holidays cannot be held all year round, mocking the idea of having breaks from work.

J2232.r: Wienert FFC LVI 84 (ET 510), 119 (ST 291); Jacobs Aesop 220 No. 80.
J2232.p: An imitator of a pig's cries is applauded, but a fool who brings a real pig to the same contest fails.

J2233.r: Clouston Noodles 87; *Wesselski Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXXII 23; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2233.p: A thief on trial blames a mason for a poor house, and the blame passes through a chain of people until an innocent shopkeeper is convicted.

J2233.1.p: An innocent man is executed simply because his neck fits the noose, or something similarly arbitrary.

J2233.1.1.p: After a young colonist accidentally kills an Indian, the men hang an old bedridden weaver instead of the valuable young man, and the tribe demands punishment.

J2234.r: Clouston Noodles 12; Nouvelles Récréations No. 71; Christensen DF XLVII 224 No. 87; England, Scotland: Baughman.
J2234.p: Someone is asked whether a person is them or their brother, and gives a foolish or confused answer about their identity.

J2235.r: Fool shoots full of holes a garment left out at night to dry. “It is a good thing I did not have it on or I would have shot myself.” Clouston Noodles 90; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 230 No. 79.
J2235.p: A foolish person is described as ready to shoot himself, showing a ridiculous or reckless lack of sense.

J2236.p: A fool judges a house by its latrine, faulting it because the latrine is too small for the dining table to fit inside. The joke is that the complaint has no logic.

J2237.p: A fool sings in a small bathroom but cannot be heard from the minaret, so he wants a bathroom built on the minaret to make his voice carry.

J2238.r: Chauvin II 82 No. 3; B[ö]dker Exempler 273 No. 3; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2238.p: A man thinks he is wise just because he owns a book, which he uses without understanding it.

J2241.p: A fool sets out to fetch the doctor, but his wife changes her mind. He still goes on to tell the doctor he is no longer needed.

J2241.1.r: But he cannot see the use of the trip when she already knew this word. India: Thompson-Balys.
J2241.1.p: A fool goes to an astrologer to get a name for his child but forgets it on the way home. His wife later happens to say the name and reminds him, so the trip was pointless.

J2241.2.p: A servant is sent to fetch the doctor, but the trip proves pointless: the doctor may be out, may not give medicine, or the medicine may not help, since everyone dies eventually.

J2242.p: A man away from home writes a letter to his wife but cannot find a messenger, so he carries the letter himself and then returns to where he was.

J2242.1.p: A scribe cannot write a letter because of his bad leg, so the letter must be carried in person, since no one else can read his writing.

J2242.2.p: A fool writes a letter so slowly that the recipient cannot read it quickly enough, so the message is delayed.

J2243.p: A fool sleeps in order to avoid being idle, a foolish way of dealing with idleness.

J2244.r: Bolte Frey 222 No. 18; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2244.p: A peasant falls out of a tree, and a neighbor advises him to climb down with the same skill and speed he used to climb up, rather than simply not climbing trees.

J2245.p: A fool tastes every piece of fruit before handing it to his master, making the fruit useless to his master.

J2254.p: Fools scold one another for talking during prayers, while they themselves are talking as they do so.

J2255.p: Travelers say they will not have time to draw their swords when attacked, so they draw them in advance as a preliminary step.

J2258.p: A schoolboy cannot read a book printed in smaller letters than the ones he was used to at school.

J2260.p: A general heading for foolish or absurd theories about science, with the individual theories listed under it.

J2270.p: A general heading for foolish or absurd theories about the heavens and the stars, with the individual theories listed under it.

J2271.p: A general heading for foolish or absurd theories about the moon.

J2271.1.r: Numskull greets old moon as if it were new. “I haven’t seen it before, for I have just come to the city.” (Each town thought to have a different moon.) *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 218 No. 52; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2271.1.p: A foolish notion that the moon is a local object near at hand rather than a distant body in the sky.

J2271.2.p: A foolish puzzle about what becomes of the old moon when it wanes and a new moon appears.

J2271.2.1.p: Lightning is believed to be made from the old moon, which is thought to be burned up or broken into bits that fall as fire.

J2271.2.2.p: Stars are believed to be made from the old moon, which has been cut up or scattered into pieces that become the stars.

J2271.3.p: Foolish simpletons try to throw the moon over a cliff, apparently thinking it can be disposed of that way.

J2271.4.p: Numskulls try to capture the moon and haul it home on a sledge, but they reach the top of the hill a few minutes too late to catch it.

J2272.p: Foolish ideas about the sun, held by people who misunderstand what the sun is or how it behaves.

J2272.1.r: *Vossische Zeitung 17. Sept. 1910; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Hopi): Voth FM VIII 176 No. 55.
J2272.1.p: A rooster believes his crowing makes the sun rise, and is disappointed when the sun rises anyway without his help.

J2272.2.p: Foolish people ask whether today's sun is the same sun that rose yesterday, treating this as a real puzzle.

J2272.3.p: Fools believe the sun goes to sleep at a certain woman's house each night.

J2273.p: Foolish ideas about the sky, held by people who misunderstand what holds it up or what it is.

J2273.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 606; *Chauvin II 112 n. 2; Liebrecht *Zur Volkskunde 102; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2273.1.p: A bird believes the sky will fall down unless he holds it up with his legs, and so he props it up.

J2274.p: Foolish ideas about the earth, held by people who misunderstand its nature or how it works.

J2274.1.p: A foolish explanation for why not everyone lives in the same place: if all people crowded into one spot, the earth would become unbalanced and tip over.

J2274.2.p: A fool believes the air is the same at home as abroad, reasoning that because the stars are the same, the air must be too.

J2274.3.p: A fool believes the climate is the same at home and abroad, reasoning that his body parts look the same in both places.

J2275.p: Foolish ideas about the stars, held by people who misunderstand what stars are or what happens to them.

J2275.1.p: A falling star is supposed to have been shot down by an astronomer, a foolish explanation for why it fell.

J2276.p: Foolish ideas about time, held by people who misunderstand how time passes or is measured.

J2276.1.p: Dinner time comes sooner in the mountains because the thin air makes time pass faster there.

J2277.p: Foolish ideas about clouds, held by people who misunderstand where clouds come from.

J2277.1.p: Clouds are supposed to come from smoke, a foolish belief about where clouds originate.

J2280.p: A catch-all for other foolish scientific beliefs that Thompson did not list separately. Fools in such tales hold ridiculous theories about how the natural world works.

J2281.r: Guests of host who waters his wine put little fishes into the wine jug. “Now I confess that I put water into the wine; otherwise the fishes could not be there.” *Wesselski Bebel II 109 No. 32.
J2281.p: A fool comes up with a ridiculous explanation for how fish ended up in a particular place, such as in a lake or pond.

J2282.r: No part of his body will absorb water.” Wesselski Bebel II 143 No. 134.
J2282.p: A drunk man falls overboard, but the skipper leaves him in the water because he believes someone soaked in wine cannot drown.

J2283.r: Bolte Frey 247 No. 86; Nouvelles Récréations No. 2; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2283.p: A fool finds a nun in bed with a bishop, cannot see her face, and so announces that the bishop must have four feet.

J2284.p: Peasants find a dead wolf and argue about what killed it. A learned man decides it froze from the inside after eating cold flesh.

J2285.p: A fool wrongly interprets omens, reading signs in ordinary events as sure predictions of what will happen.

J2285.1.p: A fool who trusts omens refuses to prepare for death. For example, a bird chirps five times and he takes this to mean he has five more years to live.

J2287.p: A fool believes an island can be moved to a new location by towing it with ships.

J2300.p: A broad heading for tales in which people are foolish in being easily fooled or deceived.

J2301.r: (Cf. J2311.0.1., J2311.2, J2311.7, J2312, J2313, J2314, J2315, J2316, J2324, J2331.) *Types 1313, 1406; *Liebrecht Zur Volkskunde 124; Bédier Fabliaux 265ff., 475; *Crane Vitry 227 No. 231; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 225 No. 66; *BP III 337; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 866; B[ö]dker Exempler 280, 296 Nos. 24, 59; Christensen DF XLVII 59; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2301.p: A broad heading for tales in which husbands are too easily fooled, especially about their wives' behavior.

J2301.1.p: A husband takes his unfaithful wife back after she swears on oath that she will be faithful from now on.

J2301.2.p: A husband is convinced his wife has become a widow, because a numskull has bought cloth that only widows use.

J2301.3.p: A gullible husband takes dust from his wife's garment and concludes from it that she has been lying with another man.

J2302.p: A broad heading for tales in which wives are too easily fooled.

J2303.p: A broad heading for tales in which a mother is too easily fooled.

J2310.p: A broad heading for tales that show the nature of gullibility, in which people are led to believe things that are not true.

J2311.p: A person is tricked into believing he is dead, and acts as if he were.

J2311.0.1.r: (Cf. J2301.) *Type 1406; Bédier Fabliaux 475; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 866; *Clouston Noodles 166; Christensen DF L 59; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2311.0.1.p: A wife tricks her husband into believing he is dead.

J2311.1.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 216f. No. 49; *Fb “æsel”; Köhler-Bolte I 135, 486, 505.
J2311.1.p: A numskull is told he will die when his horse breaks wind three times. When it does, he lies down as if dead.

J2311.1.1.p: A man believes he is going to die when he breaks wind, and so he lies down as though dead.

J2311.1.2.p: A numskull is told he will die when his mouth bleeds, and he believes it. The tale turns on his gullibility about a supposed sign of death.

J2311.1.3.p: A man believes he will die when water falls on his head, and he takes the idea to heart. He is fooled by a supposed sign of death.

J2311.1.3.1.p: A numskull believes he is dead when a pumpkin falls on his head. A harmless blow convinces him that the predicted death has come.

J2311.1.4.p: A man believes he will die when a scarlet thread gets onto his coat. He is fooled by a harmless object taken as a sign of death.

J2311.1.5.p: A fool is told that yellowing soles of his feet are a sure sign he will die. He digs his own grave and lies down in it.

J2311.2.r: *Type 1313; *BP III 337; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 237 No. 522; *Wesselski Morlini 49; *Bolte Frey 214; *Clouston Noodles 122; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 4.
J2311.2.p: A wife tells her husband that a pot of preserves is poison. He decides to kill himself, eats the preserves, and then lies down believing he is poisoned to death.

J2311.3.r: Robbers see him and ask what he is doing. “It is my grave. I went out to get a breath of air.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 206 No. 6.
J2311.3.p: A man hides from robbers by taking refuge in an open grave, where he pretends to be a dead man returned from the grave.

J2311.4.r: He speaks up, “I always went that way when I was alive.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 216f. No. 49; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys. Cf. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 860.
J2311.4.p: A numskull who has lain down believing he is dead is carried off on a bier, and the bearers lose their way. The supposed corpse then speaks up.

J2311.5.r: The “dead” man speaks: “It’s no use, friend, to try to dissuade them.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 239 No. 121; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2311.5.p: Neighbors who have heard of a numskull's death insist on his funeral even though he is alive and well. He is persuaded to be carried on a bier, and they try to recruit a busy man to join the procession, but he refuses because he has business.

J2311.5.1.p: A supposed dead man lying on a bier threatens the men carrying him.

J2311.6.r: A numskull lies in an old grave to see the Day of Judgment. He hears bells and thinks that the Last Day has come. He is beaten by mule-drivers when he tells them that he is a dead man. He returns home and tells his wife that he returns from the dead. “How goes it in heaven?” “For one thing, avoid mule-drivers.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 216 No. 46.
J2311.6.p: A man who pretends to be dead is punished for his trick.

J2311.7.r: Wolves eat his ass. “Lucky for you that his master is dead!” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 225 No. 66; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2311.7.p: A man is told that a dead person can be recognized by cold hands and feet. He chills his own hands and feet and lies down pretending to be dead.

J2311.8.r: Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 270, Coster-Wijsman 73 No. 11.
J2311.8.p: Parents are made to believe they are dead and so they marry each other again.

J2311.9.p: Foolish peasants carry a couple to burial, but when the supposed corpses speak they flee in terror.

J2311.10.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 6; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2311.10.p: A drunken man insists that he be beheaded. He is struck with the flat of a sword and, believing he is dead, accepts it.

J2311.11.p: A simpleminded man tells his mother that he has been dead for twelve years.

J2311.12.p: A supposed dead man is roused back to life by being whipped.

J2312.r: *Types 1406, 1620; *Clouston Noodles 163; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 866; H. C. Andersen “Kejserens ny Klæder”; Christensen DF L 64; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2312.p: A naked person is made to believe he is dressed, showing how easily a gullible person can be fooled. He goes about without clothes while thinking he is decent.

J2314.r: *Type 1406; *Bédier Fabliaux 265, 468; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 866; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2314.p: A layman is made to believe that he is a monk.

J2315.p: A wife convinces her husband that she has only been gone a moment. She actually stayed away a week, going to a neighbor's to cook a fish, and returns with a freshly cooked fish to make it seem so.

J2315.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2315.1.p: A wife leaves home and offers herself to a lover. Her quick return is what persuades her husband that she has not been away.

J2315.2.p: A wife tricks her gullible husband into believing he has cut off her nose: she gets him to throw a razor at her, and when it flies past she claims it has sliced her nose off.

J2316.r: *Type 1406; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 274 No. 298; Bédier Fabliaux 266; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2316.p: A wife and her helpers convince her husband that his house has moved while he was away, turning it into an inn with tables, signs and drinkers, so that he cannot find his own home.

J2316.1.p: A man fails to recognize his own house because an emperor has turned it into a mansion.

J2317.r: *Chauvin VI 138 No. 291; Clouston Noodles 161; Clouston Tales II 30ff.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 869.
J2317.p: A healthy man is persuaded that he is sick.

J2317.1.p: A man believes he has diabetes, because rascals have sewn his trouser leg so tight that it seems to confirm his illness.

J2318.p: A dim-witted fellow is persuaded that he is a thief: after cheese is stolen, he is told the thief is whoever fails to eat all his cheese, a stone is hidden in his portion, and he confesses to the theft.

J2321.r: Chauvin V 185 No. 107; Penzer V 69; von der Hagen Gesammtabenteuer II *ix, 49 No. 24; Boccaccio Decameron IX No. 3 (Lee 277); Christensen DF XLVII, DF L 78; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; U.S.: Baughman.
J2321.p: A man is made to believe that he has become pregnant and given birth.

J2321.1.r: (Cf. J1734.1, K1955.2.) *Type 1739; *BP I 317 n. 1; *Fb “kalv”; *Wesselski Bebel I 232 No. 148.
J2321.1.p: A parson is made to believe that he will bear a calf, after a cow's urine is mistakenly substituted for his in a doctor's examination; when a calf appears in the house, he thinks he has borne it.

J2321.2.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 3; Christensen DF XLVII 228 No. 93.
J2321.2.p: A man believes he has given birth to a child when he lets out wind.

J2321.3.p: A husband convinces his wife and mother-in-law that he will bear a sheep, though his wife was already pregnant when he married her.

J2322.r: *Type 1531; Köhler-Bolte I 68; Wesselski Archiv Orientální I (1929) 80 f.; Shakespeare Induction to Taming of the Shrew; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2322.p: A drunken man is made to believe he has visited both heaven and hell: he is dressed as a rich lord and fed fine food and drink, then returned to his own clothes and assumes he has been to heaven.

J2323.p: A dim-witted man believes he has married another man, after two men join hands in jest while saying "I marry you"; he thinks a bishop must annul the marriage.

J2324.r: Type 1406; Bédier Fabliaux 266ff.; Herbert III 20; *Crane Vitry 238 No. 248; Boccaccio Decameron VII No. 9 (Lee 231); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2324.p: A wife persuades her husband to have a good tooth pulled.

J2325.p: A husband is made to believe that his yarn has changed into tow because of his own carelessness, so his lazy wife is spared from spinning.

J2325.1.p: A fool believes gold in a bag has turned to ashes because a child urinated on it; actually the bag held only ashes.

J2326.r: *Type 1540; **Aarne FFC XXII 3—109; *Clouston Noodles 204—217 passim; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 463; *Wesselski Bebel I 189 No. 50; Christensen DF L 35; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 73 No. IV.
J2326.p: A student tells a woman he comes from Paris, but she hears "from paradise" and gives him money and goods to carry to her husband.

J2326.1.p: A foolish woman gives money to a swindler claiming to bring it to her parents in heaven.

J2326.2.p: A swindler explains a dream as a dead father's demand for horses, and the dupe hands the horses over to him.

J2326.3.r: Blindfolded and put on an ass. India: Thompson-Balys.
J2326.3.p: An emperor wants to travel to paradise.

J2326.4.p: A man claiming to be a messenger from relatives in distress is given goods to deliver to them.

J2327.p: A man asks for good weather and is handed a box of hornets, which he believes contains the weather itself. The joke is on his gullibility.

J2328.r: To see whether the church is moving someone lays down his coat in front of it. It is stolen. They think that the church has passed over it. Type 1326; Köhler-Bolte I 324; Christensen DF L 218 No. 79.
J2328.p: A fool is fooled into believing that a church tower is moving, a gullible mistake about what he sees.

J2331.p: A dim-witted person with a minor or unimportant job brags about his position to others.

J2331.1.p: A proud sheriff boasts of ruling over only nine farmers, a tiny and laughable jurisdiction.

J2331.2.r: “Administrador de la yesca.” Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 138 No. 1689A*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2331.2.p: A fool is given a made-up office and boasts about holding it, though the post does not really exist.

J2332.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 137 No. 1684; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2332.p: A fool is shut in a dark room and convinced that it is perpetual night, believing the darkness never ends.

J2333.p: Sledges are secretly turned around at night so they head back the way they came, while the travelers think they are still going forward.

J2334.p: A master is talked into buying a large fish on the claim that small fish crawl out of every part of his body, a deceptive sales pitch.

J2335.r: When the bag is opened, one cries, “Oh Jesus, we have shot a stag with iron shoes!” Köhler-Bolte I 325.
J2335.p: Hunters shoot a stag and hide it, but another person secretly swaps it for a dead donkey, so the hunters carry off the wrong animal.

J2336.r: *Wesselski Mönchslatein 65 No. 53; *Wesselski Bebel I 213 No. 104; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1864; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2336.p: A Jewish woman tricks her parents into believing she will give birth to the Messiah, but she actually bears a girl.

J2337.r: Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 3 (Lee 254); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2337.p: A dupe is persuaded that he is invisible, a gullible man who is made to believe a false claim about himself.

J2338.p: An adulterous wife convinces her husband that the mixed-race child she bore came about through suggestion rather than infidelity, so he accepts her explanation.

J2341.p: A near-sighted man is talked into believing by a doctor that he can see clearly, though his sight has not improved.

J2342.p: A husband refuses to believe that his wife is being unfaithful despite the evidence against her.

J2342.1.p: A husband still refuses to believe his wife is unfaithful even after he catches her in the act.

J2342.2.p: A husband who has been away for three years accepts the children born during his absence as his own.

J2342.2.1.p: A woman gives birth fourteen months after her husband leaves, yet he is persuaded the child is legitimate.

J2342.2.2.p: A wife tells her husband that she became pregnant while he was away, claiming she did exactly as he had instructed, so he is cuckolded but accepts it.

J2342.3.p: Accused of adultery, a wife denies it, and her husband dismisses the truthful accusers because he thinks she knows her own faults better than anyone.

J2342.4.p: A husband praises his wife's fidelity, but a trickster tests her and finds she is not faithful.

J2342.5.p: A husband is the last to find out about his wife's affairs, and he refuses to believe the rumors even when others tell him.

J2345.p: A foolish man is kissed while asleep and dreams it is a fairy, but the one kissing him is actually a pig.

J2346.p: A newcomer, apprentice, or ignorant person is sent on a pointless or impossible errand to fetch something that does not exist or is absurd.

J2347.p: Experienced workers play pranks or tricks on new employees, who are fooled into doing ridiculous things.

J2348.p: A gullible person is convinced that burying money will make it grow, and is cheated out of his savings.

J2349.p: Miscellaneous tales in which people are fooled because of their gullibility, not covered by more specific headings.

J2349.1.p: A gullible dupe is persuaded that a horse can fly.

J2349.2.p: A wife convinces her husband that her lover is Death, so he is frightened away and she can keep meeting the lover.

J2349.3.p: A credulous king reads about an ocean of milk and believes the book's claims about its properties.

J2349.4.r: “Yes, that is why he sang so well in the morning.” (First edition X941.) *Type 1931.
J2349.4.p: A woman who asks for news from home receives absurd answers, which she accepts as true, such as a cock having become a sexton.

J2351.p: An animal gives itself away to its enemies by talking when it should stay silent.

J2351.1.r: *Type 154; **Krohn Mann und Fuchs 11; *BP I 518 n. 1; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 33 No. *135C.
J2351.1.p: A fox talks to his own body parts, drawing attention to himself, and is caught when he sticks his tail out of his hiding place in excitement.

J2351.2.p: A wolf hiding from hunters gives himself away by talking.

J2351.3.p: A dupe loses his loot because he sings while carrying it, which reveals his location.

J2351.4.p: A wolf or bear boasts that he has eaten horses, but when a horse strikes sparks with its hooves, a lion picks up the boaster to see the horse and squeezes him to death.

J2352.p: A talkative man reveals his companion's faults or secrets, and when his own faults are pointed out, he claims to be better than his companion, who is then investigated.

J2352.1.p: One brother is refused the sacrament because he cannot pray, and he retorts that his brother cannot pray either, so both are denied it.

J2353.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 395; Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 244 No. 542; Chauvin VIII 168, 197; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 68—69; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Gaster Exempla 196 No. 56; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2353.p: A man tests whether a woman can keep a secret by telling his wife a crow flew from his belly, and the story grows with each retelling until there are fifty crows.

J2353.1.p: A man boasts to his boss that his brother can do twice his work and is hired, but the brothers then say their father can outwork the boys, so the boss fires them and asks for the father.

J2355.p: A numskull boasts about his secret instructions, which lets a cheat take advantage of him, such as being told not to serve a red-bearded man or to save sausage for winter.

J2355.1.r: *Type 563; **Aarne JSFO XXVII 1-96; BP I 349ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 1.
J2355.1.p: A foolish man loses magical objects because he talks about his secret instructions, and so lets himself be tricked and cheated out of them.

J2355.2.p: A boy blurts out his secret instructions, which reveals that his father has been stealing. He had been told to avoid his companions so they would not smell what he had been eating.

J2356.r: Thieves stumble over him as he lies on the ground. “What is this, a log?” The fool: “Does a log have five annas in its pocket?” When they have robbed him he says, “Ask the merchant in the tree if my money is good.” They rob the merchant. Clouston Noodles 100.
J2356.p: A fool's chatter leads to himself and his companions being robbed.

J2357.r: *Penzer V 55 n. 3; *Chauvin II 90 No. 31; B[ö]dker Exempler 285 No. 33; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Japanese: Ikeda.
J2357.p: A tortoise is carried through the air by a bird, holding a stick in its mouth; when it speaks, it loses its grip and falls.

J2358.p: A young heir is too frank at his father's funeral, telling the mourners he will come to mourn their fathers in turn, and so is branded a fool.

J2362.p: Talking animals anger their master, and he punishes them by feeding them twice-threshed straw.

J2363.p: A dim-witted person entertains others with rambling, roundabout nonsense talk.

J2364.p: A secret lover of a married woman overhears her lover discussing their affair with others, and she ends the relationship.

J2365.p: A fool reveals a woman's adultery, and her lover kills him for it.

J2366.p: A warrior announces where his camp is, wanting his enemies to know he is not afraid, and the enemies go there ahead of him.

J2367.p: A fool shows evil spirits where someone is hiding, and they find the hiding place.

J2370.p: A fool who asks an endless stream of questions, often too difficult or foolish for anyone to answer.

J2370.1.p: Children ask their parents questions that are too difficult to answer.

J2371.p: A fool makes absurd scientific speculations, asking foolish questions about nature and society.

J2371.1.p: A fool asks why the sea does not rise when it rains into it and nothing flows out.

J2371.2.p: A fool asks why the sea smells bad when it is full of salt.

J2371.3.p: A fool asks why rats do not poke their own eyes out in the straw.

J2371.4.p: A fool asks why the poor, who are the majority, do not kill off the rich.

J2372.r: The judge: “You are wonderful; I have tried it thirty times and succeeded only once.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 266 No. 248.
J2372.p: A judge asks how a theft was carried out, and the witness explains it.

J2373.p: A man is woken by a neighbor who reports that his she-ass has given birth to a foal with no ears or tail. He lies awake all night worrying about how the donkey will keep its harness on.

J2374.r: The second wants to see just how it happened and kills himself too. Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 156 No. 2.
J2374.p: A foolish man copies another who jumps from a palm tree using a looped rope, and the copycat kills himself.

J2375.r: When he comes to his senses, the fool says, “I had a hard time, but my curiosity is satisfied.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 231 No. 82; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2375.p: A fool climbs onto the enormous horns of his sleeping ox, and when the ox wakes it throws him off.

J2376.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 230 No. 76; *Clouston Noodles 86; U.S.: Baughman.
J2376.p: An accused man claims the plaintiff bit off his own ear; the judge tries to bite his own ear to test this and falls and breaks his head.

J2377.r: Where did he put the soil?” The third time: “I was wondering who would carry the saddle now that the horse is stolen.” *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXX-XXXII 51; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 23.
J2377.p: A master tells his servant to guard his horse at night, and the servant gives absurd answers about what he was thinking of when asked if he is asleep, such as who made the stars or who dug the sea.

J2378.r: Chauvin II 82 No. 4; B[ö]dker Exempler 273 No. 4; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2378.p: A man who is curious to see what a robber will do waits to watch, then goes back to sleep instead of stopping him.

J2381.r: A man’s head is snatched off by accident and his companions do not see what has happened. Debate: did he ever have a head? *Type 1225; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 192 No. 374; *Bolte Frey 220 No. 12; Christensen DF XLVII 192—93 No. 19; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2381.p: A fool asks an absurd question about whether a certain man ever had a head at all.

J2382.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 236 No. 110; Köhler-Bolte I 497; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII 69 No. 8.
J2382.p: A fool hides his purse on a pole on a cliff, and a trickster swaps the money for cow dung. The fool only wonders how a cow could have climbed the pole.

J2383.r: On Good Friday an old woman who has heard the Passion Story exclaims, “How hard it was for the Jews who had to watch all night with Christ!” Wesselski Bebel I 228 No. 138.
J2383.p: A foolish person expresses pity for the Jews, in a joke that turns on a misunderstanding.

J2387.p: A fool experiments by walking with his eyes shut to learn how blind men get about, and he gets lost.

J2391.p: A fool wonders which has greater pull toward the earth, a cup or its contents, and his father demonstrates gravity by pulling on the fool's back and a stick.

J2400.p: A general heading for stories in which a foolish person blindly copies what someone else does, usually with bad results.

J2401.r: (Cf. J2411.1, J2411.2, J2413.4.2, J2422.) *Types 1060-1114 passim; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 120 No. 1075; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 353 n. 271b.
J2401.p: A foolish imitation that ends in death: someone copies an action that was safe for another and is killed by it.

J2410.p: A heading grouping the different kinds of foolish imitation, such as copying miracles or magic.

J2411.p: A fool tries to copy a miracle or act of magic and fails, usually harming himself or others.

J2411.1.r: (Cf. J2401.) *Types 531, 753; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 633f.; Spanish: Espinosa III Nos 168—171; Missouri French: Carrière; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 121 n. 4; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2411.1.p: A foolish person tries to copy a magical rejuvenation, such as making himself young again, and it does not work.

J2411.1.1.p: A fool imitates a miracle in which a person pretends to die and then comes back to life, but he cannot bring himself back.

J2411.1.2.p: A foolish imitation of a god's miracle goes wrong: instead of men coming out of the furnace covered in gold and silver, lions come out.

J2411.2.r: (Cf. J2401.) Type 753; Dh II 168ff.; Lowes Romanic Review V 368ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2411.2.p: A foolish person tries to copy a miraculous horse-shoeing: he takes off a horse's foot to shoe it, but fails to put it back. Christ's version succeeded.

J2411.3.r: (Cf. J2425.) Type 552B; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 80; West Indies: Flowers 489.
J2411.3.p: A foolish person tries to copy a magical production of food and it fails.

J2411.4.p: A foolish person tries to imitate a magician and fails, injuring himself.

J2411.5.p: A dupe is persuaded by a false story that someone came back from the dead carrying bags of gold, and so he tries to copy the feat to get rich.

J2411.6.p: A fool tries to copy someone who jumped into fire without being hurt, and he is burned to death.

J2411.6.1.p: A goddess's sister tries to copy her trick of being cooked without harm, and dies trying.

J2411.7.p: A fool tries to copy a magical act that produces a garden and a lake, and fails.

J2411.8.p: A fool tries to copy someone's magical sewing and fails.

J2411.9.p: An obedient wife's pestle stays magically floating in the air when she is told to leave it there.

J2412.p: A fool tries to copy a healer's cure and makes things worse or fails.

J2412.1.r: Herbert III 63; Hervieux IV 278 No. 34; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 36; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2412.1.p: A fool applies a hot onion to a sick eye, because a friend cured his foot with this remedy.

J2412.2.p: A fool pulls out his eye to stop the pain, copying a man who had a tooth pulled and felt better.

J2412.3.p: A peasant, envious of a doctor's fee, poses as a doctor and gives wrong treatments and predictions, such as promising a son to a eunuch and giving a plaster for heart disease.

J2412.4.r: The son imitates. He sees an ass’s saddle. Diagnosis: you have eaten too much ass’s flesh. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 250 No. 167; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 792; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2412.4.p: A doctor claims to diagnose a patient by observation, and his son learns the trick is simply noticing clues, such as feathers on the road, that show what the patient ate.

J2412.4.1.p: A fool pretends to diagnose by observation, claiming to have noticed a stick under a table.

J2412.5.p: A man whose wife will not speak, recalling that a priest regained his voice by drinking black cherry juice, decides instead to cure her by beating her with a cherry tree branch.

J2412.6.p: A fool hangs a sick woman in a well to cool her off, and she drowns.

J2412.7.p: A foolish doctor tries to stop a cartwheel from creaking by cauterizing it as if it were sick, and ends up burning it up.

J2412.8.p: A fool claims he can cure goitre by striking the swelling, having seen a melon knocked out of a camel's throat that way.

J2413.p: An animal foolishly tries to imitate another animal's actions, going beyond its own abilities.

J2413.1.r: *Crane Vitry 139 No. 15; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 79; Jacobs Aesop 202 No. 10; Wienert FFC LVI 46 (ET 45), *90 (ST 19); Halm Aesop No. 331; Spanish Exempla: Keller; West Indies: Flowers 489f.
J2413.1.p: A donkey tries to fawn on his master the way a dog does, and is driven off.

J2413.1.1.p: A donkey, copying a dog, brays to wake his master when thieves are robbing him.

J2413.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 46 (ET 44), *90 (ST 18); Halm Aesop No. 338.
J2413.2.p: A donkey tries to leap onto the roof the way an ape does, and fails.

J2413.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 297), 93 (ST 65); Halm Aesop No. 8.
J2413.3.p: A jackdaw tries to carry off a lamb the way an eagle does, but gets tangled in the lamb's fleece and is caught.

J2413.4.p: An animal foolishly cuts off one of its own limbs, believing it is copying another animal's trick.

J2413.4.1.p: A fowl tricks another animal into believing he has lost a leg: he hides his leg under his wing and claims he was paid well, and the other animal cuts off the leg and the fowl bleeds to death.

J2413.4.2.r: (Cf. J2401.) Africa (Thonga): Junod 216; American Negro: Parsons JAFL XXX 190, 226, MAFLS XVI 34, Work JAFL XXXII 401.
J2413.4.2.p: A fowl tricks another animal into believing he has lost his neck: he hides his neck under his wing, and the hare cuts it off and the fowl dies.

J2413.4.3.p: A monkey cuts his own throat, believing he is imitating a cobbler's action.

J2413.5.r: He asks the cat: “Is my back bristled, etc.” The horse kills him with a kick. (Cf. K1121.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *106; Russian: Andrejev No. *119.
J2413.5.p: A dog foolishly tries to imitate a wolf, intending to kill a horse.

J2413.6.p: A monkey sneezes in the king's presence in imitation of a rabbit, and so behaves foolishly before the king.

J2413.7.p: A crane foolishly tries to catch fish the way a hawk does, and ends up stuck in the mud at the water's edge.

J2413.8.p: A jackal tries to roar like a lion at an elephant, imitating a larger animal's voice without success.

J2413.9.p: A raven tries to walk with a dove's graceful step, and breaks his bones in the attempt.

J2415.r: He is disappointed. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3252, 3255, 3594, 3691; Arab: Azov JPASB II 412; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; West Indies: Flowers 490.
J2415.p: A foolish person copies someone who has had good luck, expecting to receive the same good luck.

J2415.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 798; BP III 188ff., *191; *Gaster Exempla 190 No. 25; Köhler-Bolte I 136; England: Baughman; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 490.
J2415.1.p: A farmer brings an unusually large beet to the king as a gift and is richly rewarded. A companion, hoping for the same reward, brings a fine horse, but the king repays him with the beet.

J2415.1.1.p: A ruler rewards a clever donkey given as a gift. A greedy nobleman, hoping for a similar reward, sends two donkeys in rich trappings, and the ruler says he regrets that the gift will deprive the donor of worthy companionship.

J2415.1.2.p: A famous poet gives the king some poems and is richly rewarded. Another poet gives the king poetry too, and the king hands him the first poet's verses instead of rewarding him.

J2415.2.p: One man is rewarded with forty crowns for picking a louse from the king's robe, while an imitator who tries to pick a flea is given forty lashes instead.

J2415.3.p: A crab tries to imitate a bird that lays an egg in a pot of boiling water, expecting a reward, but falls into the pot instead.

J2415.4.p: Fairies help a forgotten child, but when another child tries to copy this good luck, the fairies strangle that child instead.

J2415.5.p: An ascetic imitates a Brahmin's religious practices hoping for the same reward, but the Brahmin goes to heaven and the ascetic goes to hell.

J2415.6.p: A pig sees a goat return decked with ornaments and plenty of food, goes out to copy the goat's trick, but is beaten instead.

J2415.7.p: A stepmother, seeing her stepdaughter appear decorated with jewels after marrying a snake, wants her own daughter to have a snake husband too, but the daughter is swallowed by the snake instead.

J2416.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2432*; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2416.p: A poor man foolishly copies a rich man's behavior or spending and comes to ruin because of it.

J2417.p: A fool blindly copies what a leader does, even when the copying makes no sense in his own situation.

J2417.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1694*; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 285 No. 64, FFC CXXVIII 244f. No. 148.
J2417.1.p: A leader is caught by the foot in a wheel and calls for help, and his followers keep repeating his cry as if it were a song.

J2417.2.p: A leader slips, and his foolish followers copy him so that they all fall to the floor.

J2420.p: A miscellaneous group of tales in which a fool imitates someone else's action with foolish and harmful results.

J2421.p: A fool copies a smith by spitting on something hot, but he spits into a pot of hot porridge instead of onto iron.

J2422.p: A fool sees a scythe cut off one man's head and assumes it will do the same to everyone, so he and the others all have their heads cut off.

J2423.p: A trickster sees a man take out his eyes, toss them in the air, and put them back. He copies this, but he may use the power only a limited number of times; when he goes beyond that limit he loses his eyes and usually receives animal eyes in their place.

J2424.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 299 n. 95; S. A. Indian (Warrau, Carrib, Shipaya): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (3) 55.
J2424.p: A trickster sees a man sharpen his leg and copies him. He is allowed to do it only four times without harm, but he breaks that rule and ends up with his leg stuck in a tree.

J2425.r: (Cf. J2411.3.) N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 301 n. 103, Speck U Pa I 141 n. 2; Lepers Island: Dixon 128; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 27 n. 1; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 280 No. 97.
J2425.p: A trickster animal visits other animals who get food by their special powers, then invites them back and tries to feed them in similar ways. He fails and usually narrowly escapes death.

J2426.p: A dim-witted man sees another man being shaved and thinks the barber is cutting off his ears, so he orders his wife to cut off his ears.

J2427.p: A dim-witted man cannot sell his cow until he claims she is with calf. When suitors come for his daughter, he tries the same trick by claiming she is pregnant, and it goes badly.

J2428.r: He throws down a penny and says, “You may like it or not, but I want money in the exchange, too.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 566.
J2428.p: A foolish simpleton, hearing that great lords invest in the exchange where he sees piles of money, puts his own money into the market to join the business.

J2431.r: *Type 1408; *BP I 321; Bolte Frey 222 No. 20; Fb “øl” III 1175a; Nouvelles Récréations No. 45.
J2431.p: A man decides to do his wife's household work himself, and everything goes wrong for him.

J2431.1.p: A husband and wife swap chores, each hoping to outdo the other, but each is cheated and finds the other's work harder.

J2434.p: A man is pulled out of a well with a rope, and a fool tries the same method to rescue a man from a tree with disastrous results.

J2442.p: A man sees a stork shelter someone from rain with its wing, so he tries to shelter his wife from rain with his arm.

J2450.p: A fool takes words or instructions so literally that he misses their obvious meaning and causes trouble.

J2460.r: Gaster Oldest Stories 167; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 282.
J2460.p: A fool obeys instructions to the letter, even when the result is absurd or harmful.

J2460.1.p: A fool misunderstands instructions and follows them in a way that causes disaster, such as burning the land and then sowing seed.

J2461.r: *Type 1696; *BP I 315, III 145; *Taylor JAFL XLVI 78 No. 1696; **Haavio FFC LXXXVIII 94ff.; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 251f. No. 169; *Fb “tosse” III 831b; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 1691*, 1691A*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC No. 1363A; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 286; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 54ff. Nos. 79—82; Africa: Werner African 217f.
J2461.p: A person is taught what to say or do in various situations and applies those words absurdly literally, always being punished for it.

J2461.1.p: A fool asks what he should have done in a situation and then literally carries out the action he is told, with silly results.

J2461.1.1.r: *Type 1696; Fb “potte” II 867a; *BP I 315; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 141 No. 1703, Espinosa III 147.
J2461.1.1.p: A dim-witted person drags a pig home on a string, having been told by someone that he should have led it that way; he takes the instruction too literally.

J2461.1.2.p: A dim-witted person, told to be cheerful at a fire, responds by being merry about it; he had wept at a wedding and was told to be gay.

J2461.1.2.1.p: A dim-witted person sings cheerful songs as he faces death, taking an instruction about a fire too literally.

J2461.1.3.p: A dim-witted person pours water on a pig roasting on the spit; he was told he should have thrown water on the fire when the house burned.

J2461.1.4.p: A dim-witted person cuts peas into quarters; he had eaten pancakes whole and was told he should have cut them up.

J2461.1.4.1.p: A dim-witted cook is told to boil a few peas for five people, and he cooks only five peas; next time he is told to cook plenty.

J2461.1.4.2.p: A dim-witted person, told to boil three measures of rice, puts three empty measures into the pot.

J2461.1.5.r: *Type 1696; *BP I 315; *Wesselski Bebel I 128 No. 26; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 762.
J2461.1.5.p: A dim-witted person, having lost his gloves on a trip, puts the hawk inside his shirt and so kills it; he had been told to keep the gloves in his bosom.

J2461.1.6.p: A dim-witted person kills a sparrow through stupidity and is told he should have carried it in his hand; he takes the advice literally and carries a harrow in his hand.

J2461.1.7.p: A dim-witted would-be thief, told by accomplices to steal something heavy, brings back a millstone.

J2461.1.7.1.p: A dim-witted thief tries to carry off a grindstone when told to bring out heavy things; told to bring shiny things, he brings out a mirror.

J2461.1.8.r: Africa (Hausa): Mischlich 164ff. No. 22 (=Frobenius Atlantis IX 277ff., 287ff., Nos. 74, 75).
J2461.1.8.p: A dim-witted person ruins his inherited property, because his sister has told him not to object to whatever he does, and he takes that as permission.

J2461.2.r: *Type 1696; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 251f. No. 169; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2461.2.p: A dim-witted person follows instructions too literally. He is told how to give a greeting, then tries it in a situation where the conditions do not fit, so the advice fails.

J2461.2.1.p: A dim-witted person kisses a pig; he had been told he should have kissed the old woman.

J2461.2.2.p: A fool learns to repeat stock phrases and by chance uses them to frighten off his wife's suitors.

J2461.3.p: A dim-witted person laughs at the death of his own child, taking a literal or mistaken view of what he should have done.

J2461.4.p: A master sarcastically tells a servant to take a year over an errand; the servant takes him at his word, stays away a year, and then returns to claim his wages.

J2461.5.p: A dim-witted person is told not to forget the handsel (a small extra token given with a purchase); he brings the token but forgets the goods he was sent to buy.

J2461.6.p: A dim-witted traveler is told to follow his nose on a journey; he runs his head into a tree and then climbs it.

J2461.7.p: A fool is told to sell a piece of cloth for four rupees, and he refuses to accept six rupees for it.

J2461.8.p: A servant asks a favor only when his master is in a good mood, waiting until the master is laughing at the servant's own foolishness.

J2461.9.p: A simple-minded person is told to get a girl's attention by tossing a pebble at her, and he throws a large stone instead, which breaks her head.

J2462.r: *Type 1685; *BP I 311; *Fb “brud” IV 64b; Gaster Oldest Stories 167; U.S.: Baughman; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
J2462.p: A foolish bridegroom carries out his instructions word for word, with absurd results.

J2462.1.r: *Type 1685; *BP I 311; Köhler-Bolte I 65; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1006A; Russian: Andrejev No. *1012 II.
J2462.1.p: The foolish bridegroom is told to put parsley in the soup, and he throws in his dog, which happens to be named Parsley.

J2462.2.r: *Type 1685; *BP I 311; *Fb “øje” III 1166a; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 762; Spanish: Espinosa III 147.
J2462.2.p: The foolish bridegroom is told to cast sheep's eyes at the bride, so he buys sheep's eyes from the butcher and throws them at her.

J2462.3.p: A foolish husband, having heard that a beautiful wife is an enemy, puts out his wife's eyes at night.

J2463.p: A foolish bride, who acts on everything literally, makes a series of disastrous mistakes.

J2463.1.p: While her parents are away, a foolish bride follows her mother's advice so literally that she hands her dowry over to a matchmaker and a suitor who are tricksters.

J2463.2.r: The girl shortly to be married complains: “It was all very well for you, mother, to marry father, but I am to marry a complete stranger.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1468; Russian: Andrejev No. *2078A; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2463.2.p: A foolish bride marries a stranger.

J2464.r: The servant, “You don’t see at all.” (Or the master coughs and apologizes; the servant says that he coughs all night.) *Type 1688; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 221; Scala Celi 126b No. 688; Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. IX 88 No. 46; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 24.
J2464.p: A servant keeps exaggerating his master's boasts to a girl, until the master finally says he has poor eyesight, which the servant then tries to top.

J2465.p: A person follows instructions so literally or stupidly that the result is a disaster.

J2465.1.p: A wife is told to feed the pigs wet meal, so she throws the meal into the well and the pigs follow it in.

J2465.1.1.p: A fool is told to water the cow, and he pours water on it instead of giving it water to drink.

J2465.2.p: A woman is told to pile up the pottery, so she smashes all the pots into fragments and heaps them up.

J2465.3.p: A fool is told to feed the child, and he gives it steaming hot food, which kills it.

J2465.3.1.p: Simple-minded men are told to shove the boy along if he is lazy about weeding, so they push him with their weeding-knives and kill him.

J2465.3.2.p: A fool is told to feed his mother, and he stuffs her with food until she dies.

J2465.4.p: A fool is told to wash the child, and he uses boiling water, which kills it.

J2465.4.1.p: A fool heats water for a woman to wash in, and he pours the boiling water over her.

J2465.5.p: A fool is told to clear out the room, so he throws out all the furniture.

J2465.6.p: A fool is told to wash the room, and he floods it.

J2465.7.p: Foolish helpers take an old woman's instruction about where to put grain so literally that they put it on her head, and the result is that they smother her. The fools obey the words without thinking about what is meant.

J2465.8.p: A fool is told to cut at the plow if it sticks on roots, and so he cuts at the bullock's legs instead of the roots. The literal obedience harms the animal.

J2465.9.p: A fool is told to sew shirts for servants and sews them to trees instead of making them as clothes. The fool takes the words too literally.

J2465.10.p: A fool is told to collect goats under a tree and ends up piling up their dead bodies there. He takes the instruction literally and kills the goats.

J2465.11.r: Cuts off child’s ears. India: Thompson-Balys.
J2465.11.p: A fool hears a threat made to a child and treats it as a command to carry out. He acts on the words as though they were an order.

J2465.12.p: Told to plow above a certain tree on a hillside, the fools haul their oxen and plow into the tree, destroying the oxen. They misread the instruction and wreck the animals.

J2465.13.p: A fool is told to plow out potatoes and literally plows them out of the ground. The literal reading ruins the crop.

J2466.p: A general heading for fools who follow an instruction to count something literally, such as counting sins or days, with absurd results.

J2466.1.p: A man who cannot remember how many sins he has committed is told by the priest to put a pebble in a sack for each sin. He comes to confession carrying three large sacks of pebbles.

J2466.2.r: Asked the day of the month, he says that it is the 125th. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 207 No. 9.
J2466.2.p: A man counts the days of the fast month by tossing a pebble into a pot each day. His daughter throws in a handful of pebbles, so the count is wrong.

J2466.3.r: If the clock is still striking it must be 50 o’clock. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 207 No. 9; Scotland, U.S.: Baughman.
J2466.3.p: A literal-minded counting tale in which a long day is reckoned absurdly. The headline gives the gist: someone takes a counting instruction too literally so that the day seems to last forever.

J2469.p: A general heading for miscellaneous fools who follow instructions word for word, with foolish results.

J2469.1.p: A person asks for lentil soup and the cook puts in just one lentil, because the request did not say more lentils were wanted. The literal cook says that more should have been requested.

J2469.2.p: A fool takes a prescription by eating the paper it is written on, rather than the medicine it describes. He follows the words literally.

J2469.3.p: Following advice to divide everything they own, people cut their beds, houses and other possessions in two. The literal division destroys their property.

J2469.3.1.r: Slave cut in two. India: Thompson-Balys.
J2469.3.1.p: A man gives up half his property by following advice literally, so he halves things that cannot be divided without being ruined.

J2469.4.p: A boy is asked to cool the women's ears, and he breaks the milk vessels they carry on their heads so the milk in them can cool their ears. He takes the request literally and ruins the milk.

J2469.5.p: A general heading for fools who are told to do something involving an experience they have never had, and take the instruction literally.

J2469.5.1.p: A fool is told by his father to feed a visitor on food he has never eaten, and so he serves the visitor dog flesh. He follows the advice literally.

J2469.5.2.p: A woman asks a soldier to show her something she has never seen in her life, and he breaks her oil pot in two with his sword. He takes her request literally and destroys her property.

J2470.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Wyandot): Barbeau GSCan XI 224 No. 68.
J2470.p: A fool takes figures of speech at face value and acts on their literal meaning.

J2471.p: A fool literally copies someone's conduct or model, such as stealing a picture from a church after being told to take a picture of good conduct.

J2472.p: A servant hears his master say he will skin some farmers, meaning cheat them, and takes the words literally. When a farmer asks for a tanner, the servant sends him to the master.

J2473.p: A peasant is asked to open his mouth so his wife can share the rich food he ate at a rich man's house, and he literally opens his mouth in front of everyone after a large meal.

J2474.p: A count asks his chaplain to read a hunter's mass, meaning a short one, and the chaplain searches the prayerbook in vain for such a mass.

J2475.r: *Crane Vitry 149 No. 38; *Herbert III 68; Hervieux IV 301 No. 93; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 124; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 22; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
J2475.p: A woman bribes a judge by putting butter on his hands, taking the phrase about greasing a judge's palms literally.

J2476.p: A guest finds that his host meant literally the invitation to share bread and salt. Later, when the host threatens a pushy beggar, the guest tells the beggar to flee because the host means what he says.

J2477.r: St. Peter is to give Christ to a woman as husband. She hears people say, when they are asked for money, “When Christ pays me, I will pay you.” The woman says that Christ has too many debts. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 657; Irish: Beal XXI 305.
J2477.p: A saying about Christ having debts is taken literally, as if Christ really owed money.

J2478.r: The merchant: “It is as good as butter.” He decides on butter. The merchant: “It is as sweet as oil.” He decides on oil. The merchant: “It is as clear as water.” He decides on water. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin II 241 No. 536.
J2478.p: A dull-witted person goes to market to buy water and instead just looks at bread, showing a muddled, literal understanding.

J2481.r: It is started by a pole, not by spurs.” *Wesselski Arlotto I 188 No. 9.
J2481.p: Men are told a horse will go like a ship. It will not move when spurred, so a man hits it with a pole, it moves, and he declares that it goes like a ship.

J2482.r: He wonders. He didn’t know that the son had a ghost to give up. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 250 No. 166.
J2482.p: A fool is told that his son has given up the ghost, meaning died, and takes the euphemism literally.

J2483.r: A fool and his son meet women mourning a dead man. “He goes to the place where there is darkness and nothing to eat or drink.” The son: “They must be coming to our house.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 262 No. 229; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2483.p: A fool takes a claim about a house having no food or drink at face value.

J2484.p: A father says he was scratched by hairy rascals, meaning monkeys, and his son takes the words literally and attacks hairy holy men.

J2485.p: A wife says she has cooked what is behind her husband. He looks and sees the door, and tries to cook it.

J2488.p: A fool demands to see an abstract quality, such as courage or wisdom, as if it were a physical thing.

J2488.1.p: A dragon who is a fool demands to see courage as if it were a visible object.

J2488.2.p: A sultan tries to prove to Adversity that he cannot be caught at a set time, so he hides in a sewer, and in doing so he experiences the very adversity he sought to avoid.

J2489.p: Miscellaneous cases in which a fool takes figurative expressions literally, not falling into a more specific category.

J2489.1.p: A fool takes figurative or slang expressions about drinking literally.

J2489.2.p: A fool takes an instruction to keep control of everyone literally, as though he should hold their locks of hair in his hand.

J2489.3.p: A fool takes the idiom "bite the ear" literally when told to speak secretly, so he bites someone's ear instead of whispering.

J2489.4.p: A fool hears "cutting the paper of the accounts" (meaning falsifying records) and literally cuts up the account books.

J2489.5.p: Told to "quiet the patient," a fool quiets him by killing him.

J2489.6.p: A fool gives away half his savings, believing the saying that whoever gives charity gets double back.

J2489.7.p: Told to "have a black look" (meaning to frown), a fool blackens his face with charcoal.

J2489.8.p: Told to "cover with straw," a fool covers his mistress with straw and smothers her, when he should have thatched the roof.

J2489.9.p: Told to "stick fast to everything you undertake," a foolish son grabs an ass by the tail and gets kicked.

J2489.10.r: Offered money, fools insist on “something or other.” India: Thompson-Balys.
J2489.10.p: A literal-minded fool takes a vague instruction about payment literally and pays with "something or other."

J2489.11.p: Told not to let paint wear off his bride's feet, a bridegroom carries her upside down across a river and drowns her.

J2489.12.p: A stupid peasant takes the saying "rupees make more rupees" literally and sticks his only rupee into a hole, losing it.

J2489.13.p: Told "never show your head again," a jester later appears with a large pot over his head.

J2490.p: A miscellaneous tale in which a fool takes words or instructions too literally and acts on the bare wording.

J2491.p: A master is told to clothe his servant, and the servant insists that the master put on his clothes for him.

J2492.r: Now give him his money.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 266 No. 246.
J2492.p: A plaintiff asks the judge to put some fear into the debtor defendant, and the judge covers the defendant's eyes and shouts "Boo!"

J2493.p: A thief hears a man call his dogs named "The Shepherd" and "Get the stick" and thinks he is ordering someone to fetch a stick.

J2494.r: *Type 1372; Fb “ørefigen” III 1182; *Jacobs list s.v. “Box on ears”; Christensen DF XLVII 208 No. 62.
J2494.p: A man is advised to cure his wife with a box on the ears, so he goes to the pharmacy and buys one, and it cures her.

J2495.r: West Indies: Flowers 491; Irish: Beal XXI 333, O’Suilleabhain 105.
J2495.p: A fool takes religious words or prayers so literally that the absurd literal reading makes them ridiculous.

J2495.1.r: The other: “That place is too far away; she can’t be here in time to help.” He prays to the Virgin of a nearer town. *Wesselski Bebel I 188 No. 47.
J2495.1.p: A man prays to a nearby image of the Virgin rather than to a distant one, reading the request too literally.

J2495.2.r: I forgive my debtors but my debtors do not forgive me.” *Wesselski Bebel I 140 No. 50.
J2495.2.p: A literal-minded person misreads the Lord's Prayer's line about forgiving debtors and concludes that the prayer has little power.

J2495.3.r: He throws the cross down: “The devil may be God; I won’t.” *Wesselski Bebel II 109 No. 34.
J2495.3.p: An actor playing Christ in a Passion Play is beaten by the Jews in the play.

J2495.4.r: They say yes. “If we don’t like him we can kill him ourselves.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 409.
J2495.4.p: An artist ordered to make a crucifix asks peasants whether they want a living God instead, taking the request too literally.

J2495.5.p: Foolish people believe God is resting on a leaf and so decide to cross a river by riding on the leaf.

J2496.r: *Type 700*; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker an Sinclair 95 No. 18.
J2496.p: A stranger hears the phrase "I don't know" so often, when asking locals questions in a language he does not understand, that he takes it to be a person's name.

J2496.1.p: A boy who was hired to work for "nothing at all" goes to town and asks for "nothing at all" as if it were a thing he could claim.

J2496.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *2420; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2496.2.p: People misunderstand one another because one does not know the language of the other.

J2497.p: A foolish son, asked by his mother for a sweet word, answers "Honey is sweet," taking her request too literally.

J2498.r: Field Pent Cuckoo 8; England: Baughman; West Indies: Flowers 491.
J2498.p: A fool told to repeat part of a church ceremony keeps repeating everything he hears, without sense or limit.

J2498.1.p: A minister who has forgotten his spectacles asks the congregation to excuse him; the choir sings his words back to him, and when he apologizes they sing the apology too.

J2498.2.r: Keeps repeating “Who are you?” “Where do you come from?” India: Thompson-Balys.
J2498.2.p: A man sent to a priest for a religious service repeats the priest's words back to him instead of carrying out the errand.

J2499.p: A general heading for further tales of literal-minded fools that do not fit the other motifs listed under this group.

J2499.1.p: A mother tells her daughter to knead the dough until the front of the oven sweats, and the daughter kneads until her own forehead sweats.

J2499.2.p: A woman who is asked to be unclothed answers that she is not naked but has a hood on, and she confesses to having had relations with the priest.

J2499.3.p: A fool admits to a crime but argues that the accusation gets the details wrong.

J2499.4.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 61; Alphabet No. 718; Mensa Philosophica No. 187.
J2499.4.p: A simple monk, to bring back stolen abbey cattle, eats as much of them as he can so they will be carried back home inside him.

J2499.5.p: A fool who hears that God is everywhere concludes that he is therefore inside an angry elephant and trusts it.

J2499.6.p: A polite greeting inviting someone to share a meal is taken literally, so the person is expected to join in and share it.

J2499.7.p: Three foolish sons are sent out to learn trades, and each applies his skill literally and disastrously: a hunter kills his father, a musician plays and dances at his father's death, and so on.

J2511.r: *Type 1351; Child No. 275; **Brown Amer. Journ. of Philol. XLIII 289; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 263; Clouston Tales II 15; *Basset 1001 Contes II 401; Chauvin VIII 132 No. 124; Clouston Noodles 108, 184; Fb “tie” III 792a; Christensen DF L 79; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
J2511.p: A husband and wife bet over who will speak first, and the one who breaks silence, often by scolding out of jealousy, loses the wager.

J2511.1.p: A couple wagers over who will rise first in the morning, and each refuses to give in even when they are carried toward the funeral pyre.

J2511.1.1.p: To win the wager a husband pretends to be dead to spite his wife; when she tells the neighbors they may take his property, he jumps up.

J2511.1.2.p: A husband and wife who are keeping a silence wager are taken for dead, and they stand up when the king offers a reward for information about their deaths.

J2511.2.p: Two foolish men make a wager over who can keep silent longer, so each stays quiet and nothing gets done or said. The joke is that both are too stubborn to speak first.

J2512.r: The third time: “What difference does it make whether you have a nose or not?” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 41. Cf. Type 2014.
J2512.p: A fool, asked where a visitor got his large nose, is thrown out of the room, then returns to make amends by telling the visitor he has a small nose, and is thrown out again. The joke is his tactless blundering.

J2513.p: A fool who hears that holy water forgives sins pours the whole supply over himself to get the full benefit. The joke is taking a sensible idea to a ridiculous extreme.

J2514.p: In a land where sickles are unknown, a newly bought sickle cuts off a man's head, and the sickle is then returned to its original owner. The tale is a foolish-extreme joke about a tool used in a way no one expected.

J2516.p: A servant or youth follows his master's directions so literally that the master ends up harmed or distressed. The point is that obeying words without using sense brings disaster.

J2516.0.1.p: A servant misreads an order literally and, as a result, the hero gets revenge on the one who gave it. The tale turns the literal misreading into a payback.

J2516.1.r: *Type 1562; Chauvin VIII 170 No. 187; cf. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 387.
J2516.1.p: A youth obeys his master's advice to think before speaking so literally that he keeps silent even when he sees the master's coat on fire. The joke is that he should have spoken up.

J2516.2.r: *BP III 151; Christensen DF XLVII 226 No. 92; Japanese: Ikeda.
J2516.2.p: A youth told to pick up everything picks up far too much, so his master then orders him to pick things up only on a signal. The master falls into a hole and cannot give the signal, leaving the youth to keep picking up.

J2516.2.1.p: A fool told to pick up everything loads his master with horse dung. It is a crude literal misreading of the order.

J2516.3.p: A youth told to do nothing but attend to the horse obeys so strictly that he almost lets his master drown. He ignores everything else, including the rescue.
