J2516.3.1.r: She goes home to see what his instructions on this point are. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 139; Christensen DF XLVII 226 No. 92.
J2516.3.1.p: A wife follows written instructions her husband left on a card, and as a result he falls into a brook and is nearly drowned. The card's literal instructions leave her unable to help him.

J2516.3.2.p: Pupils are taught to clap and say "God bless you" whenever someone sneezes. While they are hauling a drowning man out on a rope, he sneezes, and they clap, so he falls back into the water.

J2516.3.3.p: A king is let drown in his bath because his attendant was commanded to use only one phrase and could say nothing else to warn or help him.

J2516.3.4.p: A fool told only to light the fire does nothing else, and so lets the house burn down. He does not put out the blaze or save anything.

J2516.3.5.p: A servant told to report only very good news keeps to that rule even when reporting disasters, so the master learns of trouble too late or not at all.

J2516.4.p: A youth told never to leave his master's side obeys so absurdly that he becomes a constant nuisance, following his master everywhere.

J2516.5.p: An officer calls on householders to hang out lanterns. One hangs out an unlit lantern, and on later nights the householder keeps misreading the call, hanging out lanterns with unlit candles and never lighting them.

J2516.6.p: Told to let no one in, a fool burns his house down to drive out a lizard that has come in. The literal obedience and his extreme reaction ruin his home.

J2516.7.p: A sleepy servant, told to remove his master's turban as his last duty, takes the turban off while the master is still in a council meeting, creating an embarrassing scene.

J2516.8.p: A boy told to draw out the fence stakes and throw them down pulls them out and throws them into the river, misreading where they should go.

J2516.9.p: A fool carries out instructions so literally that he causes the very harm the giver wanted to avoid. Told to call a doctor for his sick master, he also calls the undertaker.

J2517.r: The overzealous visitor rides naked to see his friends. Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 233 No. 93.
J2517.p: A foolish person is so eager or impatient that he does not stop to get dressed before acting.

J2518.p: A fool's despair is carried to an absurd extreme over trivial losses.

J2518.1.p: A fool, in despair because a sparrow has taken one grain from his field, kills himself.

J2518.2.p: A fool, in despair because his ox has been killed, kills himself.

J2521.p: A person shows extreme prudishness, seeing impropriety or sexual meaning where none exists.

J2521.1.p: A prudish person wrongly accuses a man of running a brothel, though he is only keeping a bull for breeding.

J2521.2.r: Bolte Frey 245 No. 79; England: Baughman; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2521.2.p: A woman who has lost her hair to sickness is scolded for going bareheaded in public. To obey, she covers her head with her dress and leaves her body exposed.

J2521.3.p: A girl marries a man so that she will not be ashamed to undress in his presence.

J2522.p: A king smashes all the glassware himself so that his subjects cannot break it, removing the temptation.

J2523.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 232 No. 84; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2523.p: A husband takes his wife's mild permission to go away for a while so literally that he stays gone for days. He then sends a messenger to ask whether he has been away long enough.

J2523.1.p: A husband obeys his wife too literally and hangs her. She had only wanted to test how much he loved her.

J2523.2.p: A husband who has been given leave to go away walks home slowly, arriving only after dawn, so that his wife's lover has already left.

J2524.p: A fool who likes salt decides to eat nothing but salt.

J2525.r: Penzer V 88; Christensen DF XLVII 211 No. 67.
J2525.p: A fool refuses to drink from a river because he cannot drink all of it.

J2526.p: Twelve fools, wanting to prove they are equal, sleep on the ground and put their feet on the single bed meant for their chief.

J2527.p: A thief, out of force of habit, steals from his own purse.

J2528.p: A fool believes a letter reporting his uncle's death even though he has just seen his uncle alive.

J2532.p: Officials argue over who should put out a fire in the palace, and the palace burns down while they debate.

J2541.r: India: *Thompson-Balys. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1691*, 1691A*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC No. 1363A*; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 286. Cf. the same story with risque ending: U.S. (Ozarks): Randolph Who Blowed Up the Church House (New York, 1952) 16, 185.
J2541.p: A fool takes the advice not to eat greedily so literally that he starves himself at table. Later he hunts for food around the house and gets into trouble.

J2561.p: A fool thanks God that he was not sitting on the donkey when it was stolen.

J2562.p: A fool's meat is stolen by a hawk, and he is grateful that at least the recipe was left behind.

J2563.r: *Type 1689; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 227 No. 71; *Clouston Tales II 407ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
J2563.p: A man brings a gift of unripe figs to the king instead of peaches, the king throws them in his face, and the man is relieved they were not peaches.

J2564.p: A fool thanks God that camels have no wings, reasoning that winged camels might fly about and kill people.

J2565.p: A fool thanks God for building a palace without columns, since otherwise the stones might fall and kill people.

J2566.p: A man ferrying blind men across a stream for a fee has one drown, and he consoles the others that there is one fewer to pay for.

J2568.r: He thanks God. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2568.p: A man who has been promised a beating lives in constant dread until the beating finally happens, and then he is relieved it is over.

J2569.p: A philosopher loses all his wealth at sea and thanks Fortune for ending his business, so he can now devote his life to philosophy.

J2571.p: A man insists melons should grow on tall trees rather than slender vines, and when a falling nut hits him on the nose, he is thankful it was not a melon.

J2572.p: A man is told it is well he did not win the girl he loved, because his heart might not have been able to bear it.

J2600.p: A fool who is a coward is frightened by ordinary things and runs from them.

J2611.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 303 n. 109f.; West Indies: Flowers 492.
J2611.p: A person is so frightened that he falls down a cliff.

J2612.r: (Cf. J1736.1.) *BP II 556, III 286; Christensen DF XLVII 220 No. 82; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 307 No. 34.
J2612.p: Seven men make elaborate plans to attack a fierce animal, but when one of them screams with fright, the animal runs away instead.

J2613.r: Fool steps on a rake and falls down crying, “I surrender!” *BP II 555.
J2613.p: A fool surrenders to a rake, mistaking it for an enemy weapon or attacker.

J2614.p: Fools are frightened by the slightest stirring of an animal and flee.

J2614.1.r: Think it is a drum. *BP II 555; Christensen DF XLVII 194ff. No. 20.
J2614.1.p: Fools are frightened by the humming of bees.

J2614.2.p: A fool army flees at the sudden whirr of a quail taking flight.

J2614.3.p: Lions flee at the crowing of a white cock, and elephants flee at the grunting of swine.

J2615.p: A fool is frightened by the creaking of a wheelbarrow.

J2615.1.r: North Carolina: Brown Collection I 697; India: Thompson-Balys.
J2615.1.p: A fool is frightened by the noise of a mill.

J2616.r: The snipe: “It is a bill, but it is good for nothing (weak).” The hawk is no longer afraid. Type 229*; Russian: Andrejev No. 229.
J2616.p: A hawk is frightened by the bill of a snipe.

J2617.r: Africa (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 407 No. 5.
J2617.p: A man wakes with his knees raised in the air and, mistaking them for a lion, splits them with his axe.

J2618.r: *Wesselski Bebel II 119 No. 59; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2618.p: A man sleeping beside a gallows is teased by pranksters who invite the hanged man to join them; the sleeper wakes and replies that he will come at once, and the pranksters run away in terror.

J2621.p: A dead girl is mistaken for sleeping, and her lover talks to her; when he learns she is dead he is terrified, and her father, hearing the lover, thinks her ghost is speaking.

J2622.p: A fool is so frightened by a gust of wind that he falls onto a knife and kills himself.

J2623.p: A tailor puts a thimble on his head as protection against a slug, a foolish precaution against a harmless creature.

J2624.p: A coward is frightened by the glowing eyes of animals he sees in the dark.

J2625.p: A coward panics when his clothing snags on a thistle, thinking he has been seized by an enemy.

J2626.p: A coward boasts about what he would have done to an enemy, but only once the danger has passed.

J2626.1.r: Admits guilt. Husband: “Had you denied it I would have killed you!” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
J2626.1.p: A man caught with another's wife threatens her husband, boasting of what he would do, though he is cornered and afraid.

J2627.p: A fool is frightened by fireworks, fleeing or cowering from the bright bursts and noise.

J2631.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *650B; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 650B; Finnish: Aarne FFC V, XXXIII No. 650B; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 261f. No. 129.
J2631.p: A boastful coward, faced with strong opponents, hides inside the trousers of a plowman who is fighting the men.

J2632.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3444; Legends Nos. 867, 869f.
J2632.p: Two fools try to frighten each other, but each is scared by the other and both run away.

J2633.p: A tiger is frightened by a leak in the house, fearing the water or sound of dripping.

J2634.p: A fool worries that an earthquake will make him fall onto an open knife.

J2650.p: A general case of a clumsy, bungling fool whose blunders cause trouble.

J2661.p: A bungling fool suffers a chain of accidents, one mishap after another.

J2661.1.p: A foolish man accidentally kills his own child and then loses the body.

J2661.2.p: A fool seeking a midwife accidentally kills the dog, drowns the midwife, and kills the child.

J2661.3.p: Two women try to catch a squirrel and to fetch a cooking pot; one falls from the tree and dies, and the other breaks the pot.

J2661.4.r: Clothes stolen. Goes into barrel of tar to hide. In tar and feathers. *Type 1681.
J2661.4.p: A foolish boy causes a series of disasters: he kills his horse, throws his axe into a lake to kill a duck, and undresses to retrieve the axe.

J2662.p: A foolish man finds a treasure and brings some of it to a judge to buy influence, but the judge sends him back to fetch the rest of the money. The fool is tricked into handing over more.

J2665.p: A servant is clumsy and does things in an absurdly literal or unhelpful way, so that his efforts backfire on his master.

J2665.1.p: A servant girl serves a cup to the emperor badly: with one handle she holds it, with two handles she holds one in each hand, and with three she points the third handle toward herself.

J2665.2.p: A servant hurts his master while massaging or shampooing him, slapping him hard enough to break the skin.

J2666.p: A foolish man speaks in a clumsy, tactless or badly judged way, making his words backfire.

J2666.1.r: One woman says to another, “You are an adulteress and a thief, and I know that I am just as good as you are.” *Wesselski Bebel I 136 No. 38.
J2666.1.p: A fool answers a boast or insult by claiming he is just as good as the other person, and thereby makes a blunder.

J2667.r: I saw him hit him over the head with an axe but don’t know whether he hit him or not.” *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 816.
J2667.p: A fool, called as a witness in court, testifies that he was drunk and asleep on a bench at the time, so his testimony is useless.

J2668.p: A fool's brothers escape, but he is captured and stupidly reveals where they are hiding.

J2671.p: A fool is so forgetful that he cannot remember or carry out simple instructions, and his mistakes cause trouble.

J2671.1.p: A master sends his servant to fetch a girl, with a code: a fox means he has one, a hare means he has none. The servant forgets the code and reports that he does not know whether it was a fox or a hare, but the girl is downstairs.

J2671.2.p: A fool repeats his instructions aloud over and over so he will not forget them.

J2671.2.1.p: A fool repeats a word aloud to remember it, but changes the word so that his muttering sounds like insulting greetings to the people he passes.

J2671.3.p: A fool forgets the name of an elephant and calls it an earth egg, confusing it with the word for potatoes.

J2671.4.p: A foolish messenger garbles the message he has been given and delivers it wrongly.

J2672.r: “About the bed cover. When they got it, the quarrel was over.” Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 230 No. 77.
J2672.p: A man hears a noise outside at night and goes out wrapped in his bed cover to investigate. Robbers take the bed cover and run off, and when his wife asks what the quarrel was about, he has nothing to show.

J2675.r: Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 178 No. 313; Indonesia: Coster-Wijsman 43 No. 44.
J2675.p: A bungling man tries to rescue a woman caught by a crab, but gets caught himself and ends up in an embarrassing position.

J2685.p: A buyer, placing an order, draws a picture of a grindstone on his list, forgetting to draw the hole in the middle, so the grocer sends him a cheese.

J2700.p: A simple problem is made needlessly difficult through foolish overthinking or blundering, so that it becomes hard to solve.

J2711.r: Fool gives three explanations: (1) It was formerly a deep well; dug up and set out; (2) it was built by a very tall man; (3) it was built flat on the ground and then set up. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 243 No. 27.
J2711.p: Foolish people explain or attempt the building of a tower in a silly, muddled way, as a humorous account of how it was built.

J2712.r: (Ring). “In its first state it was in the mountains; it is round and flat.” Fool: “A millstone.” Chauvin VIII 170 No. 188.
J2712.p: A riddle-like challenge in which someone asks what object is being held in the hand, and the answer turns out to be an obvious or absurd trick.

J2712.1.p: A riddle asks the solver to guess what is held in a hand, and the answer is a hollowed turnip filled with carrots. The fool is tricked into thinking the problem is hard when it is simple.

J2712.2.p: A trickster asks someone to guess how many eggs he has, promising to give all seven if they guess right. It is a foolish riddle-like bargain that exposes the fool's simplicity.

J2713.r: The fool seeks advice as to how to answer this question: Who is the father of Stoffer’s three sons? Stoffer, of course. Then who was the father of Noah’s three sons? Stoffer. Danish: MS (SK 41 in Dansk Folkemindesamling).
J2713.p: A riddle whose answer is a man who fathered Noah's sons, meaning Noah himself. The solver is made to overthink a simple question.

J2716.p: A foolish attempt to work out whether it is raining, where the fools go about the problem in a roundabout and silly way. It is a fool's tale about a simple matter made absurdly difficult.

J2716.1.p: Men go to look into a pool to see whether rain is falling, mistaking the water's surface for a sign of rain. It is a foolish method of checking the weather.

J2716.2.p: A man sets out tubs to find out whether rain is still falling. It is a foolish way of checking the weather by collecting rain.

J2721.r: One fool to another: “What would happen if you cut off your nose?” “I couldn’t smell.” “What would happen if you cut off your ears?” “I couldn’t see.” “Why couldn’t you see?” “My hat would fall down over my eyes.” U.S.: *Baughman.
J2721.p: A fool is asked why he cannot see, and his foolish explanation is the joke. It is a simple-minded answer to an obvious question.

J2722.p: Two fools who own similar horses try to tell them apart by harming them, such as docking tails or notching ears, and end up marking both alike. Finally they measure heights, and the black horse is found to be two inches taller than the white.

J2751.p: A trickster, greedy while hunting, is left behind and abandoned by his companions because of his greed. It is a moral tale about greed bringing a foolish punishment.
